FAQ 11.233.1 – Consignment arrangement: when should an entity in the retail and consumer industry recognise revenue?
Reference to standard: IFRS 15 App B para B78 Reference to standing text: 11.233

A manufacturer provides household products to a retailer on a consignment basis. The retailer does not take title to the products until they are scanned at the register, and the retailer has no obligation to pay the manufacturer until they are sold to the consumer unless the goods are lost or damaged while in the retailer’s possession. Any unsold products, excluding those that are lost or damaged, can be returned to the manufacturer, and the manufacturer has discretion to call products back or transfer products to another customer.
When should the manufacturer recognise revenue?

The manufacturer should recognise revenue when control of the products transfers to the retailer. Control has not transferred if the manufacturer is able to require the return or transfer of those products. Revenue should be recognised when the products are sold to the consumer, or lost or damaged while in the retailer’s possession.
FAQ 11.233.2 – Consignment arrangement: when should an entity in the industrial products industry recognise revenue?
Reference to standard: IFRS 15 App B para B78 Reference to standing text: 11.233
Entity Y develops a new type of cold-rolled steel sheet that is significantly stronger than existing products, providing increased durability. The newly developed product is not yet widely used.

A manufacturer enters into an arrangement with entity Y whereby entity Y will provide 50 rolled coils of the steel on a consignment basis. The manufacturer is required to pay a deposit upon receipt of the coils. Title transfers to the manufacturer upon shipment, and the remaining payment is due when the manufacturer consumes the coils in the manufacturing process. Each month, both parties agree on the amount consumed by the manufacturer. The manufacturer can return, and entity Y can demand return of, unused products at any time.
When should entity Y recognise revenue?

Entity Y should recognise revenue when the coils are used by the manufacturer. Although title transfers when the coils are shipped, control of the coils has not transferred to the manufacturer, because entity Y can demand return of any unused product.

Control of the steel would transfer to the manufacturer upon shipment if entity Y did not retain the right to demand return of the inventory, even if the manufacturer had the right to return the product. However, entity Y needs to assess the likelihood of the steel being returned and might need to recognise a refund liability in that case. See paragraph 11.212 onwards.
EX 11.234.1 – Other arrangements that are not repurchase rights
Reference to standard: IFRS 15 App B para B64 Reference to standing text: 11.234

Some arrangements do not include a repurchase right, but instead provide a guarantee in the form of a payment to the customer for the deficiency, if any, between the amount received in a resale of the product and a guaranteed resale value. The guidance on repurchase rights (described in paras 11.237 and 11.241 onwards) does not apply to these arrangements because the entity does not reacquire control of the asset. The guarantee payment should be accounted for in accordance with the applicable guidance on guarantees. See EX 11.77.1 for further discussion of guarantees.
EX 11.238.1 – Decision tree to be considered when accounting for forwards and call options
Reference to standard: IFRS 15 App B para B66 Reference to standing text: 11.238
FAQ 11.238.2 – Repurchase rights: should an entity account for a call option as a lease or a financing transaction?
Reference to standard: IFRS 15 App B para B66 Reference to standing text: 11.238
Entity Z sells machinery to a manufacturer for C200,000. The arrangement includes a call option that gives entity Z the right to repurchase the machinery in five years for C150,000.
Should entity Z account for this transaction as a lease or a financing transaction?

Entity Z should account for the arrangement as a lease. The five-year call period indicates that the customer is limited in its ability to direct the use of, or obtain substantially all of the remaining benefits from, the machinery. Entity Z can repurchase the machinery for an amount less than the original selling price of the asset, so the transaction is a lease. Entity Z would account for the arrangement in accordance with the leasing guidance.
EX 11.238.3 – Conditional call rights
Reference to standard: IFRS 15 App B para B66 Reference to standing text: 11.238

Some call rights are not unilaterally exercisable by the seller, but instead only become exercisable if certain conditions are met. The revenue standard does not provide specific guidance for assessing conditional repurchase features; therefore, judgement will be required to assess the impact of these provisions. Conditional rights should be accounted for based on their substance, with an objective of assessing whether control has transferred to the customer.

As noted in paragraph 11.238, the likelihood of the entity exercising an active call right should not be considered when assessing whether control has transferred. In certain circumstances, however, an entity might conclude a conditional call right does not preclude transfer of control. For example, if the call right only becomes active based on factors outside of the entity’s control, this might indicate that control has transferred to the customer despite the existence of the conditional call right.
To assess whether a conditional call right precludes transfer of control to the customer, management should consider the following factors, among others:
- the nature of the conditions that result in the rights becoming active;
- the likelihood that the conditions will be met that result in the rights becoming active; and
- whether the conditions are based on factors within the seller’s or customer’s control.
EX 11.242.1 – Decision tree to be considered when accounting for put options
Reference to standard: IFRS 15 App B para B70; IFRS 15 App B para B72; IFRS 15 App B para B73; and IFRS 15 App B para B74 Reference to standing text: 11.242
FAQ 11.245.1 – How should a trade-in right be accounted for under IFRS 15?
Reference to standard: IFRS 15 App B para B70
Reference to standing text: 11.245

A trade-in credit is a right offered by a seller that allows the customer to trade in a purchased product for a credit against the purchase price of a new product in the future. The seller has an obligation to repurchase the asset at the customer’s request. That obligation is contingent on the customer purchasing a new asset.
A trade-in credit could be viewed as:
- a put option held by the customer under which the seller can be required to repurchase the product at the customer’s request – paragraphs B70–B76 of IFRS 15 apply to put options; or

- a call option held by the customer that permits the customer to purchase a new product in exchange for consideration that will be partly non-cash – paragraphs B39–B43 of IFRS 15 apply to such call options, and the entity would need to consider whether the arrangement contains a material right.
The accounting treatment under these two approaches might be significantly different, as summarised below:
How should a trade-in right be accounted for under IFRS 15?

Determining whether the put option guidance (in paras B70–B76 of IFRS 15) or the material right guidance (in paras B39–B43 of IFRS 15) applies requires judgement and depends on each transaction’s circumstances. An entity is required to assess the substance of the arrangement and to exercise judgement when determining which approach applies.
The entity should determine whether the substance of the trade-in credit is to enable the customer to return the ‘old’ asset, or to promote sales of the ‘new’ asset.
The following factors indicate that the put option guidance might be applicable:

- Whether the entity also leases the same assets through operating lease contracts. Where an entity also leases the same assets, judgement is required to determine whether the substance of the trade-in and leasing arrangements are significantly different. Leasing or selling second hand assets for more than scrap value as a separate activity might suggest that the trade-in credit is an incentive for the customer to return the ‘old’ asset.

- Significance of the expected residual value of the used asset relative to the stand-alone selling price of the new asset. A significant residual value implies that the ‘predominant’ right is the put option, because the entity would be inclined to recover the ‘old’ asset and sell it on the secondary market. An insignificant residual value might suggest that the predominant component is a call option of the customer (the option to buy a new asset) and the trade-in credit is an incentive to sell a new asset.

- Limitations on the customer’s ability to access the secondary market on the same conditions as the entity. Limited access to the secondary market might indicate that the customer gives more importance to the put option because there is no other outlet for the old asset.
- A volatile or illiquid secondary market might indicate that the customer sees more value in the put option.
FAQ 11.246.1 – Should an entity account for a put option as a right of return?
Reference to standard: IFRS 15 App B para B71 Reference to standing text: 11.246

Entity A sells machinery to a manufacturer for C200,000. The manufacturer can require entity A to repurchase the machinery in five years for C75,000. The market value of the machinery at the repurchase date is expected to be greater than C75,000. Entity A offers the manufacturer the put option because an overhaul is typically required after five years. Entity A can overhaul the equipment, sell the refurbished equipment to a customer, and receive a significant margin on the refurbished goods. Assume that the time value of money would not affect the overall conclusion.
Should entity A account for this transaction as a sale with a return right, a lease or a financing transaction?

Entity A should account for the arrangement as the sale of a product with a right of return. The manufacturer does not have a significant economic incentive to exercise its right, since the repurchase price is less than the expected market value at the date of repurchase. Entity A should account for the transaction in a way that is consistent with the model discussed in paragraph 11.212 onwards (rights of return).
FAQ 11.246.2 – Should an entity account for a put option as a lease?
Reference to standard: IFRS 15 App B para B71 Reference to standing text: 11.246

Entity A sells machinery to a manufacturer for C200,000 and stipulates that the manufacturer can require entity A to repurchase the machinery in five years for C150,000. The repurchase price is expected to significantly exceed the market value at the date of repurchase. Assume that the time value of money would not affect the overall conclusion.
Should entity A account for this transaction as a sale with a return right, a lease or a financing transaction?

Entity A should account for the arrangement as a lease in accordance with the leasing guidance. The manufacturer has a put option to resell the machinery to entity A and has a significant economic incentive to exercise this right, because the guarantee price significantly exceeds the expected market value at the date of repurchase. Lease accounting is required, given that the repurchase price is less than the original selling price of the machinery.
EX 11.248.1 – Overall framework for accounting for licences
Reference to standard: IFRS 15 App B para B53 Reference to standing text: 11.248
FAQ 11.248.2 – Is a software licence distinct from installation services?
Reference to standard: IFRS 15 App B para B53 Reference to standing text: 11.248

Entity B provides a perpetual software licence to an engineer. Entity B will also install the software as part of the arrangement. Entity B offers the software licence to its customers with or without installation services, and the engineer could select a different vendor for installation. The installation does not result in significant customisation or modification of the software.
Is the licence in this arrangement distinct?

The software licence is distinct, because the engineer can benefit from the licence on its own, and the licence is separable from other promises in the contract. This conclusion is supported by the fact that entity D licenses the software separately (without installation services) and other vendors are able to install the software. The licence is separately identifiable, because the installation services do not significantly modify the software. The licence is therefore a separate performance obligation that should be accounted for in accordance with the guidance in paragraph 11.254 onwards.
FAQ 11.248.3 – Is an IP licence distinct from R&D services?
Reference to standard: IFRS 15 App B para B53 Reference to standing text: 11.248

Entity C licenses a drug compound to entity D. Entity C also provides research and development (‘R&D’) services as part of the arrangement. The contract requires entity C to perform the R&D services, but the services are not complex or specialised – that is, the services could be performed by entity C or another qualified third party. The R&D services are not expected to significantly modify or customise the initial IP (the drug compound).
Is the licence in this arrangement distinct?

The licence is distinct, because it is capable of being distinct and is separately identifiable from the other promises in the contract. Entity D can benefit from the licence together with R&D services that it could perform itself or obtain from another vendor. The licence is separately identifiable from other promises in the contract because the R&D services are not expected to significantly modify or customise the IP.

Whether a licence is distinct from R&D services depends on the specific circumstances. In a very early stage IP (for example, within the drug discovery cycle) where the R&D services are expected to involve significant further development of the initial IP, an entity might conclude that the IP and R&D services are not distinct and, therefore, constitute a single performance obligation.
FAQ 11.248.4 – Is a software licence distinct from data storage services?
Reference to standard: IFRS 15 App B para B53 Reference to standing text: 11.248

‘Hybrid cloud’ arrangements typically include both a licence to on-premise software and access to software-as-a-service (SaaS). Assessing whether the licence to the on-premise software is distinct or should be combined with the service will require an understanding of the stand-alone functionality of each and the degree to which the licence and the service affect each other.

A software company enters into a contract with its customer for on-premise data analytics software and cloud data storage. The on-premise software utilises the customer’s data stored on the cloud to provide data analysis. The on-premise software can also utilise data stored on the customer’s premises or data stored by other vendors.
Is the licence in this arrangement distinct?

It is likely that the software company would conclude that the on-premise software licence is distinct from the cloud data storage service. The cloud data storage could be provided by other vendors and is capable of being distinct. The software licence and cloud data storage service are separately identifiable because a customer could gain substantially all of the benefits of the on-premise software when data is stored on the customer’s premises or with another vendor.

Alternatively, if the software company’s on-premise software and cloud data storage are used together in such a manner that the customer gains significant functionality that would not be available without the cloud data storage service, the software company might conclude that the licence is not distinct from the storage service.
EX 11.256.1 – Right to access criteria
Reference to standard: IFRS 15 App B para B58 Reference to standing text: 11.256
The licensor will undertake activities that significantly affect the IP

The first criterion requires an assessment of whether the licensor will undertake activities that significantly affect the IP to which the customer has rights, but that are not otherwise performance obligations. These activities could be specified in the contract, or they could be expected by the customer based on the entity’s published policies or customary business practices. See paragraph 11.257 for further guidance on this criterion.

The rights granted directly expose the customer to the effects of the above activities

The second criterion requires that any activities identified in the first criterion affect the customer (licensee), either positively or negatively. Activities that do not affect what the licence provides to the customer, or what the customer controls, do not meet this criterion. An entity is only changing its own asset if its activities do not affect the customer; therefore, the rights that the licence provides are not affected.
The licensor’s activities do not otherwise transfer a good or service

The third criterion requires that the activities that might affect the IP are not additional performance obligations in the contract. The retailer is required to use the latest image of the characters from the television show. There are no other goods or services provided to the retailer in the arrangement. When entering into the licence agreement, the retailer reasonably expects that entity E will continue to produce the show, develop the characters, and perform marketing to enhance awareness of the characters. The retailer can start selling consumer products with the charac

Entity E’s continued production and marketing of the show, and development of the characters, indicates that entity E will undertake activities that significantly affect the IP (the character images). The retailer is directly exposed to any positive or negative effects of entity E’s activities, as the retailer is required to use the latest images that could be more or less positively received by the public as a result of entity E’s activities.
