EX 15.140.2 – Sale of an asset by a manufacturer lessor with advance deposit payment by the lessee
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 para 71 Reference to standing text: 15.140

Entity A (a manufacturer lessor) signed an agreement on 1 January 20X8 to lease specific equipment to entity B (the lessee). Entity A committed to deliver the equipment to entity B on 1 January 20X9. Entity A will manufacture the equipment, and it estimates that the fair value will be C15,000. The estimated cost to build the asset is C10,000. The lessor has not incurred any initial direct costs in negotiating and arranging the lease. The term of the arrangement is four years, commencing when the equipment is delivered. The estimated useful life of the asset is four years and there is no residu
Inception of the lease is on 1 January 20X8, when the lease agreement is signed, and commencement of the lease is on 1 January 20X9, when the underlying asset is made available for use to the lessee.

There is no detailed guidance on how to account for lease payments prepaid at inception but before the commencement date. In our view, at inception, the lessor recognises the upfront payment of C5,000 as a liability and accretes it over the time between inception and commencement (when the asset is ready for use) of the lease. The upfront payment is, in substance, a prepayment or a loan that the lessee provides to the lessor during the construction period. The lessor should recognise finance expense as the upfront payment accretes until commencement.

Entity A determines the interest rate implicit in the lease on 1 January 20X8 by comparing the present value of lease payments discounted to 1 January 20X9 and the estimated fair value of the asset on 1 January 20X9 (in this example, the residual value and initial direct costs are assumed to be zero). Assuming that the interest rate implicit in the lease is 5%, the liability accretes over the time between inception and commencement (1 January 20X9) to C5,250. The accreted prepayment of C5,250 is treated as part of the lease payments.

At commencement of the lease on 1 January 20X9, the lessor is expecting to initially recognise a profit on disposal amounting to C5,000 and a finance lease receivable of C9,750, being the discounted amount of the future lease payments amounting to C15,000 less the set-off of C5,250 liability.
FAQ 15.148.1 – Can the lease classification be determined without performing a detailed split of the rentals?
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 App B para B56 Reference to standing text: 15.148
Question Can the lease classification be determined without performing a detailed split of the rentals?

Answer Classifying the buildings element is often more difficult than the land element. In many cases, it is possible to determine the classification of the lease of the building without performing a detailed split of the rentals between the land element and the buildings element of the lease.

With the exception of the present value test, the criteria for lease classification can be considered without obtaining a split of the rentals. For example, a building with a relatively short life, perhaps built to a customer’s specification or for a specific use, might well be treated as being held under a finance lease. Long leases of a building (usually 99 to 999 years) are likely to be finance leases.
EX 15.148.2 – Lease classification using qualitative criteria
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 App B para B56 Reference to standing text: 15.148
It might be possible to determine that a lease of a building is an operating lease using only the qualitative classification criteria in IFRS 16. Consider the following lease:

Property type: Non-specialised office building Lease term: 25 years Economic life: 50 years Initial rentals: Market rates Rent reviews: Every 5 years, upwards only, to market rates Options to purchase: None Residual value guarantees: None Cancellation clauses: None Option to extend: Lessee can extend lease by 5 years on payment of market rentals

It is relatively clear that the lessee does not have substantially all of the risks and rewards of the building’s ownership. The lease term is not for a major part of the asset’s economic life, the lessee has no interest in the residual, and rentals are set at market rates. It would therefore be reasonable to conclude, without performing a present value test, that both the lease of the land and the lease of the building are operating leases.
FAQ 15.149.1 – Why are the lease payments allocated between the land and buildings in proportion to the relative fair values of the leasehold interests?
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 App B para B56 Reference to standing text: 15.149
Question Why are the lease payments allocated between the land and buildings in proportion to the relative fair values of the leasehold interests?

Answer The fair value of a leasehold interest in land or buildings is different from the fair value of the land or buildings themselves. Allocating the lease payments simply by reference to the relative fair values of the land and buildings would not reflect the fact that land often has an indefinite economic life and would be expected to maintain its value beyond the lease term. In contrast, the future economic benefits of a building are likely to be used up, at least to some extent, over the lease term. Therefore, it would be reasonable to expect that the lease payments relating to the build

That is why the allocation of the minimum lease payments should be weighted to reflect their role in compensating the lessor, and not by reference to the relative fair values of the land and buildings. In other words, the weighting should reflect the lessee's leasehold interest in the land and the buildings.
FAQ 15.149.2 – How is the fair value of the lessee’s leasehold interest calculated?
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 App B para B56 Reference to standing text: 15.149
Question How is the fair value of the lessee’s leasehold interest calculated?
Answer The fair value of the leasehold interest is derived from the following equation:
Fair value of leasehold interest = Fair value of freehold interest – Present value of the residual interest at inception of the lease

In the case of the fair value of a freehold building, the residual value might be lower, pro rata, than the land, due to obsolescence; therefore, in order for the equation to balance, it follows that the fair value of the leasehold interest in the building will be higher, pro rata, than the land. This results in the lease payments being weighted towards the building.

There is no detailed guidance on how to determine the fair value of the leasehold interests. Nonetheless, there are several different ways in which this calculation can be approached. Whichever method is used, it is likely that the valuation inputs will remain the same, namely:
- The property’s fair value at the lease's inception.
- A split of this fair value between land and buildings.
- The property’s residual value on expiry of the lease.
Whichever method is adopted, the input of property valuation specialists will be required.
EX 15.149.3 – Rental allocation
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 App B para B56 Reference to standing text: 15.149

The inputs discussed in FAQ 15.149.2 need to be analysed further, in order to split the lease payments. The underlying rationale for the rental split is that the land component is unlikely to depreciate and, therefore, any diminution in value between the fair value at inception of the lease and the residual value at lease expiry is usually a measure of the loss in value of the buildings during the lease period. Consider the following examples:
Example 1 – Rental allocated on a leasehold value basis

Freehold value of property: C100m Value of land at inception: C40m Lease term: 25 years Initial annual rental: C6.25m Expected residual value of property: C65m (today's prices) Expected real return on property: 6.0%

If it is assumed that all of the loss in value of the property over the lease term is attributable to the building, and the residual values are discounted using the expected real return on the property, the rentals can be split as follows:

Land Buildings Total (Cm) (Cm) (Cm) i Freehold value 40 60 100 ii Residual value 40 25 65 iii Present value of residual 9 6 15 i – iii Leasehold value 31 (36%) 54 (64%) 85 (100%) Rent allocation (% × C6.25m) 2.25 4.00 6.25
Example 2 – Rental allocated on a capital value basis

An alternative methodology is to assess the loss in value of the buildings during the lease period and, thereafter, to calculate what proportion of the rentals needs to be allocated to compensate the lessor for the loss in building value during the lease period. In the example below, a rate of 6% has been used to determine the amount of rent allocated to amortisation.

In practice, property valuation specialists might vary in their views as to what is the most appropriate rate to be used to allocate rent. For example, a government bond rate or a real return rate might be considered appropriate. It is therefore important to seek guidance from property specialists when determining the rate to be used.

Land Buildings Total (Cm) (Cm) (Cm) i Freehold value 40 (40%) 60 (60%) 100 ii Residual value 40 25 65 i – ii Amortisation 0 35 35 Rental iii Rent allocated for amortisation (C0.60m) − 0.60 0.60 iv Balance (% × C5.65m) 2.26 3.39 5.65 iii + iv Rent allocation (Cm) 2.26 3.99 6.25

C0.60m is the annual rental paid in advance which, when compounded over the 25-year lease term at the expected real return on property of 6%, results in C35m, the difference between the freehold value and the building’s residual value.
Sale and leaseback transactions
FAQ 15.153.1 – When would a sale and leaseback not qualify as a sale in accordance with IFRS 15?
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 para 99 Reference to standing text: 15.153

Question Entity A sells a building with 30 years’ remaining useful life to bank B for the market value of C100m. For the purpose of this example, disregard the lease of land. The entity then leases the building back from bank B and, over the next 10 years, entity A pays to bank B a C5m per annum rental.
At the end of year 10, entity A has the option to purchase back the building for C70m.
Does this transaction qualify as a sale and leaseback?

Paragraph B66 of IFRS 15 specifies that “if an entity has an obligation or a right to repurchase the asset (a forward or a call option), a customer does not obtain control of the asset because the customer is limited in its ability to direct the use of, and obtain substantially all of the remaining benefits from, the asset”.
In this case, entity A’s option to repurchase the building means that it does not qualify as a sale in accordance with IFRS 15, and therefore it does not qualify as a sale and leaseback.
EX 15.155.1 – Accounting for a sale and leaseback transaction (example)
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 paras 100, IE11(example 24) Reference to standing text: 15.155

A seller-lessee sells a building to an unrelated buyer-lessor for cash of C2,000,000. The fair value of the building at that time is C1,800,000; the carrying amount immediately before the transaction is C1,000,000.

At the same time, the seller-lessee enters into a contract with the buyer-lessor for the right to use the building for 18 years, with annual payments of C120,000 payable at the end of each year. The interest rate implicit in the lease is 4.5%, which results in a present value of the annual payments of C1,459,200.
The transfer of the asset to the buyer-lessor has been assessed as meeting the definition of a sale under IFRS 15.
How is the transaction accounted for?
Since the consideration (C2,000,000) exceeds the fair value (C1,800,000) of the building, the agreement contains a financing transaction:
Cash C200,000 Financial liability C200,000

The seller-lessee initially recognises a right-of-use asset as the proportion of the previous carrying amount (C1,000,000) that reflects the right of use retained. The proportion is calculated by dividing the present value of the lease payment (C1,459,200), less the part of the lease payments that is just a repayment of the financing granted to the seller-lessee (C200,000) [= C1,259,200], by the fair value of the asset (C1,800,000). This results in a right-of-use asset of C699,555.

The gain on sale is calculated as a proportion of the total gain of C800,000 (purchase price less financing element less carrying amount of the building), representing the ratio between the rights effectively transferred to the buyer (= fair value of the building (C1,800,000) less the present value of the lease payments (C1,259,200)) and the fair value of the building (C1,800,000). This results in a gain of C240,355.
The final accounting entries are as follows:
Cash C1,800,000 Right-of-use asset C699,555 Building C1,000,000 Financial liability C1,259,200 Gain C240,355
FAQ 15.155.2 – How do you initially account for a sale and leaseback transaction where the lease payments are entirely variable?
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 para 100 Reference to standing text: 15.155
Question How do you initially account for a sale and leaseback transaction where the lease payments are entirely variable?

Answer The IFRS Interpretations Committee (‘IC’) was asked how the seller-lessee measures the right-of-use asset arising from a leaseback, and thus determines the amount of any gain or loss recognised at the date of the transaction where the lease includes variable payments. The ‘IC’ noted that paragraph 100 of IFRS 16 states that “if the transfer of an asset by the seller-lessee satisfies the requirements of IFRS 15 to be accounted for as a sale of the asset: (a) the seller-lessee shall measure the right-of-use asset arising from the leaseback at the proportion of the previous carrying amount

Consequently, to measure the right-of-use asset arising from the leaseback, the seller-lessee determines the proportion of the property, plant and equipment (PP&E) transferred to the buyer-lessor that relates to the right of use retained. It does so by comparing, at the date of the transaction, the right of use that it retains via the leaseback to the rights comprising the entire PP&E. IFRS 16 does not prescribe a method for determining that proportion. In this variable payment scenario, the seller-lessee could determine the proportion by comparing, for example, (a) the present value o

The gain or loss that the seller-lessee recognises at the date of the transaction is a consequence of its measurement of the right-of-use asset arising from the leaseback. Because the right of use that the seller-lessee retains is not remeasured as a result of the transaction (it is measured as a proportion of the PP&E’s previous carrying amount), the amount of the gain or loss recognised relates only to the rights transferred to the buyer-lessor. Applying paragraph 53(i) of IFRS 16, the seller-lessee discloses gains or losses arising from sale and leaseback transactions.

The ‘IC’ agenda decision explained that the seller-lessee should also recognise a liability at the date of the transaction, even if all of the payments for the lease are variable and do not depend on an index or rate. The initial measurement of the liability is a consequence of how the right-of-use asset is measured, and the gain or loss on the sale and leaseback transaction is determined, applying paragraph 100(a) of IFRS 16.

The IASB has an ongoing project in relation to how a seller-lessee should apply the subsequent measurement requirements in IFRS 16 to the lease liability that arises in the sale and leaseback transaction.
Transition and effective date
FAQ 15.166.1 – What is the lease term when estimating the incremental borrowing rate at the date of initial application?
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 App A, IFRS 16 para C8 Reference to standing text: 15.166
Question What is the lease term when estimating the incremental borrowing rate at the date of initial application?
Answer For leases previously classified as operating leases, a lessee applying the simplified transition approach uses its incremental borrowing rate at the date of initial application.

When determining an incremental borrowing rate, one factor that lessees have to consider is the lease term. The question arises whether the lessee should use the original lease term or the lease term remaining on initial application.

The commencement date of a property lease is 1 January 2001 (at which time the lease term was 20 years), and the adoption date of IFRS 16 is 1 January 2019. In this example, should the lessee determine its incremental borrowing rate for two years (the remaining lease term on initial application) or 20 years (the original lease term)?

The transitional requirements for IFRS 16 do not specify whether the lease term, when determining the incremental borrowing rate, should be the original lease term or the remaining lease term. In our view, using either would be appropriate, and the entity has an accounting policy choice. The policy chosen should be consistently applied and disclosed.

If the entity calculates the right-of-use asset retrospectively, applying paragraph C8(b)(i) of IFRS 16, it uses the same incremental borrowing rate to calculate the retrospective right-of-use asset and to calculate the lease liability.
FAQ 15.167.1 – What are the impairment requirements for right-of-use assets resulting from leases previously classified as operating leases on transition on IFRS 16?
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 App C para C10(b) Reference to standing text: 15.167

Question A retailer leases 90 stores under leases that, under IAS 17, are classified as operating leases. Prior to the adoption of IFRS 16, the retailer decided that it would no longer use 18 of the stores for trading, but it would sub-lease them to third parties. It therefore assessed whether the underlying lease contracts were onerous, applying the guidance in IAS 37, and it concluded that, for 10 lease contracts, a provision for onerous contracts was needed.
- 72 contracts: No assessment made.
- 10 contracts: Assessment made; provision recognised.
- 8 contracts: Assessment made; no provision recognised.
At transition to IFRS 16, the retailer chooses the ‘simplified approach’.

How does the retailer, at the date of initial application, assess whether the right-of-use asset recognised for each contract needs to be impaired? The store is a separate cash-generating unit, as defined in IAS 36.

At the date of initial application, the lessee has to assess whether the right-of-use asset that is recognised for each lease contract needs to be impaired. [IFRS 16 App C para C8(c)]. The way in which this test is performed depends on whether or not the lessee has already made an assessment based on IAS 37 before transition.
Contracts for which the entity has already made an assessment based on the guidance in IAS 37

For contracts for which the entity has already made an assessment based on the guidance in IAS 37 (in this example, 18 contracts), paragraph C10(b) of IFRS 16 allows it to rely on that assessment. If the entity decides to apply that practical expedient, it adjusts the right-of-use assets at the date of initial application by the amount of any provision for onerous contracts recognised immediately before the date of initial application.
Looking at the example, this means that:
- The right-of-use assets that relate to the 10 stores for which a provision for onerous contracts has been recognised are reduced by an amount equal to the carrying amount of that provision.

- The right-of-use assets that relate to the eight stores for which no provision for onerous contracts has been recognised are not adjusted; for them, no further impairment review has to be performed.

If the entity does not use the practical expedient, it has to apply the guidance in IAS 36. It will therefore have to assess whether, at the date of initial application, there is an indicator that an impairment loss has occurred (for example, because the rentals of the sub-lease differ from the rentals of the head lease). If this is the case, the entity has to calculate the recoverable amount of the right-of-use asset, in accordance with the guidance in IAS 36, and recognise an impairment if necessary. If there is no indicator present, the entity does not have to calculate the recoverable amou
Contracts for which the entity has not made an assessment based on the guidance in IAS 37

For contracts that have not already been assessed based on the guidance in IAS 37 (in this example, 72 contracts), we are of the view that the entity has an accounting policy choice. It can perform an assessment (as described in paras 66 to 69 of IAS 37) before transition to IFRS 16, and rely on the outcome of that assessment (that is, adjust the right-of-use asset by the amount of any provision for onerous contracts). Alternatively, it can apply the guidance in IAS 36 in the way described above.

Please note: The example above considered retail stores, where each right-of-use asset is also a cash-generating unit as defined in IAS 36. In a situation where the right-of-use assets are not also cash-generating units, an entity must still apply IAS 36 as normal, to determine when an impairment review is required and what the cash-generating units are.
FAQ 15.167.2 – If an entity incorporates its IAS 37 onerous lease provision into a right-of-use asset on transition, what is the deemed cost for future impairment reversals?
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 App C para C10(b) Reference to standing text: 15.167
Question If an entity incorporates its IAS 37 onerous lease provision into a right-of-use asset on transition, what is the deemed cost for future impairment reversals?

Answer A lessee that, on transition to IFRS 16, chooses the ‘simplified approach’ has to ensure that right-of-use assets resulting from lease contracts previously classified as operating leases are not impaired. It therefore either applies IAS 36 to the right-of-use asset on transition; or it relies on its assessment of whether leases are onerous, applying IAS 37, made before the date of initial application, as explained in FAQ 15.167.1. In the latter case, the lessee adjusts the right-of-use asset by the amount of any provision for onerous leases recognised in the statement of financial posit

A retailer leases a store under a lease that, under IAS 17, is classified as an operating lease. The store is a separate cash-generating unit as defined in IAS 36. Before the date of initial application of IFRS 16, the lessee has assessed whether the underlying lease contract is onerous, applying the guidance in IAS 37, and concluded that a provision for onerous contracts is needed. The carrying amount of the provision, immediately before the date of initial application, is C20.

At transition to IFRS 16, the retailer chooses the ‘simplified approach’ and decides to rely on the IAS 37 assessment, instead of applying the guidance in IAS 36. Before taking into account the provision for onerous contracts, the right-of-use asset is measured at an amount of C100; after the adjustment, the carrying amount is C80.
Can the adjustment made at the date of initial application be reversed in a future period?
This question is not addressed in IFRS 16. The lessee has an accounting policy choice on how it interprets the adjustment made on transition:

- It could interpret the initial carrying amount of the right-of-use asset (C80) as a gross amount of C100 minus a loss allowance of C20. Under this view, the adjustment is reversed to the extent that an impairment test in a subsequent period shows that the value of the right-of-use asset has recovered. Adjusting the right-of-use asset by the amount of any provision for onerous contracts under IAS 37 is solely a practical alternative approach to applying the guidance in IAS 36. The subsequent accounting of the right-of-use asset should not be impacted by whether or not that practical expedient

- Alternatively, the lessee could interpret the initial carrying amount of the right-of-use asset (C80) as its deemed cost that cannot be exceeded. Under this view, the adjustment is not reversed, regardless of whether an impairment test based on IAS 36 in a subsequent period shows that the value of the right-of-use asset has recovered.
The accounting policy chosen has to be applied consistently.
FAQ 15.167.3 – How do you apply the low-value asset exemption on transition?
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 App C para C9(a) Reference to standing text: 15.167
Under the ‘simplified approach’ for transition, a lessee could apply the low-value asset exemption to existing lease contracts previously classified as operating leases. [IFRS 16 App C para C9(a)].
Question Can the low-value asset exemption also be applied to lease contracts that, under IAS 17, are classified as finance leases?

Answer Yes. If the underlying asset is of ‘low value’ (as defined in IFRS 16), the lessee is not required to recognise a right-of-use asset and a corresponding lease liability. Following this principle, the lessee can apply the low-value asset exemption at the date of initial application to both lease contracts previously classified as operating leases and lease contracts previously classified as finance leases.
EX 15.167.4 – Applying the practical expedients on transition
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 App C para C10 Reference to standing text: 15.167

A lessee applying the simplified transition approach can choose various practical expedients when recognising leases previously classified as operating leases, including hindsight, and allocating payments between lease and non-lease components.

A lessee is allowed to use hindsight on transition (para C10(e) of IFRS 16), and the example given in the standard relates to determining which options to include in the lease term. Hindsight can therefore be applied to other judgements, such as estimated dismantling costs. In our view, hindsight should not be applied to areas that do not involve judgement or estimation. For example, for a lease where payments vary with CPI and a lessee chooses to calculate the right-of-use asset retrospectively, the lessee cannot measure it on the basis of the lease payments as at transition; instead, the les
Allocating payments between lease and non-lease components

If a lease includes payments for lease and non-lease components, the lessee must allocate the payments applying IFRS 16. Under IFRS 16, the allocation of payments between lease and non-lease components is based on the estimated consideration and stand-alone selling price at lease commencement. In our view, allocating payments based on the estimated consideration and stand-alone selling price on the date of initially applying IFRS 16, rather than at lease commencement, would be acceptable.
FAQ 15.167.5 – How do you account for finance leases on transition?
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 App C para C11 Reference to standing text: 15.167
Question How do you account for finance leases on transition?

Answer A lessee applying the simplified transition approach, which had leases classified as finance leases under IAS 17, is required to use the carrying amount of the lease asset and lease liability immediately before the date of initial application on transition. The measurement principles in IFRS 16 would only be applied after initial application. If there is a difference in measurement (for example, residual value guarantees as discussed in FAQ 15.69.1), any remeasurement would occur immediately after initial application and not as a transition adjustment (that is, it would not be taken to
EX 15.169.1 – Initial recognition of a finance lease resulting from a sub-lease on transition to IFRS 16
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 App C para C15 Reference to standing text: 15.169

On transition to IFRS 16, an intermediate lessee uses the ‘simplified approach’. It measures the right-of-use asset that results from the head lease, which was classified as an operating lease under IAS 17, using the guidance in paragraph C8(b)(i) of IFRS 16. This means that it calculates the initial carrying amount as if IFRS 16 had been applied since the commencement date, but it uses the incremental borrowing rate at the date of initial application.

The sub-lease, which also was classified as an operating lease under IAS 17, is re-assessed on the date of initial application. [IFRS 16 App C para C15]. Based on this re-assessment, it is now classified as a finance lease, and hence the lessee accounts for the sub-lease as a new finance lease entered into at the date of initial application. [IFRS 16 App C para C15(b)]. It de-recognises the right-of-use asset related to the head lease, and it recognises a receivable at an amount equal to the net investment in the sub-lease.
Does the recognition of the net investment in the sub-lease have an effect on profit or loss?

The effect of recognising the right-of-use asset relating to the head lease is presented as an adjustment to the opening balance of retained earnings (or other component of equity, as appropriate) at the date of initial application. [IFRS 16 App C para C7]. The standard is, however, not explicit on whether the same is true for the effect of recognising the net investment in the sub-lease. Since both effects relate to the initial application of IFRS 16, we think that it is appropriate to present both within retained earnings (or other component of equity, as appropriate).
The resulting accounting entries would be as follows:
Dr Right-of-use asset Cr Lease liability Cr Opening retained earnings Dr Net investment in the lease Cr Right-of-use asset Cr Opening retained earnings
The objective of the accounting entries is to illustrate the general principle; depending on the particular facts and circumstances, there could alternatively be a decrease in retained earnings.
Sale and leaseback transactions
EX 15.172.1 – Requirements for transactions before the date of initial application
Reference to standard: IFRS 16 App C paras C16, C19 Reference to standing text: 15.172

Regardless of whether a lessee applies the full retrospective or ‘simplified approach’ on transition, there are various transitional provisions that it must comply with, because they are requirements and not options. For example:

An entity that entered into a sale and operating leaseback before the date of initial application must account for the leaseback in the same way as any other operating lease (apart from adjustments for off-market terms). It cannot choose to retrospectively apply the sale and leaseback guidance in IFRS 16.

An entity that has previously recognised assets or liabilities for favourable/unfavourable lease contracts in a business combination must de-recognise that asset or liability and adjust it against the related right-of-use asset on initial application. It cannot revisit the acquisition accounting to recognise a right-of-use asset at fair value as at the business combination date.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.1 A liability is a “present obligation of the entity arising from past events, the settlement of which is expected to result in an outflow from the entity of resources embodying economic benefits”. A provision is “a liability of uncertain timing or amount”. IAS 37 sets out the requirements for recognition, measurement and disclosure of provisions. It also sets out the presentation and disclosure requirements for contingent liabilities and contingent assets.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

text: 16.3 Executory contracts are contracts under which neither party has performed any of its obligations, or both parties have partially performed their obligations to an equal extent. Executory contracts encompass commitments to purchase goods or to deliver services where performance has not yet happened. An executory contract might be onerous, in which case the requirements in IAS 37 for onerous contracts are applied (see further para 16.71 onwards).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

Some financial guarantee contracts might be within the scope of either IFRS 9 or IFRS 4. Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets that require settlement in cash which does not yet arise from a contract (for example, a contingent payable or receivable for a court judgment) is not a financial instrument. text: 16.7 The word ‘provision’ could be used to describe amounts that are deducted from assets to arrive at their balance sheet carrying amount. text: 16.9 A provision is “a liability of uncertain timing or amount”. Provisions differ from other liabilities in the degree of certainty about the amount or the timing of the payment. So, there is a clear distinction between provisions and other liabilities such as trade payables and accruals.

text: 16.11 A present obligation can arise from a legal agreement (a ‘legal obligation’) or might arise from an entity’s past practice, published policy or current statement (a ‘constructive obligation’).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.12 It will usually be straightforward to establish whether a legal obligation exists, because it derives either from a contract (through its explicit or implicit terms), from legislation or from the operation of the law.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.13 Proposed legislation moves through various stages before it is finally enacted. A proposed law only creates an obligation for which provision is made when it is virtually certain to be enacted as drafted. This means that an obligation to comply with legislation only arises when that legislation is enacted or virtually certain to be enacted. IAS 37 does not specify a single event to identify when enactment of a law is virtually certain.

text: 16.15 The expectation of other parties is critical to the existence of a past event, but it is not necessary to know the other party’s identity for an obligation to arise.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.16 A constructive obligation might arise where a potentially obligating event has taken place (such as environmental damage), but where no legal obligation exists. The entity could create a constructive obligation by making a public statement that it will rectify the damage. The public announcement creates a constructive obligation if it is sufficiently specific that it leaves the entity no realistic alternative but to carry out the rectification work.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Uncertainty as to whether a present obligation exists

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.17 In rare circumstances, it might not be clear whether a past event results in a present obligation. In these situations, a past event gives rise to a present obligation if, after taking account of all the available evidence, it is more likely than not that a present obligation exists at the balance sheet date.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.18 IAS 37 requires that:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - Where it is more likely than not that a present obligation exists at the balance sheet date, the entity should recognise a provision (if the recognition criteria are met).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - Where it is more likely that no present obligation exists at the balance sheet date, the entity should disclose a contingent liability, unless the possibility of an outflow of resources embodying economic benefit is remote, in which case no disclosure is required (see para 16.31).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - It is sometimes unclear whether a present obligation exists in connection with litigation where the events are disputed by the parties. In this situation, it might be necessary for an entity to obtain an expert’s opinion to determine whether a present obligation exists.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.19 Further information might become available between the balance sheet date and the date on which an entity’s financial statements are finalised. Where this happens, that information should be taken into account in determining whether or not a present obligation exists at the balance sheet date. A provision should not be made at the period end where the obligating event occurs after the balance sheet date. See chapter 9 para 2 for further guidance on events after the reporting period.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.19.1 – How should management account for a situation where it is not possible to reliably assess whether a present obligation exists?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.20 A liability exists only when something has happened in the past (a ‘past event’) to trigger a present obligation. The past event is known in IAS 37 as the ‘obligating event’. An ‘obligating event’ is “an event that creates a legal or constructive obligation that results in an entity having no realistic alternative to settling that obligation”. Many obligating events are obvious; for example, the obligating event giving rise to the need to make a warranty provision is the original sale of the warrantied goods. Similarly, with the contamination of land, the obligating event is the original

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.21 No obligation arises from a past event if there is a realistic possibility that the entity can avoid settlement. An entity has no realistic alternative to settling an obligation only where:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - the settlement of the obligation can be enforced by law; or

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - the event, in the case of a constructive obligation, creates a valid expectation in others that the entity will discharge the obligation.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.22 Only past events existing independently of an entity’s future actions will trigger provisions.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.22.1 – Does provision need to be made for costs arising from future operation?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Probable outflow of economic benefits

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.23 Once it has been established that a present obligation exists as a result of a past event, it is necessary to determine whether it will result in a probable outflow of resources embodying economic benefits to settle the obligation. IAS 37 states that “an outflow of resources or other event is regarded as probable if the event is more likely than not to occur …”. No provision is necessary where the outflow is not probable, but a contingent liability exists and should be disclosed unless the possibility of an outflow is remote.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.24 Obligations arising from a group of similar transactions should be considered together. IAS 37 requires the probability that an outflow of resources will be required in settlement to be determined by considering the class of obligations as a whole. A typical example of this is product warranties.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.25 In extremely rare cases, it will not be possible to make a reliable estimate of the obligation. In such cases, the liability is disclosed as a contingent liability. IAS 37 does not provide further guidance on what might be ‘extremely rare cases’.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.26 IAS 37 states that, in nearly all cases, an entity will be able to determine a range of possible outcomes and to make an estimate of an obligation that will be sufficiently reliable to use in recognising a provision. Judgement will be needed where the amount is uncertain. A variety of estimation techniques might be used to make the estimate (see para 16.47).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Continued recognition and reversal

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.27 Provisions should be based on circumstances at the balance sheet date but adjusted to reflect the current best estimate. The current best estimate will be based on information available up to the date when the financial statements are authorised for issue. If it is no longer probable that an outflow of economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation, the provision should be reversed.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.28 A provision should only be used for the expenditures for which it was originally recognised. Where the original provision was charged as an expense, any subsequent reversal should be credited to the same line in the income statement. Changes in provisions that were originally recognised as part of the cost of an asset are dealt with in EX 16.85.7.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: [IAS 37 para 61]. [IAS 1 para 45].

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.28.1 – How should the reversal of a provision be reflected in the income statement?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Contingent liabilities and contingent assets

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.29 IAS 37 uses the term ‘contingent’ for liabilities and assets that are not recognised because their existence will be confirmed only by the occurrence or non-occurrence of one or more uncertain future events that are not wholly within the entity’s control. The term ‘contingent liability’ is also used for liabilities that do not meet the recognition criteria in IAS 37.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.30 Contingent liabilities arise where there is a:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - possible obligation as a result of a past event that might, but will probably not, require an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits; or

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - present obligation as a result of a past event:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - that probably requires an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits, but where the obligation cannot be measured reliably; or

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - that might, but will probably not, require an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.30.1 – What is the spectrum of liability?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.31 A contingent liability should not be recognised. It should be disclosed, unless the possibility of an outflow is remote.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: [IAS 37 para 27]. [IAS 37 para 28].

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.32 Sometimes, entities are jointly and severally liable for an obligation. Joint and several obligations often arise in joint arrangements where two or more parties co-operate to build, develop or exploit a particular product. Where joint and several obligations arise, the part of the obligation that is expected to be met by other parties is treated as a contingent liability. The guidance in IAS 37 is applied to the part of the obligation that will be met by the entity itself.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.33 A contingent asset is “[a] possible asset that arises from past events and whose existence will be confirmed only by the occurrence or non-occurrence of one or more uncertain future events not wholly within the control of the entity”.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.34 Contingent assets generally arise from unplanned or other unexpected events that give rise to the possibility of an inflow of resources embodying economic benefits to the entity.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.35 IAS 37 does not permit the recognition of contingent assets. Contingent assets are disclosed only when an inflow of economic benefits is probable. This is different from contingent liabilities, where disclosure is required unless an outflow is remote.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: [IAS 37 para 31]. [IAS 37 para 34].

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.36 A contingent asset is not recognised, because it might result in the recognition of income that is never realised. When it becomes virtually certain that an inflow of economic benefits will arise, the asset is no longer a contingent asset and should be recognised in the period in which the change occurs (that is, when the future event occurs and confirms the asset’s existence, or when it becomes virtually certain that the future event will confirm the asset’s existence and it is virtually certain that the asset will be realised).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.36.1 – What is the spectrum of contingent assets?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.36.2 – How should deposits relating to taxes other than income tax be accounted for?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.37 Where some or all of the expenditure required to settle a provision is expected to be reimbursed by another party, the reimbursement should be recognised only when it is virtually certain that reimbursement will be received if the entity settles the obligation. The entity typically remains liable for the entire obligation, and reimbursements are therefore presented separately as assets. The amount recognised should not exceed the amount of the related provision.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.37.1 – How should provisions and related reimbursements be recognised?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.37.2 – What are the implications of post balance sheet date events for the recognition of insurance recoveries?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.38 Expenses relating to a provision can be presented net of the amount recognised for a reimbursement in the income statement (see also FAQ 16.37.2).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.39 An entity is sometimes able to transfer the obligation to another party and, as a result, it will no longer be liable for the loss, even if the party assuming the obligation fails to pay. The entity no longer has a liability for the costs arising under the obligation or bears the credit risk of the counterparty assuming the obligation, so those costs should not be included in the provision.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Measurement (paras 16.40 - 16.54)

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.40 A provision should be measured at the best estimate of the expenditure required to settle the present obligation at the balance sheet date.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.41 This is the amount that an entity would rationally pay to settle the obligation or to transfer it to a third party at the balance sheet date. It will sometimes be impossible to settle or transfer the obligation at the reporting date and, in these cases, entities often provide for the cost of fulfilling the obligation as an estimate of the amount that an entity would rationally pay to settle.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.42 Estimating the cost to settle, transfer or fulfil an obligation requires judgement, taking into account experience in similar situations and, in some cases, the views of independent experts. For example, management will often have experience of the type and number of warranty claims that have been made in the past that can be used to develop an estimate of future claims. Management might seek the advice of an expert (for example, in connection with litigation).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.43 The risks and uncertainties about the amount and timing of cash flows are taken into account in estimating the expenditure required to settle the present obligation at the balance sheet date. Where provisions involves significant judgements and estimation uncertainties, an entity should make disclosures in accordance with IAS 1. These requirements are considered in more detail in chapter 4 para 149.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.44 In deciding the amount to be provided, the entity takes into account any additional evidence provided by events that take place after the balance sheet date.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.45 A provision is measured before tax. The tax consequences of a provision are dealt with in accordance with IAS 12. Accounting for deferred tax is considered in chapter 14 para 25.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.46 Future events which might impact on measuring the provisions should be reflected where there is sufficient objective evidence that they will occur.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.46.1 – What are the implications of future changes in technology?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.47 Provisions are generally estimated using:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - the single most likely outcome; or

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - a weighted average of all of the possible outcomes (the ‘expected value’ method). This method can be applied to a large population of similar claims, as well as a single obligation with various possible outcomes.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.47.1 – How should a warranty provision be estimated using expected value (example reproduced from IAS 37)?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.47.2 – When might the expected value approach not be appropriate?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.47.3 – When might the most likely outcome approach not be appropriate? FAQ 16.47.4 – How are risks reflected under the two estimation methods?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.48 A provision is measured at the present value of the expected outflow where the effect of the time value of money is material.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.49 The discount rate should be a pre-tax rate that reflects the current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks specific to the liability. The discount rate should not, however, reflect risks for which future cash flow estimates have been adjusted. Therefore, where risk has been built into the cash flows, the discount rate should not be adjusted for the same risks.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.49.1 – What factors influence the discount rate to be used for measuring the present value of provisions? FAQ 16.49.2 – Does a negative discount rate reflect time value? FAQ 16.49.3 – How does the discount rate reflect risks specific to the liability? FAQ 16.49.4 – How does inflation affect the discount rate? FAQ 16.49.5 – Should own credit risks be considered? FAQ 16.49.6 – What factors might impact setting the discount rate?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.50 The unwinding of the discount due to the passage of time should be included as an element of borrowing costs in arriving at profit or loss for the year.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.50.1 – What discount rate should be used to calculate the borrowing costs that arise from the unwinding of a provision?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Other changes in provisions

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.51 Provisions should be re-assessed at the end of each reporting period and adjusted to reflect current best estimates. This re-assessment should include the estimated cash flows and the discount rate. A re-assessment should be undertaken at least once every reporting period. The discount rate should be a current rate (rather than a longer-term average) at each reporting date.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.51.1 – How should re-assessment of provision from changes in estimated cash flows and discount rates be accounted for?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.51.2 – What is the effect of a change in the discount rate?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Expected disposal of assets

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.52 The measurement of a provision should not take account of any gains from the expected disposal of assets, even if the expected disposal is closely linked to the event giving rise to the provision. For example, a restructuring provision cannot be reduced by an expected gain on disposal of a factory that is being sold as part of the restructuring. The gain is recognised when the factory is sold.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.53 Future operating losses do not meet the definition of a liability and the recognition criteria for provisions. This is because future operating losses do not result from a past event (see para 16.20). Therefore, a provision for termination of operations cannot include future operating losses up to the date of closure.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.53.1 – Can future operating losses of a disposal group be recognised as a provision?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.54 Expected future operating losses are an indication that an impairment review is required in accordance with IAS 36. Such a review would determine whether those assets have suffered an impairment and need to be written down. Anticipated future operating losses might indicate that an entity has an onerous contract. Onerous contracts are covered in detail in paragraph 16.71 onwards.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Restructuring (paras 16.55 - 16.70)

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.55 IAS 37 explains how to determine when an obligating event has occurred in connection with a restructuring. IAS 37 also applies to provisions for restructuring when there is a discontinued operation. Where a restructuring meets the definition of a discontinued operation in IFRS 5, additional disclosures might be required. Discontinued operations are dealt with in chapter 30 para 39.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.56 A ‘restructuring’ is:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: “A programme that is planned and controlled by management, and materially changes either: (a) the scope of a business undertaken by an entity; or (b) the manner in which that business is conducted.”

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.57 IAS 37 gives some examples of situations that fall within the restructuring definition:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The sale or termination of a line of business.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The closure of business locations or the relocation of business activities.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - Changes in management structure.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - Fundamental re-organisations that have a material effect on the nature and focus of the entity’s operations.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Applying the recognition criteria

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.58 A restructuring provision is recognised only when an obligating event has arisen. The obligation for a restructuring is often constructive. A constructive restructuring obligation arises only when both of the conditions below exists:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - A detailed formal plan for the restructuring, which identifies at least:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - the business or part of a business concerned;

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - the principal locations affected;

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - the location, function and approximate number of employees who will be compensated for terminating their services;

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - the expenditures that will be undertaken; and

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - when the plan will be implemented.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - A valid expectation, in those affected, that the entity will carry out the restructuring by starting to implement that plan or announcing its main features to those affected by it.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.59 Evidence demonstrating that an entity has started to implement a restructuring plan includes:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - Public announcement of the plan’s main features.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.60 A constructive obligation arises from a public announcement only when it raises a valid expectation in employees (or their representatives), customers, suppliers or others affected by it in a ‘sufficiently specific manner’ that the entity has no alternative but to discharge its responsibilities.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.60.1 – Is an announcement of a restructuring plan to some of those parties affected by the plan sufficient to recognise a liability for the total expected restructuring provision?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.61 The announcement must therefore address the main features of the restructuring plan in a sufficiently specific manner to raise a valid expectation that the entity will carry out the restructuring.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.61.1 – Is an announcement of an intention sufficient to recognise a restructuring provision?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.61.2 – Do individual employees have to be notified to recognise a restructuring provision?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.62 A management or board decision to restructure taken before the balance sheet date does not, in itself, give rise to a constructive obligation.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.62.1 – What are the implications of a management announcement of restructuring after the balance sheet date?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.63 A board decision and a formal plan might be all that is necessary to give rise to an obligation in some territories. This might also occur, for example, where the board includes worker representatives and management representatives.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.63.1 – What are the circumstances in which board approval crystallises the obligation?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.64 Many entity re-organisations take a number of years to complete. Some or all of the re-organisation might not be an obligation at the first year end following a board decision if the entity is realistically able to change its plans. It is unlikely that the plan will raise a sufficiently valid expectation on the part of others that the entity is committed to restructuring in these circumstances.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.64.1 – Does a restructuring that takes a long time to implement create a constructive obligation?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.65 An obligation to sell exists only when there is a binding sale agreement evidencing a commitment to sell part of the business. An entity has an obligation for restructuring related to the sale only when it has found a purchaser and signed an unconditional contract. The unconditional sale agreement must be signed before the year end for an obligation to arise at the year end.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.66 It might be necessary to consider the carrying value of the cash-generating unit to which the operations relate in the period between the board decision and the unconditional contract, particularly if management expects a loss on disposal. Impairment reviews are considered in more detail in chapter 24 para 9.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.67 The sale of an operation might be a small part of a larger restructuring, in which case a constructive obligation might arise for other aspects of the restructuring plan before a formal sale agreement has been reached.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.68 A restructuring provision should include only the direct expenditures arising from the restructuring, which are those that are both:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - necessarily entailed by the restructuring; and

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - not associated with the ongoing activities of the entity.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.69 Retraining or relocating continuing staff, marketing, or investment in new systems and distribution networks should not be included in a restructuring provision. This is because these costs relate to the future conduct of the business; they do not represent an obligation arising from a past event.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.69.1 – What are the costs generally included in, and those generally excluded from, a restructuring provision?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.70 Employee termination benefits are often lump-sum payments, but can also include enhancement of pensions and salary until the end of a specified period if the employee renders no further service that provides economic benefits to the entity. Employee termination benefits are dealt with by IAS 19 and considered in detail in chapter 12 para 4.

text: Practical application (paras 16.71 - 16.85)

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.71 An onerous contract is a contract under which the unavoidable costs of meeting the obligations under the contract exceed the economic benefits expected to be received under it. The present obligation under an onerous contract is recognised and measured as a provision.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.71.1 – How should the term ‘economic benefits expected to be received’ be understood?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.72 ‘Unavoidable costs’ under a contract are defined as being the least net cost of exiting the contract. This will be the lower of the cost to exit or breach the contract and the cost of fulfilling it.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.72.1 – Is it necessary to include overheads to determine whether a contract is onerous and to measure any resulting provision?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.73 An entity should recognise any impairment that has occurred on assets ‘dedicated to that contract’ before an onerous contract provision is recognised.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.73.1 – What are assets dedicated to a contract?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.74 IAS 37 does not apply to executory contracts unless those contracts are onerous (for example, a long-term purchase contract that has a higher unit cost than unit sales price).

text: Waste electrical and electronic equipment

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.75 The European Union’s Directive on Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (2002/96/EC) (the ‘WEEE Directive’) regulates the collection, treatment, recovery and environmentally sound disposal of electronic and electrical equipment waste. The IFRS IC issued an interpretation, IFRIC 6, providing guidance on the obligating event in certain circumstances under the WEEE Directive.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.76 IFRIC 6 provides guidance on the recognition, in the financial statements of producers, of liabilities for waste management of WEEE in respect of sales of historical household equipment.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.77 A public authority could impose a levy on entities based on measures such as gross revenues for a specified period or on assets or liabilities at a specified date. IFRIC 21 addresses the accounting for a liability to pay a levy recognised in accordance with IAS 37 and the liability to pay a levy whose timing and/or amount is certain. It sets out guidance for recognising an obligation to pay a levy that is not within the scope of other standards (such as income taxes), and it excludes fines or penalties for breaches of the legislation, and payments in exchange for an asset or service. App

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The following transactions are likely to be within the scope of IFRIC 21:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - non-refundable import duties;

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

text: When an entity issues a financial guarantee contract, is it within the scope of IAS 37?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: No, such a financial guarantee contract is outside the scope of IAS 37.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A financial guarantee contract is defined as: “...a contract that requires the issuer to make specified payments to reimburse the holder for a loss it incurs because a specified debtor fails to make payment when due in accordance with the original or modified terms of a debt instrument”. [IFRS 9 App A].

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: This definition typically applies to financial guarantees given by or to financial institutions, but could also apply to contractual guarantees given by parent entities to their subsidiaries and other intra-group guarantees and are within the scope of IFRS 9. Financial guarantee contracts are dealt with in chapter 42 para 88. The definition does not apply to guarantees that are not contractual; these are dealt with under the provision recognition and measurement criteria under IAS 37.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An exception to the IFRS 9 rules is where an issuer has previously asserted explicitly that it regards a financial guarantee contract as an insurance contract and has used accounting applicable to insurance contracts. In that case, the issuer can elect to apply either IFRS 9 or IFRS 4 to such financial guarantee contracts. The issuer can make that election on a contract-by-contract basis, but the election for each contract is irrevocable. [IFRS 9 para 2.1(e)].

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Environmental damage has occurred before period end, but there is no current law that requires clean-up, and the entity has not taken any action that creates a constructive obligation. However, a new law requiring the entity to rectify the damage will be passed shortly after the period end. The new legislation will create a present obligation that results from a past event (because the contamination has already taken place). Does any provision need to be made at the balance sheet date?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Management should determine whether it is virtually certain, at the balance sheet date, that the new law will be enacted as drafted. There is an obligating event and a present obligation if the legislation is virtually certain to be enacted. However, there is no obligation where enactment is not virtually certain because, although the potentially obligating event has taken place (that is, the contamination of the land), there is no obligation that can be enforced by law.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Some constructive obligations will be obvious – for example, some retailers have a policy of giving cash refunds to dissatisfied customers, whether or not the goods that they bought are faulty. Such a policy might be over and above any legal obligation, but a constructive obligation arises from the retailer’s established or published practice. It might be less clear whether there is an obligation for ad hoc refunds, and judgement is required.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

In these cases, a past event gives rise to a present obligation if, taking account of all available evidence, it is more likely than not that a present obligation exists at the balance sheet date. Management therefore considers all the available evidence, including evidence obtained

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Does provision need to be made for costs arising from future operation?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity might be required to operate in a particular way or to take specific actions in the future, but these do not create a legal or constructive obligation if they can be avoided.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: For example, an airline might be required, by local legislation, to undertake major engine overhauls on all of its aircraft at regular intervals. The airline cannot renew its licence and continue to fly each aircraft without completing the overhaul. There is no present obligation, because no obligating event arises before the overhaul is carried out. The airline can avoid the cost of the overhaul by, for example, selling the aircraft or otherwise discontinuing its use.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Accounting for overhaul costs in connection with owned assets is dealt with in IAS 16 (see chapter 22 para 62). A provision is not recognised, but the costs of each overhaul are capitalised and depreciated over the period to the next overhaul. [IAS 37 App C Example 11B]. (See EX 16.85.4.)

Management should also disclose the litigation as a contingent liability, unless the possibility of an outflow of economic benefits is remote. At one extreme, where the possibility of an outflow of economic benefits to settle the obligation is remote, no disclosure is required. chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: At one extreme, where an entity begins to pursue a claim through the legal process, the probability of an inflow might be low. The inflow of economic benefits is not probable, and a contingent asset is not required to be disclosed.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The claim might subsequently become probable of success before the judgment is made. It would be rare for the outcome of the case to be virtually certain before the judgment is made. The asset is therefore not recognised, but a contingent asset is disclosed.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: At the other extreme, where the inflow is virtually certain because the entity has received an award following a favourable judgment in court and the definitive conclusion of the case, the asset is no longer contingent and is recognised along with a gain.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Where a court judgment is subject to appeal, the entity will need to consider the specifics of the judgment, the applicable laws and appeal process to determine if the inflow is virtually certain:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - An appeal might indicate that the judgment is not definitive, and therefore a contingent asset continues to exist (for example, an award that is not legally enforceable as a result of an appeals process might indicate that the judgment is not definitive).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The appeal might also be a separate legal process, in which case management would need to assess whether the inflow is virtually certain.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

However, the entity will also need to assess the likelihood of a successful appeal. If it is more likely than not that an appeal will be successful, a provision should be established for the amount expected to be repaid.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

When the entity takes into account all available evidence, it is more likely than not that the dispute will be resolved in the entity’s favour. Given the evidence, the entity applies IAS 37 and discloses a contingent liability, without recognising a liability. To avoid possible penalties, the entity has also deposited the disputed amount with the tax authority. When the dispute is resolved, the tax authority will be required to either refund the tax deposit to the e

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: In January 2019, the IFRS IC issued an agenda decision which noted that such a deposit to the tax authority gives the entity a right to obtain future economic benefits, either by receiving a cash refund or by using the payment to settle the tax liability. Therefore the right is not a contingent asset as defined by IAS 37, because it is an asset, and not a possible asset, of the entity. The nature of the tax deposit (whether voluntary or required) does not affect the entity’s right and therefore does not affect the conclusion that there is an asset.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: As part of the IFRS IC agenda decision, the Committee noted that no standard specifically applies to the asset. As a consequence, an entity would need to apply IAS 8 and use judgement in developing and applying an accounting policy for the asset. The agenda decision observes that the accounting for the tax deposit could be similar or related to that for monetary assets. If this is the case, the entity would need to refer to requirements relating to monetary assets.
