33.14 Contracts to sell biological assets are accounted for either under IFRS 9 or as executory contracts. Contracts fall within the scope of IFRS 9 if they meet the definition of a derivative or if they can be net settled and are not expected to result in physical delivery of goods to meet the entity's own purchase, sale or usage requirements.
[IFRS 9 para 2.5]. [IFRS 9 para 2.6].
EX 33.14.1 – Contract within the scope of IFRS 9 EX 33.14.2 – Contract outside the scope of IFRS 9 EX 33.14.3 – Existence of an onerous contract

33.15 Common activities in the agricultural sector include the use of grower contracts or outsourcing contracts whereby the cultivation of biological assets are outsourced to farmers. IAS 41 does not deal specifically with grower contracts or outsourcing contracts. Consideration should be given to the requirements of:
- IFRS 10, to establish whether the farming operation should be consolidated by someone other than the farmer; see chapter 26 para 58;
- IFRS 16, to assess whether the outsourcing contract contains a lease to which IFRS 16 applies; see chapter 15 para 5; and

- IFRS 15, to establish whether a sale can be recognised on transfer of the biological assets to the grower or farmer, for example the sale of seeds and related products with an obligation to repurchase the harvested produce; for revenue recognition criteria, see chapter 11 para 153 and, for agent-principal assessment, see chapter 11 para 264.
33.16 Biological assets, including produce growing on a bearer plant and agricultural produce, should be recognised when:
- an entity controls the asset as a result of past events;
- it is probable that future economic benefits associated with the asset will flow to the entity; and
- the fair value or cost of the asset can be measured reliably
EX 33.16.1 – Point of recognition for offspring of biological assets FAQ 33.16.2 – When is the point of recognition of bearer biological produce?

33.17 Biological assets, including produce growing on a bearer plant, should be measured, both at initial recognition and at each subsequent reporting date, at fair value less costs to sell, except where fair value cannot be reliably measured. The fair value model accrues the additional value related to the biological asset as biological transformation takes place, rather than at the time of harvest.
FAQ 33.17.1 – How is the fair value of bearer produce ascertained? FAQ 33.17.2 – Do you include tax cash flows in the fair value model?
33.18 At the point of harvest, agricultural produce should be measured at fair value less costs to sell. This amount will then represent cost for the purposes of IAS 2 or another applicable standard.
33.19 Costs to sell are the incremental costs incurred in selling the asset, and they exclude finance costs and income tax expense.
FAQ 33.19.1 – What are costs to sell?

33.20 Fair value, in the context of IAS 41, has the same meaning as in IFRS 13 – that is, “the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date”. [IAS 41 para 8]. Guidance that is specific to the fair value measurement of biological assets and agricultural produce is contained in chapter 5 para 137.
33.21 Gains or losses that arise on measuring biological assets or agricultural produce at fair value less costs to sell are recognised in the income statement in the period in which they arise.
[IAS 41 para 26]. [IAS 41 para 28].
EX 33.21.1 – Recognition of valuation gains and losses FAQ 33.21.2 – How do you account for subsequent expenditure? FAQ 33.21.3 – How do emission trading schemes affect a forest's fair value?
Inability to measure fair value reliably

33.22 There is a presumption in IAS 41 that fair value can be measured reliably for a biological asset. This presumption can be rebutted only on initial recognition. Therefore, measurement at cost is permissible only when a reliable measure of fair value is unavailable at the point of initial recognition. An entity that has measured biological assets at fair value less costs to sell cannot revert to a cost model if a reliable measure of fair value ceases to be available.
EX 33.22.1 – Disruption of an active market after initial recognition

33.23 When fair value cannot be reliably established, biological assets should be measured at cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment losses, if any. [IAS 41 para 30]. Cost, depreciation and impairment losses should be determined in accordance with IAS 2, IAS 16 and IAS 36 as appropriate. [IAS 41 para 33]. Refer to chapter 25 para 18, chapter 22 para 79 and chapter 24 para 6 respectively.

33.24 Although a reliable measure of fair value might not be available at the point of initial recognition, it might subsequently become available (for example, if an active market opens). Biological assets are measured at fair value less costs to sell from the point at which the reliable measure of fair value becomes available.

33.25 Biological assets that are measured at fair value less costs to sell are excluded from the measurement provisions of IFRS 5. [IFRS 5 para 5]. However, where biological assets are classified as held for sale (or are included in a disposal group that is classified as held for sale), fair value is presumed to be reliably measurable. Biological assets previously measured at cost must be carried at fair value less costs to sell where the classification criteria of IFRS 5 are met. [IAS 41 para 30]. Refer to chapter 30 para 20.
33.26 IAS 41 presumes that the fair value of agricultural produce at the point of harvest will always be measurable. The cost approach is not permissible.

33.27 IAS 41 contains guidance on recognising, in profit and loss, grants receivable in respect of biological assets measured at fair value less costs to sell. These grants are outside IAS 20’s scope.

33.28 An unconditional grant is recognised as income when it becomes receivable. A conditional grant, on the other hand, should be recognised as income only when the conditions are satisfied. The threshold is thus higher than under IAS 20 which requires recognition when there is reasonable assurance that the conditions will be complied with.
[IAS 41 para 34]. [IAS 41 para 35].
EX 33.28.1 – Government grant subject to annual planting EX 33.28.2 – Government grant paid up-front EX 33.28.3 – Government grant subject to certification

33.29 Where biological assets are carried at cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment losses, the recognition in profit or loss of any government grants related to those assets is dealt with in accordance with IAS 20. Grants that do not relate specifically to biological assets (for example, a grant to build a new milking stable) fall within IAS 20’s scope, refer to chapter 17 para 2.

33.30 A number of jurisdictions have introduced emission trading schemes relating to agricultural activities, particularly forestry. There is no detailed guidance on accounting for emission trading schemes relating to agricultural activities.
Accounting for bearer plants
33.31 A bearer plant is defined as “a living plant that:
- is used in the production or supply of agricultural produce;
- is expected to bear produce for more than one period; and
- has a remote likelihood of being sold as agricultural produce, except for incidental scrap sales.”
33.32 The following are not bearer plants:
- Plants grown to be harvested and sold as produce, such as lumber.
- Annual crops which do not bear produce for more than one period, such as maize and wheat.

- Plants cultivated to produce agricultural produce, where the bearer plant will also be harvested and sold as agricultural produce (for example, trees that are cultivated both for their fruit and their lumber). If the sales from the wood are incidental scrap sales, the tree still meets the definition of a bearer plant.
33.33 Bearer plants that no longer bear produce are commonly cut down and sold as scrap at the end of their life. Such incidental scrap sales would not prevent the plant from being a bearer plant.
FAQ 33.33.1 – What are considered bearer plants?
33.34 Biological assets that meet the definition of ‘bearer plants’ are measured either at cost or revalued amounts, less accumulated depreciation and impairment losses under IAS 16.
[IAS 16 para 29]. [IAS 16 para 30]. [IAS 16 para 31].
FAQ 33.34.1 – How do you measure bearer plants?

33.35 Immature bearer plants are similar to an item of property, plant and equipment being constructed before its intended use and are measured at accumulated cost until the bearer plants are in the location and condition necessary for them to be capable of operating in the manner intended by management (that is, when bearer plants reach maturity).
FAQ 33.35.1 – How do you determine when bearer plants reach maturity?
Presentation - Balance sheet
33.36 The aggregate carrying value of biological assets within IAS 41’s scope should be presented separately on the face of the balance sheet.
FAQ 33.36.1 – How are bearer plants presented in the balance sheet? FAQ 33.36.2 – Are biological assets current or non-current?
Presentation - Income statement

33.37 Disclosure of the aggregate gain or loss arising during the current period on initial recognition of biological assets and agricultural produce, and from the change in fair value less costs to sell of biological assets, is required. [IAS 41 para 40]. There is no detailed guidance on where the aggregate gain or loss should be presented, so this disclosure can be made on the face of the income statement or in the notes to the financial statements. IAS 1 requires separate presentation on the face of the income statement where such presentation is relevant to an understanding of an entity’s
FAQ 33.37.1 – Where should gains or loss be presented in the income statement? FAQ 33.37.2 – Should gains or losses be disaggregated?

33.38 Agricultural activity is often exposed to climatic, disease and other natural risks, which could result in a material item of income or expense. [IAS 41 para 53]. The nature and amount of that item should be presented separately on the face of the income statement or in the notes, in accordance with IAS 1.

33.39 IAS 41 includes a broad range of disclosures relating to biological assets. Qualitative disclosures include a description of each group of its biological assets, the nature of the entity’s activities involving each group of biological assets and entity’s financial risk management strategies related to agricultural activity.
[IAS 41 para 41]. [IAS 41 para 46]. [IAS 41 para 49(c)].

33.40 Quantitative disclosures include non-financial measures or estimates of physical quantities of biological assets and a reconciliation of changes in the carrying amounts of biological assets, either in total or per group of biological assets if this gives more relevant information. This reconciliation should show, amongst other things, fair value gains or losses, purchases, sales and decreases due to harvest.
[IAS 41 para 46]. [IAS 41 para 50].
33.41 The carrying value of each group of biological assets does not need to be disclosed separately, but such disclosure is encouraged.

33.42 An entity is encouraged to disclose, by group or otherwise, the amount of the change in fair value less costs to sell included in profit or loss due to physical changes and the amount due to price changes. However, the standard acknowledges that this information is generally less useful where the production cycle is less than one year.

33.43 The standard requires specific disclosures where biological assets are measured at cost less any accumulated depreciation and impairment losses. The disclosures include, amongst other things, a description of the biological assets, an explanation of why fair value cannot be measured reliably, the depreciation method and useful lives used, and the gross carrying amount and accumulated depreciation at the beginning and end of the period.
[IAS 41 para 54]. [IAS 41 para 55].

33.44 If the fair value of biological assets previously measured using the cost model becomes reliably measurable during the period, there should be disclosure of a description of the biological assets, an explanation of why fair value has become reliably measurable, and the effect of the change.

33.45 Other disclosures include biological assets whose title is restricted or pledged as security, the amount of commitments for development or acquisitions, the entity's financial risk management strategies related to agricultural activity, and details about government grants related to agricultural activity, and details about government grants related to agricultural activity.
[IAS 41 para 49]. [IAS 41 para 57].

FAQ 33.4.1 – What are some examples of biological assets?
Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 5 Reference to standing text: 33.4
Biological assets include, amongst others, the following:
- Sheep, pigs, beef cattle, dairy cattle, poultry and fish.
- Plants for harvest (such as wheat, maize and vegetables).
- Trees, plants and bushes from which agricultural produce is harvested (such as fruit trees, tea bushes, vines, tobacco plants and sugar cane).
Bearer plants are accounted for under IAS 16. All other biological assets when they relate to agricultural activity are accounted for under IAS 41.
FAQ 33.4.2 – Are all living organisms biological assets?
Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 5 Reference to standing text: 33.4
Apart from obvious agricultural organisms, are other living organisms (such as cultures, cells, bacteria and viruses used in the pharmaceutical and biotechnology industries) biological assets?

Generally, such organisms would not be regarded as animals or plants under either the common or scientific usages of those words. The Collins English Dictionary defines a plant as "any living organism that typically synthesises its food from inorganic substances, lacks specialised sense organs, and has no powers of locomotion". Arguably, such a definition could encompass cultures, etc.

However, agricultural activity is the management by an entity of the biological transformation of biological assets for sale, into agricultural produce, or into additional biological assets. It is implicit throughout the standard that the kind of activities anticipated to be within its scope are ‘normal’, commonly understood agricultural activities. There is a further implication in IAS 41 that it applies to homogeneous (or, at least, highly comparable) assets or groups of assets. Many of the organisms used in the pharmaceutical and biotechnology industries are unique, or even patented, and th
Cultures, cells, bacteria, viruses and similar organisms used in the pharmaceutical and biotechnology industries are not considered to be biological assets that fall within IAS 41’s scope.

Also, the development of organisms for research purposes does not qualify as agricultural activity, as they are not being developed for sale or for transformation into agricultural produce or additional biological assets.

However, if a pharmaceutical or biotechnology company does undertake agricultural activity (for example, it grows plants from which particular drugs are developed or it develops cultures for use in dairy products), that activity will fall within IAS 41’s scope.

FAQ 33.9.1 – What are examples of agricultural activity?
Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 5 Reference to standing text: 33.9
Examples of agricultural activity include:
- Raising livestock, fish or poultry.
- Stud farms (for example, breeding horses or cattle).
- Cultivating vineyards, orchards or plantations.
FAQ 33.10.1 – What is biological transformation?
Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 5 Reference to standing text: 33.10

Biological transformation is a natural change in a biological asset. It includes growth of living animals or plants, reduction in output due to age or disease, and the production of new biological assets through a managed reproductive programme. The following are examples of biological transformation in the context of cattle:
- Calves are born (procreation).
- Calves grow into mature cattle (growth).
- Dairy cattle yield milk (production).
- Beef cattle are reared for meat (production).
All of these changes are observable, measurable and have a direct relationship to future economic benefits. Hence, biological transformation has an effect on the value of biological assets.
FAQ 33.12.1 – What are examples of management of biological transformation?
Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 6(b) Reference to standing text: 33.12
The following are examples of management of biological transformation:
- Providing shelter and food for cattle as well as maintaining their health.
- Growing fish in net cages for subsequent slaughter or sale.
- A managed breeding programme carried out to produce animals for sale.
EX 33.12.2 – Absence of management of biological transformation
Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 6(b) Reference to standing text: 33.12
A company manages a game park in South Africa. It has stocked the park with a range of wild animals indigenous to South Africa, as well as exotic animals from other continents.

The game park offers customers guided safari-type tours. The park is also used for incidental hunting as part of a culling programme. It is run with a view to profit, but this does not represent agricultural activity as there is, in this case, no management of the transformation of the biological assets; only control of the number of animals. Hence, the game park does not fall within IAS 41’s scope.

Similarly, zoos, aquariums and other parks where animals are held mainly for recreational purposes rather than agricultural activity would not be within IAS 41’s scope. The breeding that takes place is incidental to the main activity of providing a recreational facility. It is likely that such animals should be accounted for as tangible assets in the scope of IAS 16 (refer to chapter 22 para 8).
EX 33.13.1 – Classification of agricultural land ultimately destined for sale
Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 2 Reference to standing text: 33.13

An entity purchases land that it cultivates for agricultural purposes. The land will be used to grow various crops such as sugar cane, cotton and corn. The entity’s business plan is to continue with agricultural activity for a number of years, which will achieve two strategic objectives: first, to generate cash flows to fund investments; and, secondly, to demonstrate the viability of the land for agricultural purposes. At the end of the period, the land will be sold, in lots, to third parties.

While the land is being used for agricultural purposes, it should be classified as property, plant and equipment. A classification as non-current assets held for sale is only appropriate when the held for sale criteria in IFRS 5 are met. If a transfer to investment property is appropriate, the criteria governing transfers in IAS 40 should be complied with.
EX 33.13.2 – Classification of agricultural land where agricultural use is considered incidental
Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 2 Reference to standing text: 33.13

Entity A purchases vacant land that is to be used for the construction of a shopping mall. Permissions and administrative approvals, which need to be obtained prior to the commencement of construction, are expected to take up to 18 months to obtain. Entity A uses the land for agricultural activity for the period prior to obtaining the required approvals.

The agricultural use of the land can be seen as incidental to the principal objective of building a shopping mall. Classification of the land as investment property might be appropriate from initial recognition.
EX 33.13.3 – Logging road not expected to be used during more than one period
Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 2 Reference to standing text: 33.13
Entities in the forestry industry often construct roads to provide them with access to their forest holdings. These roads are typically referred to as ‘logging roads’.

An entity incurs costs in the construction of a temporary logging road that will be discarded once the forest area to which it provides access is cleared. Clearance of the land accessed by the road will take place over a three month period. The entity prepares financial statements annually, and the three months fall within one accounting period.

Any costs incurred in the construction of the logging road should be expensed as incurred, because the entity does not expect to use the logging road during more than one period as required by IAS 16.
EX 33.13.4 – Logging road expected to be used during more than one period
Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 2 Reference to standing text: 33.13
Entities in the forestry industry often construct roads to provide them with access to their forest holdings. These roads are typically referred to as ‘logging roads’.
An entity incurs costs in the construction of a logging road that is expected to provide future access to the entity’s forests. The road is expected to be used for a period of 10 years.

The costs incurred in the construction of the logging road should be capitalised as an asset under IAS 16 and should be depreciated over the estimated useful life of 10 years. This is because the road will be used during more than one period and will enable the entity to access the future economic benefits embodied in its forests.
EX 33.13.5 – Treatment of consumable biological assets after harvesting
Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 3 Reference to standing text: 33.13
Entity A raises cattle, slaughters them at its abattoirs and sells the carcasses to the local meat market.

The cattle are biological assets while they are living animals. When they are slaughtered, biological transformation ceases and the carcasses meet the definition of agricultural produce. Hence, entity A should account for the cattle in accordance with IAS 41. At the point of harvest, the fair value less costs to sell of the carcasses is taken as the cost of the inventory for the purpose of IAS 2, which applies thereafter.
[IAS 41 para 13]. [IAS 2 para 20].
EX 33.13.6 – Treatment of produce growing on bearer biological assets before and after harvesting
Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 3 Reference to standing text: 33.13
Entity B is involved in planting vines, harvesting grapes and producing wine.
While the grapes (the produce) grow on the vines, they are biological assets. When the entity harvests the grapes, their biological transformation ceases and they become agricultural produce.

Entity B should account for the grapes on the vine in accordance with IAS 41. At the point of harvest, the harvested grapes should be recognised at fair value less costs to sell and treated as inventory in accordance with IAS 2.

The exclusion of agricultural produce, after the point of harvest, from IAS 41’s scope means that the standard does not deal with activity such as the processing of grapes into wine or raisins. The Board considered including such activity within IAS 41’s scope, but concluded that it could not be differentiated with sufficient clarity from other manufacturing processes.
EX 33.14.1 – Contract within the scope of IFRS 9
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para 2.6(b) Reference to standing text: 33.14

Entity A grows cocoa beans. At the beginning of the cocoa growing season, it entered into a contract to sell 100 tonnes of cocoa beans at a fixed price. Entity A has a past practice of settling similar contracts net, because it has entered into the contract as part of its hedging strategy and has no intention of making a physical delivery of the cocoa beans to this counterparty.

Entity A has a contract to sell a non-financial item. The contract does not qualify for the ‘own use’ exemption in paragraph 2.5 of IFRS 9, because entity A has a past practice of settling similar contracts net. [IFRS 9 para 2.6(b)]. Hence, this and all similar contracts fall within the scope of IFRS 9 and are measured at fair value in accordance with that standard.
EX 33.14.2 – Contract outside the scope of IFRS 9
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para 2.6(b)Reference to standing text: 33.14
Entity B grows sugar beet. At the beginning of the growing season, it entered into a contract to sell its entire harvest to a local sugar processor at a fixed price.

The contract is intended to be settled by the physical delivery of sugar beet in accordance with entity B's normal sales practice. There is no history of entity B settling similar contracts net. Accordingly, this contract falls outside the scope of IFRS 9, so it is not measured at fair value. However, such a contract might meet the definition of an onerous contract under IAS 37 and would be measured in accordance with that standard (refer to chapter 16 para 71). The existence of a contract, whether onerous or not, does not affect the biological asset's fair value.

Entity X grows salmon commercially for sale. It has entered into a contract to deliver the salmon in the future at a fixed price. EX 33.16.1 – Point of recognition for offspring of biological assets
Reference to standard: IAS 41 paras 10, 11 Reference to standing text: 33.16

A pregnant ewe is a biological asset, as defined by IAS 41. Its offspring will also be biological assets, but they will not be recognised as separate assets until the recognition criteria in paragraph 10 are satisfied. Control of livestock may be evidenced by legal ownership and the branding or otherwise marking of the animal on acquisition, birth or weaning.

Control of new-born lambs would therefore be evidenced on birth and not only on weaning. Separate biological assets will be recognised when the lambing has proved successful and the offspring are healthy. FAQ 33.16.2 – When is the point of recognition of bearer biological produce?
Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 10 Reference to standing text: 33.16

IAS 41 provides no specific guidance for produce growing on bearer plants, other than the general recognition criteria. Bearer produce is therefore likely to be recognised immediately after the preceding harvest. The entity controls the bearer produce, because it controls the bearer plant. The previous harvest is evidence that there will be future economic benefit. The fair value can be measured reliably in most cases, but could be close to zero. We would not expect a material gain on initial recognition of bearer produce immediately after the last harvest.

Without any other evidence, fair value of the bearer produce would accrue evenly between harvests, taking into account major cash outflows related to periodic activities including fertilising, pruning or other value increasing activities. However, if evidence of specific growing cycles can be obtained, the fair value of the bearer produce could accrue exponentially.
For example, fresh fruit bunches growing on palm oil plants should be fair valued while they grow and not only once it is harvested.

Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 12 Reference to standing text: 33.17

A cash flow model is the most likely valuation method for bearer produce. The cash flow model should include all directly attributable cash inflows and outflows. The inflows will be the expected price in the market of the harvested produce. The outflows will be those incurred in growing the asset and getting it to market (for example, direct labour, fertiliser and transport to market). Contributory asset charges will be included for both the land and the bearer plant if they are owned by the entity. FAQ 33.19.1 – What are costs to sell?
Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 5 Reference to standing text: 33.19
Costs to sell are the incremental costs incurred in selling the asset and include:
- commissions to brokers and dealers;
- levies by regulatory agencies and commodity exchanges; and
- transfer taxes and duties.
The word ‘incremental’ in the definition of ‘costs to sell’ excludes costs that are included in the fair value measurement of a biological asset, such as transport costs.

The relevant costs to sell are those that would be incurred when selling the biological asset in its current state. If fair value is determined based on a cash flow model, costs to sell the final produce would also be included as a cash outflow. When measuring agricultural produce, there will only be one ‘costs to sell’.

Reference to standard: IAS 41 para B62 Reference to standing text: 33.21

IAS 41 does not explicitly prescribe how to account for subsequent expenditure related to biological assets. Such costs could include feeding, veterinary services, planting, weeding, irrigation, fertiliser, and harvesting and slaughtering costs. The Board did not prescribe the accounting for subsequent expenditure as it was seen as unnecessary with a fair value measurement approach. Costs incurred affect the fair value and, ordinarily, costs and fair value changes are both taken to profit or loss.

Many agricultural businesses follow a policy of capitalising some of these costs, particularly those relating to the development of immature plants or livestock up to the point at which they are productive. However, difficulties might be encountered in defining what should be capitalised and what should be expensed. Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 8 Reference to standing text: 33.21

A number of jurisdictions have introduced emission trading schemes relating to agricultural activities, particularly forestry. In the forestry industry, emission trading schemes typically involve the forester receiving credits from a government agency as carbon is sequestered by the growing trees. The forester is liable to surrender credits when the trees are harvested or otherwise lost (for example, through fire). EX 33.22.1 – Disruption of an active market after initial recognition
Reference to standard: IAS 41 para 31 Reference to standing text: 33.22

An entity is involved in raising cattle (biological assets) and recognises them at fair value less costs to sell. The fair value was based on a market-determined price at local cattle markets. A series of natural disasters has impacted cattle prices, making them highly volatile. The entity considers that the prices in these markets reflect abnormal conditions, and as such are unreliable, and wishes to adopt a cost-based approach for the current period.
Can the entity revert to the cost model for biological assets that were previously measured at fair value less costs to sell, when fair value cannot be measured reliably?

No, the entity cannot revert to the cost model. The entity has measured the biological assets at fair value less costs to sell from initial recognition. It should continue to apply the fair value model. The entity could provide additional disclosures around the price volatility, in order to give relevant information to users.
EX 33.28.1 – Government grant subject to annual planting
Reference to standard: IAS 41 paras 34, 35 Reference to standing text: 33.28

Entity A is in the business of growing and selling rice. The costs of rice plantation activities are high and the government has offered grants to growers as an incentive to remain in the industry and maintain the food supply. These grants will be awarded when the entity plants its crop. There are no other conditions attached to the grant. The grants are available for a three-year period.
The grant should be recognised in profit or loss when the conditions attaching to the government grant are met which would be at the point in each of the three years when the price crop is planted.
EX 33.28.2 – Government grant paid up-front
Reference to standard: IAS 41 paras 34, 35 Reference to standing text: 33.28

Entity B is in the business of growing and selling rice. The costs of rice plantation activities are high and the government has offered grants to growers as an incentive to remain in the industry and maintain the food supply. These grants will be awarded when the entity plants its crop, provided that the entity continues in the business. The purpose of the grant is to reduce the entity’s operating costs during each year. The grants are available for a three-year period.

The full grant is paid at the beginning of the three-year period, but is partially repayable if entity B ceases its rice business. The amount repayable depends on how much of the three-year period remains outstanding.

The grant should be recognised as income when it becomes unconditional. Hence, at the point in each year when an amount of the grant becomes non-refundable, that amount should be recognised as income. The balance is deferred to future periods.
EX 33.28.3 – Government grant subject to certification
Reference to standard: IAS 41 paras 34, 35 Reference to standing text: 33.28

For many years, entity C has grown fruit trees using traditional methods. From 20X0, the entity wishes to switch to organic methods. In order to assist with the costs of converting to organic farming, annual grant aid is available for three years, provided certain conditions are met. For example, the land must be registered as ‘in conversion to organic farming’ with an Organic Inspection Body (OIB) throughout the three-year period. A condition of the grant is that the registration must be certified by the OIB every year to signify that the company complies with the organic requirements.

The grant should be recognised as income when it becomes unconditional. Hence, at the point in each year when the land is certified by the OIB to be compliant and a portion of the grant becomes non-refundable, the relevant amount will be recognised as income.
Accounting for bearer plants
FAQ 33.33.1 – What are considered bearer plants?
Reference to standard: IAS 41 paras 5A, 5B Reference to standing text: 33.33

An entity farms walnut trees for the harvest of walnuts and, ultimately, for the valuable timber obtained at the end of the trees’ productive lives. Should the trees be accounted for under IAS 16 or IAS 41?

The last criterion in the definition of bearer plant is that the likelihood that the plant will be sold as agricultural produce must be remote, except for incidental scrap sales. If part of the objective of growing the trees is to harvest valuable lumber at the end of the trees’ productive lives, it seems unlikely that this criterion will be met. The walnut tree would be within the scope of IAS 41.
Can the bearer plant accounting be applied, by analogy, to livestock reared solely as breeding animals?
No, all biological assets that are animals remain within the scope of IAS 41.
Is there a choice to continue to account for bearer plants under IAS 41, rather than under IAS 16?
No. If the plant meets the definition of a bearer plant, it must be accounted for in accordance with the requirements of IAS 16.
FAQ 33.34.1 – How do you measure bearer plants?
Reference to standard: IAS 16 para 43 Reference to standing text: 33.34
What depreciation method should be applied to bearer plants?

The depreciation method chosen should reflect the pattern in which the future economic benefits of the plants are expected to be consumed by the entity. IAS 16 does not specify a particular method that must be used, so judgement will need to be applied.
Are bearer plants subject to impairment?
Bearer plants accounted for under IAS 16 will fall in the scope of IAS 36 for impairment testing. This applies irrespective of whether the cost or revaluation model is used.
Can borrowing costs be capitalised as part of cost?

Yes. Borrowing costs are capitalised until substantially all of the activities necessary to prepare the bearer biological asset for its intended use are complete. This is likely to be when the bearer plant reaches maturity and depreciation commences.
Can notional land rent be capitalised as part of the cost of bearer plants?

No. The notional land rent is not a cost under IAS 16 and therefore cannot be included in the cost of bearer plants. If the land is actually leased from a third party, the right-of-use asset depreciation can be capitalised as part of the cost of the bearer plant. Interest on the lease liability might also be eligible for capitalisation, refer to borrowing costs above.
Can bearer plants be measured under the revaluation method?
Yes. The choice of using the revaluation method in IAS 16 is available. It has to be used for all assets within the same class. Bearer plants could be such a class.
FAQ 33.35.1 – How do you determine when bearer plants reach maturity?
Reference to standard: IAS 16 para 22A Reference to standing text: 33.35

Maturity is often referred to as the condition that the bearer plant is in when it is capable of operating in the manner intended by management. There is no specific guidance on when a bearer plant reaches maturity. For example, a palm oil tree might start to grow produce after two years, but only reach its maximum yield after seven years. A grape vine might take many years to produce the right quantity and quality of fruit. Entities will need to determine their own reasonable accounting policy for determining when bearer plants reach maturity.
Presentation – Balance sheet
FAQ 33.36.1 – How are bearer plants presented in the balance sheet?
Reference to standard: IAS 1 para 54 Reference to standing text: 33.36
Should the same physical biological asset be treated as two different assets in the balance sheet?
Yes. IAS 41 makes a difference between:
- a bearer plant which is accounted for under IAS 16; and
- produce growing on bearer plants which is a biological asset under IAS 41.
There is also a different category of asset (that is, the agricultural produce which is the harvested produce of the entity’s biological assets).
The entities will have to recognise and measure the produce growing on the bearer plant and the bearer plant separately.
IAS 1 requires property, plant and equipment to be disclosed separately from biological assets within the scope of IAS 41.
FAQ 33.36.2 – Are biological assets current or non-current?
Reference to standard: IAS 1 para 66 Reference to standing text: 33.36

The presentation of biological assets as current or non-current will depend on their nature. Normally, consumable assets (such as wheat or broiler chickens) would be presented as current assets, whereas bearer assets (such as dairy cattle) would be presented as non-current assets. Consumable biological assets will typically be an integrated part of the operating cycle. However, where the period to maturity of consumable assets (such as forests) is long, presentation as non-current might be appropriate.
Presentation – Income statement
FAQ 33.37.1 – Where should gains or losses be presented in the income statement?
Reference to standard: IAS 1 para 85 Reference to standing text: 33.37
If an entity chooses to show gains and losses arising under IAS 41 on the face of the income statement, the question arises as to where they should be presented.

The standards are silent on this issue. While the final sale of agricultural produce typically falls within the scope of IFRS 15, gains and losses are not revenue under IFRS 15. Fair value gains are income in accordance with the Conceptual Framework. Fair value losses are expenses. Fair value gains can be shown as part of total income but separately from revenue.

The example following IAS 41 indicates that the change in fair value could be presented near the top of the income statement. Because the change in fair value can be either a positive or a negative amount, it is most appropriate to present the change in fair value after revenues and other income, but before expenses. The presentation should take into consideration the characteristics of the entity’s production.
The appendix to IAS 41 provides an illustrative example of how the presentation and disclosure requirements of the standard might be put into practice.
FAQ 33.37.2 – Should gains or losses be disaggregated?
Reference to standard: IAS 1 para 85 Reference to standing text: 33.37
The standard does not require or encourage disaggregating the gain or loss. Income under IAS 41 might be classified into:

- Gain or loss on initial recognition of biological assets. Initial losses on biological assets typically arise when a biological asset is purchased. The cost of the biological asset is often higher than the fair value less costs to sell, as the latter represents an exit price, and transaction expenses therefore create a loss. Initial gains on biological assets arise when new biological assets are generated (for example, when a calf or a piglet is born).

- Changes in fair value less costs to sell of biological assets. This represents the difference in value from period to period, normally on an aggregated basis. It is, therefore, sometimes difficult to distinguish from the initial gain due to procreation. The value typically increases due to growth, procreation and higher prices, but could decrease due to degeneration, sickness and lower prices.

- Gain or loss on harvest and initial recognition of agricultural produce. At the point of harvest, the agricultural produce is required to be measured at fair value less costs to sell. There is, therefore, a final fair value amount that must be recognised as income that reflects the last stage of the value creation of the biological process, up to the point when harvested produce is transferred to inventory. There could be further costs involved in preparing the inventory for market.

34 - Service concession arrangements (IFRIC 12)

Introduction and scope (paras 34.1- 34.23)
34.1 IFRIC 12’s objective is to establish general principles on recognising and measuring the obligations and related rights in public-to-private service concession arrangements.
What is a service concession?
34.2 A service concession typically involves a public sector entity (‘the grantor’) entering into a contract with a private sector entity (‘the operator’) and with the following features:
- The arrangement involves providing services that give the public access to major economic and social facilities. Such facilities typically involve the use of infrastructure.
- The operator provides services to construct and/or upgrade infrastructure and/or to operate and maintain the infrastructure for the period of the concession.
- The grantor pays the operator for its services, or grants it the right to charge users of the service during the period of the arrangement, or a combination of both.
- A contract governs the terms and conditions of the arrangement, including the service performance standards, how the price is determined, and penalties for service failures.
- The operator transfers the infrastructure to the grantor, usually in a specified condition, at the end of the arrangement.

34.3 Governments are generally responsible for the construction, operation and maintenance of infrastructure for public services, such as roads, railways, bridges, schools, hospitals, prisons, airports, water distribution and waste management systems, energy supply and telecommunication networks.

34.4 Some countries have developed private finance initiative (PFI) and public private partnership (PPP) arrangements, under which the public sector procures the provision of such public services from the private sector. These arrangements are generally referred to as ‘service concession arrangements’. The private sector designs, builds, finances and operates the infrastructure in order to provide the contracted services.

FAQ 34.4.1 – What types of private provision of public services are within the scope of IFRIC 12? FAQ 34.4.2 – Is a construction-only contract with a pre-determined margin within the scope of IFRIC 12? FAQ 34.4.3 – Is a construction and operations contract with a pre-determined margin within the scope of IFRIC 12? FAQ 34.4.4 – Are movable assets, such as buses and trains, excluded from the scope of IFRIC 12?
Public service obligation

34.5 A key feature of public-to-private service concession arrangements in the scope of IFRIC 12 is that the nature of the obligation undertaken by the operator is a public service. A public service is one where a government’s policy is for the service to be provided to the public, irrespective of who provides it.

FAQ 34.5.1 – What is a public service obligation? FAQ 34.5.2 – Does the public need to have access to the infrastructure? FAQ 34.5.3 – Does the operator need to provide the services to the public itself? FAQ 34.5.4 – Does the grantor need to be a public sector body, or to be controlled by one?
Decision tree for arrangements falling within IFRIC 12’s scope
34.6 IFRIC 12 provides a decision tree for determining whether a public-to-private service concession arrangement is within its scope.
[IFRIC 12 Information note 1].
Control of the infrastructure by the grantor

34.7 An operator accounts for a public-to-private service concession arrangement in accordance with IFRIC 12 where the grantor controls the infrastructure. The grantor controls the infrastructure where the following conditions are met:
- the grantor controls or regulates what services the operator must provide with the infrastructure, to whom it must provide them, and at what price; and
- the grantor controls – through ownership, beneficial entitlement or otherwise – any significant residual interest in the infrastructure at the end of the arrangement’s term.
EX 34.7.1 – Grantor has a non-controlling interest in the operator
Control or regulation of services

34.8 The grantor’s control or regulation of services need not be by contract (an agreement or a licence), and it could instead be through some other form of regulation. It includes situations where the grantor buys all of the output and those in which some or all of the output is purchased by other users. The operator considers the grantor and any of its related parties together when making this assessment. Where the grantor is a public sector entity, the operator regards the public sector as a whole, along with any regulators acting in the public interest, as being related to the grantor.
FAQ 34.8.1 – When could the government and a regulator together be considered as the grantor?

34.9 The term ‘price’ refers to the amount that the grantor pays to the operator for providing the public service, or the amount that the operator charges the general public for the services. The grantor does not need to have complete control of the price. It is sufficient if the grantor can regulate the price itself, by the contract, or through a regulator.

34.10 A government or regulator might set or regulate prices in various ways, ranging from fixed price arrangements to those based on a formula. A formula might be linked to performance that is within the operator’s control, or it might be linked to an inflation index which neither the grantor nor the operator controls. The grantor controls the price provided that the basis or the framework under which the prices are set is subject to control or regulation.

34.11 The operator considers the arrangement’s substance where the grantor controls or regulates the price through a capping mechanism. The operator ignores a price cap that will apply only in remote circumstances, because it has no substance. Similarly, the operator ignores other pricing mechanism features that are not substantive. The operator might have freedom to set its prices but, under the contract, it must pay any excess profit over an agreed minimum to the grantor. In this case, the operator’s return is capped, and so the grantor controls the price.
EX 34.11.1 – Control or regulation of pricing FAQ 34.11.2 – Price capping mechanism: does it have substance? EX 34.11.3 – Grantor’s formal approval of the price
Control of residual interest

34.12 The condition of control is satisfied where the grantor controls any significant residual interest in the infrastructure asset. Again, if the grantor is a public sector entity, the operator regards the public sector as a whole, including parties such as a regulator, as related to the grantor.
[IFRIC 12 para 5(b)]. [IFRIC 12 para AG2].
FAQ 34.8.1 – When could the government and a regulator together be considered as the grantor?
34.13 The grantor controls any significant residual interest where it restricts the operator’s ability to sell or pledge the infrastructure.

FAQ 34.13.1 – How might a grantor control any significant residual interest in the infrastructure? FAQ 34.13.2 – Are infrastructure assets in regulated industries ‘controlled’ within the meaning of IFRIC 12?
EX 34.13.3 – Control of the residual interest in some, but not all, of the infrastructure
34.14 The infrastructure’s residual interest is the operator’s estimate of current value of the asset as if it were already of the age and in the condition expected at the end of the arrangement.
FAQ 34.14.1 – Does the infrastructure asset have a significant residual interest?
EX 34.14.2 – Significant residual interest: discontinuance of the public service EX 34.14.3 – Significant residual interest: technical obsolescence and commercial viability

34.15 A ‘whole-of-life’ infrastructure asset is one where the operator uses the asset in the service concession arrangement for its entire useful life, and so it is likely to have no significant residual interest at the end of the concession period. In such cases, the operator disregards the condition in paragraph 5(b) of the IFRIC, and considers only the condition in paragraph 5(a) to determine whether the grantor controls the infrastructure.

34.16 The operator might have to replace part of an item of infrastructure asset that is used up in the service concession. For example, the operator might be required to resurface a toll road or the roof of a hospital building during the life of the agreement. The residual interest criterion is met in these arrangements for the whole of the infrastructure (referred to as a ‘holistic’ approach), including the part that is replaced, if the grantor controls any significant residual interest in the final replacement of that part.
FAQ 34.16.1 – How does the operator consider replacement components? (1) FAQ 34.16.2 – How does the operator consider replacement components? (2)
34.17 The grantor might regulate only part of the infrastructure. IFRIC 12 considers two such situations:

- Where the operator uses any infrastructure entirely for unregulated purposes, the asset is physically separable and can be operated independently, and it meets the definition of a cash-generating unit under IAS 36, the operator analyses it separately. An example would be a private wing in a public hospital.

- Where the operator has unregulated activities which are purely ancillary in nature (for example, a hospital shop) it disregards these when applying the control tests because these do not detract from the grantor’s control of the infrastructure.

34.18 The operator might, in substance, lease the separable infrastructure or the facility for providing the unregulated ancillary services from the grantor. If so, the operator accounts for the lease in accordance with IFRS 16.
Infrastructure assets within scope
34.19 IFRIC 12 applies to two types of infrastructure assets that the operator uses in delivering the service arrangement. These are:
- infrastructure that the operator constructs or acquires from a third party; and
- the grantor’s existing infrastructure to which it gives the operator access.
FAQ 34.19.1 – Does IFRIC 12 apply to assets that the operator leases from third parties?
Existing assets of the operator

34.20 The operator does not apply IFRIC 12 to its existing infrastructure assets which it recognised as property, plant and equipment and which it uses in the service concession arrangement. The operator continues to recognise such assets, unless they meet the conditions for derecognition in IAS 16.
EX 34.20.1 – Operator’s existing assets used in the arrangement
Inter-relationship of IFRIC 12 with IFRSs and IFRS 16

34.21 IFRIC 12 does not cover all public-to-private service concession arrangements. It includes a table, set out below, to help concession operators identify the relevant IFRS for service concession arrangements. IFRIC 12 applies to arrangements in the shaded area, where the application of IFRSs is most unclear. The table highlights the continuum of arrangements and it confirms that ‘bright lines’ do not exist between arrangements or between the accounting requirements.

34.22 Arrangements within the scope of IFRIC 12 might be very similar to arrangements that contain leases. If a service arrangement is within the scope of IFRIC 12, it is not within the scope of IFRS 16.
Private-to-private arrangements

34.23 An entity might apply the guidance in IFRIC 12 to private-to-private arrangements by analogy, through the accounting policy hierarchy set out IAS 8 where no standards or interpretations apply directly (see chapter 3 para 8). This might be appropriate where the arrangement meets similar requirements to those specified in IFRIC 12, that is:
- the arrangement meets the requirements for control by the grantor set out in paragraph 5 of IFRIC 12; and
- the arrangement embodies a public service obligation as described in paragraph 3 of IFRIC 12.

Accounting for service concession arrangements (paras 34.24 - 34.53)
34.24 The issues addressed in IFRIC 12 are:
- The treatment of the operator’s rights over the infrastructure.
- Recognition and measurement of consideration.
- Construction or upgrade services.
- Subsequent accounting treatment of a financial asset and an intangible asset.
- Items provided to the operator by the grantor.
Treatment of the operator’s rights over the infrastructure

34.25 The operator does not recognise infrastructure within the scope of IFRIC 12 as property, plant and equipment, because the contractual service arrangement does not convey to it the right to control the infrastructure. The operator has access to operate the infrastructure to provide the public service on the grantor’s behalf in accordance with the contract’s terms. This applies whether the infrastructure is constructed or acquired by the operator or is provided by the grantor for the purposes of the concession.

34.26 Control is different from management. If the grantor retains both the degree of control described in paragraph 5(a) of IFRIC 12 and any significant residual interest in the infrastructure, the operator is only managing the infrastructure on the grantor’s behalf – even though it might have wide managerial discretion.
Recognition of consideration given by the grantor to the operator

34.27 The operator recognises an asset for the consideration that it receives from the grantor in exchange for providing construction or upgrade services. The consideration received can take a variety of forms. The consideration given by the grantor to the operator might be rights to:

34.28 The operator determines the nature of the consideration given by the grantor by reference to the terms of the contract and, where relevant, contract law. The operator classifies both types of consideration as a contract asset during the construction or upgrade period, in accordance with IFRS 15. The operator also considers the substance of any payments that it makes to the grantor.
EX 34.28.1 – Consideration of amounts payable by the operator to the grantor
Operator recognises a financial asset

34.29 The operator recognises a financial asset to the extent that it has an unconditional contractual right to receive cash or another financial asset from, or at the direction of, the grantor for the construction services. This right arises where the grantor has little or no discretion to avoid payment, usually because the agreement is enforceable by law.
EX 34.29.1 – Operator’s unconditional right to receive cash for construction services
Specified or determinable amounts
34.30 Where the grantor agrees to pay the operator a specified or determinable amount, the operator has an unconditional right to receive cash, and so it recognises a financial asset.

EX 34.30.1 – Operator’s contractual right to receive specified or determinable payments from the grantor or from users EX 34.30.2 – Operator’s contractual right to receive specified or determinable payments from the grantor
Shortfall in user payments guaranteed by the grantor

34.31 The grantor might give the operator the right to charge users while guaranteeing to pay the operator any shortfall between the amounts received from users and a specified or determinable amount. The operator has an unconditional right to receive cash. Consequently, the operator recognises a financial asset for the full amount of the cash guaranteed by the grantor.
EX 34.31.1 – Users pay the operator, but any shortfall is guaranteed by the grantor
Operator’s cash flows are contingent on performance or availability
34.32 The operator recognises a financial asset, even where its right to receive cash is contingent on meeting specified quality or efficiency requirements.
FAQ 34.32.1 – What happens where the operator’s cash flows are contingent on performance of services or availability of the infrastructure asset?
Operator recognises an intangible asset

34.33 The operator recognises an intangible asset to the extent that it has a right to charge users of the public service. The operator’s right to charge users is not an unconditional right to receive cash, because the amounts are contingent on the extent to which the public uses the service.
EX 34.33.1 – Operator has a right to charge users of the services EX 34.33.2 – Operator’s revenue is conditional on usage EX 34.33.3 – Operator receives a substantially fixed return
Operator recognises both a financial asset and an intangible asset

34.34 The operator accounts separately for each component of the consideration where it receives payment for the construction services partly by a financial asset and partly by an intangible asset. The operator recognises both components initially in accordance with IFRS 15.
EX 34.34.1 – Operator recognises both a financial asset and an intangible asset FAQ 34.34.2 – How does the nature of the operator’s rights affects the type of asset recognised?
Recognition and measurement of revenue
34.35 The operator is regarded as a service provider, delivering construction or upgrade services during the construction phase and operational services during the operation phase.
34.36 The operator recognises, and measures, revenue for the services that it performs, in accordance with IFRS 15, by:
- identifying the separate performance obligations in the arrangement;
- determining the total transaction price for the arrangement;
- allocating the total transaction price to the separate performance obligations on the basis of their relative stand-alone selling prices; and
- recognising revenue for each performance obligation over time, or at a point in time, as appropriate.

FAQ 34.36.1 – How is the transaction price allocated between construction and operational services when applying IFRS 15? (1) FAQ 34.36.2 – How is the transaction price allocated between construction and operational services when applying IFRS 15? (2)
Recognition and measurement of construction or upgrade revenue
34.37 The operator accounts for construction or upgrade services in accordance with IFRS 15.

FAQ 34.37.1 – How do you determine whether the operator is an agent or principal for construction services when applying IFRS 15? FAQ 34.37.2 – How do you recognise and measure revenue for construction services when applying IFRS 15? FAQ 34.37.3 – How do you recognise revenue where the operator receives an intangible asset for construction services?

FAQ 34.37.4 – How do you recognise revenue when applying IFRS 15 and the operator receives an intangible asset for construction services? FAQ 34.37.5 – Why does the amount of revenue that the operator recognises differ between the financial asset and intangible asset models?
FAQ 34.37.6 – What is the difference in revenue recognition between the financial asset and intangible asset models?
Recognition and measurement of operations revenue
34.38 The operator accounts for operation services in accordance with IFRS 15.

FAQ 34.38.1 – How is contract revenue allocated during the operation phase when applying IFRS 15? EX 34.38.2 – Recognition of operations revenue from users as services are delivered, when applying IFRS 15 EX 34.38.3 – Recognition of operations revenue from the grantor as services are delivered, when applying IFRS 15
Accounting for construction asset
34.39 The operator accounts for the financial asset in accordance with the financial instruments standards – IAS 32, IFRS 7 and IFRS 9.
34.40 The operator classifies the financial asset into the appropriate category under IFRS 9:
- fair value through other comprehensive income; or
- fair value through profit or loss.
FAQ 34.40.1 – How is the recognition, initial and subsequent measurement of the financial asset when applying IFRS 9 in a service concession arrangement?
34.41 The operator accounts for the intangible asset in accordance with IAS 38.
34.42 The operator initially measures the intangible asset at cost.
34.43 The operator subsequently measures the intangible asset over its useful economic life at cost less accumulated amortisation and impairment losses.

FAQ 34.43.1 – What is the subsequent measurement of the intangible asset? FAQ 34.43.2 – What is the useful life of the intangible asset? FAQ 34.43.3 – When does the operator start to amortise the intangible asset? FAQ 34.43.4 – When should an entity start amortisation in an arrangement which contains both a financial asset and an intangible asset? FAQ 34.43.5 – How should the intangible asset be amortised?
Arrangements which contain both a financial and an intangible asset

34.44 The operator might recover part of its investment in the infrastructure asset through payment from the grantor and the remainder through a right to charge service users. The operator accounts separately for the financial asset and the intangible asset.
34.45 This accounting can be complex. IFRIC 12 includes an illustrative example.
[IFRIC 12 Illustrative example 3].
Arrangement does not give rise to construction or upgrade services

34.46 Service concession arrangements need not involve the operator undertaking construction or upgrade activities. The grantor can give the operator access to its existing assets, for the purpose of the public service arrangement, that require little or no upgrade. The grantor might pay the operator directly, or it might give the operator the right to charge users based on usage, but pricing is regulated. Such arrangements are within the scope of IFRIC 12, but the interpretation does not provide specific guidance.

FAQ 34.46.1 – How should an entity account for an arrangement that does not give rise to construction or upgrade services but the grantor pays the operator a fixed sum? FAQ 34.46.2 – How should an entity account for an arrangement that does not give rise to construction or upgrade services but the grantor gives the operator the right to charge users? FAQ 34.46.3 – How should an entity account for an arrangement that does not give rise to construction or upgrade services but the operator pays the grantor for the right to charge users? FAQ 34.46.4 – How should an entity account for an arrangemen
Borrowing costs incurred by the operator

34.47 The operator capitalises borrowing costs under IAS 23 where it has a contractual right to receive an intangible asset. Borrowing costs are expensed when incurred under IAS 23 where the operator has a right to a financial asset (see chapter 22 para 42).

34.48 The intangible asset in respect of the operator’s right to charge users of the public service meets the definition of a qualifying asset, because generally the licence would not be ready for use until the infrastructure was constructed or upgraded. A financial asset does not meet the definition of a qualifying asset.
EX 34.48.1 – Borrowing costs
Obligations for infrastructure maintenance during the operation phase

34.49 The operator might have obligations under the contract to replace or refurbish infrastructure assets during the operation phase. The operator might have to maintain the infrastructure to a specified level of service at all times, or it might have to restore the infrastructure to a specified condition before it is handed back to the grantor. An operator recognises and measures such contractual obligations, except for any upgrade element, in accordance with IAS 37 (see chapter 16 para 10).

FAQ 34.49.1 – How does an operator account for obligations related to infrastructure maintenance during the operation phase when applying IFRS 15? FAQ 34.49.2 – Why is IAS 37 relevant for major refurbishments and renewals?
Enhancement or new infrastructure (upgrade)

34.50 The operator does not recognise a provision in advance of the upgrade where it has a contractual obligation to enhance or upgrade existing infrastructure or to construct new infrastructure during the operation phase. Instead, the operator accounts for upgrade services in accordance IFRS 15.
FAQ 34.50.1 – Is IFRS 15 applicable to the construction of enhancements or new infrastructure (upgrade)?
Items provided to the operator by the grantor

34.51 The grantor might contribute infrastructure assets which are required for the operator to carry out its obligations under the contract. These assets remain the property of the grantor, and the operator does not recognise them as assets.

34.52 The grantor might provide other items to the operator for it to keep or do with as it pleases, and which form part of the consideration payable by the grantor for the services rendered. These items are not government grants under IAS 20. The operator includes the fair value of such non-cash consideration as part of the transaction price in accordance with IFRS 15.

EX34.52.1 – Items provided by the grantor: operator is applying IFRS 15 and recognises a financial asset EX 34.52.2 – Items provided by the grantor: operator is applying IFRS 15 and recognises an intangible asset
34.53 IFRIC 12 does not specify the accounting by grantors.

Presentation and disclosure (paras 34.54 - 34.59)

34.54 IFRIC 12 does not require any specific disclosures. SIC 29 contains disclosure requirements relating to service concession arrangements for both operators and grantors. An entity might need to include disclosures required by other standards applicable to certain aspects of service concession arrangements, such as IAS 16, IFRS 16 and IAS 38.
34.55 IFRS 7 also applies where an operator recognises a financial asset.
Transitional arrangements on first-time adoption of IFRS
34.56 A first-time adopter of IFRS can use the transitional relief in IFRIC 12.
34.57 Where management considers that applying the requirements retrospectively in full is impracticable, the operator instead:
- recognises financial assets and intangible assets that existed at the start of the earliest period presented;
- uses the previous carrying amounts of those financial and intangible assets (however they were previously classified) as their carrying amounts as at that date; and

- tests financial and intangible assets recognised at that date for impairment, unless this is not practicable, in which case it tests the amounts for impairment as at the start of the current period.

FAQ 34.57.1 – What should an operator consider where retrospective application is impracticable on first-time adoption of IFRS for the financial asset model? FAQ 34.57.2 – How does an operator apply the transitional relief for reclassifying to an intangible asset? FAQ 34.57.3 – How does an operator apply the transitional relief when reclassifying to both an intangible asset and a financial asset? FAQ 34.57.4 – Transitional relief: can the ‘fair value as deemed cost’ exemption be applied to intangible assets associated with concession agreements on first-time adoption of IFRS?
Presentation of cash flows
34.58 An entity presents the service concession cash flows in a manner which is most appropriate to its business.
FAQ 34.58.1 – What is the interaction between IFRIC 12 and IAS 7 for the presentation of cash flows related to construction activity?
