chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: FAQ 40.79.1 – How should an entity account for a prepayment of a commodity?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 39 paras 5, 6; IFRS 9 paras 9.2.4–9.2.6 Reference to standing text: 40.79

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Company A has made a prepayment to a commodity supplier, company B. The prepayment will be settled by company B delivering the physical commodity to company A. The physical commodity is highly liquid and thus readily convertible to cash.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: How should the prepayment be accounted for by company A?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: The accounting by company A depends on the facts and circumstances. The prepayment could be:

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: - outside the scope of IFRS 9 if it meets the ‘own use’ criteria in paragraph 9.2.4 of IFRS 9;

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: - measured at FVTPL if in a trading business model; or

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: - a loan measured at amortised cost, FVOCI or FVTPL, depending on company A’s business model and whether the prepayment meets the SPPI criterion.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: An ‘own use’ contract not within the scope of IFRS 9

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: If company A entered into the contract and continues to hold it for the purpose of securing physical delivery of the commodity to meet its expected sale, purchase or usage requirements, the prepayment meets the ‘own use’ criteria in paragraph 9.2.4 of IFRS 9. In this case, the prepayment is not within the scope of IFRS 9 and is accounted for as a non-financial asset.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Note that company A should consider whether it needs to recognise interest revenue from the prepayment if the contract contains a financing component. This results from the IFRIC agenda decision from November 2015 on long-term prepayments in inventory supply contracts.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Held in a trading business model, so at FVTPL

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: If the prepayment is held in a trading business model, its purpose is to ensure the physical delivery of the commodity so that company A can sell it within a short period after delivery for the purpose of generating a profit from short-term fluctuations in price. Furthermore, the commodity is readily convertible to cash. Accordingly, the contract fails the ‘own use’ criteria in paragraph 9.2.4 of IFRS 9 and is within the scope of IFRS 9.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Furthermore, under paragraphs B4.1.5 to B4.1.6 of IFRS 9, a trading business model is an ‘other’ business model (that is, neither ‘held to collect’ nor ‘held to collect and sell’). Hence the prepayment is measured at FVTPL.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: A loan at amortised cost, FVOCI or FVTPL

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: If the prepayment is held in a lending business model, the prepayment will not be held for the purpose of delivery of the commodity in accordance with company A’s purchase, sale or usage requirements. Furthermore, the commodity is readily convertible to cash. Accordingly, the contract fails the ‘own use’ criteria in paragraph 9.2.4 of IFRS 9 and is within the scope of IFRS 9.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: The accounting by company A could be amortised cost, FVOCI or FVTPL, depending on:

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: - the business model in which the prepayment is held (see chapter 42 paras 42.20–42.32); and

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: - whether it meets the SPPI criterion. In assessing whether the prepayment meets the SPPI criterion, similar considerations apply as are set out in FAQ 42.35.2 for assets that are settled in shares. If the prepayment will be settled by the delivery of a fixed volume of the commodity, it will expose company A to commodity risk, which is inconsistent with the definition of SPPI. In this case, the prepayment will not meet the SPPI criterion and will be measured at FVTPL. If, on the other hand, the prepayment will be settled by the delivery of a variable volume of the commodity, further analysis i

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: If the prepayment is accounted for at amortised cost or FVOCI, IFRS 9’s impairment requirements will apply.

text: Commodity price and foreign exchange price movements between the date of order and settlement might expose an entity to risks when purchasing inventories. Commodity price risk arises where an entity enters into a contract to purchase a commodity which varies. Foreign exchange risk arises where the entity pays for the inventory in a foreign currency.

text: To mitigate or hedge commodity price risk, the entity could enter into a forward contract to buy the commodity at a fixed price at a future date. Would the contract meet the ‘own use’ exception, or be treated as a derivative?

text: If the contract is entered into and continues to be held for the purpose of the delivery of the commodity in accordance with the entity’s expected purchase or usage requirements, the entity does not recognise the forward contract as a derivative. If the entity has a practice of settling net (either with the counterparty or by entering into offsetting contracts or by taking delivery of the commodity and selling it within a short period after delivery for the purpose of generating a profit from short-term fluctuations in price or dealer’s margin), the forward contract will have to be recognised

For example, a commodity futures contract could be bought and sold readily for cash, because it is listed for trading on an exchange and might change hands many times. However, the parties buying and selling the contract are, in effect, trading the underlying commodity. text: FAQ 40.84.2 – What does ‘own-use’ mean in practice?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard:IAS 32 paras 8–10; IFRS 7 para 5; IAS 39 para 5; IFRS 9 para 2.4 Reference to standing text: 40.84

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: To qualify for the exception, a contract’s terms must be consistent with the terms of an entity’s normal purchases or sales (the quantity specified in the contract must be expected to be used or sold by the entity over a reasonable period in the normal course of business). Other factors to consider in determining whether or not the contract qualifies for the exception include the locations to which delivery of the items will be made, the period of time between entering into the contract and delivery, and the entity’s prior practices with regard to such contracts.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: FAQ 40.84.3 – Is the ‘own use’ exemption met in a contract to sell copper where an entity has no history of net settlement?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 32 paras 8–10; IFRS 7 para 5; IAS 39 para 5; IFRS 9 para 2.4 Reference to standing text: 40.84

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Entity A owns a copper mine and enters into a fixed-price forward contract to sell one million kilograms of copper in accordance with a counterparty’s expected usage requirements. The contract permits physical delivery of the copper at the end of the 12 months, or payment of a net settlement in cash based on the change in the fair value of copper during the 12-month period. The counterparty cannot choose to refuse delivery.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Entity A intends to settle the contract by delivering the copper, has no history of settling similar contracts net in cash, and has sufficient production capacity to provide the required quantity of copper to meet the delivery requirements.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: From entity A’s perspective, is this contract an ‘own use’ contract?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: The ‘own use’ criteria are likely to be met. There is an embedded derivative (being the net settlement provision based on the change in the fair value of copper), but it does not require separation. Although the contract allows net settlement, it will still qualify as ‘own use’ as long as it has been entered into and continues to be held for the expected counterparties’ sales/usage requirements.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: FAQ 40.84.4 – Is the ‘own use’ exemption met in a contract to purchase oil where an entity has an established pattern of settling net before delivery?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 32 paras 8–10; IFRS 7 para 5; IAS 39 para 5; IFRS 9 para 2.4 Reference to standing text: 40.84

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: An entity enters into a forward contract to purchase oil. The entity has an established pattern of settling such contracts net, before delivery, by contracting with a third party. The entity settles any market value difference for the contract price directly with the third party. Is the ‘own use’ exemption met?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: No. The forward contract to purchase oil is recognised as a derivative. IAS 39/IFRS 9 applies to a contract to purchase a non-financial asset if the contract meets the definition of a derivative and it does not qualify for the exemption for delivery in accordance with the entity’s expected purchase or usage requirements. The entity does not expect to take delivery. A pattern of entering into offsetting contracts that effectively accomplishes settlement on a net basis means that the transaction does not qualify for the exemption for delivery in accordance with the entity’s expected purchase or

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: FAQ 40.84.5 – What factors should be considered when determining whether a contract meets the ‘own use’ exemption? Do both counterparties have to reach the same conclusion?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 39 para IG A1; IFRS 9 para A1 Reference to standing text: 40.84

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Entity XYZ enters into a fixed-price forward contract to purchase one million kilograms of copper in accordance with its expected usage requirements. The contract permits entity XYZ to take physical delivery of the copper at the end of 12 months, or to pay or receive a net settlement in cash based on the change in fair value of copper. Does this contract meet the ‘own use’ exemption for entity XYZ and its counterparty?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: This contract needs to be evaluated to determine whether it falls within the scope of the financial instruments standards. The contract is a derivative instrument, because there is no initial net investment, the contract is based on the price of copper, and it is to be settled at a future date. However, if entity XYZ intends to settle the contract by taking delivery, and has no history (for similar contracts) of settling net in cash or of taking delivery of the copper and selling it within a short period after delivery for the purpose of generating a profit from short-term fluctuations in pric

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: It is possible for entity XYZ and the counterparty to reach different conclusions about whether the contract falls within IAS 39/IFRS 9’s scope. For example, a ‘normal’ sale by the counterparty might not be a ‘normal’ purchase by entity XYZ, that would treat the contract as a derivative. This is one of the few areas of IAS 39/IFRS 9 where a contract might be treated as a derivative by one party, but not be treated as a derivative by the other party.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: FAQ 40.85.1 – How do you determine whether you have/do not have a written option?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 39 para IG F.1.3 (b); IFRS 9 BC6.153 Reference to standing text: 40.85

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: The following cumulative factors should be considered to ascertain whether an interest rate collar, or other derivative instrument that includes a written option is not a net written option:

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: - no net premium is received either at inception or over the life of the combination of options. The distinguishing feature of a written option is the receipt of a premium to compensate the writer for the risk incurred; and where relevant

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: - except for the strike prices, the critical terms and conditions of the written option component and the purchased option component are the same (including underlying variable or variables, currency denomination and maturity date). The notional amount of the written option component is not greater than the notional amount of the purchased option component.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: If no premium can be identified, other terms of the contract need to be examined to determine whether the contract contains a written option (in particular, whether the buyer is able to secure economic value from the option’s presence).

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: FAQ 40.86.1 – Is the ‘own-use’ exemption met in a contract to buy electricity where there is volume flexibility?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 32 para 10; IAS 39 para 7; IFRS 9 para 2.7 Reference to standing text: 40.86

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Entity B, an electricity supplier in the United Kingdom (where there is an active electricity market), enters into a contract to buy electricity from entity A. The contract provides for entity A to supply 100 units of electricity at a specified future date to entity B at a fixed price per unit. Entity B has the option to take between 90% and 110% of the contract quantity. Entity B can monetise the contract’s value by selling on any excess power into the market (that is, it can readily convert the electricity contract to cash). Does the contract meet the own use requirements?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Entity B is not able to take the own use exemption if the quantity specified in the contract is more than the entity’s normal usage requirement and the entity intends to net settle part of the contract that it does not need in the normal course of business or has a practise to net settle similar contract. The entity could take all of the quantities specified in the contract and sell the excess, or it could enter into an offsetting contract for the excess quantity. In such a case the entire contract falls within IAS 39/IFRS 9’s scope as a derivative for entity B.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: If the quantity specified in the contract is less than the entity’s normal usage requirement and the entity entered into the contract and continues to hold the contract for the purpose of the receipt of the electricity for the entity’s expected normal usage requirements, it will not be classified as a derivative. It is important, in this situation, that the entity also has no practice of net settling similar contracts or taking delivery and selling the electricity immediately (that is, making a profit from market price fluctuations).

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: FAQ 40.86.2 – Accounting for take or pay contract; do these violate the ‘own-use’ requirements?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 32 para 10; IAS 39 para 7; IFRS 9 para 2.7; IAS 37 para 66 Reference to standing text: 40.86

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Many contracts for the supply of goods oblige the buyer to take a minimum quantity of goods. If the buyer does not take the minimum amount of goods the contract requires a penalty which can either be based on a fixed price, the market value of the goods or some other variable. Do these take or pay feature violate the own use requirements?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: A minimum quantity commitment might create a derivative where the entity does not expect to purchase all of the guaranteed volume for its ‘own use’. If it becomes likely that the entity will not take physical delivery of the product and will, instead, pay a penalty under the contract, it accounts for the contract as follows:

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: - If the penalty is dependent on changes in the market price of the goods. The contract might meet the definition of a derivative and is measured at fair value through profit and loss. Changes in market price will affect the carrying value until the penalty is paid (See paragraph 40.30).

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: - If the amount of the penalty payable is fixed or pre-determined, there is no derivative. Such a payment of the contractual amount for the volume that was not taken is not considered a net settlement, because there is no payment based on the difference between contract price and market price. In other words, the entity will need to provide for the penalty payable once it becomes clear that non-performance is likely.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: If the quantity specified in the contract is less than the entity’s normal usage requirement and the entity entered into the contract and continues to hold the contract for the purpose of the receipt of the goods for the entity’s expected normal usage requirements, it will not be classified as a derivative. It is important, in this situation, that the entity also has no practice of net settling similar contracts or taking delivery and selling the goods immediately (that is, making a profit from market price fluctuations).

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: FAQ 40.86.3 – Volume adjustment feature with a written option with no premium; is the ‘own-use’ exemption met?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 39 para IG F.1.3(b); IFRS 9 para BC6.153 Reference to standing text: 40.86

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Entity A, a car manufacturer, enters into a contract to sell cars to entity B that is engaged in renting cars. The contracts provide for entity A to supply 50 cars of a specific model at a specified future date at a fixed price. Entity B has the option to take between 90% and 110% of the contract quantity. Available market information indicates that a similar contract for 50 cars but without volume flexibility would also be priced at the same fixed price specified in the contract. Entity B cannot monetise the value of the contract by selling on any excess cars in the market. Does the volume fl

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: The supply contract would not be considered a written option, because the pricing of the contract is the same as that for a similar contract with no volume flexibility. There is, therefore, no premium associated with the contract. Entity B cannot exercise any value from the option’s presence, so the contract is not a written option and qualifies for the own use exemption.

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: FAQ 40.86.4 – Electricity supply contract containing a written option; is the ‘own-use’ exemption met?

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 39 para IG F.1.3(b); IFRS 9 para BC6.153 Reference to standing text: 40.86

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: Entity A, an electricity producer in the United Kingdom (where there is an active electricity market), enters into a contract to sell electricity to entity B. The contract provides for entity A to supply 100 units of electricity at a specified future date to entity B at a fixed price per unit. Entity B has the option to take between 90% and 110% of the contract quantity. The total quantity taken will be priced at C0.21 per unit. Available market information indicates that a similar contract for 100 units of electricity but without volume flexibility would be priced at C0.20 per unit. Entity B

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: The pricing of the contract is not the same as that for a similar contract without volume flexibility. The price per unit includes a premium for the additional risk accepted by entity A in offering volume flexibility. So the contract contains a written option. Entity A can view the contract in two ways:

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: - as a written option in its entirety, and hence entity A cannot claim the own use exemption, with the effect that the contract will be marked-to-market in accordance with IAS 39/IFRS 9; or

chapter: 40 - Introduction to financial instruments – objectives, definitions and scope (IAS 39, IFRS 9, IAS 32, IFRS 7)
text: - as a fixed volume contract for 90 units of electricity for C0.20 per unit, for which the own use exemption could be claimed, and a written option for 20 units at C0.21 per unit, which is within IAS 39/IFRS 9’s scope.

41 - Embedded derivatives in host contracts (IFRS 9)
41 - Embedded derivatives in host contracts (IFRS 9)
This chapter provides guidance on IFRS 9. For guidance on IAS 39, please refer to chapter 6.3A.
For contracts impacted by IBOR reform, entities should refer to the guidance in Appendix 3 - IBOR Reform Amendments.
This eBook is licensed to peggy so, peggy.so@hk.ey.com,
Introduction (paras 41.1 - 41.9)

41.1 A derivative instrument that falls within the scope of IFRS 9 need not be free-standing. Terms and conditions might be embedded in a financial instrument or non-financial contract (the ‘host’ contract) that behave like a free-standing derivative. These are referred to as embedded derivatives. The combination of the host contract and the embedded derivative is a ‘hybrid instrument’.

41.2 Analysing non-derivative financial instruments and executory contracts for potential embedded derivatives might be challenging. A derivative identified in a host contract needs further evaluation, to determine whether it should be accounted for separately as a stand-alone derivative at fair value. Not all identified embedded derivatives need to be accounted for separately from the host contract.
Definition and key characteristics

41.3 An embedded derivative is a component of a hybrid instrument that also includes a non-derivative host contract. Some of the cash flows of the hybrid instrument vary in a way similar to a stand-alone derivative. An embedded derivative causes some or all of the cash flows of the contract to be modified according to a specified interest rate, financial instrument price, commodity price, foreign exchange rate, index of prices or rates, credit rating or credit index, or other variable. Variation of the cash flows over the contract’s term is a critical indicator of the presence of one or more e
FAQ 41.3.1 – What is an example of a hybrid instrument, a host contract and an embedded derivative?

41.4 A derivative that is attached to a financial instrument but is contractually transferable independently of that instrument, or has a different counterparty from that instrument, is not an embedded derivative, but a separate financial instrument.
FAQ 41.4.1 – What is an example of a separate derivative?

41.5 A financial asset host that is within the scope of IFRS 9 is not assessed for embedded derivatives, because the solely payments of principal and interest (SPPI) criterion is applied to the entire hybrid contract to determine the appropriate measurement category.
FAQ 41.5.1 – Do embedded derivatives as identified under IAS 39 in financial assets prevent the SPPI criterion from being met under IFRS 9?
Conditions for separation
41.6 An embedded derivative should be separated from the host contract and accounted for as a derivative if all of the following three conditions are met:
- the economic characteristics and risks of the embedded derivative are not closely related to the economic characteristics and risks of the host contract;
- a separate instrument with the same terms as the embedded derivative would meet the definition of a derivative (see chapter 40 para 30); and
- the hybrid instrument is not measured at fair value, with changes in fair value recognised in profit or loss.
41.7 The requirements are summarised in the following diagram.
If embedded derivative is not separately measurable, the entire instrument is recorded at fair value through profit or loss.

41.8 An entity could avoid separating an embedded derivative from a host contract by electing the fair value option. If a contract contains one or more embedded derivatives and the host is not an asset within the scope of this standard, an entity could designate the entire hybrid contract at FVTPL unless:
- the embedded derivative(s) does not significantly modify the cash flows that otherwise would be required by the contract; or

- it is clear, with little or no analysis, when a similar hybrid instrument is first considered, that separation of the embedded derivative(s) is prohibited; for example, a pre-payment option embedded in a loan that permits the holder to pre-pay the loan for approximately its amortised cost.

Examples of eligible host contracts are financial liability host contracts within the scope of IFRS 9, as well as non-financial host contracts such as executory contracts for the purchase of goods or services that are outside the scope of IFRS 9 (for example, a host contract for the future purchase of renewable energy credits).

41.9 The requirement to separate embedded derivatives from host contracts applies to both the issuer and the holder of a hybrid instrument. However, the two parties to the contract might reach different accounting treatments. An interest payment dependent on the FTSE 100 on a debt instrument will lead to the instrument failing the SPPI test and, as such, it is carried at fair value by the holder of such instrument. However, from the issuer’s perspective, the equity-indexed interest is an embedded derivative which is bifurcated, unless the issuer elects to value the whole contract at fair value
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.6].

Interpretation of ‘closely related’ (paras 41.10 - 41.21)

41.10 Once an embedded derivative is identified, it is necessary to consider whether its economic characteristics and risks (that is, the factors that cause the derivative to fluctuate in value) are closely related to the economic characteristics and risks of the host contract. IFRS 9 provides specific examples of embedded derivatives that are, or are not, closely related to the host contract, rather than a definition. The examples focus on whether the underlying economic characteristics and risks of the embedded derivative behave in a manner similar to the host contract’s economic characteris

41.11 A key determinant in the ‘closely related’ assessment is risk. Risk in a derivative is determined by the underlying (such as interest rate, foreign exchange, prices etc), and by any leverage in the formula for determining settlement. An embedded derivative such as a cap or floor on the interest rate (interest rate risk), that bears a close economic relationship to its host debt contract, would be considered closely related. Conversely, where a derivative that is embedded in a debt instrument embodies an equity instrument’s economic characteristics, the economic characteristics of the der
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.5].
FAQ 41.11.1 – Should an entity consider both quantitative and qualitative factors to assess the closely related criteria?
Embedded leverage features in host contracts

41.12 Embedded leverage features can significantly modify some or all of the cash flows that otherwise would be required by the host contract. IFRS 9 does not define the term ‘leverage’. A hybrid instrument contains embedded leverage features if some or all of its contractually required cash flows, determined by reference to changes in one or more underlying, are modified in a manner that multiply or otherwise exacerbate the effect of those changes. The effect of leverage is only relevant for those embedded derivatives that would otherwise be ‘closely related’ to the non-derivative host contra
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.8(b)].

41.13 There is no quantification of how much leverage is acceptable, for an embedded derivative to still be considered closely related. Any embedded feature that leverages the exposure of the host contract to more than an insignificant amount would require separation. However, the standard does not provide guidance as to what would constitute an acceptable threshold and, as such, not all leveraged contracts require separation. A threshold frequently used in practice is the notion of at least doubling the holder’s interest rate of return in relation to embedded derivatives in which the underlyi
[IFRS 9 Appendix B para B4.3.8(b)].
FAQ 41.13.1 – What is an example of a leverage feature that does not require separation?
Identifying the terms of embedded derivatives and host contract

41.14 An assessment of whether an embedded derivative is ‘closely related’ to the host contract requires an understanding of the economic characteristics and risks of both the host contract and the derivative. The nature of the embedded derivative and the type of host contract must be determined.

41.15 The economic characteristics and risks of the host contract are generally readily apparent, and determining the nature of the contract is most often not difficult in practice. Common host contracts for embedded derivatives are:
- Executory contracts, including purchase and sales contracts.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.5].

41.16 A thorough evaluation of the terms must be performed to determine whether the contract contains an embedded derivative. Certain terms and phrases might indicate the presence of an embedded derivative, including:
- Pricing based on a formula.
- The right to purchase/sell additional units.
- Exchange/exchangeable into.
- Indexed to/adjusted by/referenced to.
- The right to cancel/extend/repurchase/return.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.5].

41.17 Another method of determining whether a contract has an embedded derivative is to compare the terms of a contract (such as interest rate, maturity date(s), cancellation provisions, etc) with the corresponding terms of a similar, non-complex contract. Any differences between typical market terms and the terms of the contract that is being evaluated can indicate an embedded derivative.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.5].
FAQ 41.17.1 – What are common examples of host contracts and embedded derivatives?

41.18 The entity makes its own judgement of the terms of a contract, in the absence of stated terms. However, in exercising such judgement, the entity should not seek to create a component that is not specified in the contract. Nor should it establish the terms of the host debt instrument in a manner that would separate an embedded derivative that is not clearly present in the hybrid instrument. It cannot create a cash flow that does not exist.
FAQ 41.18.1 – What is an example of determining a cash flow that does not exist?
Assessment at inception or contract modification

41.19 An entity should assess whether an embedded derivative is required to be separated from the host contract and accounted for as a derivative when the entity first becomes a party to the contract. An entity would become party to the contract when the debt is issued at inception, bought in the secondary market or on the date of a business combination in which the debt was acquired. This initial assessment is not revised, unless the contractual terms change and the change significantly modifies the expected future cash flows associated with the embedded derivative, the host contract or both,
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.11].

41.20 The acquirer in a business combination is required to re-assess all contracts of the acquired entity for embedded derivatives at the acquisition date. The acquirer becomes a party to the contract at the acquisition date. Re-assessment might result in more embedded derivatives being separated from host contracts in the new group’s consolidated financial statements. Some of the criteria for separating embedded derivatives are driven by market conditions existing at the time when the company becomes a party to the contract. The assessment performed at acquisition date uses market conditions
FAQ 41.20.1 – Should an embedded derivative be separated following a business combination?
Application of ‘closely related’ criterion to different types of host contracts

41.21 The application guidance to IFRS 9 provides examples of situations where the embedded derivative is, or is not, closely related to the host contract. This guidance is not an exhaustive list of contract features or embedded derivatives, but it does contain many of the common features found in typical host contracts. Judgement will be required to analyse situations that are not included in these examples. We have included additional relevant examples to assist in making this determination.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.5].

Embedded derivatives in debt host (paras 41.22 - 41.46)

41.22 A contract which meets the definition of a financial instrument but is not an equity instrument is a debt instrument. An identified embedded derivative would need to have debt characteristics to be regarded as closely related.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.2].

41.23 The value of a debt instrument is determined by the interest rate that is associated with the contract. The interest rate stipulated in the debt instrument is a function of the following factors:
- Risk-free interest rate.

Embedded derivatives that affect the yield on debt instruments because of any of the above factors would be considered to be closely related, unless they are leveraged (see para 41.12) or do not change in the same direction as interest rates (see para 41.24). Embedded derivatives that have economic characteristics and risks such as equity or commodity features that are unrelated to interest rates are not closely related to the debt host.
FAQ 41.26.3 – Should an inverse SONIA feature in a leveraged inverse floater be separated?
Index-linked interest payments

41.24 Floating rate loans are commonly priced off a benchmark interest rate such as SONIA. More complex debt instruments contain embedded interest rate indices that can change the amount of interest that would otherwise be paid or received, such as leveraged inverse floaters or range floaters. An embedded derivative in which the underlying is an interest rate or interest rate index, that can change the amount of interest that would otherwise be paid or received on an interest-bearing host debt contract (or insurance contract), is usually closely related to the host contract. However, if either
- the combined instrument can be settled in such a way that the holder would not recover substantially all of its recognised investment; or

- the embedded derivative could at least double the holder’s initial rate of return on the host contract and could result in a rate of return that is at least twice what the market return would be for a contract with the same terms as the host contract.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.8(a)].

41.25 The condition that “the holder would not recover substantially all of its recognised investment” applies to situations in which the holder can be forced to accept settlement at an amount that causes the holder not to recover substantially all of its recognised investment. The term ‘substantially all’ is not defined in IFRS 9, and so judgement should be exercised after considering all of the relevant facts and circumstances.
FAQ 41.25.1 – What is an example of an instrument where the holder would not recover ‘substantially all’ of a recognised investment?

41.26 The second condition has two parts. An embedded derivative should be able to at least double the initial rate of return and, at the same time, it should be able to result in a return which is at least twice that of the market rate at the time of the change. Both of these parts should be met for the embedded derivative not to be considered closely related. So, for example, if the embedded derivative feature results in doubling the initial return under a possible future interest rate scenario (no matter how remote) but, at the same time, that interest rate scenario would not result in a ra
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.8(a)].

FAQ 41.26.1 – Should a plain vanilla SONIA feature in floating-rate debt be separated? FAQ 41.26.2 – Should a complex SONIA feature in floating-rate debt be separated? FAQ 41.26.3 – Should an inverse SONIA feature in a leveraged inverse floater be separated? FAQ 41.26.4 – Should an interest rate option in fixed-rate debt be separated?
Inflation-linked interest and principal payments

41.27 The guidance on inflation adjustment features in lease host contracts is usually applied to assess inflation adjustments in debt contracts, because IFRS 9 is silent. An embedded inflation-related index is closely related to the lease host contract if the index is not leveraged and it relates to inflation in the entity’s own economic environment under that guidance. Similar considerations are applied to debt instruments in practice. See specific discussion of lease contracts at paragraph 41.67 onwards.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.8(f)].

41.28 An embedded inflation adjustment in a debt instrument would not be closely related if it is considered to be leveraged. If the leverage is greater than one, the indexation is not simply compensating for the time value of money, and so it is not closely related.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.8(f)].

41.29 The inflation index should be a recognised measure of general inflation in the relevant economic environment. If the inflation index relates to a different economic environment from that of the debt, or it is not a commonly used measure of general inflation, the underlying inflation index will not be regarded as closely related to the debt host.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.8(f)].

FAQ 41.29.1 – Is the inflation rate for the Eurozone closely related to a particular country? EX 41.29.2 – Correlation as alternative to inflation guidance FAQ 41.29.3 – Should the inflation feature in an inflation-linked bond be separated? FAQ 41.55.1 – Should inflation features in lease rentals be separated?
Equity- and commodity-linked interest and principal payments

41.30 Interest and principal payments in a debt instrument that are linked to an equity index, a commodity index or any other non-financial index are not closely related to the debt instrument host contract and must be accounted for separately unless the index is a non-financial variable specific to the entity. The risks inherent in equity-indexed interest or principal payments embedded in a host debt instrument or insurance contract are not closely related to the host instrument, because the risks inherent in the host and the embedded derivative are dissimilar. Similarly, commodity-indexed in
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.5].

41.31 The holder of a debt instrument might have the right to put the debt instrument back to the issuer in exchange for an amount of cash or other financial assets that varies on the basis of the change in an equity or commodity index. These instruments are another example of an equity- or commodity-linked payment. The embedded derivative must be separately accounted for, unless the issuer on initial recognition designates the instrument as a financial liability at fair value through profit or loss.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.6].

FAQ 41.31.1 – Should a cash-settled put option and a conversion option in a convertible bond be separated? FAQ 41.31.2 – Should a call option linked to an equity index in a debt instrument be separated? FAQ 41.31.3 – Should linkage to an unrelated entity’s share price in a debt instrument be separated? FAQ 41.31.4 – How should an equity-linked embedded call option be separated? FAQ 41.31.5 – Should contingent payments based on the gold price in a commodity-linked bond be separated? FAQ 41.31.6 – Should an equity kicker in a subordinated loan be separated?
Interest rate caps, floors and collars
41.32 An embedded floor or cap on the interest rate on a debt contract is closely related to the host contract, provided that, when the instrument is issued:
- the floor is at or below the market rate of interest (out of the money); or
- the cap is at or above the market rate of interest (out of the money); and
- the cap or floor is not leveraged in relation to the host contract.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.8(b)].

41.33 In January 2016 the IFRS Interpretations Committee (IC) discussed the application of this guidance and in particular how to determine the floor or cap rate in the contract and the market rate of interest. The IC clarified that an entity should compare:
- the overall interest rate floor or cap for the hybrid contract; to
- the market rate of interest for a similar contract without the interest rate floor or cap (the host contract).

The IC observed that the overall interest rate floor or cap for the hybrid contract is the benchmark interest rate referenced in the contract plus contractual spreads and if applicable any premiums, discounts or other elements that would be relevant to the calculation of the effective interest rate. When determining the appropriate market rate of interest for the host contract an entity is required to consider all specific terms of the host contract and the relevant spreads (including credit spreads) appropriate for the transaction.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.8(b)]. [IFRIC Update January 2016].

41.34 The term ‘market rate of interest’ is linked to the concept of fair value as defined in IFRS 13, ‘Fair value measurement’, and is described as the rate of interest “for a similar instrument (similar as to currency, term, type of interest rate and other factors) with a similar credit rating”. As the market rate of the host instrument typically includes a receipt of premium for the floor, it is expected the IFRIC guidance will lead to floors being closely related to host contracts unless they are leveraged.
[IFRS 9 App B para B5.1.1].

41.35 The IC also observed that the guidance in paragraph AG33(b) of IAS 39 (equivalent to para B4.3.8(b) of IFRS 9) is applied in a negative interest rate environment in the same way as it would be applied in a positive interest rate environment.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.8(b)]. [IAS 39 para AG33(b)].

41.36 An interest rate cap or floor embedded in a variable-rate debt instrument, that was out of the money when the debt instrument was initially recognised, would not be separated from the host debt, even if interest rates change so that the cap or the floor is in the money. Similar considerations apply to caps (see para 41.19 above).
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.11].
FAQ 41.36.1 – Should an interest rate collar in debt be separated?
Calls, puts and pre-payment options
41.37 Embedded calls, puts and pre-payment options are not closely related to the host debt contract, unless:
- the option’s exercise price is approximately equal, on each exercise date, to the host debt instrument’s amortised cost, or

- the exercise price of the pre-payment option reimburses the lender for an amount up to the approximate present value of lost interest for the host contract’s remaining term. Lost interest is the product of the outstanding principal amount multiplied by the interest differential. The interest differential is the difference between the effective interest rate on the host contract and the effective interest rate that could be obtained by the lender if it invested the principal at the repayment date for the host contract’s remaining term in a similar contract.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.5(e)].
FAQ 41.37.1 – Should a call/put in a debt instrument be separated? FAQ 41.37.2 – Should a pre-payment option in a debt instrument be separated?
FAQ 41.37.3 – Should embedded puts and calls be taken into account when determining the expected life of convertible debt?

41.38 An interest or principal cash flow stream that has been separated and payable at different dates is an interest-only or principal-only strip. An embedded pre-payment option in an interest-only or principal-only strip is closely related to the host contract, provided that the host contract:
- initially resulted from separating the right to receive contractual cash flows of a financial instrument that did not itself contain an embedded derivative; and
- does not contain any terms that are not present in the original host debt contract.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.8(e)].

41.39 A debt instrument might include clauses that allow the issuer to extend the debt’s term beyond its original maturity (option to extend). This feature might be considered either an option to extend the maturity of the instrument or a loan commitment from the holder of the instrument. The accounting for the option to extend will depend on how the entity views the option. If the entity considers the extension an option, it is an embedded derivative in a debt instrument. If the entity considers the extension a loan commitment, it might not be a derivative within IFRS 9’s scope, and it does n

41.40 An option or automatic provision to extend the remaining term to maturity of a debt instrument is not closely related to the host debt instrument, unless there is a concurrent adjustment to the approximate current market rate of interest at the time of the extension.
[IFRS 9 para App B B4.3.5(b)].
FAQ 41.40.1 – Should a term-extending option with a reset to market rates be separated? EX 41.40.2 – Comparison of put and extension options
41.41 Certain loan commitments fall within the scope of IFRS 9 and might need to be considered for separation. Only the following loan commitments are within the scope of IFRS 9:
- Instruments that the entity designates as financial liabilities at fair value through profit or loss.
- Loan commitments that can be settled net in cash or by delivering or issuing another financial instrument.
- Commitments to provide a loan at a below-market interest rate.

Loan commitments that are not within the scope of IFRS 9 do not meet the definition of a derivative, because all derivatives must be financial instruments or other contracts within the scope of IFRS 9. An option to extend the term of a debt instrument that is considered to be a loan commitment could not be an embedded derivative that needs to be assessed for separation (see para 41.6).
[IFRS 9 para 2.3]. [IFRS 9 App A].

FAQ 41.41.1 – If an issuer treats a term-extending option as loan commitment, how should it account for the change in interest rate when it extends the loan? FAQ 41.41.2 – Should a term-extending option without a reset to market rates be separated?

41.42 The holder of a debt instrument might write a call option on the debt instrument to a third party. The issuer regards the call option as extending the term to maturity of the debt instrument, provided that the issuer can be required to participate in or facilitate the re-marketing of the debt instrument as a result of the call option being exercised. As such, the issuer needs to determine whether the extension option needs to be bifurcated according to the guidance above on extension options.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.5(b)].
Credit-sensitive payments and credit derivatives

41.43 The creditworthiness of the issuer is a key factor in setting the level of interest rate on the debt instrument, although IFRS 9 does not deal specifically with payments based on the creditworthiness of the issuer. A debt instrument that provides an interest rate reset if there is a change in the issuer’s published credit rating or creditworthiness contains an embedded derivative. However, the embedded derivative is closely related to the debt host, because the risks are similar, and so it would not be separated from the host contract.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.5(f)].
FAQ 41.43.1 – Not used FAQ 41.43.2 – Should ‘green variability’ features be separated? FAQ 42.121.2 – How should changes in cash flows due to ‘green variability’ be reflected?

41.44 Credit derivatives that are embedded in a host debt instrument and allow one party (the ‘beneficiary’) to transfer the credit risk of a particular reference asset, which it might not own, to another party (the ‘guarantor’) are not closely related to the host debt instrument. Such credit derivatives allow the guarantor to assume the credit risk associated with the reference asset without directly owning it.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.5(f)].

FAQ 41.44.1 – Should the embedded credit derivative in a credit-linked note be separated? FAQ 41.44.2 – Should non-viability clauses be separated? FAQ 41.44.3 – Do cash CDOs contain embedded derivatives that must be separated from the host financial liability by the issuer?
Equity conversion features

41.45 An equity conversion option is found in debt securities that are convertible into the issuer’s equity shares at the investor’s option. The written equity conversion option is an equity instrument for the issuer and is excluded from IFRS 9’s scope, provided that it meets the conditions for equity classification under IAS 32 (see chapter 43 para 59). However, if a debt instrument is convertible or exchangeable into shares of another entity, the embedded derivative is not closely related and the issuer would have to separate the embedded derivative from the host contract. The holder of such
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.2].
Foreign currency features

41.46 An entity might issue debt in a currency other than its functional currency. Such a foreign currency loan is accounted for under IAS 21, which requires foreign currency gains and losses on monetary items to be recognised in profit or loss. The foreign currency gains or losses are already recognised, so a foreign currency derivative embedded in such a host debt instrument is considered closely related and is not separated. This also applies to an embedded foreign currency derivative that provides a stream of interest payments that are denominated in a different foreign currency and are em
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.8(c)].

FAQ 41.46.1 – In a dual currency bond, should the embedded swap be separated? FAQ 41.46.2 – Should a foreign currency option in a loan be separated? FAQ 41.46.3 – Should a feature linking interest payments to foreign currency exchange rates be separated?

Embedded derivatives in equity host (paras 41.47 - 41.51)

41.47 A host contract that encompasses a residual interest and that involves the rights of ownership is usually an equity host. A host contract that has a stated or pre-determined maturity might not represent a residual interest in the entity’s net assets (see chapter 43 para 35). The value of an equity instrument is a function of the underlying equity price or index. An embedded derivative in an equity host would need to possess equity characteristics related to the same entity in order to be regarded as closely related.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.2].

41.48 Preference shares must first be analysed to establish if they are more akin to an equity instrument or a debt instrument, in order to determine which guidance on embedded derivatives is applicable. Following this analysis, any put or call options embedded in the preference shares are considered for separation as embedded derivatives.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.2].

41.49 A call option embedded in an equity instrument, that enables the issuer to re-acquire that equity instrument at a specified price, is an equity instrument, provided that it meets the conditions for that classification under IAS 32, in which case it is excluded from IFRS 9’s scope. The holder of such instruments would account for such instruments at fair value, because the instrument fails the SPPI test.

41.50 A put option that requires the issuer to re-acquire an equity instrument at a specified price is a written option that gives the counterparty the right to sell the issuer’s own equity instrument to the entity for a fixed price. The issuer recognises a financial liability equal to the present value of the redemption amount, being the present value of the option’s exercise price. See further chapter 43. The holder of such instruments accounts for them at fair value, because the instrument fails the SPPI test.

41.51 In the case of a puttable instrument that can be put back at any time for cash equal to a proportionate share of the entity’s net asset value (such as units of an open-ended mutual fund or some unit-linked investment products), the effect of separating an embedded derivative and accounting for each component is to measure the combined instrument at the redemption amount that is payable at the balance sheet date if the holder exercised its right to put the instrument back to the issuer.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.7].
FAQ 41.51.1 – Should a put option in puttable preference shares be separated? FAQ 41.51.2 – Should a conversion option in convertible preference shares be separated?
This eBook is licensed to peggy so, peggy.so@hk.ey.com,
Embedded derivatives in lease host contracts (paras 41.52 - 41.59)

41.52 Embedded derivatives might be present in lease host contracts under IFRS 16. No specific embedded derivative guidance is included for extension, termination and purchase options or residual value guarantees so the general principles for embedded derivatives apply.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.8(f)].

FAQ 41.52.1 – Are extensions, termination and purchase options in lease agreements embedded derivatives? FAQ 41.52.2 – Not used FAQ 41.52.3 – Are residual value guarantees in lease agreements embedded derivatives?
Inflation-indexed rentals

41.53 An embedded derivative in a host lease contract is closely related to the host contract if the embedded derivative is an inflation-related index, such as an index of lease payments to a consumer price index, provided that:
- the lease is not leveraged; and
- the index relates to inflation in the entity’s own economic environment.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.8(f)].

41.54 An embedded inflation adjustment in the lease contract would not be closely related if it is considered to be leveraged. An inflationary adjustment of greater than one would be considered sufficiently leveraged for the inflation feature to be accounted for separately. The market expects the prices of goods and services to move in line with inflation, all other factors being equal. Therefore, any inflationary adjustments in a lease contract that increase the indexed cash flows by more than the normal rate of inflation are considered to be leveraged.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.8(f)].

41.55 IFRS 9 is silent as to whether this means inflation in the lessee’s or the lessor’s economic environment. 41.56 Lease contracts might include contingent rentals that are based on certain related sales of the lessee. Contingent rental embedded derivatives are considered to be closely related to the lease host contract and would not be accounted for separately.

41.57 Where a lease contract includes contingent rentals based on variable interest rates, the contingent rental-related embedded derivative is typically considered to be closely related to the lease host contract and would not be accounted for separately. The lease contract is similar to a debt instrument, and so the obligation to make future payments for the use of the asset and the adjustment of those payments to reflect changes in a relevant variable interest rate index (such as SONIA) are considered to be closely related.

41.60 Contracts to buy or sell a non-financial item that can be settled net in cash or another financial instrument or by exchanging financial instruments, but that are entered into to meet the entity’s expected purchase, sale or usage requirements (‘own use contracts’) are accounted for as executory contracts and not as if they were financial instruments. This might include some commitments and take or pay contracts. Although these contracts can be settled net in cash or another financial instrument or by exchanging financial instruments, they are outside the scope of IFRS 9 under the own use

41.61 There is some specific guidance in IFRS 9 for foreign currency features relating to derivatives embedded in such contracts. The general guidance on embedded derivatives is applied to such contracts, and so it is necessary to consider carefully the economic characteristics and risks of such contracts. Both quantitative and qualitative factors should be considered. Relevant guidance for other types of host contract should be considered.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.8(d)].
Price adjustment features

41.62 Normal purchase and sale contracts outside the scope of IFRS 9 might contain price clauses that modify the contract’s cash flows. It is necessary to establish whether the underlying in a price adjustment feature is related or unrelated to the cost or fair value of the goods or services being sold or purchased in assessing the closely related criterion.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.5(d)].

Volume adjustment features

41.64 Many contracts for the supply of goods give the buyer the right to take either a minimum quantity of goods or any amount based on the buyer’s requirements. From the buyer’s perspective such a feature will need to be included in the analysis of whether the contract as a whole is entered into and continued to be held for the purpose of the receipt of a non-financial item in accordance with the entity’s expected purchase, sale or usage requirements (see chapter 40 para 81).
41.65 From the supplier’s perspective volume flexibility in the contract can be viewed in two ways:

- The whole contract is viewed as one instrument containing a written option. Written options have to be accounted for in accordance with IFRS 9 if they can be ‘net settled’(see chapter 40 para 85). ‘Net settled’, in this context, means either that the contract allows net settlement in cash or another financial instrument or that the item that is the subject of the contract is readily convertible into cash. The supplier would be prevented from classifying a contract containing a written option as ‘own use’.

- The contract is viewed as two components: an ‘own use’ fixed volume host contract outside IFRS 9’s scope for any contractually fixed volume element; and an embedded written option potentially within IFRS 9’s scope for the volume flexibility element. The latter would be within IFRS 9’s scope if the option can be net settled, as explained under the first view.

41.66 Inflation escalator clauses are included in executory contracts to protect the seller’s margin in real terms. An embedded inflation-related index is closely related to the lease host contract if the index is not leveraged and it relates to inflation in the entity’s own economic environment (see para 41.53).

41.68 An embedded foreign currency derivative is closely related to the host contract, provided that it is not leveraged, does not contain an option feature and requires payments denominated in one of the following currencies:

- The currency in which the price of the related goods or service that is acquired or delivered is routinely denominated in commercial transactions around the world (such as the US dollar for crude oil transactions).

- A currency that is commonly used in contracts to purchase or sell non-financial items in the economic environment in which the transaction takes place (for example, a relatively stable and liquid currency that is commonly used in local business transactions or external trade).

Accounting for embedded derivatives (paras 41.77 - 41.85)

41.77 A financial instrument containing an embedded derivative is recognised at the fair value of the entire instrument. A day 1 gain or loss might arise if the consideration paid or transaction price is not equal to the fair value of the instrument as a whole. A day 1 gain or loss is recognised only where the fair value of the entire instrument is evidenced either by other observable current market transactions in the same instrument (without modification or packaging) or by a valuation technique whose variables include only data from observable markets (see chapter 42 para 100).
[IFRS 9 App B para B5.1.2A].

41.78 An embedded derivative that is required to be separated from a host contract is measured at fair value on the balance sheet, with changes in fair value being accounted for through profit or loss. This is consistent with the accounting for a free-standing derivative. The host contract’s carrying value at initial recognition is the difference between the fair value of the entire instrument as a whole and the embedded derivative’s fair value. A day 1 gain or loss will not arise as a result of separating the embedded derivative from the host contract.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.3].

41.79 It might not be possible to determine reliably the fair value of an embedded derivative on the basis of its terms and conditions. The fair value of the embedded derivative, in that situation, is the difference between the fair value of the entire instrument and the fair value of the host contract. If the entity cannot determine the fair value of the embedded derivative (either at initial recognition or subsequently), the entire instrument is fair valued and designated as at fair value through profit or loss.

41.80 The host contract is accounted for in accordance with IFRS 9, if it is a financial instrument, and in accordance with other appropriate standards if it is not a financial instrument, following separation of an embedded derivative. Alternatively, an entity can elect to measure the entire instrument at fair value if it meets certain criteria (see para 41.8).
Separating a non-option-based embedded derivative

41.81 A non-option-based embedded derivative, such as a forward or swap, is separated from its host contract on the basis of its stated or implied substantive terms. The result should be a fair value of zero at initial recognition.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.3].

Separating an option-based embedded derivative

41.82 An embedded option-based derivative (such as an embedded put, call, cap, floor or ‘swaption’) is separated from its host contract on the basis of the option feature’s stated terms. The host instrument’s carrying amount at initial recognition is the residual amount after separating the embedded derivative.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.3].

41.83 The economic behaviour of a hybrid contract with an option-based embedded derivative depends critically on the strike price of the embedded derivative. Therefore, the separated option should be based on the specified strike price in the contract and not so as to obtain a zero fair value or zero intrinsic value at inception:

- If an entity were required to identify the terms of an embedded option-based derivative so as to achieve a fair value of the embedded derivative of zero, the strike price (or strike rate) generally would have to be determined so as to result in the option being infinitely out of the money. This would imply a zero probability of the option feature being exercised. However, since the probability of the option feature in a hybrid instrument being exercised is generally not zero, it would be inconsistent with the likely economic behaviour of the hybrid instrument to assume an initial fair value

- Similarly, if an entity were required to identify the terms of an embedded option-based derivative so as to achieve an intrinsic value of zero for the embedded derivative, the strike price (or strike rate) would have to be assumed to equal the price (or rate) of the underlying variable at the initial recognition of the hybrid instrument. In this case, the option’s fair value would consist only of time value.

The separated embedded derivative could have a zero intrinsic value if the agreed strike price was equal to the price (or rate) of the underlying variable at the initial recognition of the hybrid instrument.
Multiple embedded derivatives

41.84 A host contract might contain more than one embedded derivative. Each derivative must be identified and assessed to see whether they warrant separate accounting from the host contract. Generally multiple embedded derivatives in a single hybrid contract are treated as a single compound embedded derivative when bifurcated and valued (see para 41.77). If the embedded derivatives relate to different risk exposures and are readily separable and independent of each other, they are accounted for separately from each other.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.4].

Embedded derivatives as hedging instruments

41.85 Embedded derivatives that are accounted for separately can be designated as hedging instruments, like any free-standing derivatives, as long as the hedge accounting criteria are met. IFRS 9 does not restrict the circumstances in which a derivative can be designated as a hedging instrument, provided that the hedge accounting criteria are met, subject to some limitations on written options (see chapter 46 para 33).

Such a quantitative analysis could take the form of a regression analysis that demonstrates a statistically significant relationship between the interest rate for the maturity of the debt instrument and the inflation measure specified in that instrument.
FAQ 41.29.3 – Should the inflation feature in an inflation-linked bond be separated?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para B4.3.8(f) Reference to standing text: 41.29

A UK entity issues an inflation-linked sterling bond that pays a fixed interest of 5% per annum. The return of the principal amount is linked to the UK retail price index (RPI), which is a recognised headline measure of inflation in the economic environment of the currency in which the bond is denominated. Should the inflation feature be separated?

The coupon on the bond is 5%, and the underlying principal of the bond is £100, so the bond pays £5 interest per annum. If the inflation index increases to 10%, the principal of the bond would increase to £110 and the interest payment would increase to £5.50 (5% × C110).

The principal payment is not leveraged and it is indexed to the headline measure of inflation in the economic environment of the currency in which the bond is denominated, and so the inflation index is regarded as closely related to the host debt instrument.
FAQ 41.31.1 – Should a cash-settled put option and a conversion option in a convertible bond be separated?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para B4.3.6 Reference to standing text: 41.31

Entity A issues convertible bonds to entity H. The term of the bonds is three years and the par value is C2 million. Each bond pays fixed interest annually at 6% a year and it is convertible by entity H, at any time until maturity, into a fixed number of entity A’s ordinary shares. Entity H also has the option to put the convertible bond back to entity A for cash at par at any time.

Entity A has determined that the market rate for a loan with comparable credit status and providing substantially the same cash flows on the same terms, but without the conversion option, is 7%. Should the embedded features be accounted for separately?

Entity A’s management should separate the convertible bond’s equity and liability elements. [IAS 32 para 28]. The conversion option is an equity instrument of entity A, provided that it can only be settled by physical delivery of a fixed number of shares for a fixed amount of cash or other financial assets. It is not accounted for as a derivative. [IFRS 9 para 2.1(d)].

The fair value of a liability with a demand feature is not less than the amount payable on demand, discounted from the first date that the amount can be required to be paid. Hence, entity A would record the liability at its nominal value, with any residual consideration received being attributed to the equity component. [IFRS 13 para 47].

The option to put the convertible bond back to entity A for cash at par is an embedded derivative. This option is closely related to the host debt instrument, because the exercise price (par) is approximately equal to the bond’s amortised cost before separating the equity element under IAS 32.
[IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.5(e)].
FAQ 41.31.2 – Should a call option linked to an equity index in a debt instrument be separated?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para B4.3.6 Reference to standing text: 41.31

An entity issues a debt instrument at par with a term of five years. The debt is callable by the issuer three years after issue. If called, the holder will receive a sum that is the greater of the par value of the debt and the par value as adjusted by the percentage increase in the FTSE 100 index. Is the call feature closely related?

The embedded call option, exercisable three years after the issue of the debt instrument, is not closely related to the debt host, because the pay-off is indexed to an equity index. The equity-linked feature provides an upside to the investor, linked to an index representing different risks from those of the ordinary debt instrument. Therefore, the option should be separated from the host debt instrument and accounted for at fair value through profit and loss.
FAQ 41.31.3 – Should linkage to an unrelated entity’s share price in a debt instrument be separated?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para B4.3.6 Reference to standing text: 41.31

An entity issues a debt instrument at par with a term of five years. The debt is redeemable at par at any time. The loan agreement provides that, during the term of the loan, the entity will either receive or pay an amount based on the changes in the share price of an unrelated listed company, A plc; the reference point is the market price of A plc at the date of issue of the debt instrument. Is the equity feature closely related?

The interest payments are based on changes in the price of an equity instrument (equity risk), so they are not closely related to the host debt instrument (characterised mainly by interest rate and credit risk). Therefore, the embedded equity-linked amounts should be separated from the host debt instrument and accounted for at fair value through profit and loss.
FAQ 41.31.4 – How should an equity-linked embedded call option be separated?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para B4.3.6 Reference to standing text: 41.31

Entity A purchases a one-year debt instrument, issued by bank B for its principal amount of C1,000 on the issue date. Bank B will make no interest payments during the life of the instrument. At maturity, entity A will receive the principal amount plus any increase in the S&P 500 index since the issue date. The fair value of an at-the-money European option maturing in one year is C48 at issuance date.
How should the embedded call option be separated by bank B?

Bank B should recognise the hybrid instrument as a combination of a call option and a zero-coupon debt instrument, having first determined the option contract’s fair value and strike price. [IFRS 9 App B para B4.3.3].

Since bank B only pays increases in the value of the index since the issue date, the embedded option is at the money at the date of issue, and its fair value consists only of its time value and no intrinsic value. So its fair value at the issue date is C48, and the balance of the consideration given (C1,000 − C48 = C952) is attributed to the carrying amount of the zero-coupon debt instrument.

The zero-coupon host contract should be recognised at amortised cost, with interest accreted at the original effective interest rate of 5% to reach C1,000 at maturity. The option should be separated from the host debt instrument and accounted for at fair value through profit and loss.
FAQ 41.31.5 – Should contingent payments based on the gold price in a commodity-linked bond be separated?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para B4.3.6 Reference to standing text: 41.31

A gold mining company issues a debt instrument with a face value of C10 million and contingent interest payments in addition to a guaranteed minimum interest payment of 4% per annum. The contingent payments are linked to the price of gold, such that an additional interest payment of 0.5% would be paid for every US$100 increase in the gold price above US$1,000. The price of gold at issue date was US$1,100 per ounce. The market rate for a fixed-interest loan without such additional features is 5%. Should the gold features be separated?

A commodity-linked bond, such as the one described, enables the issuer to reduce its financing cost by offering contingent payments to investors, whilst the investor is assured of a guaranteed minimum but is able to participate in any increase in the price of gold.

In this situation, the issuer would be viewed as having (a) issued a host debt instrument at a market rate of interest of 5%, and (b) sold a call option contract under which the issuer receives a premium of 1% fixed interest and pays a variable amount that varies with the movement in the gold price above US$1,000. The option contract is not closely related to the debt instrument, because the factors that cause the option to change in value (commodity price risk) are not the same as the factors that cause the debt host to change in value (interest rate risk).
Therefore, the embedded option contract should be separated from the host debt instrument by the issuer and accounted for at fair value through profit and loss.
FAQ 41.31.6 – Should an equity kicker in a subordinated loan be separated?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para B4.3.6 Reference to standing text: 41.31

A venture capital entity provides a subordinated loan that, in addition to interest and repayment of principal, contains terms that entitle it to receive shares of the borrower, free of charge or at a very low price (an ‘equity kicker’), if the borrower undergoes an initial public offering (IPO). As a result of this feature, the interest on the subordinated loan is lower than it would otherwise be. Should the borrower separate this feature?

The ‘equity kicker’ meets the definition of a derivative, even though the right to receive shares is contingent on the future listing of the borrower. Paragraph BA.1 of IFRS 9 states that a derivative could require a payment as a result of some future event that is unrelated to a notional amount. An ‘equity kicker’ feature is similar to such a derivative, except that it does not give a right to a fixed payment, but an option right, if the future event occurs.
