FAQ 45.73.3 – Cash collateral held for trade receivables or lease receivables: recognition and impact on measurement of ECL
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para B5.5.55 Reference to standing text: 45.73

As a result of the impact of COVID-19, suppliers might require customers to provide cash collateral before goods or services are provided. The cash collateral might be held indefinitely by the supplier and only returned once the customer no longer procures goods or services from them. Similarly, some lessors might require lessees to provide cash collateral that is only returned after the lease term has ended. This FAQ assumes that management has determined that the cash collateral does not represent a prepayment for goods or services or lease rentals.
How should the supplier or lessor recognise such cash collateral, and how should it reflect the collateral when measuring the expected credit loss (ECL) for trade or lease receivables?
NB. The solution below focuses on trade receivables, but the same principles apply to cash collateral on lease receivables, except where stated.

Management should first consider whether the cash collateral results in derecognition of any trade receivable balances in accordance with paragraph 3.2.3 of IFRS 9, or whether it should be offset against them in accordance with paragraph 42 of IAS 32. In most cases, it is unlikely that the receipt of cash collateral would result in settlement of the trade receivables and hence in their derecognition. The offsetting criteria are also unlikely to be met, since there is generally no intention to settle net (and some of the other conditions for offsetting might also not be met). This is because th

When determining the ECL of trade receivables, cash collateral would be considered a credit enhancement in terms of paragraph B5.5.55 of IFRS 9, since the collateral will reduce the amount of loss in the event that the debtor defaults. As such, the collateral will be reflected in the measurement of the ECL. However, the collateral does not affect whether a significant increase in credit risk has occurred (for receivables not measured using the simplified approach), nor whether a receivable is credit-impaired (when giving the disclosures required by paragraph 35M of IFRS 7). [IFRS 9 App B para
For entities that use a provisions matrix in calculating the ECL on trade receivables, the cash collateral might have the following impacts:

- Grouping of trade receivable balances: It is unlikely that customers providing cash collateral and those not providing cash collateral will be similar in nature and have similar credit risk. As such, it would be expected that trade receivables that are subject to cash collateral would be grouped and analysed separately from trade receivables that are not.
- Calculating the loss rate: In determining appropriate loss rates, the cash collateral would reduce the loss on a default, and so it should be considered.
The following disclosures should be provided in accordance with IFRS 7:
- the effect of collateral on the amounts arising from ECLs (para 35K of IFRS 7); and

- where there is a legal right to offset the collateral against trade receivables, the offsetting disclosures in paragraphs 13A–13E of IFRS 7. Please note that these disclosures apply regardless of whether, on the balance sheet, the collateral is offset against the trade receivables where they are subject to a master netting arrangement or similar agreement.

The considerations above for recognition, ECL and disclosures would apply equally to cash collateral held for lease receivables. However, whilst lessors are required to provide quantitative information about collateral held, they are not required to provide a narrative description of such collateral. [IFRS 7 para 35A].
FAQ 45.78.1 – Accounting for modified loans under IFRS 9
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para B5.5.27 Reference to standing text: 45.78
The issues below were discussed by the IFRS Transition Resource Group for Impairment of Financial Instruments (‘ITG’) in its April 2015 meeting.
When an originated loan is renegotiated in a way that does not result in derecognition, IFRS 9 requires that a ‘modification gain or loss’ is recognised.
How should an entity calculate the modification gain or loss?

IFRS 9 is clear that the modification gain or loss should be measured as the difference between the previous gross carrying amount of the loan and the revised gross carrying amount of the loan, with the latter calculated as the present value of the new estimated cash flows discounted at the original effective interest rate. The estimated expected cash flows should not consider the ECL. If a write-off of the loan occurred before the modification, the gross carrying amount used would be after deduction of the write-off, as a write-off is a derecognition event.
How should the entity measure the new lifetime ECL?

Although the entity might consider, after the modification, that there is a lower probability of a credit event occurring, the ECL cannot be nil. This is because the expected cash flows used for the purposes of the ECL measurement take into account the possibility of credit losses, whereas the revised gross carrying value does not.
How should the modification gain or loss and movement on the expected credit loss allowance be presented?

The modification gain or loss and movement on the expected credit loss allowance should be presented in a way that is most relevant to an understanding of the entity’s performance. This might result in the modification gain or loss and the movement on the expected credit loss either being presented gross or net of each other. Materiality should also be applied in this context.
What modifications are included in the disclosure required by paragraph 35J of IFRS 7?
All modifications should be included in the disclosures required by paragraph 35J of IFRS 7 (that is, it includes modification for credit reasons).

This requirement in IFRS 9 requires the entity to track this information so as to be able to identify these ‘modification gains and losses’. This will create operational challenges; whilst most entities collect information about modifications for credit reasons, they might not collect information about modifications for commercial or other reasons. Also, preparers should consider whether to provide disclosure of financial instruments modified for credit reasons separately from other modifications.
FAQ 45.79.1 – How should modified loans, such as loans subject to ‘forbearance’, be classified within the IFRS 9 expected credit loss (ECL) impairment model?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para B5.5.27 Reference to standing text: 45.79 Banking and capital markets

When a borrower is in financial difficulty, to maximise recovery of the contractual cash flows of a loan, a bank might offer to modify the contractual terms. For example, the borrower might be offered a payment holiday. This is done with the objective of helping the borrower during their period of financial difficulty but still maximising recovery by the bank of the loan’s contractual cash flows. For loans such as retail mortgages, this also helps to avoid the need to repossess the borrower’s home. Such modifications are sometimes referred to as ‘forbearance’, although definitions of this term

When a bank grants a modification to a borrower due to their financial difficulty and this does not result in derecognition, in which ‘stage’ of the IFRS 9 ECL impairment model (that is, stage 1: ‘performing’; stage 2: ‘underperforming’; or stage 3: ‘credit-impaired’) should the loan be classified (i) at the time of modification, and (ii) subsequently? The loan was not purchased or originated credit-impaired.
Please note: This FAQ assumes that the borrower is in financial difficulty. Refer to FAQ 45.79.2 for discussion of the ‘Impact of COVID-19 payment holidays on ECL staging’.
(i) At the time of modification

The appropriate classification of the loan will depend on the specific facts and circumstances of the modification granted to the customer. The definition of a ‘credit-impaired financial asset’ (that is, stage 3) in Appendix A to IFRS 9 states that:

“A financial asset is credit-impaired when one or more events that have a detrimental impact on the estimated future cash flows of that financial asset have occurred. Evidence that a financial asset is credit-impaired include observable data about the following events: …

(c) the lender(s) of the borrower, for economic or contractual reasons relating to the borrower’s financial difficulty, having granted to the borrower a concession(s) that the lender(s) would not otherwise consider; …”
Considering each of the three possible stages:

- Stage 3 – In many cases, the loan will meet the definition of ‘credit-impaired (stage 3), because the forbearance concession has only been granted due to the borrower’s financial difficulty, the lender would not otherwise grant such a concession, and the concession has a detrimental effect on the estimated future cash flows (for example, a portion of the interest or principal payments are waived).

- Stage 2 – Where the loan does not meet the definition of ‘credit-impaired’, it should be classified in stage 2. This might be the case, for example, where a customer is not in significant financial difficulty and:

- a short-term payment holiday is granted where payments are only deferred (rather than waived) and interest accrues on the unpaid deferred amounts, with the result that there is not a detrimental impact on the estimated future cash flows of the loan.
- a loan covenant is amended or waived, which is not considered to have a detrimental impact on the estimated cash flows.
- Stage 1 – At the time of granting a modification to a borrower that is a concession due to their financial difficulty, it would not be appropriate to classify the loan in ‘stage 1’.

As well as considering the ECL implications of the modification, paragraph 5.4.3 of IFRS 9 requires the gross carrying amount of the loan to be recalculated, and a corresponding modification gain/loss to be recognised in profit or loss when the contractual cash flows of a loan asset are renegotiated or otherwise modified and this does not result in derecognition of the loan.
(ii) Subsequent classification

As described in paragraph B5.5.27 of IFRS 9, following such a modification, a loan is not automatically considered to have lower credit risk. Typically, a borrower would need to demonstrate consistently good payment behaviour over a period of time before the credit risk is considered to have decreased and the loan moves from stage 3 to stage 2, or from stage 2 to stage 1. A history of missed or incomplete payments would not typically be erased by simply making one payment on time.

The stage classification under IFRS 9 is a separate matter from whether or not a loan still meets a definition of ‘forbearance’, because the latter could reflect a regulatory definition which requires a different ‘probation’ period. That is, it should not be assumed that a regulatory ‘probation’ period can be used as the period of good payment behaviour needed to move an asset from stage 3 to stage 2, or from stage 2 to stage 1, for IFRS 9 purposes.
Appropriate disclosure should also be given in accordance with IFRS that describes how an entity determines whether:
- the credit risk of financial instruments has increased significantly since initial recognition (para 35F(a) of IFRS 7);
- financial assets are credit-impaired (para 35F(a), (d) of IFRS 7); and
- modified financial asset moves from stage 3 to stage 2, and from stage 2 to stage 1 (para 35F(f) of IFRS 7).
FAQ 45.79.2 – Impact of COVID-19 payment holidays, including subsequent extensions to such holidays, on ECL staging
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para B5.5.27 Reference to standing text: 45.79 Banking and capital markets

Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, payment holidays or ‘forbearance’ were typically initiated by a borrower known to be in financial difficulty. The lender obtained detailed financial information from the borrower that the lender used on a case-by-case basis to assess the financial position of the borrower and tailor the payment holiday to their individual circumstances. In those circumstances, the exposure was classified either as stage 2 as a minimum, or stage 3 (refer toFAQ 45.79.1 ‘How should modified loans, such as loans subject to ‘forbearance’, be classified within the IFRS 9 expected cred

Following the COVID-19 pandemic, the circumstances in which payment holidays are typically granted have changed significantly. They have been initiated both by borrowers but also governments as blanket measures, with very little, if any, financial information provided by individual borrowers. That has typically resulted in standardised payment holidays being offered to all customers in a class (for example all home mortgages) without a borrower-level assessment. In addition, the initial payment holiday granted may also subsequently be extended and only high level information obtained from the

As highlighted by the IASB in its document issued on 27 March 2020, in these changed circumstances it is not appropriate to apply previously established approaches to assessing significant increase in credit risk (‘SICR’) for payment holidays in a mechanistic manner.
What factors should be considered in assessing whether a loan granted a payment holiday related to COVID-19 should be classified in stage 1, stage 2 or stage 3?

There are a wide range of factors that may be relevant in making this assessment when a payment holiday is first granted. The relevance of each factor will depend upon the particular facts and circumstances, as well as the materiality of the possible impact. Key factors to consider are discussed below.
Subsequent extensions to payment holidays

The factors set out in this FAQ would also be expected to be relevant in assessing how a loan should be classified when an extension to the original payment holiday period is granted, when the lender does not have detailed, up-to-date financial information on the borrower. However, if an extension is granted, then the following factors should be considered in addition to those in the rest of this FAQ:

- Likelihood of SICR: Generally, the likelihood of an SICR will be greater when a payment holiday is extended than when it was first granted. That is because with the passage of time it will become less and less likely the payment holiday is necessitated only by short-term liquidity difficulties. However, this will be dependent on specific facts and circumstances. For example:

- where an extension is requested by the borrower despite ‘lockdown’ being eased in the relevant territory, with more normal economic activity having resumed so that other borrowers are able to resume normal repayments, there would be a strong presumption an SICR has occurred;

- where the original payment holiday was for a longer period of time, for example three months, an extension would be more indicative of an SICR (rather than just short-term liquidity difficulties) than if the original payment holiday was for a shorter period of time such as [1] one month; and

- where extensions are granted as a ‘blanket’ measure that does not discriminate between borrowers, that would not provide relevant information to staging at the individual loan level (refer to ‘Blanket’ vs customer-initiated below).

- Indebtedness: When the terms of the extension do not change the maturity date of the loan, the periodic repayment obligation after payments resume will be higher than before the extension. In isolation, this would be expected to increase the borrower’s probability of default and the likelihood of the loan moving to stage 2.

- Higher risk loans: For higher risk loans already in stage 2 with a higher expectation of default, there might not yet be sufficient information to identify which of those loans are credit impaired on an individual basis, and so are required to be moved to stage 3 (refer to ‘Credit impaired or stage 3 below). However, as per paragraph B5.5.5 of IFRS 9, such loans should not be grouped with less risky loans for recognition of a loss allowance on a collective basis when this obscures their heightened risk and introduces bias by underestimating ECL.

- Data gathering: When granting an extension, banks may have had more time to build processes and greater opportunity to gather customer data with which to classify borrowers more accurately, compared to when payment holidays were first granted (refer to ‘Forward planning’ below). That is because when payment holidays were initially granted, due to the importance of borrowers quickly accessing relief schemes and the speed with which banks had to put in place new processes, very little, if any, current financial information was generally requested from individual borrowers. This additional data

- ‘Double count’: As more information becomes available over time, care should be taken to avoid any ‘double counting’. This could arise where exposures are moved to stage 2 due to payment holiday extensions, but the underlying risk necessitating the extension has already been appropriately reflected in the SICR assessment via other inputs to the ECL estimate. This risk is greatest where collective approaches have been applied elsewhere in the ECL estimation, such as via overlays or in the application of multiple economic scenarios. As discussed below under ‘Practical considerations’, it might

When the lender does have detailed, up-to-date financial information on the borrower that shows they are in financial difficulty , then the guidance in FAQ 45.79.1 referred to above should be applied instead of this guidance. Similarly where a borrower requests an extension but the bank declines the extension because it determines that the borrower would not be able to service the loan even with a further deferral of payments, that would indicate the borrower is in financial difficulty and the loan should be classified in stage 2 as a minimum.
IFRS technical considerations

- ‘Blanket’ vs customer-initiated: As highlighted in the IASB document, where a payment holiday is granted to an entire class of financial instruments, that alone should not automatically result in all those financial instruments moving to stage 2. That is because if the ‘blanket’ nature of the holiday does not discriminate between borrowers, it does not provide relevant information to staging at the individual loan level. An example would be a government requiring that payment holidays are granted to an entire class of loans (for example all home mortgages) without regard to the borrower’s in

- Collective assessment: Due to the common absence of detailed information from borrowers regarding the individual cause of their payment holiday request and their broader financial circumstances, it is highly likely that initially a collective approach will be needed to determine which loans with payment holidays should be moved to stage 2 (refer to FAQ 45.42.1 – ‘Top down’ versus ‘bottom up’ approach).

- Short-term liquidity issue vs SICR: Where a borrower is only experiencing short-term liquidity difficulties and those difficulties will be mitigated by the payment holiday, perhaps in conjunction with other government reliefs that reduce the risk of default, the loan may not experience a significant increase in the risk of default and validly remain in stage 1. In addition, where the application process asks only very high-level questions, some borrowers granted payment holidays may be pre-emptively maximising their cash and not currently experiencing liquidity issues or a significant increa

- Modification vs existing clause: Some loans may contain pre-existing clauses permitting the borrower a payment holiday, so no modification to the original loan contract is needed to allow this. This guidance on payment holidays obtained via contractual modifications is likely to similarly apply to these cases.

- Credit impaired or stage 3: A loan that is granted a payment holiday will only move to stage 3 when the loan is identified as credit impaired on an individual basis. This is because the IFRS 9 definition of credit impaired does not include assets assessed only on a collective basis where the impact cannot yet be identified for individual assets (refer to FAQ 45.4.2 - ‘Would the IFRS 9 ‘stage 3’ expected credit loss provision be the same as the IAS 39 incurred loss provision?’).

- Regulatory vs accounting: Where the regulatory treatment or regulatory reporting of payment holidays is changed, this will not automatically affect the accounting analysis under IFRS 9. The impact of such changes, if any, on IFRS 9 accounting would need to be separately analysed and assessed.

Significant judgement may be needed in applying the above technical considerations and determining which loans should move to stage 2, where a bank has limited data on customers’ specific circumstances. The availability of that information will also vary by bank, by territory and over time. However, as more information naturally becomes available, the approach taken should be updated appropriately. The following considerations may be relevant:

- Impact of Multiple Economic Scenarios (MES): Practically, when assessing which loans with payment holidays move to stage 2, a lender might first apply updated macroeconomic scenarios and weightings to reflect the change in economic outlook. Attention can then be focused on those loans with payment holidays that would remain in stage 1.

- Relevant risk factors: When assessing loans with payment holidays to determine which / what portion should move to stage 2, the following risk factors may be relevant to the extent data is available:

- Industries and sectors: Dependent on the territory, borrowers in some industries or sectors, such as a nurse or a company in the health sector, might have significantly stronger future prospects than borrowers in others, such as the tourism sector.

- ‘Headroom’: Loans that prior to COVID-19 had credit risk (for example. a probability of default or ‘PD’) closer to the threshold for moving to stage 2, or other risk indicators such as recent payment arrears, are more likely to have had a significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition once the additional factor of the payment holiday is also taken into account.

- Indebtedness: Even where a borrower’s income returns to its pre-COVID-19 level, their level of indebtedness might continue to grow during the payment holiday and so increase their future debt servicing costs and risk of default. This might be the case where the borrower cannot access government reliefs, where the relief only provides short-term liquidity that needs to be repaid, or where that relief does not fully address their income shortfall (for example, as enhanced government unemployment benefit is capped so borrowers with income levels significantly in excess of the cap will see their

- Other products: Where a borrower has other financial products with the lender, such as investments, revolving credit facilities etc, where that information is not already incorporated into the SICR criteria, information about those other products may be helpful in evaluating the risk of the borrower.

- Forward planning: Lenders might consider how the situation will evolve over time and what data will become available when. That may help identify additional data, or more granularity on existing data, that can be gathered to improve identification and support of riskier customers, provide more accurate estimation of the effect on staging and ECL, and manage expectations of both internal and external stakeholders. Examples might include:
- Adding additional questions, such as the industry a retail customer works / worked in, to those that new applicants are required to answer;
- Contacting a sample of customers to better understand their circumstances and how they have changed since the payment holiday was initially granted; or
- Gathering existing unstructured data (for example, the precise nature of the customer’s employment on their paper application form) so it can be analysed.

Given the extent of judgement involved, at least in the shorter term, the staging approach adopted for customers with payment holidays is likely to be the subject of significant scrutiny by users of financial reports. Clear disclosure will therefore be essential. The nature and extent of that disclosure will vary dependent on the reporting (for example, annual vs interim, IAS 34 interim vs other types of interim reporting) but regardless, the following will likely be key:
- A clear description of the approach taken to the staging of loans with payment holidays.
- The key assumptions and judgements that have been made.
- Explanation of the potential impact if different judgements had been made.
- Analysis of the credit risk concentration of loans granted payment holidays, for example by PD banding or Loan To Value (LTV) ratio for secured exposures, as well as by stage.
- Explanation of any changes made to previously applied SICR criteria (also refer to the publication ‘Spotlight: Changes to SICR criteria’).
- Any expectations of the timescale over which the uncertainties might be resolved.

FAQ 45.80.2 – Level at which to apply the ‘no reasonable expectations of recovering’ threshold

FAQ 45.81.1 – Income statement presentation of reversals of impairment on stage 3 assets
Reference to standard: IAS 1 para 82, IFRS 9 para 5.4.1, IFRS 9 para 5.5.8 Reference to standing text: 45.81

In which line item in the income statement should an entity recognise the reversal of impairment when a stage 3 instrument moves back to either stage 1 or stage 2? In particular, can the component of the reversal relating to the interest income previously not recognised (since interest under stage 3 was recognised on the net carrying amount) be recognised as interest income?
No, the total reversal of impairment should be presented as an impairment gain.

Paragraph 5.4.1 of IFRS 9 requires interest revenue for stage 3 assets to be calculated by applying the effective interest rate (EIR) to the amortised cost, and interest revenue for stage 1 and 2 assets to be calculated by applying the EIR to the gross carrying amount. IFRS 9 does not include a provision for a 'catch up' of interest.

Furthermore, paragraph 5.5.8 of IFRS 9 requires movements in expected credit losses, including reversals, to be recognised as an impairment gain or loss. The term ‘reversals’ includes the interest revenue not previously recognised. This was confirmed in an IFRS Interpretations Committee agenda decision in March 2019 which observed that, applying paragraph 5.5.8, an entity recognises in profit or loss as a reversal of impairment the adjustment required to bring the loss allowance to the amount that is required to be recognised in accordance with IFRS 9 (zero if the asset is paid in full). Accor

This principle is further supported by the requirement in paragraph 5.5.8 of IFRS 9 for interest revenue calculated using the effective interest method to be presented as a separate line item in the income statement. For a stage 3 asset, interest income reflects the EIR applied to the amortised cost of the asset.

It is also supported by paragraph 5.5.14 for purchased or originated credit-impaired financial assets, whereby an entity is required to recognise favourable changes in lifetime expected credit losses as an impairment gain, even if the lifetime expected credit losses are less than the amount of expected credit losses that were included in the estimated cash flows on initial recognition.

As such, IFRS 9 is prescriptive and requires the total reversal of impairment to be presented as an impairment gain. Hence, a component relating to unrecognised interest cannot be presented as interest revenue.

This can be illustrated in the following simplified example which follows on from the example in FAQ 45.4.1, which was discussed by the Transition Resource Group for Impairment of Financial Instruments (ITG) at its meeting in December 2015.

An entity holds a stage 3 financial asset measured at amortised cost. The effective interest rate (EIR) is 10%. At 31 December 20X1, the gross carrying amount of the asset (before deducting the loss allowance) is CU100, and the amortised cost (after deducting the loss allowance) is CU40. Accordingly, the lifetime expected credit losses (ECL) at 31 December 20X1 are CU60.

Between 31 December 20X1 and 31 December 20X2, there were no contractual cash flows, no cash settlements and no change in the expected timing or amount of cash flows on the asset. (For the purposes of this illustration, the effects of compound interest have been ignored.)
The table below summarises the application of the EIR in 20X2 and the carrying amounts at 31 December 20X2.
At 31 December 20X1 (A) CU Application of EIR in 20X2 (B) = (EIR × (A)) CU At 31 December 20X2 (A + B) CU Gross carrying amount 100 10 110 Expected credit loss (60) (6) (66) Amortised cost 40 4 44

Interest revenue for the 12 months to 31 December 20X2 is CU4, being the application of the EIR to the amortised cost of the asset. This comprises the unwinding of the discount (at the EIR) on the amortised cost of CU40 @ 10% (that is, the gross carrying amount (CU10 = CU100 × 10%) less the unwinding of the discount (at the EIR) on the ECL (CU6 = CU60 × 10%)).
During 20X3, the credit risk of the customer recovers and it settles its total contractual balance due, being CU110 (plus any further interest charged up to the date when the customer pays).
The full reversal of the impairment of CU66 should be presented as an impairment gain. The reversal cannot be split into CU60 impairment gain and CU6 interest income.

Qualifying criteria for hedge accounting (paras 46.33-46.55)

46.33 An entity’s risk management strategy is central to the objective of hedge accounting under IFRS 9. However, hedge accounting is an exception to the normal accounting rules, and so some restrictions are necessary to determine whether or not a proposed hedging relationship qualifies for hedge accounting. An entity is only allowed to apply hedge accounting if it meets the specified qualifying criteria, which are as follows:
- The hedging relationship consists only of eligible hedging instruments (see para 46.97 onwards) and eligible hedged items (see para 46.56 onwards).
- There is formal designation and documentation of the hedging relationship and risk management objective and strategy at inception of the hedge (see para 46.34 onwards).
- The hedge relationship meets the hedge effectiveness requirements (see para 46.37 onwards).

46.34 Formal designation and documentation must be in place at the inception of the hedge relationship. The documentation should identify:
- the risk management objective and strategy;
- the hedging instrument;
- the nature of risk being hedged; and
- how management will assess hedge effectiveness, including giving a description of sources of expected ineffectiveness and how the hedge ratio was determined.

46.35 Since there must be formal designation and documentation of the hedging relationship at the inception of the hedge, a hedge relationship cannot be designated retrospectively. - an economic relationship exists between the hedged item and hedging instrument;

46.41 An economic relationship must exist between the hedged item and the hedging instrument. This means that there must be an expectation that the value of the hedging instrument and the value of the hedged item would generally move in the opposite direction as a result of having the same or economically related underlyings or hedged risk. For example:
- Forecast fixed interest payments on a bond and an interest rate swap that receives fixed interest payments and pays variable interest have the same underlying (the fixed interest rate).

A deliberate imbalance is not permitted. This requirement is to ensure that entities do not introduce a mismatch of weightings between the hedged item and the hedging instrument to achieve an accounting outcome that is inconsistent with the purpose of hedge accounting. - availability of hedging instruments and nature of the underlying of those hedging instruments (and, as a consequence, the level of the risk of differences in value changes involved between the hedged item and the hedging instrument);
- tolerance levels in relation to expected sources of hedge ineffectiveness (which determine when the hedging relationship is adjusted for risk management purposes); and
- costs of hedging (including the costs of adjusting an existing hedging relationship).

46.50 IFRS 9 introduces the concept of ‘rebalancing’. Rebalancing refers to adjustments to the designated quantities of either the hedged item or the hedging instrument of an existing hedging relationship for the purpose of maintaining a hedge ratio that complies with the hedge effectiveness requirements. This allows entities to respond to changes that arise in the relationship between the underlying or risk variables. Rebalancing does not result in de-designation and re-designation of the hedge. It is accounted for as a continuation of the hedging relationship that, in many cases, will reduce

46.51 Rebalancing is consistent with the requirement of avoiding an imbalance in the weightings between the hedged item and the hedging instrument, not only at inception of the hedge but also at each reporting date and on any significant change in circumstances. Entities should not need to rebalance very often if they have a good risk management strategy in place and the economic relationship is stable.
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.4.10].

46.52 An entity must update its documentation of the analysis of the sources of hedge ineffectiveness that are expected to affect the hedging relationship during its remaining term, when rebalancing a hedging relationship.
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.5.21].

46.53 Rebalancing is not always applicable. An example is where the changes in the hedge relationship – which might arise from changes in the derivative counterparty credit risk – cannot be compensated by adjusting the hedge ratio. Rebalancing is also not allowed if the risk management objective has changed. Hedge accounting should be discontinued.
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.5.15].

e) Discounted cash flows for measuring hedge ineffectiveness

46.54 Hedge accounting does not change the measurement of the hedging instrument, it only affects where the change in its carrying amount is presented. Hedging instruments are subject to measurement at either fair value or amortised cost, both of which take into consideration the time value of money.

46.55 The hedged item is also measured on a present value basis. Subsequent changes would include the effect of the time value of money; for example, an undiscounted spot approach cannot be used in a foreign currency hedge. This requirement ensures that the measurement of the effectiveness of the hedge relationship reflects the time value of money, and that any mismatches in timing between the hedged item and the hedging instrument are recognised as ineffectiveness. See also paragraph 46.76 for information on partial term hedges.
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.5.4].

Eligible hedged items (paras 46.56- 46.96)

46.56 A hedged item can be a recognised asset or liability, unrecognised firm commitment, highly probable forecast transaction, or net investment in a foreign operation. The hedged item can be a single item or a group of items, but it must be reliably measurable.
[IFRS 9 para 6.3.1]. [IFRS 9 para 6.3.2]. [IFRS 9 para 6.3.3].

46.57 A hedged item must normally expose the entity to risk of changes in the fair value or future cash flows that could affect P&L. This could be in the current or future periods. Hedge accounting cannot apply to any items included in equity or transactions that directly affect equity, except for equity instruments for which an entity has elected to present changes in fair value in OCI. Such an equity instrument can be a hedged item in a fair value hedge, provided the hedged exposure is one that could affect OCI. In that case, any hedge ineffectiveness is also recognised in OCI.
[IFRS 9 para 6.5.2]. [IFRS 9 para 6.5.3].

46.58 Items (including net positions) can be grouped together and designated as a hedged item, if:
- the items are individually eligible hedged items; and

46.61 Hedges of a net position are permitted, but the gains and losses on recycling are presented as a separate line item in P&L or OCI (separate from the hedged items). - the hedged net position changes in size over the life, and the entity uses eligible hedging instruments to hedge the net risk;
- hedge accounting is normally applied to such net positions; and
- not applying hedge accounting to the net nil position would give rise to inconsistent accounting outcomes.

46.97 The main qualifying hedging instruments are:
- derivative instruments, including separate embedded derivatives in financial liabilities or non-financial contracts;

- non-derivative financial instruments measured at fair value through P&L (FVTPL) (except for financial liabilities designated at FVTPL where changes in fair value as a result of credit risk are presented in OCI); and
- the foreign currency component of non-derivative financial instruments (except for equity instruments for which changes in fair value are presented in OCI).
[IFRS 9 para 6.2.1]. [IFRS 9 para 6.2.2]. [IFRS 9 para 6.2.3].
46.98 Any combination of derivatives (or a proportion of them) and non-derivatives (or a proportion of them) can be jointly designated as a hedging instrument. See further paragraph 46.130 onwards.

46.99 Most derivative financial instruments (except for some written options) can be designated as hedging instruments (see para 46.102), provided they are entered into with an external party. Intra-group derivatives and other contracts do not qualify as hedging instruments in consolidated financial statements, although they might qualify in the separate financial statements of individual entities in the group or for segmental reporting, provided the information reported to the chief operating decision maker (CODM) is on that basis. In consolidated financial statements, consistent with paragra
[IFRS 9 para 6.2.3]. [IFRIC 16 para 14].

The circumstances in which such a single external contract can be treated as a hedging instrument on consolidation is considered in the examples in the context of interest rate risk and foreign currency risk management.

46.101 An entity’s risk management objectives and strategies might require it to enter into a master netting agreement with a counterparty, under which the entity is required to settle all external derivative contracts with that counterparty on a net basis (for example in the event of a default of one of the counterparties). Although netting arrangements have the effect of allowing an entity to settle profitable and loss-making contracts on a net basis in certain circumstances, this, in itself, would not give rise to there being only a single derivative contract, and hence would not preclude t
FAQ 46.101.1 – Can net settled external derivatives with the same counterparty be designated in separate hedging relationships?

46.102 Freestanding derivatives, or a proportion of them, can be designated as a hedging instrument for one or more types of risk, except for some written options. A written option or net written option cannot be a hedging instrument, unless it is designated as an offset to a purchased option, including one embedded in another financial instrument, or is jointly designated with another hedging instrument so that, in combination, they do not result in a net written option. See further paragraph 46.111 onwards.
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.2.4].

46.103 Contracts for purchases or sales of non-financial assets that are accounted for as derivatives under IFRS 9 (that is, contracts that can be settled net or by exchanging another financial instrument and that are not for own use) can be used as hedging instruments. This is not applicable to contracts that do meet the ‘own use’ criteria; however, in certain circumstances an alternative to hedge accounting exists by allowing an irrevocable designation at FVTPL (as described in paras 46.155 and 46.156).

46.104 An embedded derivative that is accounted for separately from its host contract can be used as a hedging instrument. Because derivatives embedded in financial assets are not separated under IFRS 9’s classification and measurement requirements (see chapter 41 para 5), this will only be relevant for separate derivatives embedded in financial liabilities or non-financial contracts. In January 2016, the IFRS IC issued an agenda decision that makes separation of floors and caps in debt instruments unlikely (see chapter 41 para 33). Embedded derivatives that are not separated cannot be designa
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.2.1]. [IFRS 9 para 6.2.1].

46.105 An entity does not need to enter into a new derivative contract every time it enters into a new hedging relationship. Provided the hedge accounting criteria are met, a pre-existing derivative instrument that has been held for some time can be designated as a hedging instrument in a new hedging relationship, as can a derivative that has been designated previously as a hedging instrument in a hedge relationship that no longer qualifies for hedge accounting.
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.5.28].

Portions and proportions of a hedging instrument

46.106 A derivative cannot be designated as a hedging instrument for a part of its changes in fair value that result from only a portion of the remaining life of the derivative (such as the next three years of a swap with a remaining life of five years). But it is possible to designate a proportion of the entire instrument, such as 50% of the nominal amount. The proportion that is not designated as a hedge can be designated as a hedging instrument in another hedge relationship; otherwise, it will be measured at FVTPL.
FAQ 46.106.1 – Is it possible to use proportions of derivatives as hedging instruments?

46.107 There is normally a single fair value measure for a hedging instrument in its entirety, and the factors that cause changes in fair value are co-dependent. Thus, a hedging relationship is designated by an entity for a hedging instrument in its entirety. It follows that a derivative instrument cannot be split into components representing different risks, with only certain components designated as a hedging instrument. The only exceptions permitted are:
- separating the forward element and spot element of a forward contract and designating only the change in the spot element as the hedging instrument;
- separating and excluding the foreign currency basis spread from the designated hedging instrument; and
- separating the intrinsic value and time value of an option contract and designating only the change in intrinsic value of an option as the hedging instrument.

46.108 These exceptions are permitted because the separate elements can generally be measured separately. Furthermore, all of the forward element of a forward contract, cross-currency basis spreads and the time value of an option are seen by IFRS 9 as a ‘cost of hedging’, that is, a cost of achieving the risk mitigation inherent in the hedge. In line with this ‘cost of hedging’ rationale, the timing of the related cost in P&L is matched to that of the item being hedged. This is described in more detail in paragraph 46.117 onwards.

46.109 Options, in contrast to forward contracts and swaps, give the holder the right but not the obligation to exercise the instrument and exchange the underlyings. A purchased option has potential gains equal to or greater than losses, so can reduce P&L volatility from changes in fair values or cash flows. As it has the potential to reduce risk exposure, it can qualify as a hedging instrument.

46.110 An entity can designate as the hedged item only changes in the cash flows or fair value above or below a specified price or other variable (a ‘one-sided risk’). In a hedge of one-sided risk, entities are permitted to designate the hedged risk as the intrinsic value of a purchased option that has the same principal terms as the hedged item, but cannot include the time value of the option. For example, an entity can designate the variability of future cash flow outcomes resulting from a price increase of a forecast commodity purchase. 46.111 A written option (as opposed to a purchased option) exposes its writer to the possibility of unlimited loss, but it limits the gain to the amount of premium received. A written option is not effective in reducing the P&L exposure of a hedged item. Therefore, a written option does not qualify as a hedging instrument on its own, unless it is designated as an offset to a purchased option. A written option can also be designated as an offset to a purchased option that is embedded in another financial instrument. For example, in a callable debt that allows the issuer of the debt to repay
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.2.4].

46.112 Nevertheless, a written option might be an eligible hedging instrument when combined with other purchased options (regardless of whether they arise from one or several different contracts), provided that the combination does not represent a net written option (for which a net premium is received). For example, an entity’s hedging strategy might involve entering into a combination of a written put option and a purchased call option to form a collar. The objective is to protect the entity from loss below a certain value (the floor/written put) and limit the upside potential for gain above

46.113 An interest rate collar might be designated as a hedging instrument, if the combination is a net purchased option or zero cost collar (that is, it is neither a net written nor a net purchased option). Typically, such an instrument would not be a net written option, provided that:

- No net premium is received, either at inception or over the life of the combination of options. The distinguishing feature of a written option is the receipt of a premium to compensate the writer for the risk incurred.

- Except for the strike prices, the critical terms and conditions of the written option component and the purchased option component are the same (including underlying variable or variables, currency denomination and maturity date).
- The notional amount of the written option component is not greater than the notional amount of the purchased option component.

46.114 Where a collar whose fair value was zero at inception is designated as a hedging instrument some time into its life, it might have some fair value on the date of designation. If its fair value on the date of designation is negative, the first condition in paragraph 46.113 would be failed, and such a collar would not be allowed for designation as a hedging instrument. However, if the negative fair value is only due to the deferral of a premium, then the negative nature does not create an exposure linked to net written options, and therefore the instrument could be designated as a hedging

46.115 If a combination of a written option and a purchased option (such as an interest rate collar) is transacted as a single instrument with one counterparty, an entity cannot split the derivative instrument into its written option component and purchased option component and designate the purchased option component as a hedging instrument. This is because a hedging relationship is designated by an entity for a hedging instrument in its entirety, and the remaining written option is not, on its own, an eligible hedging instrument.
[IFRS 9 para 6.2.6]. [IFRS 9 para BC6.153].

46.116 The fair value of an option can be divided into two portions: the intrinsic value, which is the difference between the strike price and current market price of the option’s underlying; and the time value, which is the option’s remaining value and depends on the volatility of the price of the underlying, interest rates and the time remaining to maturity. Changes in the option’s time value will not be offset by an equivalent change in the value or cash flows of the hedged item.
FAQ 46.116.1 – Not used FAQ 46.116.2 – How should an entity calculate the intrinsic value of an option?
Separating the intrinsic and time value of an option

46.117 IFRS 9 introduces the concept of ‘cost of hedging’. Where a purchased option is designated as a hedging instrument, IFRS 9 views the option as similar to purchasing insurance cover, with the time value being the associated cost.

46.118 Many entities might choose to designate only the intrinsic value of an option as the hedging instrument, particularly (as described in para 46.110) where the hedged item is a one-sided risk and so the time value cannot be designated as part of the hedged risk. However, in a more dynamic hedging model, an entity might choose to designate all fair value changes in the hedging relationship.

46.119 If an entity elects to designate only the intrinsic value of the option as the hedging instrument, it must account for the changes in the aligned time value (see para 46.121) in OCI and hold them in a hedging reserve in equity, regardless of whether the hedge is a cash flow or fair value hedge. The subsequent release of the time value of the option depends on whether the hedge is transaction related or time-period related:

- For a transaction-related hedge that results in the recognition of, or a firm commitment for, a non-financial asset or non-financial liability, the time value of the option is removed from equity and recorded in the initial cost or other carrying amount of the asset or liability. This is not a reclassification adjustment and does not affect other comprehensive income.

- For other transaction-related hedges, the time value of the option is reclassified from equity as a reclassification adjustment to profit or loss in the same period or periods that the hedged cash flows affect profit or loss. Any amount that is not expected to be recovered in one or more future periods should be immediately reclassified into profit and loss.

- For time-period-related hedges, the time value of the option is amortised on a systematic and rational basis over the period during which the option’s intrinsic value could affect profit or loss (or other comprehensive income where the hedged item is an equity instrument whose fair value is recorded through other comprehensive income). This is recorded as a reclassification adjustment.

46.120 Once an entity designates the intrinsic value of the option, the accounting in IFRS 9 is not optional, but mandatory. However, this accounting limits P&L volatility for option-based hedges. It removes an obstacle to sensible risk management practice.

46.121 The accounting for the initial time value of purchased options applies only to the extent that the time value relates to the hedged item. This is called the ‘aligned time value’. Where the hedging instrument and hedged item are not fully aligned, entities need to determine the aligned time value – that is, how much of the time value included in the premium paid (actual time value) relates to the hedged item – and apply the accounting treatment to that portion. This can be determined using the valuation of an option that would have critical terms that perfectly match the hedged item.
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.5.32].

46.122 If the actual time value is higher than the aligned time value at inception, the amount recorded in a separate component of equity is based on the aligned time value. Differences in the fair value changes between the two are recorded in P&L. If the actual time value is lower at inception, the amount to be recorded in equity is the lower of the cumulative change in fair value of the actual and aligned time values. The residual amount is recognised in P&L. It might be difficult to obtain the ‘perfect’ option, and so entities will need to address these accounting complexities.
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.5.33].

Hedging with forward contracts

46.123 A forward is a contract to exchange a fixed amount of a financial or non-financial asset on a fixed future date at a fixed price. The use of forward contracts as hedging instruments is a common hedging strategy. The first requirement is to decide whether the hedging instrument can be accounted for as a forward contract.
FAQ 46.123.1 – What is a forward contract?
Separating the forward and spot elements of a forward contract

46.124 The fair value of a forward contract is affected by changes in the spot rate and changes in the forward points. In the case of a foreign currency forward contract, the forward points arise from the interest rate differential between currencies specified in a forward contract.
[IFRS 9 App B para BC6.416].

46.125 Management might want to exclude the forward points from the hedge relationship in order to improve effectiveness. Unlike the accounting for options, where it is mandatory to take movements in time value to OCI and equity if only the intrinsic value has been designated as a hedging instrument, the hedge accounting treatment for forward points is optional.
FAQ 46.125.1 – What approaches are available for entities hedging foreign currency using a forward contract?

46.126 Where the spot rate is the designated hedged risk, entities will still need to consider the time value of money and measure the hedged item using discounted spot (as discussed at paras 46.54 to 46.55). For a short-term hedge between currencies with limited interest rate volatility, the impact might not be significant.
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.5.4].
Accounting for currency basis spreads

46.127 The hypothetical derivative method is a common way of assessing whether a hedge meets the hedge effectiveness requirements. A hypothetical derivative cannot include features that do not exist in the hedged item. A hypothetical derivative cannot simply impute a charge for exchanging different currencies (that is, the currency basis spread), even though actual derivatives under which different currencies are exchanged might include such a charge (for example, cross-currency interest rate swaps).
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.5.5].

46.128 Where an entity separates the foreign currency basis spread from a financial instrument and excludes it from the designation of that financial instrument as the hedging instrument, the entity is able to account for the changes in the currency basis spread in the same manner as could be applied to the forward element of a forward contract (as noted in para 46.124 onwards). This treatment is optional but, if adopted, will help to mitigate volatility in P&L.
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.5.39]. [IFRS 9 para 6.2.4(b)].

Hedging more than one risk with a single instrument

46.129 A derivative, such as a forward contract, a swap or an option, is used as a hedging instrument to hedge a single risk (foreign currency, interest rate or equity price risk). However, an entity might use a single derivative such as a cross-currency swap (combined interest rate and currency swap) to convert a variable-rate position in a foreign currency to a fixed-rate position in the entity’s functional currency. A single hedging instrument could be designated as a hedge of more than one type of risk, provided there is specific designation of the hedging instrument and of the different r
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.2.6].

Combination of hedging instruments

46.130 A derivative could also be designated as the hedging instrument in combination with one or more other derivatives, or in combination with groups of non-derivative assets or liabilities. Two or more derivatives (or proportions of them) could be viewed in combination and jointly designated as the hedging instrument, provided together they do not create a net written option (see further paras 46.111 to 46.115).

46.131 Derivative instruments do not have to be similar to be combined, either together or with non-derivative instruments. Even where the risks arising from some derivatives offset those arising from others, the combination can still be designated as a hedging instrument.

46.132 IFRS 9 also permits derivative instruments to be combined with non-derivative instruments, or proportions of them, and the combination designated as the hedging instrument.

46.133 An ‘all-in-one’ hedge is the designation of a gross settled derivative (that is, an instrument which is settled gross by delivery of the underlying asset and the payment of the price specified in the contract, rather than by net settlement of the difference between the two legs) as the hedging instrument in a cash flow hedge of the variability of the consideration to be paid or received in the future transaction that will occur on gross settlement of the derivative contract itself, assuming the other cash flow hedge accounting criteria are met.

Non-derivative financial instruments
46.134 Non-derivative financial instruments (or components of those instruments) can be used as hedging instruments subject to some limits.
46.135 Hedging instruments must be designated in their entirety or as a proportion of the entire instrument (with limited exceptions, as described in para 46.106 onwards). See also paragraph 46.141.
[IFRS 9 para 6.2.4]. [IFRS 9 App B para B6.2.5].

46.136 Only non-derivative financial instruments measured at FVTPL can normally be used as hedging instruments, with the exception described in paragraph 46.139. Financial assets that do not meet the ‘solely payments of principal and interest’ requirements are carried at FVTPL. Financial assets measured in this way are eligible as hedging instruments.
FAQ 46.136.1 – Is it possible to use a non-derivative contract measured at FVTPL as a hedging instrument?

46.137 Financial liabilities accounted for at FVTPL, but for which the changes in the liability’s own credit risk are presented in OCI, are not eligible for designation as hedging instruments. This is because such a designation would allow credit risk on the hedging instrument to be excluded from the hedge relationship or require the credit risk amount in OCI to be reclassified to P&L.

46.138 Instruments that were designated at inception at FVTPL to mitigate an accounting mismatch (commonly referred as the ‘fair value option’) might be later designated as hedging instruments. However, this should be consistent with an entity’s risk management objective and strategy, and hence, in practice, it should arise only if the original mismatch no longer exists.
[IFRS 9 para BC6.136]. [IFRS 9 para BC6.137]. [IFRS 9 para BC6.138]. [IFRS 9 para BC6.139].

46.139 The only exception to designating the hedging instrument in its entirety is that non-derivative financial instruments can be designated as hedging instruments of foreign currency risk, provided that such non-derivative financial instruments are not investments in equity instruments for which the entity has elected to present the changes in fair value in OCI. This is because the foreign currency risk component already needs to be separated and reported in P&L in accordance with IAS 21.
[IFRS 9 para 6.2.2]. [IFRS 9 App B para B6.2.3]. [IFRS 9 para BC6.124].

Similarly, a contract to purchase the non-controlling interest in a subsidiary which is required to be recognised as a liability under paragraph 23 of IAS 32 is not accounted for as a derivative and, accordingly, could be designated as a hedged item or a hedging instrument in a hedge of foreign currency risk only. However, partial term designation is not allowed, that is, an entity cannot treat the cash flows of only a proportion of the period during which a non-derivative instrument designated as a hedge against foreign currency risk remains outstanding and exclude the other cash flows from the designated hedging relationship. Items that do not qualify as hedging instrument

46.142 An entity’s own equity instruments are not financial assets or liabilities of the entity and, therefore, cannot be designated as hedging instruments. Similarly, non-controlling interests in consolidated financial statements are treated as part of equity and, hence, cannot be designated as hedging instruments in the consolidated financial statements.
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.2.2].

46.143 Firm commitments and forecast transactions cannot be designated as hedging instruments, since they are not normally recognised in the financial statements. However, if the foreign currency component of a purchase commitment is required to be separated as an embedded derivative under paragraphs 4.3.3 and B4.3.8(d) of IFRS 9, it could be designated as a hedging instrument in a hedge of the exposure to changes in the fair value of the maturity amount of a debt attributable to foreign currency risk.

The acquirer is required to re-designate all hedge relationships of the acquired entity as if they started at the date of acquisition. Discontinuance of hedge accounting (paras 46.145 - 46. 154)

For hedges impacted by IBOR reform, Interest Rate Benchmark Reform Amendments to IFRS 9, IAS 39, IFRS 7, IFRS 4 and IFRS 16 are intended to ensure that an entity will not have to discontinue hedge accounting, solely because IBOR reform. It is likely that there will be changes to either or both the hedging instrument and hedged items.

Entities with financial asset and financial liability modifications in the context of IBOR reform should read the guidance in chapter 42 and consider Phase 2 Interest Rate Benchmark Reform Amendments to IFRS 9, IAS 39, IFRS 7, IFRS 4 and IFRS 16. Refer to Appendix 3 para A3.39 for the Phase 2 amendments issued in August 2020.

46.145 Voluntary de-designation of hedge accounting is prohibited. Hedge accounting should be discontinued prospectively only when the hedging relationship (or part of the relationship) ceases to meet the qualifying criteria for hedge accounting. Examples of ceasing to meet the qualifying criteria include:

- The hedging instrument expires or is sold, terminated or exercised. For this purpose, the replacement or roll-over of a hedging instrument into another hedging instrument is not an expiration or termination if such replacement or roll-over is part of the entity’s documented risk management objective.
- The hedged item is sold, extinguished or no longer expected to occur.
- The hedging relationship no longer meets the risk management objective (for example, because the entity no longer pursues that risk management objective).

- The hedge effectiveness requirements are not met (for example, there is no longer an economic relationship between the hedged item and the hedging instrument, or the effect of credit risk starts to dominate the value changes that result from that economic relationship).
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.5.26]. [IFRS 9 para 6.5.6].

The accounting treatment when the hedging instrument or hedged item no longer exists is explained for fair value hedges and cash flow hedges in paragraph 46.152 onwards and 46.153 onwards respectively.

Risk management objective no longer met

46.146 If a hedging relationship no longer meets the risk management objective (see paras 46.34 and 46.35), hedge accounting must be discontinued. An entity should not de-designate and discontinue a hedging relationship if the hedging relationship still meets the original risk management objective that formed the basis for the hedge, assuming all other hedging criteria are still met.
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.5.23].
FAQ 46.146.1 – Is it possible to de-designate a hedge of foreign currency exposure on forecast purchases or sales under IFRS 9?

46.147 A risk management strategy can (and often will) involve many different hedging relationships, each with a risk management objective. Hence, the risk management objective for a particular hedging relationship can change, even though an entity’s risk management strategy remains unchanged. If the risk management objective for a hedge relationship has changed, hedge accounting for the hedge relationship must be discontinued.
[IFRS 9 App B para B6.5.24]. [IFRS 9 App B para B6.5.26].

Replacement or roll-over of hedging instruments

46.148 The replacement or roll-over of a hedging instrument into another hedging instrument is not an expiration or termination if such replacement or roll-over is part of the entity’s documented risk management objective. Any such replacement or roll-over should be documented at the level of the specific hedge relationship, as it refers to the documented risk management objective and not the higher-level hedging strategy.

46.149 A novation is not an expiration or termination of the hedging instrument if the novation is a consequence of laws or regulations with the purpose of incorporating a central clearing counterparty.
FAQ 46.149.1 – What is the accounting for the novation of a derivative which was designated as a hedging instrument in a hedge relationship?
Discontinuance of part of a hedging relationship

46.150 Discontinuance of hedge accounting can affect a hedging relationship in its entirety or only part of it, depending on the facts and circumstances. Examples of where only a part of a hedging relationship is discontinued are:
- Where the volume of hedged item included in the hedging relationship has decreased due to an adjustment to the hedge ratio as part of a rebalancing exercise (see para 46.50 onwards).
- Where part of the volume of a forecast transaction is no longer highly probable.

These are contracts that can be settled net or by exchanging financial instruments, or where the non-financial item is readily convertible to cash but that were entered into for the purpose of the receipt or delivery of a non-financial item in accordance with the entity’s expected purchase, sale or usage requirements. Option to designate a credit exposure at FVTPL

46.157 The credit risk of a financial instrument, such as a loan or loan commitment, is a risk component that does not meet the eligibility criteria to be designated as a hedged item. The spread between the risk-free rate and the market interest rate incorporates credit risk, liquidity risk, funding risk and other unidentified risk components and margin elements. Credit risk cannot be isolated, and so does not meet the ‘separately identifiable’ criterion.
[IFRS 9 para BC6.470]. [IFRS 9 para BC6.503]. [IFRS 9 para BC6.504].

46.158 Credit derivatives, such as credit default swaps that are used to hedge credit risk, are accounted for at FVTPL, while credit exposures are usually measured at amortised cost or are unrecognised (such as, loan commitments). Where there is credit deterioration, gains are recognised on the credit derivative, while the impairment on the hedged item is measured on a different basis, which results in P&L volatility that does not reflect the credit protection obtained.

46.159 There is an option to designate the financial instrument (or a proportion of it) at FVTPL This option is available only where credit derivatives are used to manage all (or a proportion) of the credit risk on the instrument and if:
- the name of the credit exposure (for example, the borrower or the holder of a loan commitment) matches the reference entity of the credit derivative (‘name matching’); and
- the seniority of the financial instrument matches that of the instruments that can be delivered in accordance with the credit derivative.

46 – Hedge accounting (IFRS 9)
FAQ 46.1.1 – What is hedge accounting?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para 6.1.1 Reference to standing text: 46.1
What is hedge accounting?

Entities are exposed to financial risks arising from many aspects of their business. Different entities are concerned about different risks. For example, some entities might be concerned about exchange rates or interest rates, while others might be concerned about commodity prices. Entities implement varying risk management strategies to eliminate, reduce or modify their risk exposures.

Hedge accounting is a technique that modifies the normal basis for recognising gains and losses (or revenues and expenses) on associated hedging instruments and hedged items, so that both are recognised in P&L (or OCI) in the same accounting period. This is a matching concept that eliminates or reduces the volatility in the statement of comprehensive income that otherwise would arise if the hedged item and the hedging instrument were accounted for separately under IFRS. Hedge accounting is optional, and management should consider the costs and benefits when deciding whether to use it.
FAQ 46.2.1 – Why is macro hedging addressed as a separate project?

The reason for the IASB addressing such hedges separately is that hedges of open portfolios introduce additional complexity. As time passes, new exposures are continuously added to such hedged portfolios, and other exposures are removed, with corresponding adjustments being made to the instruments used to hedge those exposures. In addition, the hedged portfolio often comprises both assets and liabilities and only a part of the overall exposure is hedged. Lapse or surrender features that are present in many insurance contracts could be regarded as similar to a prepayment option in a loan, and they can be a source of ineffectiveness. Entity A enters into an interest rate swap contract to hedge changes in the fair value of a fixed-rate borrowing of C100m due for settlement in five years. The terms of the borrowing and the swap exactly match. Interest rates rise so that the borrowing’s fair value falls to C90m and the swap’s fair value changes from zero to minus C10m.

Under fair value hedge accounting, the swap is carried as a liability of C10m (less any settlement paid). The carrying amount of the borrowing is reduced to C90m. Both the loss and the gain are recognised in P&L. Under the amortised cost method, the C90m carrying amount of the liability would be amortised back up to C100m, giving rise to additional finance cost over the remaining period to maturity.
As noted in paragraph 46.9, IFRS 9 allows amortisation to be deferred until hedge accounting is discontinued. What is the practical impact of deferring amortisation in this example?

If the swap is in place until the borrowing’s maturity date, the debt’s carrying amount will be adjusted back to C100m through further hedge accounting adjustments. In other words, any fair value adjustments to the debt’s carrying value would be reversed by maturity, as the fair value of the liability immediately before settlement must be C100m. Therefore, no amortisation will be necessary.

For example, consider an entity that holds a fixed-rate debt instrument which is accounted for at amortised cost. IFRS 9 indicates (in para 6.3.7) that an entity may designate an item in its entirety or a component of an item as the hedged item in a hedging relationship. These adjustments are in addition to the effective interest rate adjustments made in determining the amortised cost of the hedged item. In such instances, since the fair value of the designated cash flows of the hedged item

However, in other types of designation, the cumulative change in the fair value of the hedged item arising from the hedged risk might not amount to zero. This could be the case where, for example, the designation occurs when the fair value of the designated cash flows is not at par, or where a component other than the benchmark rate is designated. FAQ 46.12.1 – Can the amounts recorded in OCI as a result of changes in fair value of the hedging instrument in a fair value hedge of an equity instrument designated at FVOCI be transferred to other components of equity?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para 6.5.8(a) Reference to standing text: 46.12

Can the amounts recorded in OCI as a result of changes in fair value of the hedging instrument in a fair value hedge of an equity instrument designated at FVOCI be transferred to other components of equity?

Company A holds equity instruments issued by an unrelated company. Since the equity instruments are not held for trading, company A voluntarily elected to designate them at fair value through OCI (FVOCI) on initial recognition. In order to mitigate its exposure to changes in fair value, company A subsequently enters into a derivative that it designates as a fair value hedge of the equity instruments.

Yes. Increases or decreases in the fair value of the equity instruments are recognised in OCI and not subsequently transferred to profit or loss. [IFRS 9 App B para B5.7.1]. However, the entity could transfer the cumulative gain or loss within equity at any time. [IFRS 9 para BC E.38].

On that basis, it would be acceptable to transfer the gain or loss on the hedging instrument and on the hedged equity instrument at the same time and to the same other component of equity, subject to jurisdiction-specific restrictions. Such a transfer would not go through the statement of comprehensive income.
As an alternative, company A could choose to keep the gains and losses in their original equity components. The chosen accounting policy should be applied consistently and disclosed.

FAQ 46.20.1 – Does IFRS 9 require debit balances in the cash flow hedge reserve to be tested for recoverability?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para 6.5.11(d)(iii) Reference to standing text:46.20

Changes in commodity prices, foreign exchange rates and other market prices may give rise to fair value movements on hedging instruments. Debit balances may be included in the cash flow hedge reserve as a result of such market movements. Does IFRS 9 require these debit balances to be tested for recoverability?

Yes. Paragraph 6.5.11(d)(iii) of IFRS 9 requires recoverability to be considered for losses in cash flow hedging reserves (that is, where the accumulated amounts are in a loss position). Where an entity expects all or a portion of such losses will not be recovered in one or more future periods, it should immediately reclassify the amount not expected to be recovered to profit or loss.

IFRS 9 does not provide specific guidance on how the recoverability test should be applied, and entities should consider their accounting policies for the assessment of recoverability of these amounts. Where such debit balances are significant, an entity should consider whether disclosure about the accounting policy – and about significant judgement in the application of that policy – is required in accordance with paragraph 122 of IAS 1.

However, prior to assessing such debit balances for recoverability, the entity should consider whether recycling of such balances is required for other reasons (for example, if a forecast transaction is no longer expected to occur). See paragraph 46.153 for the required treatment of discontinued cash flow hedges.
FAQ 46.25.1 – What amount of a net investment in a foreign operation qualifies as a hedged item in a net investment hedge?
Reference to standard: IFRIC 16 para 11 Reference to standing text: 46.25
What amount of a net investment in a foreign operation qualifies as a hedged item in a net investment hedge?
Company W, whose functional currency is the Euro, has a wholly owned US subsidiary, subsidiary D, whose functional currency is US dollars.

The carrying value of subsidiary D’s net assets is USD70 million. Subsidiary D’s net assets include an inter-company borrowing of USD10 million received from company W, which is not expected to be settled in the foreseeable future.
Subsidiary D’s management predicts that it is highly probable that it will:
- earn a profit of at least USD8 million; and
- pay a dividend of USD5 million to company W.
Company W also plan to make a capital contribution to subsidiary D in one year’s time.
Company W can hedge up to USD80 million of its net investment in subsidiary D at the date of hedge designation. The USD80 million is represented by:
- USD70 million of subsidiary D’s net assets; and

- USD10 million inter-company loan. This loan could be designated as a hedged item, because it is not expected to be settled in the foreseeable future and therefore, in substance, forms part of company W’s net investment in subsidiary D [IAS 21 para 15].

Subsidiary D’s forecast profits (USD8 million) and forecast inter-company dividend payments (USD5 million) cannot be included in the hedged item, because they do not form part of company W’s existing net investment. The undeclared forecast inter-company dividend payments (USD5 million) do not qualify as hedged items, because they will not affect reported net profit or loss. As the profits are earned, they increase the net investment and can then be included in the hedged item. When dividends are paid, the amount covered in the net investment hedge might need to be reduced correspondingly.

The forecast capital contribution is also not an eligible hedged item because the forecast cash flows will never affect profit or loss. The fair value of subsidiary D plus cash held by company W will be exactly the same before and after the contribution.
FAQ 46.25.2 – Can goodwill be included in a net investment hedge?
Reference to standard: IAS 21 para 47 Reference to standing text: 46.25 Corporate treasury
Can goodwill be included in a net investment hedge?

Entity A, a EUR functional currency company, has acquired a US subsidiary for USD200 million. After accounting for the acquisition, the entity shows in its balance sheet a net asset of USD200 million that includes goodwill (fully allocated to the purchased entity) of USD100 million.

Entity A’s management decides to hedge the foreign currency risk on its USD200 million investment by entering into a forward contract to sell USD200 million for EUR. For accounting purposes, entity A’s management wishes to designate the net asset (including the goodwill) as the hedged item in a net investment hedge relationship and apply hedge accounting.
Yes, entity A’s goodwill is a part of the net investment at the group level. As a result, it can be designated as a part of the hedged item in a net investment hedge because:

- IAS 21 requires any goodwill arising on the acquisition of a foreign operation to be treated as an asset of the foreign operation and, thus, to be expressed in the functional currency of the foreign operation and translated at the closing rate through OCI. [IAS 21 para 47].
- In the case of disposal of the foreign operation, the gains and losses arising on the retranslation will be reclassified to profit or loss.
