FAQ 46.156.1 – Can entities use the fair value option for ‘own use’ contracts to reduce P&L volatility?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para 2.5 Reference to standing text: 46.156

Entities in the utilities industry often have a large number of contracts requiring physical delivery of energy, and generally these contracts are ‘own use’ contracts under IFRS 9. These entities commonly hedge with energy derivatives. Can the utilities entities reduce P&L volatility without formally designating their physical delivery contracts in hedge relationships by using the ‘fair value option’ in IFRS 9?

Yes. By electing to designate the physical contracts at fair value through P&L, they are likely to significantly reduce the measurement inconsistency between the physical contracts and the energy derivatives, and thus achieve offsetting effects without the need to apply hedge accounting (and therefore comply with the hedge accounting criteria).
FAQ 46.156.2 – What is the meaning of ‘readily convertible to cash’?
Reference to standard:IFRS 9 para 2.5 Reference to standing text: 46.156

IFRS 9 introduced the ‘fair value option’ for ‘own use’ contracts providing certain criteria are met. It is also one of the criteria to consider in determining whether a contract is net settled and therefore eligible for own use treatment or not. What is the meaning of readily convertible to cash in this context?

There is no explicit guidance on the meaning of ‘readily convertible to cash’ in IFRS. However, in the absence of a substantive net settlement provision in the contract, an entity would only be able to apply the fair value option if:

- there was a liquid market (spot or forward) in which the non-financial item (commodity or transformed product) could be sold for a price that preserves the value of the underlying raw material; in other words, it is not significantly less than would have been received under a net settlement provision; or
- it is possible to easily convert the non-financial item back into the raw material (for which there is a liquid market) with insignificant time, effort and cost.
FAQ 46.156.3 – Fair value option alternative to hedge accounting: when does a contract meet the readily convertible to cash requirement?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 paras 2.5, 2.6 Reference to standing text: 46.156

Entities enter into fixed price purchase or sale contracts where the fair value of the contract could be derived with reference to market prices and/or components. Although IFRS 9 allows the designation of components for non-financial items as hedged items in certain circumstances, the application of hedge accounting requires additional administration such as the monitoring of designations, calculation of ineffectiveness and performing of prospective effectiveness assessments.

As an alternative to hedge accounting, IFRS 9 allows an entity to irrevocably designate and measure a contract to buy or sell a non-financial item that can be settled net in cash or another financial instrument, or by exchanging financial instruments (as if the contract was a financial instrument) at FVTPL, even if it was entered into for the purposes of the receipt or delivery of a non-financial item in accordance with the entity’s expected purchase, sale, or usage requirements (that is, an ‘own use’ contract), provided that it eliminates or significantly reduces an accounting mismatch. [IFRS

Paragraph 2.6 of IFRS 9 sets out four ways in which a contract can be settled net. Two of these (IFRS 9 para 2.6(b) and (c)) would automatically require the contract to be subject to the requirements of IFRS 9 and measured at FVTPL. For designation at FVTPL to therefore be relevant, one of the other two must be met. These are that the contract either includes a clause that permits net settlement in cash or another financial instrument (IFRS 9 para 2.6(a)), or the non-financial item that is subject to the contract is readily convertible to cash (IFRS 9 para 2.6(d)). If neither of these is met,

Note: It is assumed for the purpose of this memo that only fixed price contracts or contracts with fixed price components would qualify, since a variable price contract would most probably not give rise to material fair value adjustments.
Considering the requirements above, when would a non-financial item that is the subject of a purchase or sale contract meet the ‘readily convertible to cash’ requirements of IFRS 9?

A non-financial item is readily convertible to cash only if the net amount of cash that would be received from its sale (that is, sale proceeds minus conversion costs) in an active market is either equal to or not significantly less than the amount the entity would typically have incurred in the production or purchase of the underlying item.

This would be the case if there is a liquid market for the non-financial item in its current state and location, and the entity is able to trade the item and not derive a significantly different result than an explicit net settlement provision would provide. This determination should consider the location of the item, the transport cost in relocating it to a liquid market hub, as well as the ease/timing of converting and selling the related item within the market without being exposed to undue market movements.
With regards to processed/manufactured products, that is, products derived from items that in themselves might be readily convertible to cash, one would similarly have to consider whether:
- There is a liquid market for the product (that is, the item in its current form and location) that enables recovery of the contract price; or
- The transformed product can be converted back into the underlying product which is traded in a liquid market with insignificant cost and time.

An entity should therefore evaluate the significance of the estimated costs of converting the item to cash (or back to its liquid trading form) in determining whether it is readily convertible to cash. The assessment of the significance of those conversion costs should be performed at inception of the contract. Where a product (for example, aluminium soft drink cans) is derived from an item in a liquid trading form (for example, aluminium ingots), the conversions costs should include both the initial conversion cost (that is, the cost of converting the aluminium ingots into cans), as well as t
Consider the following example:
An entity has entered into a contract to sell aluminium soft drink cans for $1 each. The sales price of a can consists of the following components:
- a pure aluminium component amounting to $0.60;
- manufacturing and other costs of $0.35; and
- a profit margin of $0.05.

Assume that there is no liquid market for aluminium cans that enables the recovery of the contract price, and that the cost of melting down a can and recasting it into ingots which are traded in a liquid market amounts to $0.15.

In determining whether the cans are readily convertible to cash (from the seller’s point of view), the significance of the initial production/conversion cost as well as the cost of converting the item back into its ‘liquid trading’ form should be assessed against the amount that could be realised. The initial production cost, which is included in the cost of the original product (that is, the can) at inception of the contract, would essentially be lost during the subsequent conversion process and should therefore not be omitted from the analysis.

Component Amount Original aluminium component $0.60 Original manufacturing and other costs $0.35 Original cost price $0.95 Gross recoverable amount $0.60 Cost of converting product back to liquid trading form ($0.15) Net recoverable amount $0.45

In this instance, an acceptable approach to doing the analysis would be to compare the recoverable amount to the cost of $0.95. It would only be possible to derive a maximum of $0.45 (that is, $0.60 of aluminium (assuming no product losses) after incurring the melting and recasting cost of $0.15) from every can which costs $0.95 to produce.

The original cost of the product ($0.95) would be regarded as significantly different to the net recoverable amount ($0.45) and the contract would therefore not meet the readily convertible to cash requirement.

Based on the criteria mentioned above, conclusions for a commodity could therefore differ within the same commodity chain due to different locations, availability of transformation facilities and/or the extent of product modifications. Each case would therefore have to be considered based on the specific facts and circumstances.
FAQ 46.159.1 – Are index-based credit default swaps eligible hedging instruments for a portfolio of financial assets?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para 6.7.1 Reference to standing text: 46.159
Are index-based credit default swaps eligible hedging instruments for a portfolio of financial assets?

Given the IFRS 9 requirement to match the name of the borrower or seniority between the credit exposure and the credit derivative, index-based credit default swaps would not be eligible hedging instruments for a portfolio of financial assets.
FAQ 46.159.2 – If the fair value option is elected, would there be a perfect offset between the credit exposure and the credit derivative?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para 6.7.1 Reference to standing text: 46.159
If the fair value option is elected, would there be a perfect offset between the credit exposure and the credit derivative?

Even where the fair value option is available, the fair value of the financial instrument designated at fair value through P&L might be affected by other risks not present in the credit derivative (for instance, interest rate risk), and hence there will not be a perfect offset.
FAQ 46.159.3 – When can an entity designate a financial instrument at fair value through profit or loss to help it manage credit risk?
Reference to standard : IFRS 9 para 6.7.1 Reference to standing text: 46.159 , 42.59 N/A

Paragraph 6.7.1 of IFRS 9 allows an entity to designate a financial instrument at fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL) where the entity uses a credit derivative to manage the credit risk of all or part of the credit exposure on that financial instrument. If such a designation is applied to a pre-existing credit exposure, then at the time of the designation, the difference between the carrying amount of the financial instrument, if any, and the fair value is recognised immediately in profit or loss.
What are the relevant requirements and practical considerations when assessing whether a financial instrument may be designated under paragraph 6.7.1?
The following requirements apply when designating a financial instrument:

- The entity must have adopted IFRS 9 hedge accounting. That is because, as noted in paragraph 7.2.21 of IFRS 9, if an entity applies the hedge accounting requirements of IAS 39 instead of applying chapter 6 of IFRS 9, paragraph 6.7.1 cannot be used.

- The credit derivative used to manage the credit risk of the financial instrument must be measured at FVTPL. Therefore, if, for example, the credit derivative meets the definition of a financial guarantee in Appendix A to IFRS 9 and is not measured at FVTPL, the associated credit exposure may not be designated as FVTPL under paragraph 6.7.1.
- The credit derivative must be used to manage the credit risk of all, or a part, of the financial instrument.
- Where only a proportion of the credit exposure (for example, 80%) is managed for credit risk using the credit derivative, an entity may only designate that proportion as measured at FVTPL.
- The name of the credit exposure (for example, the borrower or holder of the loan commitment) must match the reference entity of the credit derivative.
- The seniority of the financial instrument must match that of the instruments that can be delivered in accordance with the credit derivative.
- The entity must document the designation concurrently.

In addition, paragraph BC6.543(b) of IFRS 9 notes the IASB’s concern that paragraph 6.7.1 could be used for earnings management. Therefore it is important to ensure that the credit derivative is genuinely being used for credit risk management purposes and not for earnings management. Relevant factors in assessing whether this is the case, as well as other practical considerations, are set out below.

Risk management documentation – Documentation of the designation would be expected to be incorporated within the entity’s normal risk management framework. The credit risk management strategy would also be expected to be reviewed, approved and monitored by the appropriate governance forum(s) applicable to other similar risk management strategies of the entity.

Discontinuation – The risk management documentation would be expected to clearly explain the circumstances in which the credit derivative could be terminated / sold, or the credit exposure could cease to be managed using the credit derivative, given that such events would discontinue the designation. If a designation were discontinued after only a short period, that would call into question whether the designation was genuinely part of the entity’s risk management and a valid designation, rather than just short-term earnings management.

Term of credit derivative versus period of credit exposure – Paragraph 6.7.1 of IFRS 9 contains no requirement for the term of the credit derivative to equal or exceed the period of the credit exposure, thus avoiding the need to ‘roll’ or re-hedge at a later date or be exposed to credit risk during the remaining life of the credit exposure. Furthermore, paragraph 6.7.3(a)(i) contemplates a designation being discontinued where the credit derivative expires before the credit exposure, indicating that a designation can be valid where the period of the credit derivative is less than the term of th

The extent of credit risk exposure managed – Where only a proportion of the credit exposure is managed for credit risk using the credit derivative, the proportion designated as FVTPL should be determined in a manner consistent with the risk management policy. For example, consider a situation where an entity has purchased a five-year credit default swap (‘CDS’) to manage the risk on a seven-year credit exposure, and where the notional amount of the CDS matches the notional amount of the credit exposure. If, due to historical correlations between five-year and seven-year credit risk, the entity

Where an entity has credit exposure arising from a variety of instruments classified as FVTPL, FVOCI and/or amortised cost, and it manages only a part of that total credit exposure with credit derivatives, unless the credit risk management policy clearly demonstrates otherwise, it would be expected that the credit derivatives would be considered to manage the credit risk of each of those instruments on a pro-rata basis.

Interaction with hedge accounting – Where the credit exposure is already designated within an accounting hedge relationship under IFRS 9 and is then designated at FVTPL under paragraph 6.7.1, there might be other considerations.

For example, where the credit exposure is the hedged item in a fair value hedge of interest rate risk, the carrying value of the instrument will already have been adjusted for changes in fair value attributable to changes in interest rate risk, which will also have been recognised in profit or loss. As a result, the gain or loss on designation (equal to the difference between the carrying amount at the time of designation – including the adjustment for the fair value hedge – and the fair value) will not include the previously recognised interest rate-related gains / losses on the credit exposu

Where the credit exposure is in a cash flow hedge of interest rate risk, following the paragraph 6.7.1 designation the balance accumulated in the cash flow hedge reserve would continue to be recycled to profit or loss over time in accordance with paragraph 6.5.11d(ii). This reflects that the credit exposure is a variable-rate debt instrument whose fair value is not affected by movements in market interest rates, and so the designation would not accelerate the timing of when the hedged expected future cash flows affect profit or loss.
Disclosure – Where an entity has designated a credit exposure in accordance with paragraph 6.7.1, it will need to disclose:
- The carrying amounts of the credit exposures designated as FVTPL. [IFRS 7 para 8(a), (e)].
- The net gains or losses recognised in respect of the credit exposures, separately from other instruments measured at FVTPL. [IFRS 7 para 20(a)(i)].
- For credit derivatives used to manage the credit risk, a reconciliation of each of the nominal amount and the fair value at the beginning and end of the period. [IFRS 7 para 24G(a)].
- The gain or loss recognised in profit or loss on designation. [IFRS 7 para 24G(b)].

- On discontinuation, the financial instrument’s fair value that has become the new carrying amount in accordance with paragraph 6.7.4(b) of IFRS 9 and the related nominal or principal amount. Except for providing comparative information in accordance with IAS 1, an entity does not need to continue this disclosure in subsequent periods. [IFRS 7 para 24G(c)].

- Any changes to its objectives, policies and processes for managing credit risk and the methods used to measure credit risk (for example, where an entity starts to manage credit exposures using credit derivatives). [IFRS 7 para 33(c)].
In addition, where there is a critical accounting judgement in connection with the designation, this should be disclosed in accordance with paragraph 122 of IAS 1.
FAQ 46.169.1 – Will an entity have to de-designate hedges on transition to IFRS 9 if it changes its method of calculating effectiveness to take account of the time value of money?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para B6.5.4 Reference to standing text: 46.169 Corporate Treasury

Entity A whose functional currency is the euro decides to hedge its foreign currency risk of USD1m highly probable sales in 9 months’ time. In accordance with its risk management policy it designates changes in the spot foreign currency rate as the hedged risk in a cash flow hedge. The designated hedging instrument is the spot component of a 9-month foreign exchange forward contract, expected to mature at the same time as the forecast sales.

IFRS 9 requires that the measurement of the effectiveness of a hedge relationship reflects the time value of money (see para 46.55 for more details). Hence, for the purpose of measuring ineffectiveness the hedged item should be measured on a present value basis (which means the spot foreign currency rate will need to be discounted). This is a change from IAS 39 under which entities often do not discount when hedging changes in the spot rate.
Is the entity required to de-designate its previous hedge on transition to IFRS 9 because IFRS 9 introduces the requirement to move to discounted spot basis for hedge effectiveness testing?

No. There is no clear guidance in IFRS 9 but, considering the nature of the change, our view is that beginning to measure hedge effectiveness using a discounted spot rather than on an undiscounted spot basis is a continuing hedge under IFRS 9. It is a refinement of the method of testing effectiveness, which is part of the required accounting rather than a change in designation. Therefore, entity A is not required to de-designate its hedge.

As an alternative, could entity A choose to change the hedged risk from changes in the spot foreign currency rate to changes in the forward foreign currency rate? In this case would entity A be required to de-designate its previous hedge?

Yes. If entity A chooses to change the hedged risk from changes in the spot foreign currency rate to changes in the forward foreign currency rate, in our view this would give rise to a new hedge relationship under both IFRS 9 and IAS 39. This is a change in the documented hedged risk, which is an essential part of the designated hedge relationship, so entity A would be required to de-designate its hedge.
EX 46.169.2 – Examples of how to transition to IFRS 9 for fair value hedges of interest rate risk
Reference to standard: IFRS 7.2.24 Reference to standing text: 45.169

The transitional provisions of IFRS 9 requires the classification of financial assets and liabilities to be applied retrospectively, irrespective of the entity’s business model in prior periods. It requires hedge accounting to be applied prospectively (in most circumstances), and allows for hedging relationships which qualified for hedge accounting under both IAS 39 and IFRS 9 to be regarded as continuing relationships.

The standard is not clear on how fair value adjustments arising from the application of fair value hedge accounting under IAS 39 should be treated on transition. The discussion below illustrates scenarios where a fixed-rate bond asset is designated in a fair value hedge relationship, but depending on its classification under IAS 39 and the interpretation of the transitional provisions of IFRS 9, different retained income opening balances could potentially be achieved regardless of the fact that the same instruments and hedging strategies were applied. For example, in a fair value hedge relatio

Bank A has invested in an unquoted fixed-rate bond. The bond asset is classified as a ‘loan and receivable’ under IAS 39. In order to hedge against changes in the fair value of the bond, the bank entered into a ‘pay fixed receive floating’ interest rate swap and designated the swap and the bond in a fair value hedge relationship. The fair value hedge accounting results in the carrying amount of the bond to be adjusted with the change in the fair value of the bond relating to the hedged risk (that is, interest rate risk), with the contra to be recognised in profit or loss.

Based on Bank A’s assessment of its business model and contractual cash flows of the bond, it has determined that on adoption of IFRS 9 the bond asset will continue to be carried at amortised cost. Hedge accounting will be continued for the relationship under IFRS 9 since the hedge relationship qualifies for hedge accounting under both IAS 39 and IFRS 9.

There is no indication that IFRS 9 requires the impact of qualifying hedge relationships to be reversed upon transition to the standard. Although the carrying amount of the bond has been adjusted with certain changes in its fair value, the adjustments are due to the application of hedge accounting and not the classification of the bond under IAS 39. Since the hedge relationship will continue under IFRS 9, no adjustment will be made to the fair value adjustment recorded against the carrying amount of the bond nor will its effective interest rate be revised.

Both the change in the fair value of the swap and the fair value of the bond recorded under IAS 39 will therefore remain within retained income, resulting in an unadjusted retained income opening balance.

Same as scenario 1 above, but due to the revised composition of the balance sheet on adoption of IFRS 9, Bank A expects that the hedging of the bond and therefore hedge accounting would no longer be required. It will de-designate the hedge relationship on transition to IFRS 9 and expects to either close-out the swap or assign it to another portfolio shortly thereafter.

Although the carrying amount of the bond has been adjusted with certain changes in its fair value, the adjustments are due to the application of hedge accounting and not the classification of the bond under IAS 39. Since the hedge relationship will not continue under IFRS 9, the effective interest rate of the bond will be revised and the revised effective interest rate will be utilised for the recognition of interest under IFRS 9.

Both the change in the fair value of the swap and the fair value of the bond recognised under IAS 39 will therefore remain within retained income, resulting in an unadjusted retained income opening balance.

Bank A has invested in a fixed-rate bond for liquid asset purposes. The bond is classified as an available-for-sale (‘AFS’) asset under IAS 39. In order to hedge against changes in the fair value of the bond, the bank entered into a ‘pay fixed receive floating’ interest rate swap and designated the swap and the bond in a fair value hedge relationship. The fair value hedge accounting results in the change in the fair value of the bond relating to the hedged risk (that is, interest rate risk) to be recognised in profit or loss rather than in OCI.

Based on Bank A’s assessment of its business model and contractual cash flows of the bond, it has determined that on adoption of IFRS 9 the bond asset will be carried at amortised cost. It has also determined that due to the revised composition of the balance sheet on adoption of IFRS 9, the hedging of the bond and subsequent hedge accounting would no longer be required. It will de-designate the hedge relationship on transition to IFRS 9 and expects to either close-out the swap or assign it to another portfolio shortly thereafter.

Although IFRS 9 requires the classification of the bond on transition to the standard to be applied retrospectively, the bond was designated in a fair value hedge relationship for a portion of its life. Based on the conclusion in scenario 2 above, the change in the fair value of the bond relating to the hedged risk recorded during the fair value hedge designation period should not be reversed (that is, only the residual fair value changes should be reversed).

The carrying amount of the bond should therefore be restated only to the extent of the ‘non-hedge accounted’ fair value adjustments. Any balance in the ‘AFS reserve’ relating to fair value adjustments on the bond should therefore be adjusted against the carrying amount of the bond (to clear out the ‘AFS reserve’ to zero).

Both the change in the fair value of the swap and the fair value of the bond (for the designated period) will therefore remain within retained income, resulting in an unadjusted retained income opening balance insofar as the interest rate risk was hedged (and hedge accounted).

Since the hedge relationship will not continue under IFRS 9, the effective interest rate of the bond will be revised based on the restated carrying amount (which consists of the amortised cost plus the hedge accounted fair value adjustments not reversed) and the revised effective interest rate will be utilised for the recognition of interest under IFRS 9.

Same as scenario 3 above, but based on the entity’s assessment of the post IFRS 9 balance sheet structure, fair value hedging is still required. Fair value hedge accounting is therefore continued as the hedge relationship qualified for hedge accounting under both IAS 39 and IFRS 9.

Same as solution 3 above. The carrying amount of the bond should be restated only to the extent of the ‘non-hedge accounted’ fair value adjustments and hedge accounting will continue uninterrupted. The effective interest rate on the bond will ignore any fair value hedge adjustments since fair value hedge accounting has not yet ceased.

Both the change in the fair value of the swap and the fair value of the bond (for the designated period) will therefore remain within retained income, resulting in an unadjusted retained income opening balance insofar as the interest rate risk was hedged.

Bank A has invested in a fixed-rate bond. The bond is designated at fair value through P&L (‘FVTPL’) under IAS 39. In order to hedge against changes in the fair value of the bond, the bank entered into a ‘pay fixed receive floating’ interest rate swap but does not apply any hedge accounting due to the natural offset obtained in profit or loss.

Based on Bank A’s assessment of its business model and contractual cash flows of the bond, it has determined that on adoption of IFRS 9 the bond asset will be carried at amortised cost. The fair value of the bond would also continue to be economically hedged with the aforementioned interest rate swap.

The carrying amount of the bond will be restated to its amortised cost. Since the change in the fair value of the swap will however remain in retained income, this will result in a mismatch in the retained income opening balance.
However, should the Bank designate the bond at FVTPL based on an accounting mismatch, it would be able to avoid the reversal of the change in the fair value on the bond.

Additional consideration: In order to pre-empt the above-mentioned issue which would arise under IFRS 9, the entity could choose to designate the bond and swap in a fair value hedge relationship (provided that it is in line with their risk management strategy) regardless of the fact that it would not result in any accounting difference under IAS 39, apart from a different presentation in profit or loss. The adjustments made to the fair value of the bond due to the fair value hedge designation would then not be reversed on adoption of IFRS 9 as suggested under solutions 3 and 4 above.
FAQ 46.171.1 – How should a basis adjustment be accounted for on transition to IFRS 9?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 paras 6.5.11(d), 7.2.22 Reference to standing text: 46.171 Corporate Treasury

An entity might elect to hedge a forecast transaction that subsequently results in recognition of a non-financial asset or a non-financial liability. When the hedged transaction occurs, IAS 39 provides the entity with an accounting policy choice to:

- recycle the amount that has been accumulated in the cash flow hedge reserve to profit or loss in the same period or periods during which the non-financial asset acquired or non-financial liability assumed affects profit or loss; or
- adjust the initial cost or other carrying amount of the non-financial asset or the non-financial liability (often referred to as ‘basis adjustment in a cash flow hedge’).

Entity A previously chose to recycle when the hedged cash flows affected profit under IAS 39 (that is, it did not basis adjust the carrying amount of the non-financial asset or non-financial liability).
How should the basis adjustment be accounted for on transition to IFRS 9?
IFRS 9 eliminates the accounting policy choice provided by IAS 39. Therefore going forward the entity must account for the basis adjustment.

On transition to IFRS 9, an accounting policy choice can be applied where the non-financial item has already been recognised at the date of initial application, but the hedging movements have been held in the hedging reserve.

An entity can apply the new hedge accounting requirements to all hedge relationships existing on the date of transition. Accordingly, the amount accumulated in the cash flow hedge reserve at the date of initial application should be removed from the reserve and included in the carrying amount of the corresponding non-financial asset or non-financial liability. Entity A (a calendar-year reporter) would make an adjustment on 1 January in the year of adoption of IFRS 9. The comparative balance sheet (at 31 December) is not adjusted. This basis adjustment is not a reclassification adjustment, and

An entity can continue to hold amounts in the hedging reserve and recycle to profit and loss when the non-financial asset or non-financial liability affects profit or loss. This is a reclassification adjustment and is therefore recorded through other comprehensive income in the period of reclassification.

This accounting policy choice exists only for those non-financial items already recognised at the date of initial application. For subsequent recognition of non-financial items recognised as a result of a hedge of a forecast transaction, a basis adjustment must be made to the initial carrying value of the non-financial asset or non-financial liability.
FAQ 46.171.2 – How should an entity account for the time value of options expiring before the date of initial application on transition to IFRS 9?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9.paras 7.2.26(a), 7.2.2 Reference to standing text: 46.171 Corporate Treasury

IFRS 9 requires, as a general rule, the hedge accounting requirements to be applied prospectively. [IFRS 9 para 7.2.22]. However, as an exception to this rule, an entity “shall apply the accounting for the time value of options in accordance with paragraph 6.5.15 retrospectively if, in accordance with IAS 39, only the change in an option’s intrinsic value was designated as a hedging instrument in a hedging relationship. This retrospective application applies only to those hedging instruments that existed at the beginning of the earliest comparative period or were designated thereafter”.

Entity H adopts IFRS 9 in its financial statements for the year ended 31 December 20X6. The date of initial application (‘DIA’) is 1 January 20X6. The entity prepares one year of comparative information in its financial statements, so the beginning of the earliest comparative period is 1 January 20X5.

In the past, entity H adopted an option-based hedging strategy, designating the intrinsic value of those options in a hedge relationship in accordance with IAS 39. However, those options expired (or were exercised) in November 20X5.

Does entity H need to restate the 20X5 comparatives in its 20X6 financial statements to account for the time value of the options that expired or were exercised prior to the DIA in accordance withparagraph 6.5.15 upon adoption of IFRS 9? Note that the retrospective application of the requirements would impact the amount of time value deferred in OCI as at 1 January 20X5 and hence the aggregate charge in the 20X5 statement of profit or loss.
Entity H has an accounting policy choice as to whether to restate the 20X5 comparatives.

Paragraph 7.2.26(a) of IFRS 9 is clear that the accounting for time value of options must be applied retrospectively to those instruments existing at the beginning of the earliest comparative period (or designated thereafter) if, in accordance with IAS 39, only the change in an option’s intrinsic value was designated as a hedging instrument in a hedging relationship. This can be read to imply the 20X5 comparatives should be restated.

However, if the qualifying criteria for hedge accounting were not met at the date of initial application as defined in paragraph 7.2.2 of IFRS 9 (that is, at 1 January 20X6 in the above example), because there was no longer a hedging instrument outstanding at that date, then hedge accounting cannot be applied under paragraph 7.2.23 of IFRS 9. If IFRS 9 hedge accounting is not being applied, there is an argument that comparatives should not be restated to apply the IFRS 9 approach to the time value of the options that expired prior to 1 January 20X6.

We believe that a policy choice of restatement or not is available to entity H. The chosen policy should be applied consistently to all options expiring before the date of initial application of IFRS 9.
FAQ 46.172.1 – How can an entity transition hedge relationships with cross-currency interest rate swaps to IFRS 9?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para 7.2.26 Reference to standing text: 46.172 Corporate Treasury

On 1 July 2015, company A entered into a five-year cross-currency interest rate swap (CCIRS) to hedge the foreign exchange risk on a foreign currency-denominated, five-year fixed-rate borrowing issued on the same date. The CCIRS swaps the fixed-rate foreign currency cash flows on the borrowing to floating-rate local currency cash flows (principal and interest).
The company applied hedge accounting under IAS 39 from the inception date of the swap. The hedge designation was a split/dual designation including:
- a cash flow hedge component (for the foreign currency risk on the credit margin component, that is, the spread above the benchmark interest rate); and
- a fair value hedge component (for the benchmark rate component, that is, the benchmark interest rate and the principal cash flow).

To measure the effectiveness of 1) above under IAS 39, the hypothetical derivative method was used. The hypothetical derivative (‘hypo’) was modelled as a derivative to mirror the hedged risk and while IAS 39 is silent on the matter, a charge for currency basis (CB) was included in the hypo’s cash flows because company A considered this charge to exist in such a stand-alone derivative. (See chapter 6.8A para 29.)

At each subsequent effectiveness testing date, changes in value of the CCIRS due to CB were similarly mirrored in the change in value of the hypo and therefore did not give rise to ineffectiveness in the hedge relationship.

At 1 January 2018, company A adopts IFRS 9. The company wishes to treat its hedge relationships as ‘continuing’ hedges under paragraph 7.2.24 of IFRS 9 to avoid possible adverse consequences from de-designation and re-designation. IFRS 9 does not allow risks, such as CB, to be modelled in the hypothetical derivative if they only exist in the hedging instrument.
Assume the hedge relationships meet the qualifying criteria under paragraph 6.4 of IFRS 9 and that company A maintains the split/dual designation as described above.
What transition approaches would enable the company to treat their hedge relationships as ‘continuing’ hedges under IFRS 9?

Transition approach Description A: Retrospectively change hedge designation to exclude CB. Retrospectively change hypo to exclude CB. Approach: Remove CB from the hedge designation. text: 47.15 A financial asset and a financial liability should be offset when, and only when, both of the following are satisfied:

text: - The entity currently has a legally enforceable right to set off the recognised amounts.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)

text: 47.16 If the offset conditions are satisfied, and the entity has the right to receive or pay a single net amount and it intends to do so, it has, in effect, only a single financial asset or financial liability. In that situation, the financial asset and the financial liability are presented on the balance sheet on a net basis. If the offset conditions are not satisfied, the financial asset and the financial liability are presented separately from each other, consistently with their characteristics as the entity’s resources or obligations.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: 47.17 There can be situations where there are transfers of financial assets that do not qualify for de-recognition and, in such cases, the entity has to recognise an associated liability (see chapter 44 para 80). De-recognising a financial instrument not only results in the removal of the previously recognised item from the balance sheet, but it might also result in recognition of a gain or loss. Offsetting does not give rise to recognition of a gain or loss. When considering presentation of particular items, recognition, de-recognition and measurement need to be considered first.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: 47.18 A right of set-off is “a debtor’s legal right, by contract or otherwise, to settle or otherwise eliminate all or a portion of an amount due to a creditor by applying against that amount an amount due from the creditor”. The conditions supporting the right might vary from one legal jurisdiction to another and, therefore, the laws applicable to the relationships between the parties would need to be considered carefully. For offsetting to be applied by a reporting entity, the legal right of set-off does not have to be held by all parties to the contract, only by the reporting entity.

text: - Market risk – the risk that the fair value or cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate, because of changes in market prices. Market risk embodies not only the potential for loss, but also the potential for gain. It comprises three types of risk, as follows:

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Interest rate risk – the risk that the fair value or future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of changes in market interest rates.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Currency risk – the risk that the fair value or future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of changes in foreign exchange rates.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Other price risk – the risk that the fair value or future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of changes in market prices (other than those arising from interest rate risk or currency risk), whether those changes are caused by factors specific to the individual financial instrument or its issuer, or by factors affecting all similar financial instruments traded in the market.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Credit risk – the risk that the counterparty to a financial instrument will cause a financial loss for the entity by failing to discharge an obligation.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Liquidity risk – the risk that an entity will encounter difficulty in meeting obligations associated with financial liabilities.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: 47.86 An entity should disclose information that enables users of its financial statements to evaluate the nature and extent of risks arising from financial instruments to which the entity is exposed at the reporting date.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: 47.87 The disclosures in the standard focus on the risks that arise from financial instruments and how they have been managed. These risks typically include, but are not limited to, credit risk, liquidity risk and market risk.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: 47.88 Providing qualitative disclosures in the context of quantitative disclosures enables users to link related disclosures and, hence, form an overall picture of the nature and extent of risks arising from financial instruments. The interaction between qualitative and quantitative disclosures will contribute to disclosure of information in a way that better enables users to evaluate an entity’s exposure.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: 47.89 An entity that uses several methods to manage a risk exposure should disclose information using the method or methods that provide the most relevant and reliable information.

text: 47.90 For each type of risk arising from financial instruments, an entity should disclose: the exposure to risk and how it arises; its objectives and policies for managing the risk; and any changes to these since the prior period.

text: 47.92 Concentrations of risk arise from financial instruments that have similar characteristics and are affected similarly by changes in economic or other conditions. text: 47.94 The credit risk disclosures should enable users of financial statements to understand the effect of credit risk on the amount, timing and uncertainty of future cash flows. To achieve this objective, credit risk disclosures should provide:

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - information about an entity’s credit risk exposure (that is, the credit risk inherent in an entity’s financial assets and commitments to extend credit), including significant credit risk concentrations.

text: 47.95 An entity should explain its credit risk management practices and how they relate to the recognition and measurement of expected credit losses. IFRS 7 requires the following disclosures:

text: - how an entity determines increases in credit risk, including how financial assets are determined to have low credit risk (para 5.5.10 of IFRS 9) and the presumption that there has been a significant increase in credit risk where financial assets are more than 30 days overdue has been rebutted (para 5.5.11 of IFRS 9);

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - how it was determined that assets were credit impaired;

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - write-off policies, including the indicators that there is no reasonable expectation of recovery and information about the policy for financial assets that are written off but are still subject to enforcement activity; and

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - how modifications of contractual cash flows have been treated.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)

text: 47.110 The factors that an entity might consider in providing a description of how it manages liquidity risk include, but are not limited to, whether the entity:

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Has committed borrowing facilities (for example, commercial paper facilities) or other lines of credit (for example, stand-by credit facilities) that it can access to meet liquidity needs.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Holds deposits at central banks to meet liquidity needs.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Has very diverse funding sources.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Has significant concentrations of liquidity risk in either its assets or its funding sources.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Has internal control processes and contingency plans for managing liquidity risk.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Has instruments that include accelerated repayment terms (for example, on the downgrade of the entity’s credit rating).

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Has instruments that could require the posting of collateral (for example, margin calls for derivatives).

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Has instruments that allow the entity to choose whether it settles its financial liabilities by delivering cash (or another financial asset) or by delivering its own shares.

text: FAQ 47.4.1 – Should derivative assets be classified as current or non-current?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 1 paras 66, 68 Reference to standing text: 47.4

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Paragraph 66 of IAS 1 identifies that an entity should classify assets as current assets when:

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - it expects to realise the asset, or intends to sell or consume it, in its normal operating cycle;

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - it holds the asset primarily for the purpose of trading;

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - it expects to realise the asset within 12 months after the reporting period; or

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - the asset is cash or a cash equivalent (as defined in IAS 7), unless the asset is restricted from being exchanged or used to settle a liability for at least 12 months after the reporting period.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Should derivatives be classified as current or non-current?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Applying the above definition, it could be argued that financial assets that meet the definition of ‘held for trading’, in accordance with IFRS 9, should be presented as current assets.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: However, paragraph 68 of IAS 1 clarifies that some, rather than all, financial assets and liabilities classified as held for trading are current assets and liabilities respectively. Non-hedging derivatives that are not held primarily for the purpose of trading are not required to be classified as current simply because they fall within the ‘held for trading’ definition in IFRS 9. Rather, the requirements of paragraph 66 of IAS 1 should be applied in determining classification. chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: The treatment of hedging derivatives will be similar. Where a portion of a financial asset is expected to be realised within 12 months of the balance sheet date, that portion should be presented as a current asset; the remainder of the financial asset should be shown as a non-current asset. This suggests that hedging derivatives which are assets should be split into current and non-current portions. The liability component of the convertible debt should be classified as non-current where it is repayable in more than 12 months, and the components of an instrument that are classified as equity should be ignored. text: FAQ 47.7.2 – Should puttable debt that is puttable by the holder within the next 12 months be classified as current or non-current?

text: Reference to standard: IAS 1 para 69 Reference to standing text: 47.7

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: An entity has puttable debt that is puttable by the holder within the next 12 months but, if not put, is repayable only beyond 12 months. Should it be classified as current or non-current?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: In this case, the puttable debt should be classified in its entirety as current, irrespective of whether IFRS 9 requires the put option to be accounted for as a separate embedded derivative and, if it does, irrespective of whether the host debt contract is reported in a separate balance sheet line item from the embedded derivative. This reflects that the put option could cause the entire instrument to be settled in a manner that is regarded as a liability under IAS 32.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: FAQ 47.15.1 – Should loans be offset against deposits and the net amount reported in the balance sheet for mortgage offset products?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 32 para 42 Reference to standing text: 47.15 Banking and capital markets

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: A financial asset and a financial liability shall be offset and the net amount reported in the balance sheet when an entity:

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - has a legally enforceable right to set off the recognised amounts; and

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - intends either to settle on a net basis, or to realise the asset and settle the liability simultaneously.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Bank A issues a mortgage offset product, which links a deposit liability and a mortgage asset, with the following terms:

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - there is no restriction on the customer’s ability to withdraw part or all of the deposit at will;

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - there is no requirement for mortgage repayment instalments to be settled using the deposit balance (interest or capital), although the customer might choose to do so; and

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - interest is calculated on the net amount of the mortgage asset and the deposit liability. The customer has waived the right to receive interest on the deposit (or it attracts 0% interest) in exchange for offsetting the deposit against the liability for the purposes of calculating the interest.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: NB Assume that both the deposit liability and the mortgage asset are measured at amortised cost under IFRS 9.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Should the deposit liability be offset against the mortgage asset and the net amount reported in the balance sheet?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: No. The amounts cannot be offset. The mortgage asset and deposit liability should be reported separately and not offset, because there is no legally enforceable right to offset, nor is there an intention to settle on a net basis or to realise the asset and settle the deposit simultaneously. [IAS 32 para 42].

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Should interest be presented as a single net income item in the income statement?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: It depends. Where the contractual basis of the arrangement is that the customer has waived the right to interest on the linked deposit (or it attracts interest of 0%) in exchange for interest being calculated on the net balance, the interest should be reported as a single net income item (or expense item where the deposit liability exceeds the mortgage asset) in the income statement.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Where the contractual basis of the arrangement is that interest is not calculated on the net balance but, for example, is calculated separately on the loan and deposit and offset for payment purposes, the interest income and expense calculated separately should be presented gross in the income statement.

text: FAQ 47.28.1 – Should cash and overdrafts covered by cash management arrangements be offset?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 32 para 50 Reference to standing text: 47.28

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Group X comprises various subsidiaries, each of which has a separate bank account with bank B. At any time, some of these accounts have a positive cash balance and others have a negative (overdraft) balance. Group X operates the following arrangements for cash management purposes:

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Zero balancing (sometimes referred to as a ‘cash sweep’), under which the balances on a number of designated accounts are transferred to a single netting account on a regular basis, including at the balance sheet date. In some cases, the amounts transferred are repaid to the relevant subsidiaries shortly afterwards. This might be agreed contractually or at the choice of group management.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Notional pooling, under which bank B calculates the net balance on a number of designated accounts, with interest being earned or paid on the net amount. There might be a transfer of balances into a netting account, but this is not always at the balance sheet date.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Is group X able to offset cash and overdraft balances, and hence present net balances in its consolidated balance sheet?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: If balances are to be presented net, both of the criteria set out in paragraph 42 of IAS 32 should be satisfied. Group X should have a currently legally enforceable right to offset, which means that it is enforceable at any time and not just in stipulated circumstances, such as an event of default or bankruptcy. Also, group X should demonstrate a clear intention to settle the period end balances with the same counterparty, as clarified by the March 2016 IFRS IC agenda decision. A notional pooling, for the purpose of calculating interest that does not involve settlement of the associated balanc

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Assuming that the agreement with bank B gives group X the necessary legally enforceable right to offset, its position will be as follows:

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Where there is zero balancing at the balance sheet date, and no repayment of funding (reversal of cash flows) takes place, either on the following day or any day thereafter, group X has a single cash balance or overdraft at the balance sheet date, and it is presented as such. The IAS 32 offsetting requirements are not relevant in this case.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Where there is zero balancing at the balance sheet date, but the amounts transferred are repaid to the relevant subsidiaries shortly afterwards as a practice of group X, there would often be a single cash balance or overdraft at the balance sheet date that should be presented as such. Again, the IAS 32 offsetting requirements are not relevant in this case. However, there might be circumstances where group X has separate cash and overdraft balances (for example, where it has a contractual obligation to return the balances to the respective subsidiaries the following day). In such circumstance

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Where there is notional pooling, but no physical transfer of balances to one account, group X will not be able to demonstrate ‘the intention to settle net’, because the arrangement does not actually involve net cash settlement. Accordingly, the balances should be presented gross.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Where there is notional pooling with regular net settlement, entities will only be able to present notional pool balances net where they have the legal right and an intention to net settle the actual balances in place at the period end date. To the extent that the balances change between the period end and settlement date, the entity cannot demonstrate an intention to net settle the previous balance.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Note that arrangements such as those described above can be complex; each arrangement should be viewed in light of its specific facts and circumstances. Further disclosure of gross balances might be necessary if the amount at the balance sheet date does not reflect normal cash balances throughout the year.

text: FAQ 47.30.1 – Does IFRS 7 apply to entities that are not in the financial services industry?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IFRS 7 para 3 Reference to standing text: 47.30

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Consistent with IAS 32 and IFRS 9, IFRS 7 applies to all entities, not just those in the financial services sector. This means that it applies to a manufacturing entity whose only financial instruments might be cash, bank loans and overdrafts, trade debtors and creditors, as well as to a bank with many and complex financial instruments. It also applies to the financial statements of subsidiaries of a consolidated group, even though, in most large groups, risks are managed at the consolidated level.

Commodity contracts that are settled net in cash and fail the ‘own use’ exemption, or are settled through other financial instruments, are within IFRS 7’s scope; those contracts that meet the ‘own use’ exemption would be outside IFRS 7’s scope, because they are not financial instruments. [IFRS 9 para 2.4]. These terms are discussed in detail in chapter 40 para 81. For internal reporting purposes, management might exclude ‘own use’ contracts when assessing the entity’s expos

text: FAQ 47.30.5 – Does IFRS 7 apply to provisions, accruals and pre-payments?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IFRS 7 para 3 Reference to standing text: 47.30

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Provisions (as defined in IAS 37) are outside the scope of IFRS 7, because they are not financial instruments. Accruals representing a right to receive cash or obligations to deliver cash are within IFRS 7’s scope. For example, an accrual for goods received but not yet invoiced is within IFRS 7’s scope. On the other hand, a pre-paid expense, which is settled by the future delivery of goods or services, is not a financial instrument and is outside IFRS 7’s scope.

text: FAQ 47.30.6 – Does IFRS 7 apply to issued financial guarantee contracts?

text: FAQ 47.55.1 – In what circumstances would the IFRS 7 definition of ‘continuing involvement’ be met?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IFRS 7 para 42C Reference to standing text: 47.55

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: The extent and substance of the linkage between the assets and any other rights or obligations should be considered on a case-by-case basis, to determine if the IFRS 7 definition of ‘continuing involvement’ is met. For example, if the liability is contractually linked to the assets, such that cash flows from the asset must be used to settle the liability, or the assets and associated liabilities are ring fenced (for example, in an SPV), we believe that they would be within the scope of the IFRS 7 disclosures.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Ongoing involvement, such as contingent price adjustments to the transfer price in respect of a transferred financial asset (for example, due to a change in tax or law that affects the asset), which does not fall within the exemptions in paragraph 42C of IFRS 7 would be considered continuing involvement for the purposes of the IFRS 7 disclosures. However, an interest rate swap or other derivative that is not linked to the transferred asset would not be a continuing involvement.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: For those transferred assets that are de-recognised in their entirety (for example, non-recourse factoring), the transferor might continue to service the assets for a fee, which could be based on a percentage of the asset value. The issue arises of whether the servicing contract is a continuing involvement in the transferred assets that falls within the scope of IFRS 7’s disclosure requirements.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: The term ‘payment’ in paragraph B30 of IFRS 7 does not include cash flows of the transferred financial asset that an entity collects and is required to remit to the transferee.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: An entity must assess a servicing contract to determine if it meets the definition of ‘continuing involvement’ in the context of paragraph 42C of IFRS 7. For example, where the servicing fee is dependent on the performance of the transferred asset, or on the timing of cash flows from the transferred asset, this will constitute a continuing involvement for the purposes of paragraph 42C.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Similarly, a servicer has continuing involvement, for the purposes of the disclosure requirements, if a fixed fee would not be paid in full because of non-performance of the transferred financial asset. In these examples, the servicer has an interest in the future performance of the transferred financial asset.

text: Similar principles apply to identifying concentrations of other risks, including liquidity risk and market risk. For example, concentrations of liquidity risk might arise from the repayment terms of financial liabilities, sources of borrowing facilities or reliance on a particular market in which to realise liquid assets. Concentrations of foreign exchange risk might arise if an entity has a significant net open position in a single foreign currency, or aggregate net open positions in several currencies that tend to move together.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: FAQ 47.93.1 – Is disclosure required if the year end credit risk exposure is unrepresentative due to seasonal fluctuations?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IFRS 7 para IG20 Reference to standing text: 47.93

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Entity Y is producing seeds for the agricultural industry. The main season for planting is the spring. 75% of entity Y’s markets are in the northern hemisphere; 25% are in the southern hemisphere. Entity Y’s account receivables are approximately C400 million in June and C100 million in December. Entity Y has a December year end. Does entity Y have to disclose additional information about its exposure to credit risk on the receivables that is representative of its exposure to risk during the year?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: In this case, the December year end exposure to credit risk is unrepresentative of the entity’s exposure during the period. Entity Y should provide further information that is representative, such as a description (with amounts) of how the exposures vary during the year, or the average (or highest) exposure to credit risk during the year.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: FAQ 47.93.2 – Is disclosure required if the year end credit risk exposure is unrepresentative due to a major acquisition?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: Reference to standard: IFRS 7 para IG20 Reference to standing text: 47.93

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: On 30 November 20X6, entity A (which has euro as its functional currency) acquires a major competitor. Due to the acquisition, US dollar-denominated receivables increased from $100 million to $300 million, and variable interest rate debt doubled from €200 million to €400 million, compared to the balances as at 30 June 20X6. Entity A has a December year end. The balances as of 31 December 20X6 are considered to be representative of the next year(s). Does entity A have to disclose additional information that is representative of its exposure to risk during the year?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: In this scenario, entity A should disclose additional information, because the quantitative data as at 31 December 20X6 is not representative of the financial period 20X6. A mere statement that the data is not representative is not sufficient. To meet IFRS 7’s requirements, the entity might disclose the highest, lowest and average amount of risk to which it was exposed during the period. However, a full high/low/average analysis might not be required if the exposure at the year end is representative for future periods and if sufficient explanations of the facts and circumstances are provided.

text: How should a credit-impaired financial asset for which ECL is also measured using the simplified approach be disclosed in accordance with the requirements in paragraphs 35H and 35M of IFRS 7?

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: As stated in paragraph 35B of IFRS 7, credit-risk disclosures should enable users of financial statements to understand the effect of credit risk on the amount, timing and uncertainty of future cash flows. To meet this objective, information should be given about the sub-set of financial assets for which ECL is measured using the simplified approach that are also credit-impaired. Such information could be given as a separate column in the disclosure tables or by means of additional narrative information.

text: - gross movements reflecting the transfers between stages of financial assets in interim periods previously reported; or

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: For example, consider the following scenarios where a financial asset moves from one stage to another within the reporting period:

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Scenario 2: the asset was in stage 1 in Q1, stage 2 in Q2, and then in stage 3 at the year end.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: If approach (a) is adopted, the changes between interim periods would be included in the annual reconciliations as follows:

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Scenario 1: there would be a transfer from stage 1 to stage 2, and another transfer from stage 2 to stage 1.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Scenario 2: there would be a transfer from stage 1 to stage 2, and another transfer from stage 2 to stage 3.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: If approach (b) is adopted, the annual reconciliations would disclose changes in a financial asset’s stage from the beginning of the reporting period to that at the end of the reporting period, ignoring all movements during the interim periods, as follows:

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Scenario 1: there would be no transfers between stages reflected in the reconciliations.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: - Scenario 2: there would be a movement from stage 1 to stage 3.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: IFRS 7 and IFRS 9 give no specific guidance, and so either approach is acceptable as a matter of accounting policy. Where information is available (as would be the case if included in interim reporting), approach (a) – that includes the transfers between interim reporting dates – might be more useful to the user of the financial statements. Conversely, approach (b) is consistent with the view that the frequency of interim reporting should not affect reporting in the annual financial statements.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: The chosen policy should be consistently applied and disclosed where the effect is material.

However, if reconciliations of gross carrying amounts are given in addition to the required reconciliations of the loss allowance, the same basis should be used for both reconciliations.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: An entity hedges its exposure to variable interest rate risk on an issued bond. The hedge is designated as a cash flow hedge. The bond and the hedging instrument (interest rate swap) have a five-year remaining life. The variable leg of the swap exactly matches the variable interest of the bond (causing no ineffectiveness).

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: The high effectiveness of the hedge does not necessarily mean that there would be no impact on equity or profit or loss due to changes in interest rate risk. The accounting for a cash flow hedge means that the fair value movement related to the effective part of the hedging instrument is included in other comprehensive income. Amounts deferred in other comprehensive income are recycled in profit or loss when the hedged transaction occurs. Hence, reasonably possible movements in the interest rate risk exposure have an impact on both profit or loss and equity.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: At the same time, reasonably possible movements in the interest rate risk exposure on the outstanding bond would have an opposite impact on profit or loss, because the bond pays variable interest.

chapter: 47 - Presentation and disclosure of financial instruments (IFRS 9, IFRS 7)
text: If the effects of recycling and ineffectiveness are not material, the entity could consider the following disclosure as an approximation for the sensitivity analysis: “The movements related to the bond and the swap’s variable leg are not reflected, because they offset each other. The movements related to the remaining fair value exposure on the swap’s fixed leg are shown in the equity part of the analysis”.

48 - Earnings per share (IAS 33)
48 - Earnings per share (IAS 33)
This eBook is licensed to peggy so, peggy.so@hk.ey.com,
Introduction and scope (paras 48.1-48.8)

48.1 Earnings per share (EPS) is a ratio that is widely used by financial analysts, investors and other users to gauge an entity’s profitability and to value its shares. Its purpose is to indicate how effective an entity has been in using the resources provided by the ordinary shareholders, and to assess the entity’s current net earnings. EPS also forms the basis for calculating the ‘price-earnings ratio’, which is widely used by investors and analysts to value shares.

48.2 Throughout this chapter, reference is made to ‘equity holders of the parent’. In paragraph 54(r) of IAS 1, ‘equity holders of the parent’ was amended to ‘owners of the parent’. IAS 33 has not been updated to reflect this change, so we have used ‘equity holders of the parent’ in line with IAS 33.

48.3 EPS is a ratio of the numerator (that is, earnings measured in terms of profits available to ordinary equity holders of the parent entity) to the denominator (that is, the weighted average number of ordinary shares). In addition to basic EPS, diluted EPS is disclosed with the objective to illustrate the effect of all dilutive potential ordinary shares. Dilution is a reduction in EPS resulting from the assumption that convertible instruments are converted, that options or warrants are exercised, or that additional ordinary shares are issued upon the satisfaction of specified conditions.
[IAS 33 para 10]. [IAS 33 para 30].
48.4 IAS 33 prescribes the principles for the determination and presentation of EPS.
48.5 IAS 33 applies to the following entities:

- Those whose ordinary shares or potential ordinary shares (such as convertible debt or warrants) are traded in a public market (that is, a domestic or foreign stock exchange or an over-the-counter market, including local and regional markets).

- Those that file, or are in the process of filing, financial statements with a securities commission or other regulatory body for the purpose of issuing ordinary shares in a public market (that is, not private placements).
48.6 EPS is required only on the basis of consolidated information even if the parent’s separate and consolidated financial statements are presented together.

48.7 An entity may choose to present EPS based on its separate (rather than consolidated) entity financial statements, as well as that based on the consolidated financial statements. The separate entity EPS figures should not be shown in the consolidated financial statements. They should be shown only on the face of the separate entity statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income (or income statement, if presented as a separate statement).

48.8 Entities whose securities are not publicly traded are not required to disclose EPS. However, where such entities choose to disclose EPS, they need to calculate and disclose EPS in accordance with IAS 33.
