The dividend was appropriately authorised and recognised by the subsidiary as a liability at 31 August 20X5. The parent prepares consolidated financial statements for the year ended 31 December 20X5 in its presentation currency of euros. The following exchange rates are relevant:
The dividend remains outstanding at the balance sheet date. The dividend is recorded in the subsidiary’s and the parent’s separate and consolidated financial statements as follows:

In subsidiary’s balance sheet (as translated for consolidation) € Dividend payable – $100,000 @ 1.75 57,142 In parent’s income statement Initially recorded at rate when dividend is declared – $100,000 @ 1.50 (transaction date) 66,667 Exchange loss on receivable recognised in the income statement (9,525) In parent’s balance sheet – Dividend receivable at year end rate – $100,000 @ 1.75 57,142

FAQ 49.60.2 – Does a parent entity need to track cumulative exchange differences individually for each of its foreign operations?
Reference to standard: IAS 21 paras 48, 49 Reference to standing text: 49.60

Yes. However, the tracking of cumulative exchange differences can be onerous. For a parent entity with more than one foreign operation, it could be tempting to aggregate these exchange differences related to all the net investments in one currency together, with the reclassification of these exchange differences on the disposal (or partial disposal) of some of those foreign operations being calculated proportionately, based on the whole investments portfolio.

IAS 21 requires reclassification whenever there is a disposal, or partial disposal, of a foreign operation, so the cumulative translation adjustment (CTA) needs to be tracked on each individual net investment. There is no requirement to separately track the CTA on a loan that forms part of the net investment in the foreign operation, because such CTA is included within the total CTA for the foreign operation.
EX 49.60.3 – Reclassification of cumulative exchange differences due to a group restructuring
Reference to standard: IAS 21 paras 48, 49 Reference to standing text: 49.60

In a group restructuring, a foreign operation is transferred from one intermediate holding entity to another. The group continues to hold a 100% interest in that foreign operation. No third parties are involved with the group restructuring.
Are the cumulative exchange differences reclassified in the group’s consolidated financial statements?

No. The key question is whether the restructuring results in an economic change that, from the group’s perspective, constitutes a partial or full disposal. The foreign operation continues to be part of the consolidated group and so, from the group’s perspective, the restructuring is not a disposal event. Accordingly, no cumulative translation adjustment (CTA) is reclassified in the group’s financial statements.
Are the cumulative exchange differences reclassified in an intermediate holding entity’s consolidated financial statements?

If the intermediate holding entity that disposes of the foreign operation prepares consolidated financial statements under IFRS and it recognises the gain or loss on the disposal of the foreign operation in profit or loss, the CTA deferred in equity (if any) that arises at that intermediate reporting level is also reclassified to profit or loss.

However, if the disposal by the intermediate holding entity is a non-reciprocal group restructuring transaction outside the scope of IFRS 10 and IFRIC 17 (a demerger), the intermediate holding entity might account for the gain or loss on disposal in equity (see chapter A1 para 37 onwards). In such a case, the intermediate holding entity has an accounting policy choice to recognise the CTA previously deferred in equity either in profit or loss (by applying IAS 21 para 48), or in equity (by applying consistent principles to those applied to recognise the gain or loss on disposal in equity as set
FAQ 49.60.4 – When is is the CTA reclassified when it arises from a different presentation currency?
Reference to standard: IAS 21 para 8, 48 Reference to standing text: 49.60 and 4.136
A Group comprises three entities:
- Parent A (domiciled in Germany). Parent A is a holding company and has few activities in its country of domicile and little or no economic exposure to the EUR.
- Direct Subsidiary B based in China with substantial operations in that country (100% owned).
- Indirect Subsidiary C also based in China with substantial operations in that country (100% owned by B).

The functional currency of each of the three entities is the RMB and, accordingly, each entity prepares financial statements in RMB. However, Parent A chooses to present its consolidated financial statements in EUR. The translation of the consolidated financial statements into EUR creates a translation adjustment, recognised in other comprehensive income, and accumulated in a separate component of equity (currency translation reserve).
Subsidiary C is disposed of in the reporting period. Is the CTA related to C reclassified to profit and loss?

IAS 21 does not contain any explicit CTA reclassification guidance where a parent, in its consolidated financial statements, disposes of an operation and both entities have the same functional currency, but the consolidated financial statements are presented in a different currency.

IAS 1.93 indicates that "Other IFRS specify whether and when amounts previously recognised in OCI are reclassified to profit and loss". IAS 1.95 also notes that an example of a reclassification adjustment is the disposal of a foreign operation. IAS 21.48 states that on the disposal of a foreign operation the amount accumulated in other comprehensive income shall be reclassified to profit and loss. A foreign operation is defined in IAS 21.8 as "an entity that is a subsidiary, associate, joint arrangement or branch of a reporting entity, the activities of which are based or conducted in a countr

One view is that the CTA arising from the translation of Subsidiary C from its functional currency of RMB to the presentation currency of EUR should not be reclassified into profit or loss. These differences arise solely from the Parent A's choice of presentation currency and do not represent gains or losses from an economic standpoint. This is because all three entities have the same functional currency and therefore it could be argued that Subsidiary C is not a foreign operation of Subsidiary B or, indirectly, Parent A. A consequence of this view is that the CTA is presented as part of items

Another view is that the CTA arising from the translation of Subsidiary C from its functional currency of RMB to the presentation currency of EUR should be reclassified into profit or loss. This CTA arose from translation from the functional currency of the operation to the parent’s presentation currency. As the definition of a foreign operation is not clear as explained above, it could be argued that Subsidiary C is a foreign operation and therefore that the CTA is subject to the reclassification requirements of IAS 21.48 .
Parent company A therefore has an accounting policy choice, which should be clearly disclosed and applied consistently.
FAQ 49.61.1 – How does an entity account for cumulative translation adjustment when there has been a partial disposal?
Reference to standard: IAS 21 para 48A Reference to standing text: 49.61

A parent sells 80% of its 100% interest in the subsidiary, and retains a 20% interest that is classified as being in an associate. The entire amount of cumulative translation adjustment (CTA) in relation to that subsidiary is reclassified to profit or loss (even though the entity retains an interest in that former subsidiary).
Partially owned subsidiary

Where the subsidiary is partially owned (that is, where a non-controlling interest exists) and the parent has sold its partial interest, the amount of the CTA that has been allocated to the non-controlling interest is de-recognised, but it is not transferred to profit or loss. De-recognition of the non-controlling interest (that includes the non-controlling interest’s share of CTA) will form part of the journal entry to recognise the gain or loss on disposal of the subsidiary.
FAQ 49.63.1 – Is a repayment of a quasi-equity loan or share capital, without a change in the parent’s proportionate percentage shareholding, a partial disposal for the purposes of IAS 21?
Reference to standard: IAS 21 para 48C Reference to standing text: 49.63

Where a subsidiary that is a foreign operation repays a quasi-equity loan or repays/returns share capital, but there is no change in the parent’s proportionate percentage shareholding, there is an accounting policy choice regarding whether the cumulative translation adjustment (CTA) should be reclassified, depending on how ‘ownership interest’ in IAS 21 is interpreted.

- Option 1 – No disposal of interest in subsidiary Since the parent continues to own the same percentage of the subsidiary, and continues to control the foreign operation, there has been no change in its proportionate ‘ownership interest’, and hence no disposal or partial disposal. Under this view, ‘ownership interest’ refers only to the proportionate interest. The CTA should not, therefore, be reclassified.

- Option 2 – Disposal of interest in subsidiary The transaction is a partial disposal, because there has been a reduction in the parent’s absolute ownership interest. Under this view, in addition to a proportionate change in ownership being a partial disposal, ‘ownership interest’ can also be interpreted as a change in the absolute interest held in a net investment. A pro rata share of the CTA should be reclassified.
The above options would equally apply to a return of capital/repayment of share capital in similar circumstances.
Entities should make an accounting policy choice between these two methods and apply this policy consistently.

Where a foreign operation pays a dividend to its parent, and the substance of the dividend payment is that of a partial return of capital or partial liquidation, the parent similarly has an accounting policy choice whether to treat such an event as a partial disposal.
EX 49.63.2 – Partial disposal of a subsidiary while control is retained
Reference to standard: IAS 21 para 48C Reference to standing text: 49.63
A parent owns 100% of a subsidiary. The subsidiary is a foreign operation. The parent sells 30% of its shareholding, retaining a 70% shareholding and control.
How much, if any, cumulative translation adjustment (CTA) should be re-attributed to the non-controlling interest?

The reduction in the parent’s ownership interest is a partial disposal under paragraph 48D of IAS 21. Because 30% of the subsidiary has been disposed of, 30% of the CTA should be re-attributed to the new non-controlling interest. This transfer is accounted for in the statement of changes in equity and is not presented in the performance statements. None of the CTA is reclassified to the income statement.
EX 49.64.1 – Partial disposal of an associate
Reference to standard: IAS 21 para 48C Reference to standing text: 49.64

An investor owns 40% of the share capital of an entity. It has significant influence over the entity, and it accounts for the investment as an associate using equity accounting. The associate is a foreign operation. The investor sells half of its total shareholding, retaining a 20% investment. It continues to have significant influence and to account for the investment as an associate.
How much, if any, cumulative translation adjustment (CTA) is reclassified to profit or loss?

The reduction in the investor’s ownership interest is a partial disposal under paragraph 48D of IAS 21. Because half of the investment in the associate has been disposed of, 50% of the CTA relating to the foreign associate is reclassified to profit or loss.
Presentation and disclosure
FAQ 49.73.1 – Where should foreign exchange differences be presented in the income statement?
Reference to standard: IAS 21 para 52 Reference to standing text: 49.73

The disclosure required in paragraph 49.73 is on an aggregate net basis. The total amount of exchange differences recognised in profit or loss includes exchange differences recognised on subsequent settlement and re-translation to closing rate on balances arising on foreign currency transactions. However, the standard is silent as to where in profit or loss they should be included.
In practice, foreign exchange differences typically tend to be classified in the same line item as the underlying transaction. Therefore:
- Foreign exchange differences arising from trading transactions are included in the results of operating activities.
- Foreign exchange differences arising from financing are included as a component of finance cost/income.
- Foreign exchange differences arising on deferred tax balances are included as part of deferred tax expense (income). [IAS 12 para 78].
FAQ 49.77.1 – When can an entity provide supplementary information in a currency that is different from its presentation or functional currency?
Reference to standard: IAS 21 para 57 Reference to standing text: 49.77

IAS 21 does not prohibit an entity from providing for its users, as supplementary information, financial statements or other financial information (such as five-year summaries) in a currency that is not its functional currency or its presentation currency.

Such supplementary information is often referred to as a ‘convenience translation’. It is normally based on translations prepared by applying a single exchange rate to all amounts appearing in financial statements presented in the entity’s functional or presentation currency. The relationships among amounts in the financial statements do not change. Such translations fail to account for the effects of changes in foreign exchange rates and, therefore, do not comply with the translation procedures set out under IAS 21.

Introduction and scope (paras 50.1- 50.7)

50.1 IFRS 4 was designed as an interim standard with the objective of specifying the accounting for insurance contracts by entities that issue such contracts. IFRS 4 requires limited improvements to accounting practices for insurance contracts, and therefore allows entities to continue with their existing accounting policies for insurance contracts if those policies meet specified minimum criteria. Entities applying IFRS 4 are required to identify and explain, to the users of financial statements, the amount, timing and uncertainty of future cash flows arising from insurance contracts.

50.2 IFRS 4 will be replaced by IFRS 17 as amended in June 2020 (see chapter 50A). IFRS 17 will apply to annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2023 (with early adoption permitted where IFRS 9 is also applied).

50.3 IFRS 4 applies to insurance and reinsurance contracts that an entity issues and reinsurance contracts that it holds. IFRS 4 also applies to financial instruments that an entity issues that have a ‘discretionary participation feature’.

50.4 IFRS 4 refers to any entity that issues an insurance contract as ‘an insurer’, whether or not the entity is regarded as an insurance company for legal or supervisory purposes. All references to an insurer shall be read as also referring to an issuer of a financial instrument that contains a discretionary participation feature.
50.5 IFRS 4 does not address other aspects of accounting by insurers, such as accounting for financial assets that they hold or financial liabilities that they issue, other than:
- permitting an insurer in specified circumstances to reclassify some or all of their financial assets at fair value through profit or loss (see para 50.42); and
- containing temporary exemptions in relation to the application of IFRS 9 (see para 50.75 onwards).
50.6 IFRS 4 does not apply to direct insurance contracts that an entity holds.
50.7 IFRS 4 does not apply in the following situations (even if the definition of an insurance contract is met):
- Product warranties issued directly by a manufacturer, retailer or dealer are within the scope of IFRS 15, (see chapter 11) and IAS 37 (see chapter 16).
- Employee benefit plans and retirement benefit obligations are within the scope of IFRS 2 (see chapter 13) IAS 19 (see chapter 12) and IAS 26.

- Contractual rights or obligations that are contingent on the use of non-financial items and a lessee's residual value guarantee embedded in a lease are within the scope of IFRS 16 (see chapter 15), IFRS 15 (see chapter 11) and IAS 38 (see chapter 21).

- Financial guarantees are within the scope of IFRS 9 or IAS 39 (see para 50.75 onwards), ‘Financial instruments: recognition and measurement’ (see chapter 40). Financial guarantee contracts will be within the scope of IFRS 9 or IAS 39 (see chapter 40), except where the issuer has previously asserted explicitly that it regards such contracts as insurance contracts and has used accounting applicable to insurance contracts, in which case the issuer can irrevocably elect, on a contract-by-contract basis, to apply either:
- IFRS 9 or IAS 39, IAS 32 and IFRS 7(see chapter 47); or
- Contingent consideration payable on a business combination is within the scope of IFRS 3 (see chapter 29).

Definition of an insurance contract (paras 50.8- 50.23)

50.8 IFRS 4 defines an insurance contract as “a contract under which one party (the insurer) accepts significant insurance risk from another party (the policyholder) by agreeing to compensate the policyholder if a specified uncertain future event (the insured event) adversely affects the policyholder”.
EX 50.8.1 – Contracts that are insurance contracts EX 50.8.2 – Contracts that are not insurance contracts

50.9 The key principle of an insurance contract is that there should be a transfer of significant insurance risk arising from an uncertain future event that adversely affects the policyholder and results in the payment of significant additional benefits.
Specified uncertain future event
50.10 Uncertainty (or risk) is the essence of an insurance contract. At least one of the following is uncertain at the inception of an insurance contract:
- whether an insured event will occur;
- how much the insurer will need to pay if it occurs.
EX 50.10.1 – Fixed-fee property maintenance contract EX 50.10.2 – Manufacturer warranty contract
Significant insurance risk
50.11 The risk accepted from the policyholder must be insurance risk. Insurance risk is any risk other than financial risk.

50.12 Financial risk is: “the risk of a possible future change in one or more of a specified interest rate, financial instrument price, commodity price, foreign exchange rate, index of prices or rates, credit rating or credit index or other variable, provided in the case of a non-financial variable that the variable is not specific to a party to the contract”.
FAQ 50.12.1 – Does an equity release mortgage with a ‘no negative equity’ guarantee transfer insurance risk?
50.13 Contracts can contain both financial and insurance risk; such contracts are not excluded from being insurance contracts, provided the insurance risk is significant.

50.14 Insurance risk is ‘significant’ if, and only if, the occurrence of an insured event could result in the payment of “significant additional benefits in any scenario, excluding scenarios that lack commercial substance (ie have no discernible effect on the economics of the transaction)”.
50.15 IFRS 4 does not set a numerical threshold for ‘significant’ insurance risk.

50.15.1 The definition of insurance risk refers to risk that the insurer accepts from the policyholder. That is, insurance risk must be a pre-existing risk that is transferred from the policyholder to the insurer as a result of the contract, and is not a new risk created by the contract.

50.16 A scenario with commercial substance can be one that is extremely unlikely. An entity needs to consider whether the benefits are greater in a scenario with commercial substance in which the insured event occurs than in any other scenario. The entity will then have to determine whether the difference between the benefits under this scenario and the benefits if no insured event occurred is significant. If that is the case, the contract is an insurance contract.
EX 50.16.1 – Payments for low probability events
50.17 ‘Additional benefits’ exclude payments conditional on an event that does not cause a significant loss to the policyholder.
[IFRS 4 App B para B24(c)].
EX 50.17.1 – Payment for insignificant loss
Adversely affects the policyholder

50.18 A contract requiring payment to the policyholder if a specified uncertain event occurs is only an insurance contract if the event creates insurance (as opposed to financial) risk and that event adversely affects the policyholder.
EX 50.18.1 – Adversely affects the policyholder EX 50.18.2 – Climatic variables
50.19 Payments under insurance contracts can be predetermined and do not need to exactly compensate the policyholder for the financial impact of the adverse event.

50.20 Payments under insurance contracts can be more than the loss suffered. One such case is ‘new-for-old’ policies where the insurer pays for the replacement cost of a new asset, rather than capping the compensation to the value of the old and damaged asset.
50.21 Insurers must accept risk from another party (a separate entity) for insurance risk to exist.
[IFRS 4 IG example 1 para 1.28].
EX 50.21.1 – Captive insurance subsidiaries
50.22 IAS 37 applies where a group self-insures, and a provision will be recognised if there is an obligation at the reporting date (see chapter 16 EX 16.85.10).
[IFRS 4 App B para B19(c)].
Existing accounting policies

50.23 Insurers are exempt from applying the criteria for developing accounting policies in paragraphs 10 to 12 of IAS 8 (see chapter 3 paras 7 to 9) to insurance contracts. Entities can continue with their existing (local GAAP) accounting policies if those policies meet certain criteria.
FAQ 50.23.1 – Can accounting policies that meet the requirements of IAS 37 meet the requirements in paragraph 13 of IFRS 4?

Recognition (paras 50.24 - 50.66)

50.24 For an insurer to recognise an insurance liability, a contractual relationship between the insurer and the policyholder must exist at the end of the reporting period. Liabilities for potential claims that might arise under future contracts cannot be recognised.

50.25 Liabilities for potential claims are often called ‘catastrophe’ or ‘equalisation’ provisions, and are created when a liability is built up over time, to be used on the occurrence of a future catastrophic loss covered by current or future contracts. They are prohibited, because they do not meet the definition of a liability under the Framework.

50.26 An insurer should only remove an insurance liability from its balance sheet when the obligation specified in the contract is discharged, or cancelled or expires. This is consistent with the treatment of financial liabilities under IAS 39 or IFRS 9 (see chapter 44 para 101).
50.27 Some insurance liabilities, such as claim liabilities, are extinguished by payments in kind or the provision of services rather than by the payment of a monetary amount.
EX 50.27.1 – Provision of services to discharge insurance obligations
50.28 The amount of an insurance liability is subject to a liability adequacy test.

50.29 If an insurer applies a liability adequacy test that meets specified minimum requirements, IFRS 4 imposes no further requirements. The minimum requirements are that the liability adequacy test considers current estimates of all contractual cash flows, related cash flows (such as claims handling costs) and cash flows resulting from embedded options and guarantees. If an insurance liability is inadequate in the light of estimated future cash flows under the liability adequacy test, the entire deficiency must be recognised in profit or loss.
50.30 If the insurer’s liability adequacy test meets the minimum requirements of paragraph 16 of IFRS 4, that test is applied at the level of aggregation specified by that test.

50.31 Where the insurer’s accounting policies do not require a liability adequacy test meeting the specified minimum requirements, the insurer should compare the insurance liability’s carrying amount (less any related deferred acquisition costs and other insurance-related intangible assets) with the provision that would be required if it were measured using IAS 37. Where the net carrying amount of an insurance liability is insufficient when compared with IAS 37 measurement, the insurer should reduce the related assets or increase the liability. The difference should be recognised in profit or

50.32 If the insurer compares the adequacy of its insurance liability with the provision that would be required by IAS 37, this comparison should be done for each portfolio of contracts. A portfolio includes all contracts managed together and that are subject to broadly similar risks.
Changes in accounting policy
50.33 Requirements in respect of changes in accounting policies apply to insurers that already apply IFRSs and to those adopting IFRSs for the first time.

50.34 Insurers can only change their existing accounting policies for insurance contracts where the change results in presenting information that is more relevant and no less reliable, or more reliable and no less relevant, than before. The criteria in IAS 8 are used to determine whether a change in policy would result in more relevant or more reliable information.
50.35 IFRS 17 gives insurers further context for judgements about whether a change in accounting policies will make their financial statements more relevant and reliable.

50.36 Insurers can change their accounting policies to measure insurance liabilities to reflect current market interest rates. This can be for designated liabilities, without applying the policy to all similar liabilities.
Continuation of certain existing practices

50.37 Some existing local GAAP accounting policies can continue to be used, but cannot be introduced as a change, because they do not satisfy the ‘more relevant and no less reliable’ or ‘more reliable and no less relevant’ criteria. These include:
- Measuring insurance liabilities on an undiscounted basis.
- Measuring contractual rights to future investment management fees at an amount that exceeds fair value.
- Using non-uniform accounting policies for insurance contracts of subsidiaries, except as noted in paragraph 50.36.

50.38 An insurer can change accounting policies for insurance contracts of subsidiaries if they are not uniform, provided the change does not make accounting policies more diverse and satisfies IFRS 4’s other requirements for a change in accounting policy.

50.39 Insurers do not need to eliminate excessive prudence if it was part of their previous accounting policies. Changes to accounting policies that introduce additional prudence are not permitted if the liabilities are already measured with sufficient levels of prudence.
Future investment margins

50.40 Existing measurement practices for insurance liabilities can include future investment margins, either by using a discount rate that reflects the estimated return on an insurer’s assets or by projecting the returns on those assets at an estimated rate of return and then discounting those projected returns at a different rate. An insurer does not need to change its accounting policies to eliminate future investment margins, but there is a rebuttable presumption that an insurer’s financial statements will become less relevant and less reliable if it introduces such a policy.

50.41 In some accounting models, realised gains or losses on an insurer’s assets have a direct effect on the measurement of its insurance contracts. An insurer is permitted, but not required, to change its accounting policies so that a recognised but unrealised gain or loss on an asset affects measurement in the same way as a realised gain or loss. The related adjustment to the insurance liability (or deferred acquisition costs or intangible assets) is recognised in other comprehensive income if the unrealised gains or losses are recognised in other comprehensive income. This practice is somet
Re-designation of financial assets

50.42 When an insurer changes its accounting policies for insurance liabilities, it can, but is not required to, reclassify some or all of its financial assets as ‘at fair value through profit or loss’. Reclassification is permitted if an insurer changes accounting policies when it first applies IFRS 4 and if it makes a subsequent policy change. The reclassification is a change in accounting policy and therefore IAS 8 applies.
Distinction between insurance and investment contracts

50.43 Investment contract is an informal term used to describe contracts which take the legal form of insurance contracts but do not transfer significant insurance risk, and they are within the scope of IFRS 9 or IAS 39 (see para 50.75 onwards) because they create financial assets or liabilities.
[IFRS 4 paras BC 22, BC 23].
50.44 There are circumstances in which IFRS 9 or IAS 39 (see para 50.75 onwards) can apply to elements within an insurance contract, and IFRS 4 can apply to investment contracts.
Unbundling insurance contracts

50.45 Deposit components are contractual components that are not accounted for as a derivative under IFRS 9 or IAS 39 (see para 50.75 onwards) and would be within the scope of IFRS 9 or IAS 39 if they were separate instruments.
50.46 Some insurance contracts have an insurance component and a deposit component. Deposit components within insurance contracts either should or could be unbundled as follows:
- Unbundling is required if:
- the insurer can measure the deposit component (including any embedded surrender options) separately (that is, without considering the insurance component); and
- the insurer’s accounting policies do not require it to recognise all obligations and rights arising from the deposit component.

- Unbundling is permitted, but not required, if the insurer can measure the deposit component separately but its accounting policies require it to recognise all obligations and rights arising from the deposit component, regardless of the basis used to measure those rights and obligations.
- Unbundling is prohibited if an insurer cannot measure the deposit component separately.
EX 50.46.1 – Loan waiver on death

50.47 Where an insurance contract is unbundled into separate deposit and insurance components, IFRS 9 or IAS 39 (see para 50.75 onwards) is used to account for the deposit component, and IFRS 4 is used to account for the insurance component.
Discretionary participation features
50.48 Contracts that contain a discretionary participation feature are often called ‘with profits’ or ‘participating’ contracts.

50.49 Discretionary participation features arise where the policyholder has a contractual right to receive additional benefits in excess of guaranteed benefits from the issuer. The additional benefits need to be:
- likely to be a significant portion of the total contractual benefits;
- contractually at the issuer’s discretion about their amount or timing; and
- contractually based on:
- the performance of a specified pool of contracts or a specified type of contract;
- realised and/or unrealised investment returns on a specified pool of assets held by the issuer; or
- the profit or loss of the company, fund or other entity that issues the contract.

50.50 Issuers of contracts with discretionary participation features can either choose to treat the whole contract as a liability or separate out the guaranteed element and recognise that element as a liability.

50.51 Where a discretionary participation feature is accounted for separately from the guaranteed element, it should be recognised as a liability, or a separate component of equity, or it can be split between the two. It should not be treated as an intermediate category that is neither debt nor equity.
50.52 It is not specified how an issuer should determine the classification of discretionary participation features between liability and equity, but it should be done consistently.
50.53 Premiums arising on contracts with discretionary participation features can be recognised as revenue, without separating any portion that relates to the equity element.

50.54 Changes in the guaranteed element of contracts with discretionary participation features, and in the portion of the discretionary participation feature classified as a liability, are recognised in profit or loss.

50.55 The portion of profit or loss attributable to any equity component of a contract with a discretionary participation feature is recognised as an allocation of profit or loss, rather than expense or income. This is similar to the presentation of non-controlling interests (see chapter 26).
50.56 If a whole discretionary participation feature in an investment contract is classified as a liability, the issuer applies the liability adequacy test to the whole contract.

50.57 If any part of a discretionary participation feature in an investment contract is classified as a separate component of equity, the liability recognised for the whole contract must be no less than the amount that would result from applying IFRS 9 or IAS 39 (see para 50.75 onwards) to the guaranteed element.

50.58 Insurance contracts can contain embedded derivatives (see chapter 41 para 73 onwards). Subject to paragraph 50.59, IFRS 9 or IAS 39 (see para 50.75 onwards) applies to embedded derivatives contained in insurance contracts, unless the embedded derivative is itself an insurance contract.

50.59 An insurer does not need to separate, and measure at fair value, a policyholder’s option to surrender an insurance contract for a fixed amount (or for an amount based on a fixed amount and an interest rate). This is an exception to IFRS 9 and IAS 39 (see para 50.75 onwards).

50.60 Payments under an insurance contract can be linked to a price index. This link can be an embedded derivative but it can also transfer insurance risk. If the transfer of insurance risk is significant, the embedded derivative will meet the definition of an insurance contract. In this case, the embedded derivative need not be separated and measured at fair value according to IFRS 9 or IAS 39 (see para 50.75 onwards).
EX 50.60.1 – Embedded derivatives
Insurance contracts acquired in a business combination or portfolio transfer
50.61 An acquirer in a business combination should measure insurance liabilities assumed and insurance assets acquired at fair value.
50.62 An acquirer in a business combination can (but is not required to) expand the presentation of the fair value of the acquired insurance contracts into two components, as follows:
- a liability measured according to the insurer’s accounting policies for insurance contracts that it issues; and
- an intangible asset, representing the fair value of the contractual insurance rights and obligations acquired, to the extent that the liability does not reflect that fair value.

50.63 An insurer acquiring a portfolio of insurance contracts can use expanded presentation (set out within paragraph 50.62 to reflect both the fair value of the liability acquired and the related intangible asset.)
50.64 Intangible assets related to acquired insurance contracts (as described in paragraph 50.62) are excluded from the scope of IAS 36 and IAS 38.
50.65 Subsequent measurement of intangible assets related to acquired insurance contracts should be consistent with the measurement of the related insurance liability.
50.66 IAS 36 and IAS 38 apply to customer lists and customer relationships that are not part of the contractual insurance rights and obligations that existed at the date of the business combination.

Presentation and disclosure (paras 50.67 - 50.74)
50.67 IFRS 4’s implementation guidance (see paras IG20 to IG24) provides guidance on how IAS 1’s presentation requirements could be met in respect of insurance contracts.
50.68 An insurer should not net reinsurance amounts against the amounts arising from the related insurance contracts.
50.69 An insurer should disclose information that identifies and explains the amounts in its financial statements arising from insurance contracts.
50.70 An insurer should disclose information that enables users of its financial statements to evaluate the nature and extent of risks arising from insurance contracts.

50.71 The required disclosures are set out in paragraphs 37, 39 and 39A of IFRS 4, and paragraphs IG25 to IG71 of IFRS 4 discuss how these requirements could be met. For entities that apply the temporary exemption from IFRS 9 or the overlay approach, see paragraphs 50.83 and 50.92 respectively for the related disclosure requirements.
EX 50.71.1 – Materiality of disclosures
Disclosure in respect of investment contracts with discretionary participation features
50.72 Investment contracts with discretionary participation features are within the scope of IFRS 7 and subject to its disclosure requirements (see chapter 47).
50.73 The interest expense disclosed in accordance with paragraph 20(b) of IFRS 7 does not need to be calculated using the effective interest method.

50.74 Fair value disclosures under IFRS 7 are not required if the fair value of the discretionary participation features cannot be reliably measured. In such instances, information should be disclosed to help users of the financial statements to make their own judgements about the extent of possible differences between the contracts’ carrying amount and fair value. These disclosures are set out in paragraph 30 of IFRS 7.

Applying IFRS 9 with IFRS 4 (paras 50.75-50.92)

50.75 The IASB published an amendment to IFRS 4 in September 2016. This amendment addresses the concerns of insurance companies about the different effective dates of IFRS 9 and IFRS 17. The amendment to IFRS 4 provides two different solutions for insurance companies: a temporary exemption from IFRS 9 for entities that meet specific requirements (applied at the reporting entity level); and the ‘overlay approach’. Both approaches are optional.

50.76 IFRS 4 will be superseded by IFRS 17, as amended in June 2020. Accordingly, both the ‘temporary exemption’ and the ‘overlay approach’ will cease to be applicable when IFRS 17 becomes effective on 1 January 2023.

50.77 Under the temporary exemption, insurers are permitted to continue to apply IAS 39, instead of adopting IFRS 9, if their activities are ‘predominantly connected with insurance’ and when IFRS 9 is not previously applied. The assessment of whether activities are predominantly connected with insurance is initially performed as at the annual reporting date immediately preceding 1 April 2016.
FAQ 50.77.1 – Can a group use the temporary exemption from IFRS 9 to continue to apply IAS 39 in its consolidated financial statements?

50.78 Reassessments of eligibility for the temporary exemption at subsequent annual reporting dates are only made where there is a significant change in the entity’s activities, as described at paragraphs 20H to 20I of IFRS 4.
FAQ 50.78.1 – Can IFRS 9 be deferred for an insurance company incorporated after 31 December 2018?

50.79 To assess whether activities are ‘predominantly connected with insurance’, two tests have to be performed. Only if both tests are passed are an insurer’s activities considered to be predominantly connected with insurance.

50.80 First, an insurer assesses whether the carrying amount of its liabilities arising from contracts within IFRS 4’s scope (including any unbundled deposit components or embedded derivatives) is significant, compared to the total carrying amount of all of its liabilities. Secondly, the insurer compares the total carrying amount of its liabilities connected with insurance with the total carrying amount of all of its liabilities.
50.81 In addition to liabilities arising from contracts within IFRS 4’s scope, liabilities connected with insurance include:
- non-derivative investment contract liabilities measured at fair value through profit or loss applying IAS 39; and
- liabilities that arise because the insurer issues, or fulfils obligations arising from, those insurance and non-derivative investment contracts.
50.82 The second test is passed if the resulting percentage is:
- less than or equal to 90% but greater than 80%, and the insurer is not engaged in a significant activity unconnected with insurance.

FAQ 50.82.1 – What activities should be included in the assessment of whether an insurer engages in ‘significant activity unconnected with insurance’ for the purpose of applying the temporary exemption?

50.83 Entities that apply the temporary exemption from IFRS 9 have to make extensive disclosures to help users to understand why they are allowed to apply the temporary exemption from IFRS 9 and how this affects their financial statements. The required disclosures are set out in paragraphs 39C, 39D, 39G, 39H, 39I and 39J of IFRS 4.

50.83.1 Insurers applying the IFRS 4 temporary exemption to apply IAS 39 should consider Phase 2 Interest Rate Benchmark Reform Amendments to IFRS 9, IAS 39, IFRS 7, IFRS 4 and IFRS 16. Refer to Appendix A3.39, for the Phase 2 amendments issued in August 2020.

FAQ 50.83.1 – If an entity applies the temporary exemption from IFRS 9, should it provide the fair value and credit risk disclosures required by IFRS 4 in its interim financial statements? FAQ 50.83.2 – Is an insurer required to present comparative information in respect of the preceding reporting period for quantitative disclosures provided in accordance with paragraphs 39E to 39G of IFRS 4 when it first applies the temporary exemption?

50.84 Under IFRS 9, certain financial assets have to be measured at fair value through profit or loss; whereas, under IFRS 4, the related liabilities from insurance contracts could be measured on a cost basis. This might create volatility in profit or loss. The ‘overlay approach’ seeks to address the additional accounting mismatches and volatility in profit or loss that might arise from applying IFRS 9 before IFRS 17. The overlay approach is only relevant to those insurers that apply IFRS 9 (that is, that are not eligible for, or choose not to apply, the temporary exemption).

50.85 Under the overlay approach, an insurer is permitted to reclassify – from profit or loss to other comprehensive income – the difference between the amount that is reported in profit or loss under IFRS 9 and the amount that would have been reported in profit or loss under IAS 39 in respect of those designated financial assets to which the overlay approach is being applied.

50.86 A financial asset is eligible for designation for the ‘overlay approach’ if it is measured at fair value through profit or loss under IFRS 9, but would not be so measured under IAS 39. In addition, the asset cannot be held in respect of an activity that is unconnected with contracts within IFRS 4’s scope .
EX 50.86.1 – Assets held in respect of activity unconnected with insurance

50.87 An insurer chooses which eligible financial assets to designate for the overlay approach when it elects to apply the overlay approach. Subsequently, it might designate eligible financial assets for the overlay approach only on initial recognition or when an asset first becomes eligible for the overlay approach subsequent to initial recognition.

50.88 If a designated financial asset no longer meets the eligibility criteria for the overlay approach (for example, because it is transferred so that it is now held in respect of an entity’s banking activities or because the entity ceases to be an insurer), it should be de-designated.
50.89 In that case, any balance accumulated in other comprehensive income relating to this financial asset is reclassified to profit or loss.

50.90 The ‘overlay approach’ is applied retrospectively. Accordingly, the difference between the fair value of the designated financial assets and its carrying amount is recognised as an adjustment to the opening balance of accumulated other comprehensive income.
50.91 If, at the beginning of any accounting period, an insurer chooses to stop applying the overlay approach, it should apply IAS 8 to account for the change in accounting policy.

50.92 If an insurer applies the overlay approach, it has to provide information that enables users of the financial statements to understand how the amount that is reclassified from profit or loss to other comprehensive income is calculated and how the reclassification affects its financial statements. The required disclosures are set out in paragraphs 39L and 39M of IFRS 4.

Definition of insurance contracts
EX 50.8.1 – Contracts that are insurance contracts
Reference to standard: IFRS 4 para B18 Reference to standing text: 50.8 Insurance
Examples of insurance contracts (if the transfer of insurance risk is significant) are:
- Insurance against theft or damage to property.
- Insurance against product liability, professional liability, civil liability or legal expenses.
- Life insurance and pre-paid funeral plans.
- Life-contingent annuities and pensions.
- Disability and medical cover.
EX 50.8.2 – Contracts that are not insurance contracts
Reference to standard: IFRS 4 paras B19, B20, B21 Reference to standing text: 50.8 Insurance
Examples of contracts that are not insurance contracts are:
- Investment contracts that have the legal form of an insurance contract but do not transfer significant insurance risk.

- Retrospectively rated contracts that pass all significant insurance risk back to the policyholder (for example, through enforceable mechanisms that adjust future premiums as a direct result of incurred losses), such as some financial reinsurance or group contracts.
- Derivatives that expose one party to financial risk (such as changes in interest rate, commodity prices, foreign exchange rates and indexes) rather than insurance risk.
- Credit-related guarantees that trigger payments, even if the holder has not incurred a credit loss.
- Catastrophe bonds that provide for reduced payment of principal, interest or both, based on climatic or geological variables not specific to a party to the contract.

If any of the contracts above create financial assets or financial liabilities, they are accounted for using IFRS 9 (unless temporary exemptions in relation to the application of IFRS 9 apply (see para 50.75 onwards)).
If any of the contracts above do not create financial assets or financial liabilities, they are accounted for using IFRS 15 (see chapter 11).
Specified uncertain future event
EX 50.10.1 – Fixed-fee property maintenance contract
Reference to standard: IFRS 4 para B2 Reference to standing text: 50.10 Insurance

Entity P owns a portfolio of properties. It outsources its property maintenance and repair on all of these properties to Entity S, a property management company, for a five-year period for a fixed fee. This fee covers both property management and the cost of repair work. All repairs and maintenance required to maintain the properties to an agreed standard, based on the condition on inception of the contract, are now the responsibility of Entity S. The contract covers normal wear and tear and certain other conditions (such as dry rot and damp, should they be discovered in the course of any reme

Where either the number of services to be performed over a period or the nature of those services is not pre-determined, there can be significant insurance risk. There is uncertainty in the situation above in the following areas:
- whether any particular repairs will be required;
- when any particular repairs will be required; and
- how much any particular repair will cost.

There is a specified uncertain event, because it is uncertain when or if any particular repair will be required and how much it might cost. The significance of the insurance risk for Entity S is assessed, on a contract-by-contract basis, under IFRS 4. Insurance risk could be significant, even though there might be a minimal probability of material losses for Entity S arising from all of its property management contracts, because a significant loss could arise on any one contract, such as the contract with Entity P. If the insurance risk is significant, this contract will be an insurance contra
EX 50.10.2 – Manufacturer warranty contract
Reference to standard: IFRS 4 paras 4(a), B2
Reference to standing text: 50.10 Insurance

Entity G sells photocopiers to small businesses. The photocopiers require servicing after each 100,000 copies are made, and they break down from time to time. The photocopiers are sold with a one-year manufacturer’s warranty. When selling a photocopier, Entity G offers its customers an extended fixed-period repair and maintenance contract. Under this extended contract, Entity G will perform servicing and repairs to the photocopier, as necessary, for a fixed annual fee.

There can be significant insurance risk where either the number of services to be performed over the term of a contract or the nature of those services is uncertain. This arises because the issuer of the warranty and the extended contract will be compensating the customer if the photocopier breaks down and the breakdown will adversely affect the customer. The potential number and extent of any breakdowns are unknown, so the warranty and the extended contract meet the ‘uncertain future event’ element of the insurance contract definition.

But paragraph 4(a) of IFRS 4 specifically excludes product warranties issued directly by a manufacturer, retailer or dealer from the scope of IFRS 4. The contracts in this example are warranty contracts that have been issued by Entity G, the retailer, and fall outside IFRS 4’s scope.

The scope exclusion would not apply if the same repairs and maintenance were to be provided by a party other than the manufacturer, retailer or dealer (such as an entity specialising in photocopier repairs or a competing retailer).
Significant insurance risk
FAQ 50.12.1 – Does an equity release mortgage with a ‘no negative equity’ guarantee transfer insurance risk?
Reference to standard: IFRS 4 App A Reference to standing text: 50.12 Insurance

An entity issues an equity release mortgage (also commonly referred to as a 'lifetime or ‘reverse’ mortgage) with a ‘no negative equity’ guarantee. The contractual terms secure the mortgage against the borrower’s property. Principal and accrued interest are payable when the borrower dies or moves into long-term care. The property is then sold and the proceeds used to repay the mortgage balance (including any accrued interest). The entity is not entitled to any excess of the sales proceeds over the amount due but it bears any shortfall where the sales proceeds are not sufficient to repay the pr
Does the contract transfer insurance risk?

Yes. The contract exposes the entity to the risk of changes in fair value of the borrower’s property (that is, a non-financial asset). That is not a financial risk, because the fair value of the property reflects not only changes in market prices for properties in general (a financial variable) but also the physical condition of the specific asset (a non-financial variable). The contract therefore transfers insurance risk, as well as financial risk, from the borrower to the entity.

Under IFRS 4, a contract is treated as an insurance contract only if it transfers significant insurance risk, which arises if an insured event could cause an entity to pay significant additional benefits in at least one scenario with commercial substance. If that is the case and the entity could pay significant additional benefits to the policyholder/mortgagee in at least one scenario with commercial substance, then the instrument is an insurance contract within the scope of IFRS 4. The instrument would also be an insurance contract within the scope of IFRS 17 (when effective). When applying I

If the contract does not transfer significant insurance risk, it is within the scope of IFRS 9. As the bank holds the equity release mortgage within a ‘hold to collect’ business model, the classification and measurement of the contract under IFRS 9 is determined based on the contractual cash flow characteristics of the financial asset (the SPPI test) in accordance with paragraph 4.1.1 of IFRS 9. In performing the SPPI test, the bank needs to consider whether the possible effect of the ‘no negative equity’ guarantee is more than de minimis and is genuine (refer to FAQ 42.51.1). In doing so, imp

- The ‘significant additional benefits’ threshold in IFRS 4 is not the same as the de minimis threshold in IFRS 9. De minimis is a stricter threshold with regard to cash flow variability and is only met when the possible effects on cash flows are clearly trivial or negligible.

- In assessing whether the cash flows under the guarantee could arise only on the occurrence of an extremely rare, highly abnormal, or very unlikely event, so are not genuine, it should be questioned why the clause was included in the contract if it has no apparent commercial purpose. The remainder of this FAQ assumes the clause is genuine.

As a result, the equity release or ‘reverse’ mortgage will be measured in one of three ways, depending upon the extent of the possible cash flow variability arising from the ‘no negative equity’ guarantee:

- as an insurance contract under IFRS 4, where significant additional benefits accrue to the borrower (in the form of forgiveness of a shortfall that would otherwise be due) in at least one scenario with commercial substance;

- as a financial instrument under IFRS 9 at fair value through profit or loss, where the additional benefits will not be significant in any scenario with commercial substance but could be more than de minimis (that is, cash flows received are not SPPI as losses are borne by the lender if proceeds on sale of the property are insufficient to repay outstanding principal and interest); or
- as a financial instrument under IFRS 9 at amortised cost, where the additional benefits could never be more than de minimis.
Each individual contract should be analysed based on its specific facts and circumstances.
EX 50.16.1 – Payments for low probability events
Reference to standard: IFRS 4 para B23 Reference to standing text: 50.16 Insurance

An entity has a contract which requires an insurer to reimburse it for the value of a property that it owns in the event of the property being destroyed by a hurricane. The likelihood of a hurricane destroying a building is low (although the scenario has commercial substance), but the payment by the insurer would be substantial. In all other scenarios, a similar payment would not be made. The contract is therefore an insurance contract, because the insurance risk is significant.
Adversely effects the policyholder
EX 50.17.1 – Payment for insignificant loss
Reference to standard: IFRS 4 para B24(c) Reference to standing text: 50.17 Insurance

A contract requires the issuer to pay CU1 million to the holder if an asset suffers physical damage causing an insignificant economic loss of CU1. The holder transfers to the insurer the insignificant loss of losing CU1. The contract also creates the non-insurance risk that the issuer will need to pay CU999,999 if the physical damage occurs. Because the issuer does not accept significant insurance risk from the holder, this contract is not an insurance contract.

A gambler places a bet that a horse will win a race. This is a betting contract which depends on the outcome of a specified uncertain event. The gambler is not adversely affected by the outcome of the race before placing his bet, so the contract is not an insurance contract.

Reference to standard: IFRS 4 para 13 Reference to standing text: 50.23 Insurance
Can accounting policies that meet the requirements of IAS 37 meet the requirements in paragraph 13 of IFRS 4?

It depends. The existing accounting policies of entities that issue insurance contracts will often be determined by regulatory accounting requirements or local accounting standards. The IFRS 4 permission to continue with those policies (subject to the minimum requirements) results in diversity in how entities account for insurance contracts. Where the issuer is not an insurance company, the choice of accounting policies for an insurance contract can be complicated by the lack of specific local GAAP standards. EX 50.27.1 – Provision of services to discharge insurance obligations
Reference to standard: IFRS 4 para 14(c) Reference to standing text: 50.27 Insurance

Entity C provides car breakdown services to customers. Customers pay a fixed fee and Entity C undertakes to provide roadside assistance or to tow the car to a nearby garage for repair. Entity C has determined that there is significant insurance risk and, therefore, the contract is within the scope of IFRS 4. Unbundling insurance contracts
EX 50.46.1 – Loan waiver on death
Reference to standard: IFRS 4 para 10, IG example 1 para 1.24
Reference to standing text: 50.46 Insurance
Entity B loans CU100,000 to a customer over a period of 10 years. If the customer dies during the period of the loan agreement, the loan’s remaining balance will be waived.

The contract between Entity B and the customer contains a deposit element (the loan) and an insurance element (waiving the remaining loan balance on death is equivalent to a cash death benefit). Unbundling the deposit component from the insurance contract is required or permitted if the criteria in paragraph 10 of IFRS 4 are met. If the insurance component is not unbundled, the contract is an insurance contract if the insurance component is significant in relation to the whole contract.
EX 50.60.1 – Embedded derivatives
Reference to standard: IFRS 4 paras 7, 8, B11 Reference to standing text: 50.60 Insurance

Entity G (who is not the manufacturer, retailer or dealer) offers a repair or replacement service for washing machines and other domestic appliances for a predetermined fee. If a faulty appliance cannot be repaired, Entity G is obliged to make a specified payment to the policyholder for a replacement appliance. This payment is based on a formula that adjusts the appliance’s original cost by an inflation index.

The link to the inflation index is an embedded derivative. However, the payment is contingent on an uncertain future event (that is, whether the appliance breaks down and needs replacing), which adversely affects the policyholder (by being unable to use the appliance). So, the payment transfers insurance risk, and the embedded derivative meets the definition of an insurance contract.

EX 50.71.1 – Materiality of disclosures
Reference to standard: IFRS 4 para IG12 Reference to standing text: 50.71 Insurance

The implementation guidance explains in more detail how an entity can satisfy its disclosure requirements. An insurer decides, in the light of its circumstances, how much detail it gives to satisfy those requirements, how much emphasis it places on different aspects of the requirements, and how it aggregates information to display the overall picture without combining information that has materially different characteristics. It is necessary to strike a balance, so that important information is not obscured either by the inclusion of a large amount of insignificant detail or by the aggregation

- A large international insurance group that operates in a wide range of regulatory jurisdictions typically provides disclosures that differ in format, content and detail from those provided by a specialised niche insurer operating in one jurisdiction.
- Many insurance contracts have similar characteristics. Where no single contract is individually material, a summary by classes of contract is appropriate.
- Information about an individual contract might be material where it is, for example, a significant contributor to an insurer’s risk profile.
Applying IFRS 9 with IFRS 4
FAQ 50.77.1 – Can a group use the temporary exemption from IFRS 9 to continue to apply IAS 39 in its consolidated financial statements?
Reference to standard: IFRS 4 paras BC 260, BC 261, BC 262, BC 263 Reference to standing text: 50.77 Insurance
Can a group use the temporary exemption from IFRS 9 to continue to apply IAS 39 in its consolidated financial statements?

It depends. The temporary exemption from IFRS 9 only applies at the level of the reporting entity. The temporary exemption can only be applied in a group’s consolidated financial statements if the whole group is eligible for the temporary exemption. When a group fails to qualify for the temporary exemption because its activities are not predominantly connected with insurance:
- The group should apply IFRS 9 in its consolidated financial statements.
- The group can provide additional information to explain the effects of applying IFRS 9 with IFRS 4.
- Eligible insurance subsidiaries of the group can continue to apply IAS 39 in their individual financial statements, but will have to prepare IFRS 9 information for consolidation purposes.
FAQ 50.78.1 – Can IFRS 9 be deferred for an insurance company incorporated after 31 December 2018?
Reference to standard: IFRS 4 paras 20B, 20G Reference to standing text: 50.78 Insurance
Can IFRS 9 be deferred for an insurance entity incorporated after 31 December 2018?

No. Paragraph 20B(b) of IFRS 4 requires an entity to assess whether its activities are predominantly connected with insurance at its annual reporting date immediately preceding 1 April 2016. Paragraph 20G(b) of IFRS 4 further requires any reassessment to be made at a subsequent annual reporting date before 31 December 2018 (that is, the effective date of IFRS 9).

FAQ 50.82.1 – What activities should be included in the assessment of whether an insurer engages in ‘significant activity unconnected with insurance’ for the purpose of applying the temporary exemption?
Reference to standard: IFRS 4 para 20F Reference to standing text: 50.82 Insurance
What activities should be included in the assessment of whether an insurer engages in ‘significant activity unconnected with insurance’ for the purpose of applying the temporary exemption?

An insurer should consider only those activities from which it might earn revenue and incur expenses. This will take into account qualitative and/or quantitative factors, including publicly available information such as the industry classification that users of financial statements apply to the insurer. There is no guidance in IFRS 4 on how the term ‘significant’ should be interpreted. In practice, this will be one of the key areas of judgement in applying the temporary exemption.
FAQ 50.83.1 – If an entity applies the temporary exemption from IFRS 9, should it provide the fair value and credit risk disclosures required by IFRS 4 in its interim financial statements?
Reference to standard: IFRS 4 para 39B,IAS 34 paras 6, 16A Reference to standing text: 50.83 Insurance

IFRS 4 allows qualifying entities, whose activities are predominantly connected with insurance, to continue applying IAS 39, instead of adopting IFRS 9 for annual periods beginning before 1 January 2023.

Entities that apply the temporary exemption from IFRS 9 are required, by paragraphs 39B to 39G of IFRS 4, to make additional disclosures to help users to understand why they are permitted to apply the temporary exemption from IFRS 9 and how this affects their financial statements. The objective of these disclosures is to provide information that permits some comparison between insurers applying the temporary exemption and entities applying IFRS 9.

If an entity applies the temporary exemption from IFRS 9, should it provide the fair value and the credit risks disclosures required by paragraphs 39B to 39G of IFRS 4 in its interim financial statements prepared under IAS 34?

No. The IFRS 4 amendment made no consequential amendments to IAS 34 (see chapter 35), and it did not introduce any specific new interim disclosure requirements. However, judgement is required to meet the general requirements of IAS 34, including paragraphs 6 and 16A(a).

Paragraph 6 of IAS 34 states that the interim financial report is intended to provide an update on the latest complete set of annual financial statements and, accordingly, it focuses on new activities, events and circumstances. The adoption of the temporary exemption is such an event or circumstance.

Paragraph 16A(a) of IAS 34 requires an entity to provide “a statement that the same accounting policies and methods of computation are followed in the interim financial statements as compared with the most recent annual financial statements or, if those policies or methods have been changed, a description of the nature and effect of the change”. The adoption of the temporary exemption is an accounting policy choice, so it would be appropriate for an insurer to provide sufficient disclosures under paragraph 16A(a) of IAS 34 to help users to understand why it is permitted to apply the temporary

If the entity has disclosed sufficient information applying paragraph 30 of IAS 8 (see chapter 3), regarding deferral of IFRS 9 in the latest financial statements, a cross-reference from the interim financial statements to the latest financial statements could be included in the interim financial statements to satisfy the IAS 34 requirements.
In certain jurisdictions, there might be local regulatory rules and requirements that need to be considered for interim reporting, in addition to the points noted above.

Reference to standard: IFRS 4 paras 39B, 47 Reference to standing text: 50.83

Entities that apply the temporary exemption from IFRS 9 are required, by paragraphs 39E to 39G of IFRS 4, to make additional quantitative disclosures to help users to understand how this affects the financial statements. The objective of these disclosures is to provide information that permits some comparison of insurers applying the temporary exemption with entities applying IFRS 9.

Is an insurer required to present comparative information in respect of the preceding reporting period for the quantitative disclosures provided in accordance with paragraphs 39E to 39G of IFRS 4 when it first applies the temporary exemption (that is, for an entity with a calendar reporting year-end, in its financial statements as at 31 December 2018)?
No, insurers are permitted, but not required, to provide comparative information for these disclosures.

The objective of the disclosure requirements in the amendment is “to enable users of financial statements to make some comparisons between insurers applying the temporary exemption and entities applying IFRS 9”. In 2017 – the comparative period – all insurers still apply IAS 39 (except for those that have decided to early adopt IFRS 9), since IFRS 9 becomes effective for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2018. Furthermore, paragraph 47 of IFRS 4 points out that “… an entity that discloses the information required by paragraphs 39B–39J shall use the transitional provisions in IFRS 9 ….”. IFRS 9 provides relief from restating comparative information. Instead, entities are required to provide the disclosures set out in paragraphs 42L to 42O of IFRS 7 in the period when they first apply IFRS 9. Disclosures for the preceding period are not required. Introduction and scope (paras 50A.1-50A.29)
This chapter provides guidance on IFRS 17. IFRS 17 is effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2023. Early application is permitted, provided that the entity also applies IFRS 9.
Scope of IFRS 17, classification of contracts by insurers
50A.1 IFRS 17 applies to:
- insurance contracts that an entity issues (see para 50A.2);
- all reinsurance contracts (that is, those that an entity issues and those that an entity holds) (see para 50A.22); and
- investment contracts with discretionary participation features that an entity issues, provided that an entity also issues insurance contracts (see para 50A.24).
– Does IFRS 17 apply to entities other than regulated insurers?

50A.2 IFRS 17 defines an insurance contract as a contract under which one party (the issuer) accepts significant insurance risk from another party (the policyholder) by agreeing to compensate the policyholder if a specified uncertain future event (the insured event) adversely affects the policyholder.

50A.3 A contract is an agreement between two or more parties that creates enforceable rights and obligations. The enforceability of rights or obligations is a matter of law. Contracts can be written, oral or implied by customary business practices. Contractual terms can be either explicit or implicit, including those terms that are imposed by law or regulation. In applying the standard to insurance contracts, an entity should consider its substantive rights and obligations arising from a contract, law or regulation. However, contractual terms that confer no discernible effect on the economics

EX 50A.3.2 – Contracts that are not insurance contracts

50A.4 An insurance contract must transfer significant insurance risk arising from an uncertain future event that adversely affects the policyholder and results in the payment of significant additional amounts. These terms are discussed further in paragraphs 50A.5 to 50A.19.
[IFRS 17 App B para B17]. [IFRS 17 App B para B18].

50A.5 The definition of insurance risk refers to risk that the entity accepts from the policyholder. That is, insurance risk must be a pre-existing risk that is transferred from the policyholder to the entity as a result of the contract, and it must not be a new risk created by the contract.
[IFRS 17 App B para B11].

[IFRS 17 App B para B27(c)].

Specified uncertain future event
50A.7 Uncertainty (or risk) is the essence of an insurance contract. At least one of the following is uncertain at the inception of an insurance contract:
- the probability of an insured event occurring;
- how much the entity will need to pay if it occurs.
Significant insurance risk
50A.8 The risk accepted from the policyholder must be insurance risk. Insurance risk is any risk other than financial risk that is transferred from the holder of the contract to the issuer.

50A.9 Financial risk is “the risk of a possible future change in one or more of a specified interest rate, financial instrument price, commodity price, currency exchange rate, index of prices or rates, credit rating or credit index or other variable, provided in the case of a non-financial variable that the variable is not specific to a party to the contract”.
50A.10 Contracts can contain both financial and insurance risk. Such contracts are not excluded from being insurance contracts, provided that the insurance risk is significant.
FAQ 50A.10.1 – Is a contract classified as an insurance contract if it insures expense risk and lapse risk?

50A.11 Insurance risk is ‘significant’ if, and only if, the occurrence of an insured event could cause the entity to pay additional amounts that are “significant in any single scenario, excluding scenarios that have no commercial substance (that is, no discernible effect on the economics of the transaction)”.
[IFRS 17 App B para B18]. [IFRS 17 App B para B19].
50A.12 IFRS 17 does not set a numerical threshold for ‘significant’ insurance risk.

50A.13 A scenario with commercial substance can be one that is extremely unlikely. An entity needs to consider whether the additional amounts that would be payable are greater in a scenario with commercial substance in which the insured event occurs than in any other scenario. The entity will then have to determine whether the difference between the additional amounts payable under this scenario and the additional amounts payable if no insured event occurred is significant.
[IFRS 17 App B para B18].

50A.14 This assessment should be made on a present value basis. The discount rate used to calculate the present value should reflect the time value of money, the characteristics of the cash flows and the liquidity characteristics of the insurance contract. The same rate is also used for measurement purposes if the contract meets the definition of an insurance contract (see para 50A.111).
[IFRS 17 App B para B20].

50A.16 The significance of the insurance risk is assessed on a contract-by-contract basis. Accordingly, the insurance risk can be significant, even if there is minimal probability of significant losses for a portfolio or a group of contracts.
[IFRS 17 App B para B22].

50A.17 A contract requiring payment to the policyholder if a specified uncertain event occurs is only an insurance contract if the event creates insurance risk (as opposed to financial risk) and that event adversely affects the policyholder.

50A.19 Payments under insurance contracts can be more than the loss suffered. One such case is ‘new for old’ insurance coverage, where the entity pays for the replacement cost of a new asset, rather than capping the compensation to the value of the old and damaged asset.

50A.20 Some contracts transfer insurance risk to the issuer only after a period of time. For such contracts, an entity has to make an assessment as to whether there is a transfer of significant insurance risk from the policyholder resulting from cash flows that are within the boundary of the contract (see para 50A.81). A contract meets the definition of an insurance contract at inception if there is a transfer of significant insurance risk arising from cash flows within the boundary of the contract.
[IFRS 17 App B para B24].

50A.21 Where a contract meets the definition of an insurance contract, it remains an insurance contract until all of the rights and obligations under the contract are extinguished, unless a contract is derecognised as a result of contract modification (see para 50A.197).
[IFRS 17 App B para B25].

50A.22 IFRS 17 defines a reinsurance contract as an insurance contract issued by one entity (the reinsurer) to compensate another entity for claims arising from one or more insurance contracts issued by that other entity (underlying contracts).

50A.23 The requirements for the assessment of significant insurance risk in a reinsurance contract are the same as for an insurance contract. However, additionally, a reinsurance contract transfers significant insurance risk if it transfers substantially all of the insurance risk resulting from the reinsured portion of the underlying insurance contract, even if it does not expose the reinsurer to the possibility of a significant loss.
[IFRS 17 App B para B19].

Investment contracts with discretionary participation features

50A.24 IFRS 17 defines an investment contract with discretionary participation features as a financial instrument that provides a particular investor with the contractual right to receive, as a supplement to an amount not subject to the discretion of the issuer, additional amounts:
- that are expected to be a significant portion of the total contractual benefits;
- the amount or timing of which is contractually at the discretion of the issuer; and
- that are contractually based on either:
- the returns on a specified pool of contracts or a specified type of contract,
- realised and/or unrealised investment returns on a specified pool of assets held by the issuer, or
- the profit or loss of the entity or fund that issues the contract.

50A.25 Investment contracts with discretionary participation features are only within the scope of IFRS 17 if the entity also issues insurance contracts. Otherwise, they are accounted for as compound instruments containing a financial liability component (within the scope of IFRS 9) and an equity component, if applicable.

50A.26 Other standards, rather than IFRS 17, apply to the following (even if the definition of an insurance contract is met):

- Product warranties provided by a manufacturer, retailer or dealer in connection with the sale of its products (either a good or a service) to a customer are within the scope of IFRS 15 (see chapter 11) and IAS 37 (see chapter 16).

- Employers’ assets and liabilities from employee benefit plans are within the scope of IAS 19 (see chapter 12) and IFRS 2 (see chapter 13); and retirement benefit obligations reported by defined benefit retirement plans are within the scope of IAS 26.

- Contractual rights or obligations that are contingent on the future use of, or the right to use, a non-financial item are within the scope of IFRS 16 (see chapter 15), IFRS 15 (see chapter 11) and IAS 38 (see chapter 21).
- Residual value guarantees provided by a manufacturer, dealer or retailer are within the scope of IFRS 15 (see chapter 11).
- Residual value guarantees for lessees embedded in a lease are within the scope of IFRS 16 (see chapter 15).

50A.28 Some contracts might meet the definition of an insurance contract but have as their primary purpose the provision of services to a customer for a fixed fee. An entity can make an irrevocable choice to apply IFRS 15 instead of IFRS 17 to these contracts if all of the following conditions are met:
- the price of the contract does not reflect an assessment of the risk with an individual customer;
- the contract compensates the customer by providing a service; and
- the insurance risk arises primarily from the customer’s use of services rather than from uncertainty over the cost of the service.

50A.29 Some contracts meet the definition of an insurance contract but limit the compensation for insured events to the amount otherwise required to settle the policyholder's obligation created by the contract (for example, loans with death waivers). An entity shall choose to apply either IFRS 17 or IFRS 9 to such contracts that it issues, unless such contracts are excluded from the scope of IFRS 17 (see para 50A.26). The choice can be made for each portfolio of insurance contracts, and the choice made for each portfolio is irrevocable.
