text: A1.5 A family-owned or managed business could consist of a number of separate entities that are not controlled by any one individual or collectively under the terms of a contractual arrangement. A control group is presumed to exist between spouses and their children. Control groups involving siblings should be considered based on specific facts and circumstances. A contractual agreement is needed to conclude that a control group exists in other circumstances. The reason for this condition is to prevent the use of ‘grooming' transactions, whereby, for a brief period immediately before the combination, the combining entities or businesses are under common control. It might otherwise be possible for combinations that should otherwise be accounted for in accordance with IFRS 3 (that is, using t

text: A1.8 Common control is not transitory when the combining entities or businesses have been under common control for a period before the combination. A re-organisation within a group, to facilitate a spin-off or an initial listing, is a business combination involving entities under common control, although the parent loses control shortly after the transaction.

text: A1.10 The key feature of a business combination among entities under common control is that there is no change in the ultimate control of the combining entities as a result of the transaction. The extent of non-controlling interests in each of the combining entities before and after the business combination is not relevant to determining whether the combination involves entities under common control.

text: A1.14 Considering facts and circumstances (see paras A1.17 and A1.18), management could refer to IFRS 3 in determining a policy for business combinations under common control and decide to adopt the acquisition method as its accounting policy. IFRS 3 is the standard that applies to most business combinations. Management could select IFRS 3 acquisition accounting for business combinations involving entities or businesses under common control, notwithstanding the fact that these transactions are excluded from the scope of IFRS 3 (see para A1.1). The requirements of IFRS 3 should be applied in fu

text: A1.15 Considering facts and circumstances (see paras A1.17 and A1.18) management could apply a method broadly described as predecessor accounting. The principles of predecessor accounting are:

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: - Assets and liabilities of the acquired entity are stated at predecessor carrying values (see paras A1.19 to A1.21). Fair value measurement is not required.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: - No new goodwill arises in predecessor accounting.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: - Any difference between the consideration given and the aggregate carrying value of the assets and liabilities of the acquired entity at the date of the transaction is included in equity in retained earnings or in a separate reserve.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: A1.16 Some commonly used methods for predecessor accounting in consolidated financial statements are:

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: - Retrospective presentation method. The acquired entity’s results and balance sheet are incorporated as if both entities (acquirer and acquiree) had always been combined, or using the results from the date when either entity joined the group, where such a date is later.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: - Prospective presentation method. The acquired entity’s results and balance sheet are incorporated prospectively from the date on which the business combination between entities under common control occurred.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: A1.17 The accounting policy that management selects will be determined by the substance and the specific facts and circumstances surrounding any particular business combination under common control. A consistent policy should be applied to transactions of a similar nature. The following criteria might be used in determining which accounting policy best reflects the substance of each business combination under common control:

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: - Existence of non-controlling interests: if non-controlling interests are affected, this might point towards acquisition accounting being an appropriate policy. Conversely, if the entities are wholly owned, this might point towards predecessor accounting being more appropriate.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: - Consideration for the transfer: if the fair value for an entity or a business is paid in full in cash, this might point towards acquisition accounting being an appropriate policy. Conversely, if the consideration for the transfer is set at the existing book values in the accounts of the transferring entity, this might point towards predecessor accounting being an appropriate policy.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: - Management of combining entities: if combining entities were managed together before and after the combination, this might point towards the predecessor method being an appropriate policy. Conversely, if the combining entities or businesses were not managed together, although still controlled by the same ultimate controlling party, acquisition accounting might be more appropriate.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: - Purpose of the transaction: if the transaction is undertaken in connection with an IPO or other change in control or significant change in ownership event, this might point towards acquisition accounting being an appropriate policy. Conversely, if the transaction is undertaken to effect an internal simplification, or it is driven perhaps by internal tax planning strategies, this might point towards predecessor accounting being an appropriate policy.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: A1.18 The above list of criteria is not exhaustive. Management might need to make a judgement, and disclose the policy chosen and reasons for it, as part of its critical judgement disclosures as required by IAS 1. Applying acquisition accounting is not a free policy choice but it requires management to demonstrate economic substance. If there is no economic substance, acquisition accounting is not considered appropriate. Applying substance when selecting a policy might result in two business combinations under common control being accounted for differently by the reporting entity where the spe

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: A1.19 As stated in paragraphs A1.11 and A1.12, there is no guidance in IFRS on the treatment for business combinations under common control; however, the IASB is currently debating the topic. Several issues were raised with the IFRS IC and subsequently the IASB decided to address the topic as part of a wider project starting with a issuance of a discussion paper expected in late 2020. Currently, the selection of predecessor accounting versus acquisition accounting would need to be made following the guidance in IAS 8, as would the selection of values used when applying predecessor accounting.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: A1.20 The controlling party might not prepare consolidated financial statements. In such situations, the book values used are generally those from the highest set of consolidated financial statements available. If no consolidated financial statements are produced, the values used would be those from the financial statements of the acquired entity.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: A1.21 Given the absence of definitive guidance in IFRS, there might be circumstances that support the use of other values as predecessor values (for example, carrying values from the financial statements of an intermediate sub-group or from the acquired entity), even where consolidated financial statements are prepared at a higher level. Careful analysis of the facts and circumstances is required to determine whether it would be more meaningful to select such alternative values. For example, we believe that the following considerations would typically be relevant in determining appropriate val

text: - Transaction in preparation for a listing. The values in the highest level of consolidation will typically be more relevant if the common control business combination is in preparation for a listing or sale. Transactions in preparation for a listing can occur in a variety of ways. For example, two existing subsidiaries might be merged into one, and the surviving subsidiary is then listed. Alternatively, a New Co might be involved and the accounting could be more complex, because the transaction might not be a business combination under common control. There is no guidance in IFRS, so the subs

text: - Identity of users. If the users of the financial statements of the reporting entity that now includes the transferred business are users that previously relied on the financial statements of the transferred business, the book values of the transferred business might be more relevant.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: - Timing of transaction. The timing of the transaction should be considered in relation to when the business over which the receiving and reporting entity now has control was originally established or acquired by the group as a whole. The longer the time period, the less relevant the values in the business’s own financial statements are likely to be if the business has been directed and operated as part of the wider group.

text: A1.22 The selection of a policy that applies predecessor or acquisition accounting is only relevant where there is a combination of two or more businesses under common control. This situation might arise in separate financial statements where a business is transferred up into an existing entity that is itself a business. It might also arise in the consolidated financial statements of a business entity that has acquired a subsidiary that also qualifies as a business.

text: A1.23 If a New Co is involved, care needs to be taken when analysing what, if any, substance New Co has and what role it plays, because the transaction might not be a business combination under common control:

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: - Conversely, there might be situations where a new company is set up as an acquisition vehicle by the purchaser and for purchaser’s benefit. In such a case – as outlined in EX 29.40.1 for the VCP Acq Co in Step C – the new acquisition company would be seen as the acquirer in a business combination, and it should apply IFRS 3 acquisition accounting.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: - It might also be the case that New Co, similar to the situation in the first bullet above, does not have any substance, but it acquires two separate and independent businesses from within the common control group. In that case, because two or more businesses are being combined, one of the combining businesses would be identified as the acquirer and one as the acquiree. In that case, a business combination exists and, similar to EX 29.39.1, acquisition accounting could be applied. text: A1.24 The acquiree could have been previously acquired by the controlling party in a business combination. The controlling party would have applied the acquisition method, and it would have recognised assets and liabilities (including goodwill) in accordance with IFRS 3. The numbers from the highest level of common control used in predecessor accounting would differ from the carrying amounts in the stand-alone financial statements of the acquiree. These numbers are not pushed down to the financial statements of the acquiree under IFRS.

text: A1.25 The combining entities are looked at from the perspective of a transfer made by the controlling party. The transaction is not seen as an equal exchange of values and a change of control from the date of the business combination. No goodwill beyond that recorded by the controlling party in relation to the acquiree can therefore arise.

text: A1.26 When the retrospective presentation method is used, the consolidated financial statements reflect both entities' full-year results, even though the business combination might have occurred part of the way through the year. The corresponding amounts for the previous year reflect the combined results of both entities, even though the transaction did not occur until the current year. This reflects the view that the transaction involves two entities controlled by a controlling party. The financial statements reflect the numbers from the perspective of that party, and they reflect the period

text: A1.29 Transactions under common control mainly occur in two ways:

text: A1.30 The acquisition of an equity investment in a subsidiary in an entity’s separate financial statements is not a business combination. The acquirer includes its interest in the acquiree as an investment in a subsidiary in accordance with IAS 27.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: A1.31 A business combination occurs in separate financial statements only if the entity acquires an unincorporated business or a set of activities and assets meeting the definition of a business.

text: Transfer of a business from a subsidiary to its parent (hive-up transactions)

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: A1.32 The transfer of a subsidiary’s business (a set of activities and assets) to its parent is often referred to as a ‘hive-up’. The consideration is often payable via an inter-company account. If a subsidiary is 100% owned, such a transaction does not result in any change from a group perspective. The issue is how to account for the transaction in separate financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: A1.33 The entity could account for the transaction using either the predecessor values method (see para A1.15) or the acquisition accounting method (see para A1.14).

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: A1.34 Acquisition accounting applied to the hive-up results in the same accounting treatment, practically speaking, as predecessor accounting if a hive-up takes place immediately after an acquisition.

Investments might be transferred at, for example, the carrying amount of the subsidiary’s net assets, or for no consideration. text: A1.37 The transfer of the subsidiary could be achieved by transferring equity instruments between entities under common control. The appropriate accounting treatment for such a transfer is based on the substance of the transaction. Judgement should be applied to determine whether a distribution from an investee to a parent is a return on capital (dividend income) or a return of capital (a reduction or reallocation of the cost of investment). See also chapter 28 paras 32 and 33 and FAQ 28.33.1, ‘How is a distribution in the form of an investment in a subsidiary accounted for?'.

text: A1.38 Dividend income should be recognised by the transferee in profit or loss and would typically be recorded at fair value. However, if the dividend income relates to the receipt of an investment in a subsidiary (which constitutes a business), there is a policy choice to record the investment received and therefore the dividend income either at the carrying amount of the investment in the transferor’s separate financial statements at the date of transfer (that is, ‘predecessor value’) or at fair value.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: A1.39 There is no specific guidance in IFRS that deals with distributions of non-cash assets that meet the definition of a business between entities under common control. Management of the transferee should select either acquisition accounting or predecessor values method, and it should apply that policy as outlined in paragraph A1.14 onwards.

text: A1.40 The transferor has an accounting policy choice as to whether to recognise the dividend at the book value or fair value of the investment that is being distributed. IFRIC 17 requires a fair value approach for certain transactions. However, IFRIC 17 does not apply to a distribution of a non-cash asset that is ultimately controlled by the same party or parties (that is, common control) before and after the distribution. text: A1.41 Complications might arise where a common control transaction involves a new company set up by the group to effect the combination of entities under common control. The combination of a new company and a single reporting entity is unlikely to meet the definition of a business combination in the context of IFRS 3. The new company will not be the acquirer; and it is not a business, so reverse acquisition accounting principles will not be available, because reverse acquisition is an application of IFRS 3. text: A1.42 The new company’s consolidated financial statements include the existing entity’s full results (including comparatives), even though the re-organisation might have occurred part of the way through the year. This reflects the view that the transaction involves two entities controlled by the same controlling party – they reflect the period over which that party has had control. The assets and liabilities of the existing entity are incorporated at their pre-combination carrying amounts without fair value uplift. This is on the basis that there is no substantive economic change.

text: A1.43 There are other common control situations involving the establishment of a new company and the combination of more than two entities. In those situations, there is a selection to be made between applying predecessor accounting and acquisition accounting (see paras A1.17 and A1.18 above). Capital re-organisation accounting will be applied in relation to the financial statements of the identified acquirer (see also para A1.45).

In the new company’s consolidated financial statements, management will have to decide, based on the specific facts and circumstances, whether to apply acquisition accounting in accordance with IFRS 3 or predecessor accounting, provided that the transaction meets the definition of a business combination. If acquisition accounting is used, the new company will not be identified as the acquirer. Instead, one of the combining entities will be the acquirer. These businesses might be seen as a single reporting entity. The transaction will not be a business combination, but rather it will be a capital re-organisation of the existing reporting entity (see further para A1.41 onwards and chapter 29 paras 39 to 41).

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: The private operating entity is seeking to obtain the listing status of the non-operating public shell corporation. This transaction is usually not considered to be a business combination, because the non-operating public shell corporation does not meet the definition of a business. This is a capital transaction of the legal acquiree and is equivalent to the issuance of shares by the private entity for the net monetary assets of the public shell corporation, accompanied by a recapitalisation. This is not a business combination under IFRS 3.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations

The deemed shares issued by the private entity (that is, the consideration for the acquisition of the public shell company) are recognised at fair value and recorded as an expense.

Any difference between the fair value of the shares deemed to have been issued by the private operating company and the fair value of the public shell company’s identifiable net assets represents a service received by the acquirer. chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: The Smith family runs a retail business. The retail outlets are operated by seven companies that are owned in different proportions by Mr. Smith, his wife, and their three children. No one member of the family has more than 50% of the equity of any of the operating companies; and there is no contractual arrangement among the members of the family. None of the companies has previously acquired a business from a member of the family.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: The family has been advised to consolidate their holdings for tax purposes. A new holding company, entity X, has been formed and will acquire all of the operating companies by issuing shares to Mr. and Mrs. Smith and their three children. Each family member will own 20% of entity X after the transaction.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: The Smith family together controls all of the combining entities before and after the transaction. The reorganisation is a business combination involving entities under common control. The combining entities are entity X and the existing operating companies. Even though there is no contractual arrangement that gives the family common control, in many cases, such an arrangement is presumed to exist due to the close family relationships.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: In such a case, management should select an accounting policy based on the substance and specific facts and circumstances surrounding the transaction – either the acquisition method or the predecessor values method, if this is the acquiring entity’s first business combination involving entities under common control. All of the requirements of IFRS 3 are applied if the acquisition method is used. Entity X cannot be the acquirer (see para A1.44).

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: If a new entity is formed to issue equity interests to effect a business combination, one of the combining entities that existed before the business combination shall be identified as the acquirer by applying the guidance in IFRS 3. All of the existing companies together should be identified as the acquirer if they are managed together as a single business. The accounting result would be similar to predecessor accounting in the case where all of the companies together are the acquirer under IFRS 3.

S1, S2 and S3 could be individual shareholders or entities that have entered into two separate joint venture agreements governing entities A and B. text: Entities D and P provide oilfield services in the North Sea. Entity D is owned by a group of individuals, none of whom have control, and who do not have a collective control agreement. Entity P is owned by a single individual, Mr X. The owners of entities D and P have decided to combine their entities. The consideration will be settled in shares of entity P.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: Entity P issues new shares, amounting to 30% of its issued share capital, to its controlling shareholder, Mr X. Mr X then transfers the shares to the owners of entity D in exchange for their interest in entity D. At this point, Mr X controls both entities D and P, owning 100% of entity D and 70% of entity P. Mr X then contributes the controlling interest in entity D to entity P. Mr X had a controlling interest in both entities D and P before and after the contribution. Is the combination of entities D and P a combination of entities under common control?

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: No. This is not a business combination of entities under common control. Mr X’s control of both entities before the business combination was transitory. The substance of the transaction is that entity P has obtained control of entity D. Entity P accounts for this transaction as a business combination under IFRS 3 using acquisition accounting.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: Transaction 1 – Yes. In the first transaction, the transfer of entity C to entity E, the non-controlling interest is not affected, because the composition of the sub-group headed by entity B remains unchanged. In entity E's consolidated financial statements, the combination with entity C qualifies for the exemption from IFRS 3 for a combination between entities under common control; this is because it is a business combination in which the combining entities (entities E and C) are controlled by the same party (entity A) both before and after the combination.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations

The non-controlling interest in entity B has disposed of part of the entity B sub-group. text: Company A is a publicly listed company with numerous subsidiaries with substantive operations. One of these subsidiaries, company G, has debt that is publicly listed. Company G has three subsidiaries – companies X, Y and Z – that constitute its operations in three different countries. In anticipation of an IPO, company X acquires company Z. Assume that company A and company G have different carrying values for the assets of company Z. What predecessor values should company X use in its consolidated financial statements?

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations
text: The consolidated figures from the highest level should normally be used for business combinations under common control (see para A1.19). That would mean that company X would use the values as recorded in the consolidated financial statements of company A with respect to company Z. However, given that this re-organisation has occurred entirely within the consolidated operations of company G, and there are third party stakeholders in company G's financial statements, using the values from the consolidated financial statements of company G might be more relevant in this case.

text: IAS 27 does not define ‘cost’, nor does it specify how an entity determines the cost of the investment in a subsidiary under a common control transaction. Historical cost, under the Conceptual Framework, is the value of the costs incurred in acquiring or creating the asset, comprising the consideration paid to acquire or create the asset plus transaction costs.

chapter: Appendix 1 - Business combinations under common control, transfers of investments within groups and capital re-organisations

This subtle change from the original wording – ‘fair value of the consideration given’ – proposed in the tentative decision suggested that fair value might not always be the only appropriate basis to measure cost.

In summary, it appears that the determination of cost in these scenarios is not straightforward.

Another approach is to use the predecessor value, where the investment is measured at the carrying amount of the investment in the transferor’s separate financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.1 Consolidated financial statements of an issuer of debt or equity securities are normally required by regulators around the world. These requirements are usually met by presenting consolidated financial statements prepared under IFRS or local GAAP.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.2 Financial information might be required for part or parts of a group, in some circumstances. This is usually in connection with a transaction of some nature – disposals, distributions, business combinations, spin-offs and initial public offerings (IPOs) are examples of transactions where a specific type of financial information is required.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.3 The financial information might be needed for parts of a group that are under common control but are not part of a legal sub-group, where the preparation of consolidated financial statements would be appropriate. Financial statements of entities that are under common control are primarily prepared for use in a transaction. These are most often described as ‘combined’ or ‘carve out’ financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.4 ‘Combined financial statements’ are financial information that includes economic activities that are bound together by common control but are not a legal group. These are usually prepared by aggregating the financial statements of segments, separate entities or components of groups that fail to meet the definition of a ‘group’ under IFRS 10.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.5 ‘Carve out financial statements’ are the financial statements of a division or lesser business component(s) of a larger entity; the term is commonly used to refer to equity carve outs, spin-offs and split-offs. Carve out financial statements may also be combined financial statements if, for example, financial information from components of separate legal sub-groups are aggregated.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.6 The term ‘new reporting entity’ is used to describe the economic activity, usually part of an existing group that is the basis of the combined financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.7 The preparation of combined financial statements can require the exercise of considerable judgement. Each transaction is different and each set of combined financial statements will present unique challenges. The nature of the transaction, the boundary of the reporting entity, the quality of the accounting records, the past practices and policies of the parent, and the views of the relevant regulator are very important.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.8 IFRS does not include specific guidance on the preparation of combined financial statements, although the Conceptual Framework and other standards include relevant information for preparing combined financial statements. However, it is accepted that there are circumstances in which combined financial statements can claim to be prepared in accordance with IFRS.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.9 There is no set method that results in combined financial statements being prepared in accordance with IFRS. There is a common set of questions that need to be asked; the answers will determine whether IFRS combined financial statements can be prepared and how that might be accomplished, as well as what disclosures might be required.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.10 This guidance is designed to assist in the preparation of combined financial statements. Each set of combined financial statements presents unique questions and challenges. Nothing should be read as overriding the accounting standards or relevant regulatory requirements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.11 This guidance sets out the questions and describes some of the common practices that are followed in preparing combined financial statements under IFRS.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.12 This guidance does not address the accounting issues that might arise in the current parent or ultimate controlling party.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.13 The preparation of combined financial statements, particularly for a capital markets transaction, always presents a unique set of issues. Management should ensure that it has consulted its auditors and professional advisers. Management should also understand the views and requirements of the relevant regulators.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.14 The five key steps in the diagram below set out the process and the considerations that are commonly encountered when preparing combined financial statements:

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Step 1: Determine the purpose of the combined financial statements and understand the relevant regulatory requirements

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.15 Consolidated financial statements and combined financial statements both present historical financial information. Consolidated financial statements require the consolidation of the parent company and all of its subsidiaries. Combined financial statements present the historical financial information of specific economic activities.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.16 A key assumption underlying the preparation of combined financial statements is that there is a binding element for the economic activities throughout the period (see further guidance in para A2.42). The binding element is not necessarily direct legal ownership, although common control is almost always present. The binding element is the characteristic based on which the economic activities are ‘bound’ together throughout a period (for example, legal ownership or common control).

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.17 ‘Carve out’ financial statements are the financial statements of a division or lesser business component(s) of a larger entity. The term ‘carve out’ arises because the business unit’s financial statements are viewed as being ‘carved out’ of the larger consolidated financial statements. There is no accounting definition of a carve out transaction; the term is commonly used to refer to equity carve outs, spin-offs and split-offs.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: What is the objective of the combined financial statements?

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.18 Combined financial statements are usually prepared in connection with a contemplated transaction, such as an initial public offering (IPO) through a spin-off of a division or major line of business, or in connection with a planned distribution to shareholders. Alternatively, the combined financial statements might serve as the basis for final purchase price discussions in a merger and acquisition transaction.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.19 The purpose and the users of the combined financial statements might influence how the financial information is prepared and presented. The working assumption in this guidance is that non-standard financial statements are required that comply with IFRS.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.20 Few countries have specific regulatory requirements for the preparation of non-standard financial statements. See FAQ A2.20.1 for examples of regulatory requirements relating to combined financial information.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: FAQ A2.20.1 – What regulatory information sources are there for combined financial statements?

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.21 If there are specific regulatory requirements, those must be followed. The resulting financial information might or might not comply with IFRS. For example, a reporting entity preparing combined financial statements under IFRS subject to SEC regulation will be expected to follow the SEC guidance. The combined financial statements would normally comply with IFRS as well. Financial information prepared on the basis of the UK’s guidance in Standards for Investment Reporting (SIR) 2000, ‘Investment reporting standards applicable to public reporting engagements on historical financial informa

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.22 Many other countries find the existing guidance of other regulators useful, but their regulators are broadly looking for combined financial statements prepared in accordance with IFRS. Most combined financial statements are prepared with a view to capital market transactions. Management should understand the perspective of the relevant regulator in the early stages, even if the regulator has not published comprehensive guidelines on preparing combined financial statements. The views of the regulator might be obvious from similar transactions that have occurred, public statements, company

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.23 Different regulators might take different views, and this could have a profound impact on the nature, extent and even acceptability of the combined financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.24 Combined financial statements might be prepared in a jurisdiction that has no specific guidance, or they might be prepared for another purpose, such as providing to lenders, suppliers or counterparties. It might be useful to voluntarily follow a set of regulatory guidance, because it is likely to be better understood by users.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.25 The basic objectives of financial reporting are to provide useful information for assessing management stewardship and allowing users to assess the ability of the reporting entity to generate cash flows. These objectives remain relevant when preparing combined financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.26 The combined financial statements are inherently a ‘temporary’ measure. They are prepared for a specific objective at a point in time for a specified number of reporting periods. It would be unusual for combined financial statements to be prepared for a number of successive periods. After a certain period of time, the reporting entity will either be in a position to prepare consolidated financial statements, or it would have been subsumed into a larger group, following the transaction or the restructuring.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Can ‘fair presentation’ or ‘true and fair view’ be achieved for combined financial statements?

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.27 Both the purpose of reporting and the relevant regulator might require a ‘clean’ audit opinion on the combined financial statements (that is, a ‘presents fairly’ or ‘true and fair view’ opinion). That requirement might define how the financial information is prepared.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.28 There are many examples of combined financial statements of a new reporting entity that assert compliance with IFRS that have been subject to a normal audit. An audit opinion might refer to ‘true and fair’ or ‘fair presentation in accordance with IFRS’.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.29 The more complex the pre-transaction structure and the more adjustments and allocations that are made during the preparation, the less likely it is that combined financial statements can be created that provide a ‘true and fair view’.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.30 However, there are circumstances in which the combined financial statements should be described as ‘drawn up in accordance with the basis of preparation described in Note X’; these ‘basis of preparation’ combined financial statements are not general purpose financial statements in accordance with IFRS.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.31 The more complex the pre-transaction structure and the more adjustments and allocations that have to be made, the further the financial information will be pushed towards a ‘basis of preparation’ and away from ‘in accordance with IFRS’. Therefore, the assurance given will refer to compliance with the basis of preparation as set out.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.32 The nature of the audit opinion is principally governed by local regulation and the nature of the financial information. ‘Basis of preparation’ is accepted by some regulators. Other regulators (for example, the Hong Kong Stock Exchange) require audit opinions that refer to full compliance with IFRS.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.33 An ‘emphasis of matter’ paragraph is also commonly used in audit opinions on combined financial statements prepared in accordance with IFRS. The ‘emphasis of matter’ paragraph might explain, for example, that the new reporting entity has not operated as a separate entity, or that the combined financial statements are not necessarily indicative of results that would have occurred if the business had been a separate stand-alone entity during the period presented.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Step 2: Determine the new reporting entity

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.34 A reporting entity in a typical capital market transaction is a group headed by a legal entity. However, if combined financial statements are required, the legal structure will seldom have been in place throughout the track record period: the legal group might only be established when the transaction is executed; or there might be a group restructuring before the transaction, so the reporting entity’s history includes common control acquisitions or combinations of entities that are not legally connected. Setting the ‘boundary’ of the new reporting entity is the basis of financial reporti

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.35 ‘Common control’ exists where control lies with the same ultimate party or parties bound by a contract.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.36 The IFRS Framework defines a reporting entity as follows: “A reporting entity is an entity that is required, or chooses, to prepare financial statements. A reporting entity can be a single entity or a portion of an entity or can comprise more than one entity. A reporting entity is not necessarily a legal entity."

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: [IFRS Framework para 3.10].

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.37 An operating segment of a larger group, a group of entities that are legally unconnected but operating together under common control to achieve a single business objective, or entities bound together by contract could all be a reporting entity in appropriate circumstances. The IFRS framework states that “if a reporting entity comprises two or more entities that are not all linked by a parent-subsidiary relationship, the reporting entity’s financial statements are referred to as ‘combined financial statements'".

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: [IFRS Framework para 3.12].

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.38 The IFRS framework acknowledges that the appropriate boundary of a reporting entity could be difficult to determine. This may be the case if the reporting entity is not a legal entity and does not comprise only legal entities linked by a parent-subsidiary relationship. The framework notes that the information needs of the primary users of the reporting entity should be taken into account when determining the appropriate boundary. Users require a faithful presentation. Therefore, according to the framework, the information presented requires that:

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - “the boundary of the reporting entity does not contain an arbitrary or incomplete set of economic activities;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - including that set of economic activities within the boundary of the reporting entity results in neutral information; and

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - a description is provided of how the boundary of the reporting entity was determined and of what constitutes the reporting entity.”

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: IFRS Framework paras 3.13 and [3.14].

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Can a ‘business’ without legal boundaries be a reporting entity?

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.39 A reporting entity does not need to be a legal entity. A separate vehicle that is not a legal entity and that does not have a separate legal ‘personality’ has the potential to be a reporting entity if it is a separately identifiable financial structure (for example, some type of partnership, branch or segment).

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.40 A reporting entity would not therefore be limited to entities structured as legal entities. It can comprise a portion of an entity, or two or more entities.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.41 The boundary of a reporting entity that is not a legal entity should be set in a way that users who rely on the financial statements will be able to obtain relevant financial information. The financial statements should represent faithfully the economic activities of the entity (see para A2.38 above).

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: What factors indicate that economic activities are bound together and form a reporting entity?

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.42 There are generally two key considerations to assess when determining whether a reporting entity exists as a basis for preparing combined financial statements, as follows:

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - whether the assets and liabilities are under common control or common management (usually with common control, see paras A2.43 to A2.48 below); and

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - whether the economic activity of the reporting entity is or will be bound together for a purpose through, for example:

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - a legal re-organisation of a group or groups that has occurred after the reporting date, but before publication of the financial statements;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - a legal re-organisation that will happen in connection with a proposed IPO, disposal or similar transaction; or

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - an agreement that was signed and in place throughout the periods covered by the combined financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Must common control be present for a reporting entity to exist?

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.43 It would be rare for a reporting entity to be identified where common control is absent.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.44 A reporting entity where the various entities or businesses are under common control will have a single governing body that governs the relevant activities. Users can assess whether that governing body has made efficient and effective use of the resources if the entities have been under common control.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.45 Combined financial statements can only be prepared for the period when entities were under common control. If the entity acquired another entity from a third party during the track record period of the combined financial statements, acquisition accounting is applied from the date when control was obtained.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Can an entity prepare combined financial statements if the economic activities of the proposed reporting entity are not under common control?

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.46 It is rarely appropriate to prepare combined financial statements where the economic activities have been under common management that is not accompanied by common control.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.47 Common management, where it is not supported by contractual arrangements or common control, is seldom a sufficient basis to establish a reporting entity.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: FAQ A2.47.1 – Can common management be a basis for common control?

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.48 A common business is seldom sufficient to establish a reporting entity. A private equity fund might decide to acquire a number of businesses in a single industry over a short period of time and then consolidate these into a group to achieve economies of scale and synergies. The purchase of each individual business is a business combination, and acquisition accounting is required. The entities acquired have a common business, and combining financial information over several years might be useful for investors. However, preparing combined financial statements for the acquired businesses an

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: When can combined financial statements be prepared?

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.49 The below FAQs illustrate some common scenarios in which a new reporting entity can be identified, and consider whether combined financial statements might be appropriate for its economic activities.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: FAQ A2.49.1 – How might a reporting entity be established from entities that will be legally bound together through a re-organisation? FAQ A2.49.2 – How might a reporting entity be established from entities that have been legally bound together under a contractual arrangement? FAQ A2.49.3 – How might a reporting entity be established from separate entities managed together as a single economic entity? EX A2.49.4 – Demerger transaction into a NewCo

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Do the principles of consolidation accounting apply when preparing the combined financial statements of the reporting entity?

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.50 Combined financial statements must follow all of the recognition, measurement and disclosure requirements of IFRS to claim compliance with IFRS. The basic objectives of financial reporting should apply, providing useful information for:

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - assessing management stewardship;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - allowing users to assess the ability of the reporting entity to generate cash flows; and

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - allowing comparability over time.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.51 A re-organisation is often effected to form a new reporting entity. A new entity might be formed to acquire only a portion of the existing legal group as the listing business.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.52 Practice varies as to whether the combined financial statements present a non-controlling interest. This is a complex area that depends on a number of factors, including whether or not the non-controlling interest survives the planned transaction. Management should consider what treatment will both provide useful information and comply with IFRS.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: What is the disposal group approach, and when might it be appropriate for combined financial statements?

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.53 A new reporting entity, when preparing combined financial statements for a transaction, might include businesses that were legally part of the reporting entity during the track record period but will not be part of the new reporting entity going forward. A re-organisation is effected at or near the point of the transaction, so that only the continuing business (the new reporting entity) forms the new legal group. Management needs to decide how to present the financial results and financial position of the reporting entity in the combined financial statements, particularly where there has

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.54 The two approaches commonly seen in practice are:

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - to exclude all businesses and activity that will not form part of the new legal group from the combined financial statements (carve out basis); or

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - to include such businesses and activity and present them as a disposal group or discontinued operations (disposal group basis).

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.55 Regulators might have a preference for one type of presentation; for example, regulators in the US would generally expect the disposal group basis approach to be followed. The approach chosen will depend on several factors and will involve the exercise of judgement.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.56 Users often prefer to have information relating only to the continuing business; so, where possible, management might seek to apply the carve out approach in the combined financial statements. It is reasonable to follow the carve out approach only where certain criteria are met. These criteria are not defined under IFRS, but regulators in some jurisdictions (for example, the UK and US) have more explicit guidance that generally shares similar concepts. These are:

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - the business that is being disposed of is dissimilar to the remainder of the new reporting entity;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - the business that is being disposed of has been separately managed; and

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - separate historical books and records exist for the business being disposed of.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.57 The disposal group approach is an alternative basis for presenting the combined financial statements of a new reporting entity. The disposal group approach has both listing and non-listing businesses (in the case of an IPO) during the track record period where it is not appropriate or possible to use the carve out approach. The disposal group approach consolidates all of the businesses to be disposed of, up to the date of disposal or discontinuance.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.58 The financial information of the disposed businesses or discontinued operations is included in the new reporting entity up until this date; they are presented as a disposal group separately from the continuing business.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.59 The concept of a ‘disposal group’, in the context of preparing combined financial statements, is similar to the definition of a disposal group in accordance with IFRS 5: “a group of assets to be disposed of, by sale or otherwise, together as a group in a single transaction, and liabilities directly associated with those assets that will be transferred in the transaction”.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.60 A disposal group does not necessarily need to meet the definition of a ‘discontinued operation’ as defined in IFRS 5. The disposal group treatment is applied only for those balance sheets where the requirements of IFRS 5 have been met as of the balance sheet date.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.61 The disposal group approach is commonly used where the new reporting entity includes entities that will not be transferred on a re-organisation.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.62 Management should consider the specific facts of each individual case.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Step 3: Consider whether the combined financial statements can comply with IFRS

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.63 Combined financial statements are those where management is seeking to claim compliance with IFRS and that are prepared based on historical data. Historical financial information is past information that has been prepared in accordance with statutory requirements and relevant accounting standards. A core assumption is that the historical financial information is drawn from distinct or separate accounting records and that the information can be audited.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.64 ‘Pro-forma financial information’, on the other hand, is hypothetical information that seeks to illustrate a particular outcome or scenario on an ‘as-if’ basis. Such financial information includes effects of events or transactions that did not occur (non-historical), or occurred earlier or later than the date recognised in the financial statements. This term is used in different ways in different jurisdictions.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.65 A new reporting entity being prepared for a transaction is rarely a neat sub-group that has prepared consolidated financial statements that present only and all of the economic activities and transactions that encompass the new reporting entity, including debt, taxes, share-based payments, share of corporate assets, management services and charges. The reporting entity can prepare and present consolidated financial statements in those circumstances.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.66 Most new reporting entities preparing for a transaction will not have the financial information in the form and nature described in paragraph A2.65. Management might need to make adjustments, including the allocation of certain assets, liabilities and expenses that are relevant to the new reporting entity but that have not been accounted for within the legal entities within the boundary of the reporting entity.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.67 Combined financial statements prepared in accordance with IFRS will frequently include adjustments or allocations to reflect the items described in paragraph A2.65. Determining what is appropriately included as historical financial information is a key area of judgement in preparing combined financial statements. The combined financial statements should avoid ‘as-if’ adjustments, but there is limited guidance on what to adjust and how. The goal is to avoid ‘as-if’ or ‘pro-forma’ financial information. The meaning and interpretation of the term ‘pro-forma’ might differ from territory to t

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: EX A2.67.1 – Historical information prepared in accordance with IFRS EX A2.67.2 – Financial statements with significant adjustments

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.68 Some jurisdictions regard the allocation of historical expenses incurred by the larger group to the reporting entity as historical information; this is because the allocation is based on actual past expenses incurred by the larger group, allocated to the reporting entity on a rational basis.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.69 Other jurisdictions might regard any allocations as a pro-forma adjustment. EX A2.67.2 sets out a basis of preparation from a set of pro-forma financial statements.
