chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Step 4: Deal with the practical issues of preparation

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Which accounting policies should be used in the combined financial statements prepared in accordance with IFRS?

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.70 Accounting policies should be appropriate for the purpose of the combined financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.71 The accounting information previously recorded about the circumscribed area of economic activities will be the basis for preparing the combined financial statements. It might then be necessary to make adjustments to present the combined financial statements in accordance with the chosen accounting policies.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.72 Different approaches are used in different circumstances:

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - Using the accounting policies followed in the consolidated financial statements of the group (the current parent) to which the respective economic activities belong. This is frequently the case where a seller is preparing information to present to its existing investors or potential purchasers, such as information on parts of a legal group that are to be sold.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - Using the accounting policies that will be applied in the financial statements of the new reporting entity to which the respective economic activities will belong. This is often appropriate where a business is being demerged from an existing group into a new and separate legal entity. The combined financial statements are intended to show the financial performance of the economic activities forming part of that new reporting entity.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - Applying the acquirer’s accounting policies where the combined financial statements of the target company are prepared for a proposed acquisition, to present the financial performance of the acquiree under the acquirer’s accounting policies. This approach is required in certain jurisdictions, including the UK.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.73 The choice of accounting policies will depend on the intended users of the financial information and the purpose of reporting. The fact that different accounting policies might be applied does not cause issues with regard to IFRS compliance; IFRS requires management to select appropriate policies that result in information that is relevant and reliable.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Purchase accounting adjustments from previous transactions

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.74 The new reporting entity might include businesses or entities that were previously acquired by the current parent. The treatment of purchase price adjustments and goodwill related to the new reporting entity, recognised by the current parent, can vary.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.75 The predecessor method of accounting for common control business combinations and re-organisations generally uses the carrying values at the highest level of common control (see Appendix 1 paras A1.19 to A1.21). The current parent is unlikely to form part of the new reporting entity. The question arises as to whether adjustments should be made to the combined financial statements of the new reporting entity, to reflect the carrying values of the current parent. Examples of such allocations are any goodwill and related purchase price adjustments recorded by the current parent that relate

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.76 Parent entities rarely allocate goodwill and purchase price adjustments when using IFRS in separate financial statements. There is no requirement for ‘push-down accounting’ under IFRS, and company law in many jurisdictions would make push-down accounting difficult.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.77 ‘Push-down accounting’ refers to establishing a new accounting basis for an acquired business in its separate financial statements following an acquisition; effectively, the parent's goodwill and purchase accounting adjustments are included in the separate financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.78 Goodwill and the related purchase price adjustments might be included in the combined financial statements of the new reporting entity. The financial track record of the new reporting entity would be seen by many users and regulators as incomplete if it did not reflect the cost of the business to the current parent entity. In essence, the goodwill and purchase accounting should not be stranded in the current parent company but should accompany the business to which it relates.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: EX A2.78.1 – Allocation of goodwill

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Tangible and intangible assets

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.79 The new reporting entity will recognise all of the assets in the combined financial statements that its constituent entities control. Challenges can arise where the new reporting entity has used corporate assets such as brands or patents, and these might or might not be transferred to the new reporting entity. Similarly, a reporting entity might have historically controlled assets that will not be transferred to it as part of the transaction.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.80 Assets might be attributed to the new reporting entity based on legal ownership, usage or through an inter-company sharing arrangement, such as an operating or lease agreement. The attribution should reflect the legal substance of arrangements that existed throughout the track record period.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.81 Assets that have been controlled by a part of the new reporting entity during the track record period might not transfer to the new reporting entity as part of the transaction. Similar to the discussion on disposal groups (see para A2.55), two approaches are seen in practice. One or the other might be preferred by the relevant regulator or might be more appropriate in the specific circumstances. The two approaches are as follows: to include the asset until the date of the transaction and make clear disclosure that it will not transfer; or to exclude the asset from the combined financial

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: FAQ A2.81.1 – How might intangible assets be allocated in combined financial statements?

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.82 The new reporting entity might have debt for which it is legally obligated, and this will be included in its combined financial statements. This will include third party debt issued directly by the legal entities that form the new reporting entity.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.83 Third party debt of the current parent might also be assigned or legally assumed by the new reporting entity. This debt should be included in the combined financial statements of the new reporting entity for all periods in which the debt was outstanding.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.84 Lease liabilities would follow the related right of use asset. The allocation of interest income and costs would follow the way in which the related debt and debt instruments have been apportioned.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.85 There might be other circumstances in which debt should be included in the combined financial statements of the new reporting entity. Management should carefully consider the presentation that is most meaningful to users of the combined financial statements. For example, if the new reporting entity will have interest-bearing obligations to the current parent, this should be presented as debt financing. The basis for allocation should be consistent with the terms of the transaction, demerger or disposal agreement as relevant.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: What income and expenses should be included in the combined financial statements of the new reporting entity?

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.86 The combined financial statements of the new reporting entity should include all economic activity arising from its business. A new reporting entity that has been part of a larger group will seldom have a free-standing financial track record.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.87 Income and expenses from its economic activities might be recorded elsewhere in the group and might need to be allocated to the new reporting entity, for its combined financial statements to be described as prepared in accordance with IFRS. All relevant expenses should be included in the combined financial statements of the new reporting entity if a reasonable basis of allocation can be established.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.88 Expenses incurred at the corporate level might be with third parties for services performed at the corporate level for lower-level entities. These might include payroll, accounting, centralised purchasing, marketing, executive management, lease expenses, advertising, legal, insurance, selling and administrative expenses. Some expenses − such as pensions, and other employee benefits − might only be recorded at the parent or corporate level.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.89 The combined financial statements should reflect a reasonable allocation of expenses from the parent or other units of the group providing the services. The method of allocation might be by specific identification, legal obligation or in a manner that best reflects the nature of how the expense is incurred, such as headcount and time usage.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.90 The allocation of corporate overhead involves judgement, but it should reflect the incremental costs incurred to service the new reporting entity. Inter-company transactions that have been eliminated in consolidated financial statements, such as purchases and sales, should be reinstated in the combined financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.91 Estimating and allocating transactions not previously allocated to the reporting entity is not the same as creating transactions that have never happened (similar to ‘pro-forma’ information). Allocations are acceptable, provided that there is an appropriate basis, and the basis is clearly disclosed in the combined financial statements. The disclosure should include how allocated items were identified, and the method and effect of allocation.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.92 The allocations should be made using high-quality information. Allocations should not be made if the information required to make reasonable and supportable estimates does not exist. Management should instead provide sufficient disclosure in the notes to enable readers of the combined financial statements to understand the nature of the expenses that have not been included in the new reporting entity.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.93 Clear and meaningful disclosure in the notes to the combined financial statements is essential for a good understanding of the financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: EX A2.93.1 – Allocations in combined financial statements

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.94 The UK’s SIR 2000 and US SEC guidance (see FAQ A2.20.1) might be useful when determining how to allocate expenses to the new reporting entity. Factors usually considered when doing an allocation include:

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - whether the assets and liabilities will be part of the new reporting entity;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - whether there was any intra-group recharge between the parent and the new reporting entity (for example, legal, accounting, finance or employee benefit expenses); and

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - whether the recharges represent amounts actually incurred, and how the basis of the recharge has been determined.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.95 There are a few areas that have specific guidance issued by regulators. These are discussed at paragraph A2.96 onwards.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.96 Accounting for income taxes in combined financial statements almost always presents challenges. The ideal situation is a new reporting entity that was a legal sub-group filing a group tax return or individual tax returns, and that will continue under the same tax regime after the transaction. This situation rarely occurs in practice. However, the new reporting entity needs to apply the requirements of IAS 12 in preparing the combined financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.97 Management needs to analyse the tax circumstances of the new reporting entity, including its legal status after the transaction, to account for income taxes. There are two approaches broadly seen in practice to apply IAS 12 to the combined financial statements of the new reporting entity: the separate tax return method; and the tax incurred method.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.98 The separate tax return method aggregates the tax position of the individual entities of the new reporting entity. Legal entities that comprise the new reporting entity and previously filed separate tax returns have a clear tax position. Current tax expense and tax assets and liabilities are accounted for in accordance with the tax returns. Deferred tax assets and liabilities arise from the individual book tax differences.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.99 However, some groups prepare consolidated tax returns that include all entities in the group and allocate tax expense under an inter-company or tax-sharing arrangement.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.100 If management chooses to follow the separate return method to determine current tax expense in the track record period, differences will arise between the tax expense or benefit (under the separate tax return basis) and taxes paid or received under the legal tax-sharing arrangement. These differences are normally treated as a capital contribution or distribution to or from the parent entity, and they are included in the reconciliation of invested capital between periods.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.101 Management needs to give careful consideration to carrying forward tax losses, and it needs to ensure that these will be available to the new reporting entity before recording deferred tax assets.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.102 The tax incurred method of determining tax expense might be appropriate if the parent recharged taxes to the entities that will comprise the new reporting entity.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.103 Management should assess the recoverability of deferred tax assets, as normal, using the financial results of the new reporting entity for all periods presented. However, assumptions made in assessing the realisation of deferred tax assets and the establishment of uncertain tax positions should reflect the facts as they existed at the historical dates; they should not incorporate the benefit of hindsight.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: EX A2.103.1 – Allocation of tax charge

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.104 Interest expense should be included in the combined financial statements of the new reporting entity if:

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - the carve out entity has historically been allocated an interest charge;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - the new reporting entity will assume the debt associated with the interest charge;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - the debt will be repaid by the new reporting entity using the proceeds of an offering of securities; or

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - the debt on the parent’s books specifically related to the activity of the new reporting entity.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.105 Capital structures are usually complex in transactions involving a new reporting entity that needs to prepare combined financial statements. A regulator might not insist on including interest expense. However, it usually allows an interest charge to be included if a reasonable allocation of interest can be made, irrespective of whether interest was previously charged to the new reporting entity.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: EX A2.105.1 – Allocation of interest income and expense

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.106 The employees of the new reporting entity might have participated and/or continue to participate in the parent’s employee benefit plans. It is rare that the new reporting entity will have its own defined benefit plans at the time of a transaction or that it will be legally assigned the pension liability for its own employees.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.107 The appropriate treatment of the employee benefit plans in the combined financial statements will depend on several factors, the most significant of which will be the nature of the plans after the transaction. Two approaches are frequently observed, as set out in paragraphs A2.108 and A2.109.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.108 The employee benefit plans of the parent might become, in effect, multi-employer plans, with the employees of the new reporting entity as participants in the multi-employer plans. Contributions to the plan are included in the profit or loss account of the new reporting entity, or it might be appropriate to allocate employee benefit expense to the new reporting entity.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.109 Alternatively, a portion of the pension assets might be assigned to the new reporting entity, which assumes all existing obligations for the employees that are transferred to it, effectively creating a new defined benefit plan for the new reporting entity. This is seldom likely to have been effected by the date of the transaction, although it is likely to have been announced or agreed with employees. It might be appropriate to reflect pension assets and liabilities in the combined financial statements, with appropriate disclosure. Calculation of pension assets and liabilities in these c

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.110 The parent of the new reporting entity might have recorded impairment charges related to non-financial assets that will be included in the new reporting entity. Likewise, it might have avoided recording impairments, because of synergies in the wider group that will no longer exist after the transaction.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.111 The new reporting entity will need to determine its cash-generating units (CGUs) for impairment testing of non-current assets, and groups of CGUs for impairment testing of goodwill and assets that benefit more than one CGU.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.112 Management will need to test goodwill and other non-current assets with indefinite lives. It will need to separately assess if any events have occurred to the stand-alone operations that would trigger the need to perform a non-financial asset impairment test for each period covered by the combined financial statements. This assessment would be made without the benefit of hindsight.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.113 Non-financial asset impairments should not be apportioned to the carve out entity; they should be based on the actual assets allocated to the carve out entity and the carve out entity’s stand-alone results.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.114 Share-based payments awarded to employees of the new reporting entity by a related party, or other holder of an economic interest in the new reporting entity (that is, parent, other group company or shareholder), as compensation for services provided to the entity are accounted for as share-based payment transactions, following the guidance in IFRS 2. This is required under IFRS, unless the transfer is clearly for a purpose other than compensation for services to the reporting entity, such as settlement of an obligation to the employee that is not related to employment.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Inter-company transactions and balances

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.115 Previous interactions between the new reporting entity and other entities in the group should be re-assessed for classification; they are likely to be ‘third party’ transactions in the combined financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.116 Entities in the previous group will normally be regarded as related parties during the track record period, and so the requirements of IAS 24 should be applied.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.117 Further to the additional disclosure requirements under IAS 24, some practical issues could arise:

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - Previous trading balances might include trading and financing elements, and these should be separated in the new reporting entity’s balance sheet.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - Classification as non-current might change.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - Receivables from related parties might not be recoverable, because parental guarantees fell away.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - Additional liabilities might crystallise on separation from the previous group.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: EX A2.117.1 – Allocation of management fees and other expenses

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.118 Combined financial statements are usually prepared in accordance with a transaction of some kind, and so the issue of transaction costs will frequently arise.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.119 There are three main issues, in practice, concerning transaction costs:

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - the IPO costs that are eligible for capitalisation;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - the allocation of IPO costs among existing shareholders and shareholders contributing new funds; and

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - whether transaction costs incurred in anticipation of an IPO can be deferred.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.120 An IPO of the new reporting entity’s shares will often follow a group re-organisation. Management should make a clear distinction between group re-organisation costs and IPO costs. The latter only represent the incremental equity issuance costs; this will not include the costs of the re-organisation, such as staff redundancies, relocation, legal expenses and tax costs. Costs of a re-organisation or restructuring should be expensed as incurred.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.121 New shares are issued to investors in an IPO to raise additional capital and, along with existing shares, they subsequently become listed on a stock exchange. Costs incurred in listing existing shares on a stock exchange are not transaction costs relating to the issue of an equity instrument. These costs are incurred to make the existing shares more marketable, and they do not relate to raising new capital.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.122 Costs incurred in issuing new shares to raise capital (‘primary offering’) in an IPO are transaction costs of the equity instruments, and they are a deduction from equity.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.123 Costs that are incurred to raise capital and to list existing shares are allocated between the new shares and the existing shares on a reasonable basis. Any costs incurred to list existing shares, or to list new shares arising from a demerger, are not equity transaction costs, and they are charged to the income statement.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.124 Qualifying transaction costs incurred in anticipation of issuing equity shares can be deferred on the balance sheet until the transaction occurs, or they can be shown as a deduction from equity. Costs must be expensed if the transaction is not assessed as probable. Costs previously written off should not be reinstated.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.125 The new reporting entity is seldom a separate legal entity throughout the entire track record period, and so it has no share capital and reserves in its own right. If the separation from the previous group has not finished, any equity represents the parent’s net investment in the new reporting entity. Typically, this is labelled ‘invested capital’ or ‘parent company investment’ in the combined financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.126 If legal share capital exists, it would be shown separately in equity (in which case, the presentation of earnings per share is also meaningful – see para A2.129).

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.127 Whether or not legal accounts (such as share capital or share premium), are shown, those ‘recyclable’ balances that require separate disclosure under other IFRSs should be disclosed separately (for example, hedging reserves).

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.128 Special attention should be given to outstanding balances that still exist between the new reporting entity and its parent. Balances without the characteristics of debt should be included as part of the invested capital.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Presentation of earnings per share

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.129 IAS 33 requires presentation of earnings per share (EPS) for an entity “that files, or is in the process of filing, its financial statements with a securities commission or other regulatory organisation for the purpose of issuing ordinary shares in a public market”.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.130 Presentation is often less meaningful, because the combined financial statements are unlikely to have legal share capital (see para A2.125). Some regulators accept omission of this disclosure in such a case. Once the shares are issued, EPS figures become meaningful for capital markets, and so they should be adjusted retrospectively. Some regulators, notably the SEC, require the shares issued to the existing investors, on formation of the combined entity legal structure, to be used as the denominator in calculating historical EPS.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: EX A2.130.1 – No EPS presented

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.131 Care should be taken if the new reporting entity’s invested capital fluctuates significantly throughout the track record period, caused by, for example, share issuances for cash or management buy-out. Where it is practicable, management should highlight the impact of such transactions on the number of shares used, for the purpose of calculating the EPS figures.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.132 The general principles of not applying hindsight and presenting the business as run by management at the time, mean that it is appropriate to keep comparative periods closed. For example, if a lawsuit is settled by the time the combined financial statements are prepared, the accruals that were made in the track record period are not ‘trued up’ to the actual settlement amount.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.133 The presentation of the carve out entity's statement of cash flows can be challenging. For example, inter-company transactions that would not have been reflected in the consolidated statement of cash flows at the parent company level should be reflected in the cash flow statement at the carve out entity level. These inter-company transactions need to be properly classified in the combined financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.134 The requirements of IFRS 1 should be applied when financial statements are prepared for a new reporting entity. This guidance focuses on specific issues related to the preparation of combined financial statements, and it does not address the general requirements of IFRS 1 that are relevant for all first-time adopters.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: There are two options set out in paragraph D16 of IFRS 1 for a subsidiary (including carve out entities) that adopts IFRS at a date later than the group headed by its parent (or entity that has significant influence or joint control over it). It can measure its assets and liabilities at either:

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - the carrying amounts that would be included in the parent’s consolidated financial statements, based on the parent’s date of transition to IFRSs … ; or

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - the carrying amounts required by IFRS 1, based on the subsidiary’s date of transition to IFRSs.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.135 IFRS 1 requires reconciliations between previous GAAP and IFRS, explaining how the transition affected the financial position and performance of the reporting entity. A new reporting entity is unlikely to have previously prepared financial statements, and so no reconciliation can be prepared.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.136 A new reporting entity that is spun off from an existing IFRS reporter would not have any reconciling items, because it can apply the same exemption that is available for a subsidiary transitioning after its parent has transitioned.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.137 IFRS 1 requires the preparation and presentation of an opening balance sheet as a starting point of the financial statements. This requirement is also applicable for combined financial statements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.138 This guidance does not address complex areas of accounting that largely depend on individual facts and circumstances or are governed by local regulations (for example, calculation and presentation of non-controlling interest or foreign currency translation differences).

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Step 5: Make clear disclosures

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.139 Clear and transparent disclosures are fundamental to the understanding of combined and carve out financial statements. This type of financial information is usually prepared to represent specific circumstances, and these are often governed by local regulatory requirements.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A2.140 Disclosure notes should address at least:

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - the purpose for which the combined financial statements are prepared;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - how the new reporting entity was identified and the significant judgements that were made; the boundary of the new reporting entity should be clearly described in the basis of preparation, including the explanation as to which entities are included in the combined financial statements;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - a list of combining entities;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - whether the combined financial statements are prepared in accordance with IFRS or a basis of preparation;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - the principal accounting policies followed in preparing the combined financial statements;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - how the allocation of assets, liabilities, income and expenses was performed;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - how inter-company transactions were reflected in the combined financial statements;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - how EPS was calculated, if applicable;

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - the critical judgements and estimates involved in the preparation of combined financial statements; and

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: - disclosure requirements of all applicable IFRSs, if the combined financial statements claim compliance with IFRS.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: A fund manager might be responsible for managing portfolios of different funds but often has no beneficial interests in those funds. The decision-making process requires the fund manager to request approval from the unit holders on major decisions. The funds are under common management, but there is no basis for aggregating all funds managed by the same fund manager.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: The aggregated funds do not represent a reporting entity; fund holders or creditors of one fund do not have access to the assets of other funds, and it is not possible to hold a residual interest in aggregate of all of the funds.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements
text: Group X has two major areas of operations – in metals and coal. Management plans a demerger that will spin-off the metals business into a new sub-group and create two new listed entities: A Metals and A Coal.

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements

The financial information has been prepared incorporating the following adjustments:

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements

chapter: Appendix 2 - Preparation of combined and carve out financial statements

Appendix 3 - IBOR Reform Amendments
Appendix 3 - IBOR Reform Amendments
This eBook is licensed to peggy so, peggy.so@hk.ey.com,

A3.1 Following the financial crisis, the replacement of benchmark interest rates such as LIBOR and other interbank offered rates (‘IBORs’) has become a priority for global regulators. The Financial Stability Board’s July 2014 report ‘Reforming Major Interest Rate Benchmarks’ set out recommendations for the reform of certain benchmarks. As a result, many jurisdictions are in the process of transitioning to alternative benchmark rates. The reforms aim to achieve a shift away from individual trader quotes to observed transaction rates and to increase the population on which those rates are based.

A3.2 This appendix provides a number of examples that explain the IBOR reform amendments in different situations. For illustrative purposes, we have based the examples on GBP LIBOR changing to SONIA, but the same principles also apply to other benchmark interest rates subject to IBOR reform that are changing in a similar way.
Who might be affected by IBOR replacement, and how?

Entities that might be affected range from corporate entities with IBOR-based debt funding, or that have hedged debt (fixed or floating) with derivatives that reference an IBOR, to financial institutions such as banks and insurers that issue products that reference an IBOR. Even if an entity does not have any contracts referencing an IBOR, it might still use an IBOR in constructing certain discount rates used in financial reporting, such as in calculating an asset’s ‘value in use’ when assessing it for impairment or fair values in accordance with IFRS 13, and so it might still be affected by t
What do the Phase 1 amendments address?

A3.4 The IASB had a two-phase project to consider what, if any, reliefs to give from the effects of IBOR reform. Phase 1 considered reliefs to hedge accounting in the period before the reform. The Phase 1 amendments were finalised by the IASB in September 2019, and they provide temporary relief from applying specific hedge accounting requirements to hedging relationships directly affected by IBOR reform. The Phase 1 amendments generally allow hedge accounting to continue during the period of uncertainty caused by benchmark reform (for example, uncertainty about whether cash flows on a particul
A3.5 In providing the relief, the IASB noted that discontinuing hedge accounting solely due to IBOR reform would not provide useful information to the users of financial statements.
[IFRS 9 para BC6.550]. [IAS 39 para BC227].
A3.6 The Phase 1 amendments are mandatory and should be applied for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2020. Earlier application is permitted.
[IFRS 9 para 7.2.26(d)]. [IAS 39 para 108G].
What do the Phase 2 amendments address?

A3.7 In August 2020, the IASB issued amendments to IFRS 9, IAS 39, IFRS 7, IFRS 4 and IFRS 16 (Phase 2 amendments) that address the issues that arise during the reform of an interest rate benchmark rate, including the replacement of one benchmark with an alternative one. The key reliefs provided by the Phase 2 amendments are as follows:

- When changing the basis for determining contractual cash flows for financial assets and liabilities (including lease liabilities), the reliefs have the effect that the changes, that are necessary as a direct consequence of IBOR reform and which are considered economically equivalent, will not result in an immediate gain or loss in the income statement.

- The hedge accounting reliefs will allow most IAS 39 or IFRS 9 hedge relationships that are directly affected by IBOR reform to continue. However, additional ineffectiveness might need to be recorded.

See paragraph A3.38 onwards for more information about the Phase 2 amendments. For more detailed guidance, see our In depth publication ‘Practical guide to Phase 2 amendments to IFRS 9, IAS 39, IFRS 7, IFRS 4 and IFRS 16 for interest rate benchmark (IBOR) reform’.

Scope of the Phase 1 amendment

A3.8 The amendments apply to all hedging relationships that are directly affected by IBOR reform. A hedging relationship is directly affected only if the IBOR reform gives rise to uncertainties about:
- a contractually or non-contractually specified interest rate benchmark that has been designated as a hedged risk; and/or
- the timing or the amount of IBOR-based cash flows of the hedged item or the hedging instrument
[IFRS 9 para 6.8.1]. [IAS 39 para 102A].

A3.9 The Phase 1 amendments apply to hedges of interest rate risk, including hedges of issued or held debt instruments and of forecast debt issuances. The amendments apply to both contractually and non-contractually specified interest rate benchmarks, and so they include hedges of both floating- and fixed-rate debt instruments. [IFRS 9 para 6.8.1(a)]. [IAS 39 para 102A(a)].

A3.10 However, the scope is broader than only hedges of interest rate risk. It includes some foreign currency hedges – in particular, hedges with cross-currency interest rate swaps where one or both of the legs of the swap references an IBOR. However, a hedge of foreign currency risk with an instrument such as a currency forward, where neither the cash flows of the hedging instrument nor the hedged risk references an IBOR, is outside the scope of the Phase 1 amendments.
[IFRS 9 para BC6.556]. [IAS 39 para BC233].

A3.11 The Phase 1 amendments also include hedging relationships in which interest rate risk is not the only hedged risk. For example, hedging relationships where an entity designates a cross-currency interest rate swap to hedge exposure to foreign currency and IBOR interest rate risk are within the scope of the Phase 1 amendments.
[IFRS 9 para BC6.557]. [IAS 39 para BC234].

A3.12 The Phase 1 amendments apply to the market-wide reform of an interest rate benchmark, such as that resulting from the recommendations set out in the Financial Stability Board’s July 2014 report ‘Reforming Major Interest Rate Benchmarks’. However, the Phase 1 amendments are not limited to the jurisdictions noted in that report. A market-wide reform is required, and so the Phase 1 amendments do not apply to changes that are only specific to the two parties to a contract. They also do not apply to interest rate benchmarks that are not subject to reform or replacement.
[IFRS 9 para 6.8.2]. [IAS 39 para 102B].

A3.13 The Phase 1 amendments might apply to only some items in a hedge relationship. For example, in a hedging relationship where the hedged item references an IBOR that is subject to reform but the hedging instrument references the replacement benchmark rate (that is not subject to reform), the Phase 1 amendments will apply to the hedged item, because its future cash flows are uncertain, but not to the hedging instrument.

A3.14 Furthermore, if the only impact of the reform is that the fair values of the items that comprise the hedging relationship are affected only by general uncertainty due to the IBOR reform, the Phase 1 amendments will not apply, because there is only an ‘indirect effect’.
[IFRS 9 para BC6.556]. [IAS 39 para BC233].

A3.15 The amendments only provide exceptions from certain aspects of hedge accounting that arise from uncertainties over the timing or amount of cash flows in the period to until the reforms occur. The IASB’s Phase 2 amendments consider other issues, including hedge designations when these uncertainties are no longer present and the accounting treatment to be applied to any changes to the terms of contracts (see para A3.38).

Key reliefs provided by the Phase 1 amendments

A3.16 The Phase 1 amendments provide temporary relief from applying specific hedge accounting requirements to hedging relationships directly affected by IBOR reform. The key reliefs provided by the Phase 1 amendments relate to:
- the ‘highly probable’ requirement;
- prospective assessments (economic relationship or expected to be ‘highly effective’);
- the IAS 39 retrospective effectiveness test.; and
- recycling of the cash flow hedging reserve.

A3.17 In some hedges, the hedged item or hedged risk is a non-contractually specified IBOR risk component. An example is a fair value hedge of fixed-rate debt where the designated hedged risk is changes in the fair value of the debt attributable to changes in an IBOR. In order for hedge accounting to be applied, both IFRS 9 and IAS 39 require the designated risk component to be separately identifiable and reliably measurable.
[IFRS 9 para 6.3.7]. [IAS 39 para 81]. [IAS 39 para AG99F].

A3.18 Under the Phase 1 amendments, a non-contractually specified risk component only needs to be separately identifiable at initial hedge designation and not on an ongoing basis. For example, in hedging relationships where an entity designates an interest rate swap as a hedge of exposure to changes in GBP LIBOR for a fixed-rate debt, and the market structure moves, over time, from being GBP LIBOR to SONIA (so the GBP LIBOR risk component is no longer separately identifiable), hedge accounting of the risk attributable to changes in GBP LIBOR can continue (subject to the other requirements for
[IFRS 9 para 6.8.7]. [IAS 39 para 102H].

A3.19 There is no relief from performing an ongoing assessment of ‘reliably measurable’; this is because, if an entity cannot reliably measure the hedged risk component, it will not be able to measure and recognise any ineffectiveness.
[IFRS 9 para BC6.575]. [IAS 39 para BC261].

A3.20 A practical effect of this is that, if IBOR quotes are no longer available such that the hedged component is no longer reliably measurable, this will lead to the discontinuance of hedge accounting. For this reason, the IASB has amended the hedge accounting requirements, as part of Phase 2, so that a change of the hedge designation to the alternative benchmark rate will not result in discontinuation of hedge accounting (see para A3.41).
How this relief for risk components applies to a dynamic macro hedge or a hedge of a group of items is discussed under ‘Group hedges’ (seepara A3.32).
‘Highly probable’ requirement

A3.22 Cash flow hedge accounting under both IAS 39 and IFRS 9 requires the future hedged cash flows to be ‘highly probable’.Where these cash flows depend on an IBOR (for example, future interest payments on a forecast issuance of a LIBOR-based debt hedged with an interest rate derivative), a question arises as to whether they can be considered ‘highly probable’ beyond the date at which the relevant IBOR might cease being published (or a fallback provision triggers a change in the benchmark rate).
[IFRS 9 para 6.3.3]. [IAS 39 para 88(c)].

A3.23 The relief provided by the Phase 1 amendments requires an entity to assume that the interest rate on which the hedged cash flows are based does not change as a result of the reform. Hence, where the hedged cash flows might change as a result of IBOR reform (for example, where the future interest payments on a hedged forecast GBP debt issuance might be SONIA+X% rather than GBP LIBOR+Y%), this will not cause the ‘highly probable’ test to be failed.
[IFRS 9 para 6.8.4]. [IAS 39 para 102D].

However, if the highly probable test is failed for other reasons (for example, if it is no longer highly probable that the entity will go ahead with the forecast debt issuance, whether due to uncertainty arising from the reforms or for any other reason), hedge accounting will still need to be discontinued.
Prospective assessments (economic relationship or expected to be ‘highly effective’)

A3.25 Both IAS 39 and IFRS 9 require a forward-looking prospective assessment in order to apply hedge accounting. IAS 39 requires the hedge to be expected to be highly effective, whereas IFRS 9 requires there to be an economic relationship between the hedged item and the hedging instrument.
[IFRS 9 para 6.4.1(c)]. [IFRS 9 App B para B6.4.4]. [IFRS 9 App B para B6.4.5]. [IFRS 9 App B para 6.4.6]. [IAS 39 para 88(b)]. [IAS 39 para AG105(a)].

A3.26 If cash flows under IBOR and IBOR replacement rates are expected to be broadly equivalent, it is likely that there would be minimal ineffectiveness. However, to the extent that cash flows are expected to differ, this would give rise to hedge ineffectiveness in the prospective assessment, in particular where the replacement of the benchmark rate is expected to occur at different times in the hedged item and the hedging instrument.

A3.27 Under the amendments, an entity assumes that the interest rate benchmark on which the cash flows of the hedged item, hedging instrument or hedged risk are based is not altered by IBOR reform. One effect of this relief is that an entity assumes that any fallback clauses will not be triggered by the reforms.
[IFRS 9 para 6.8.6]. [IAS 39 para 102F].

IAS 39 retrospective effectiveness test

A3.28 Uncertainties could also affect IAS 39’s retrospective effectiveness requirement. In particular, IBOR reform might cause a hedge to fall outside the required 80–125% range. IAS 39 has therefore been amended to provide an exception to the retrospective effectiveness test such that a hedge is not discontinued during the period of IBOR-related uncertainty solely because the retrospective effectiveness falls outside this required 80–125% range.
[IAS 39 paras 88(e), AG105(b)]. [IAS 39 para AG105(b)].[IAS 39 para 102G].
FAQ A3.28.1 – Does an entity need to identify why a hedge failed the 80–125% retrospective effectiveness test in order to apply the Phase 1 relief (IAS 39 only)?
Recycling of the cash flow hedging reserve

A3.29 The relief from recycling the cash flow hedging reserve follows a similar rationale to that for the ‘highly probable’ requirement. Under IAS 39 and IFRS 9, entities are required to recycle a cash flow hedge reserve if the hedged cash flows are no longer expected to occur. Where a hedged debt instrument depends on an IBOR, the relief requires an entity to assume that the interest rate on which the hedged cash flows are based does not change as a result of the reform. Therefore, if an entity expects the cash flows on a hedged variable-rate debt to change to a different benchmark, this will
[IFRS 9 para 6.8.5]. [IAS 39 para 102E].

Measuring ineffectiveness

A3.30 The IASB has not provided any exception to the measurement of hedged items or hedging instruments. This is because such an exception would be inconsistent with the decision not to change the requirements to measure and recognise hedge ineffectiveness.
[IFRS 9 para BC6.567]. [IAS 39 para BC253].

End of Phase 1 amendments

A3.31 The amendments prescribe when each of the Phase 1 amendments will prospectively cease. In general, the Phase 1 amendments end at the earlier of (a) when there is no longer uncertainty arising from IBOR reform over the timing and amount of the IBOR-based cash flows of the relevant item, and (b) when the hedging relationship to which the relief is applied is discontinued. More specifically, the Phase 1 amendments cease as follows:

- The ‘highly probable’ requirement – at the earlier of (a) when there is no longer uncertainty arising from IBOR reform over the timing and amount of the IBOR-based cash flows of the hedged item, and (b) when the hedging relationship of which the hedged item is part is discontinued.

- Recycling of the cash flow hedge reserve – at the earlier of (a) when there is no longer uncertainty arising from IBOR reform over the timing and amount of the IBOR-based cash flows of the hedged item, and (b) when the entire amount in the cash flow hedge reserve for a discontinued hedging relationship has been recycled to profit or loss.
- Prospective assessments (expected to be highly effective or economic relationship) –

- for a hedged item: at the earlier of (a) when there is no longer uncertainty arising from IBOR reform with respect to the hedged risk or over the timing and amount of IBOR-based cash flows, and (b) when the hedging relationship is discontinued;

- for a hedging instrument: at the earlier of (a) when there is no longer uncertainty arising from IBOR reform over the timing and amount of IBOR-based cash flows, and (b) when the hedging relationship is discontinued.

This means that the relief could end at different times for the hedging instrument and the hedged item. However, if the hedging relationship is discontinued earlier than this date, this relief ceases to apply at the date of hedge discontinuation.

- Retrospective effectiveness test (IAS 39 only) – at the earlier of (a) when there is no longer uncertainty arising from IBOR reform with respect to the hedged risk and the timing and amount of IBOR-based cash flows of the hedged item or of the hedging instrument, and (b) when the hedging relationship is discontinued.

The Phase 1 amendments did not provide an end date to the risk components relief. The Phase 2 amendments, issued in August 2020, provide an end date for the Phase 1 risk components relief (see para A3.40).

Group hedges (including macro hedges)
A3.32 This section deals with the effect of the amendments on hedges where either the hedging instrument or the hedged item (or both) comprises more than one contract or transaction. This includes:
- macro fair value hedges accounted for using the specific requirements for fair value portfolio hedges of interest rate risk in paragraphs AG114–AG132 of IAS 39;
- macro cash flow hedges (for example, as illustrated in paras IG F6.2 and IG F6.3 of IAS 39);

- other hedges of groups of assets, liabilities, firm commitments or forecast transactions (see para 78 of IAS 39 and paras 6.3.1(b) and 6.6.1 of IFRS 9), including, under IFRS 9, hedges of a net position (see paras B6.6.1 - B6.6.10 of IFRS 9);
- hedges of aggregated exposures (see para 6.3.4 of IFRS 9); and
- hedges where the hedging instrument comprises two or more derivatives or proportions of them (see para 77 of IAS 39 and para 6.2.5 of IFRS 9).
A3.33 For such hedges, it is possible that IBOR reform will affect the items that make up either the hedging instrument or the hedged item at different times or in different ways. For example:
- where the hedged item is a group of variable-rate loans, some of the loans in the group might move to the new benchmark rate sooner than others;

- where the hedging instrument is a combination of instruments (for example, a cross-currency interest rate swap and an interest rate swap, or two interest rate swaps in different currencies), one swap might be amended to the replacement benchmark rate before the other;

- in a macro fair value hedge of a portfolio of loans where there is frequent de-designation and re-designation of the hedged item, at the time when a previously designated loan is re-designated, the interest rate risk that is separately identifiable might have changed from IBOR to the replacement benchmark rate.
A3.34 The amendments include specific guidance on how to apply the amendments in such cases. More specifically, the guidance requires:

- Where the hedged item is a group of items or the hedging instrument is a combination of financial instruments, the requirements for when the Phase 1 amendments end apply to each item or financial instrument separately. [IFRS 9 para 6.8.12]. [IAS 39 para 102N]. Thus, in the example above, where the hedged item is a group of variable-rate loans, if some of the loans in the group move to the new benchmark rate sooner than others, the relief for assessing prospective effectiveness will end at different times for the various loans in the group. Similarly, in the example above, where the hedging i

- In a macro fair value hedge, for the purpose of applying the relief for determining if an IBOR risk component is separately identifiable, an entity determines whether a particular IBOR risk component is separately identifiable only when it initially designates a hedged item (that is, an individual loan) in the macro fair value hedge.

A3.35 The amendments require disclosure of:
- the significant interest rate benchmarks to which the entity’s hedging relationships are exposed;
- the extent of the risk exposure that the entity manages that is directly affected by the interest rate benchmark reform;
- how the entity is managing the process of transition to alternative benchmark rates;

- a description of significant assumptions or judgements that the entity made in applying the Phase 1 amendments (for example, assumptions or judgements about when the uncertainty arising from interest rate benchmark reform is no longer present with respect to the timing and the amount of the interest rate benchmark-based cash flows); and
- the nominal amount of the hedging instruments in those hedging relationships.

A3.36 An entity will apply the amendments retrospectively to hedging relationships that existed at the beginning of the reporting period in which the entity first applies the amendments or were designated thereafter, and to the amount recognised in the cash flow hedge reserve at the start of the reporting period.
[IFRS 9 para 7.2.26(d)]. [IAS 39 para 108G].

A3.37 The Phase 1 amendments do not allow entities to reinstate hedge accounting that has already been discontinued. However, hedge accounting can only be applied from the date when any such new hedge is designated (that is, the amendments do not allow designation in hindsight, because doing so would be inconsistent with the general requirement for hedge accounting to be applied prospectively).
[IFRS 9 para BC6.601]. [IAS 39 para BC287].

A3.38 The IASB has undertaken a two-phase project to consider what, if any, reliefs to give from the effects of IBOR reform. The Phase 1 amendments, issued in September 2019, provided temporary reliefs from applying specific hedge accounting requirements to relationships affected by uncertainties arising as a result of IBOR reform (‘the Phase 1 reliefs’). The Phase 2 amendments that were issued on 27 August 2020 address issues that arise from the implementation of the reforms, including the replacement of one benchmark with an alternative one. FAQ A3.27.1 – Can a hedging relationship fail the prospective assessment for reasons outside the scope of the relief provided by the Phase 1 amendments?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para 6.8.6; IAS 39 para 102F Reference to standing text: A3.27
Can a hedging relationship fail the prospective assessment for reasons outside the scope of relief provided by the Phase 1 amendments?

Yes. A hedging relationship might still fail the prospective assessment for reasons outside the scope of the relief in the Phase 1 amendments. An example is a variable-rate debt denominated in one currency that is hedged with an interest rate swap denominated in a different currency but that is pegged to the currency of the debt. If the two currencies subsequently cease to be pegged, the prospective assessment would likely fail and hedge accounting would have to be discontinued.

If, at a particular reporting date, the hedging instrument has moved to the alternative benchmark rate but the hedged item remains on the previous benchmark rate, the Phase 1 amendments require an entity to assume that all of the future cash flows on the hedged item remain based on the previous benchmark rate, even if it is expected that the hedged item will move to the alternative benchmark rate in the near future. Depending on the size of the impact, this could have the effect that the hedge is no longer expected to be highly effective, in which case the hedge relationship would need to be d
In addition, IBOR reform could have other implications for the prospective effectiveness test that entities will need to carefully consider. These include that:

- where an entity uses critical terms match as a method to assess prospective effectiveness, the critical terms of the hedging instrument might no longer match those of the hedged item (in particular, in the case where the hedging instrument has moved to the alternative benchmark rate but the hedged item has not); and
- where an entity uses regression analysis to assess prospective effectiveness, there might initially be a lack of directly observable data points for the replacement rate.

Under IFRS 9, an entity determines whether, prospectively, there continues to be an economic relationship between the hedging instrument and the hedged item. If, prospectively, there is no longer such an economic relationship, the hedge relationship must be discontinued. [IFRS 9 para BC6.566].
FAQ A3.28.1 – Does an entity need to identify why a hedge failed the 80–125% retrospective effectiveness test in order to apply the Phase 1 relief (IAS 39 only)?
Reference to standard: IAS 39 paras 88(e), AG105(b). Reference to standing text: A3.28
Does an entity need to identify why an hedge failed the 80–125% retrospective effectiveness test in order to apply the Phase 1 relief?

No. An entity does not need to identify why a hedge failed the 80–125% retrospective effectiveness test. Even if this is for non-IBOR- related reasons, the relief still applies. The reason is so that entities do not have to split any hedge ineffectiveness into the amount caused by IBOR reform and the amount caused by other factors. Such a split could be difficult to do in practice, and it would require an additional calculation to measure any ineffectiveness.

However, entities will still need to measure the change in fair value of the hedging instrument and the hedged item, since ineffectiveness must still be measured and reported in the income statement in the usual way. [IAS 39 para BC252]. Therefore, if a hedge is only 75% effective, whilst the entity can continue hedge accounting, the 25% ineffectiveness must be recognised in the income statement (subject to the normal ‘lower of’ test for a cash flow hedge).

Furthermore, if the prospective effectiveness assessment is failed at any reporting date, hedge accounting would need to be discontinued. Hence, it is important that entities have a robust prospective effectiveness test, since there is no longer the ‘safety net’ of potentially failing the retrospective test.
FAQ A3.29.1 – If hedge accounting is discontinued when the Phase 1 reliefs have been applied, should the balance of the cash flow hedge reserve be recycled immediately?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para 6.8.5; IAS 39 para 102E Reference to standing text: A3.29

If the outcome of a prospective test is that the hedge is not expected to be highly effective under IAS 39, or an entity determines that there is no longer an economic relationship between the hedging instrument and hedged item under IFRS 9, hedge accounting would need to be discontinued. If this is the case, should the balance of the cash flow hedge reserve be recycled immediately?

No, the balance of the cash flow hedge reserve would not be recycled through the income statement immediately, because the relief related to such recycling continues to apply. Rather, the balance of the cash flow hedge reserve will continue to be recycled to the income statement when the hedged cash flows impact the income statement.

FAQ A3.30.1 – What is the impact of the Phase 1 amendments on the measurement of the change in the fair value of derivatives designated as hedging instruments and the change in the fair value of the hedged item attributable to the hedged risk?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 paras BC6.567-BC6.570; IAS 39 paras BC253-BC256 Reference to standing text: A3.30

What is the impact of the Phase 1 amendments on the measurement of the change in the fair value of derivatives designated as hedging instruments and the change in the fair value of the hedged item attributable to the hedged risk?

The fair value of derivatives designated as hedging instruments will continue to be measured using assumptions that market participants would use when pricing that derivative, as required by IFRS 13, ‘Fair Value Measurement’. This will include any effect of IBOR reform that market participants would include when pricing that derivative. Unlike the prospective effectiveness assessment, the entity does not assume that the current benchmark rate will remain unchanged.

Similar principles apply when calculating the change in fair value of the hedged item for the purposes of measuring hedge ineffectiveness. So, for a fair value hedge, the change in fair value of the hedged item attributable to the hedged risk will include any effect of IBOR reform that market participants would include when pricing the hedged item for such changes in fair value. This includes any premium for uncertainty inherent in the hedged risk that a market participant would include. FAQ A3.30.2 – In cash flow hedge relationships under the Phase 1 amendments, does an entity assume zero cash flows after the expected date of replacement of an IBOR with an alternative benchmark?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 paras BC6.567–-BC6.570; IAS 39 paras BC253–-BC256 Reference to standing text: A3.30
In cash flow hedge relationships under the Phase 1 amendments, does an entity assume zero cash flows after the expected date of replacement of an IBOR with an alternative benchmark?

Under the Phase 1 amendments, an entity does not assume zero cash flows after the expected date of replacement of the IBOR with an alternative benchmark. Rather, it includes the effect of the reform in the measurement using market participant assumptions. A market participant might factor in the effect of the reform in a number of ways, including:

- assuming IBOR cash flows for the remaining life of the hedge but including an adjustment to the discount rate that reflects both (a) the market expectation of a change in the hedged item’s benchmark rate in the future, and (b) the uncertainty associated with that change (for example, over the timing of the change, or what the new benchmark rate or spread will be, and the effect of any pre-existing fall back clauses); or

- assuming IBOR cash flows for a certain number of remaining years and then assuming modification of the contract to the replacement benchmark rate, discounted using a discount rate that reflects only (b) above – that is, only the uncertainty associated with the change. A practical challenge with this approach is determining the cash flows in the period after the replacement, in particular the additional spread that is expected to be charged on the change to the new benchmark rate.

Under either approach, an entity might consider modelling a number of possible scenarios and probability weighting them. Other approaches could potentially be used, and the approach used by market participants could also change over time as the market evolves. However, any approach would need to reflect a market participant view of (a) the expectation/likelihood that the rate will change to the new benchmark (since this would be factored into the market’s fair value measurement of the hedged item), and (b) the uncertainties associated with the change.
FAQ A3.30.3 – What sources of ineffectiveness might there be during the transition to a new benchmark rate?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para BC6.567; IAS 39 para BC253 Reference to standing text: A3.30
What sources of ineffectiveness might there be during the transition to a new benchmark rate?

If there are any differences in how the hedged item and the hedging instrument transition to the new benchmark rate, this will likely give rise to ineffectiveness. Such differences could include the following:

- Overnight versus term alternative benchmark rate: For example, the hedging instrument moves to an overnight alternative benchmark rate (such as SONIA), but the hedged item moves to a term version of the same alternative benchmark rate (such as a three-month SONIA).

- Timing of transition: For example, if the hedging instrument transitions to the alternative benchmark rate before the hedged item, there will be a period when the hedged item references the current benchmark rate and the hedging instrument references the replacement rate. This will give rise to ineffectiveness both in the period when they reference different rates and in periods before either transitions. Furthermore, it is expected that a spread adjustment between the current benchmark rate and the alternative benchmark rate will be needed to achieve economic equivalence. If the hedging ins

- Fallback clauses: It is possible that the fallback clauses in the hedging instrument (possibly following a protocol, such as one prescribed by ISDA) and the hedged item (agreed bilaterally between contract counterparties) will be different.

- Scenario B: a contract is amended to include a clause that states that modifications of cash flows will occur, but neither a date for replacement nor the benchmark rate is specified (for example, ‘GBP LIBOR will be replaced with an alternative benchmark rate at a date to be mutually agreed by the parties to the contract’). In this case, uncertainty has not been removed, and so the Phase 1 amendments continue to apply.

- Scenario C: a contract is amended to include a clause that states that conditions specifying the amount and timing of benchmark cash flows will be determined by a central authority at some point in the future (for example, ‘GBP LIBOR will be replaced by the replacement rate determined by the Central Bank X when that replacement rate becomes effective’). FAQ A3.35.1 – Can the ‘extent of risk exposure’ disclosure be provided on a qualitative basis?
Reference to standard: IFRS 7 para 24H Reference to standing text: A3.35
Can the ‘extent of risk exposure’ disclosure be provided on a qualitative basis?

The Phase 1 amendments require disclosure of the extent of the risk exposure that the entity manages that is directly affected by the interest rate benchmark reform. The amendments are not clear whether this disclosure could be provided on a qualitative basis; however, numerical disclosures might provide more useful information to users.
FAQ A3.35.2 – What key points might management consider when explaining how the entity is managing the process of transition to alternative benchmark rates?
Reference to standard: IFRS 7 para 24H Reference to standing text: A3.35
Under the Phase 1 amendments, what key points might management consider when explaining how the entity is managing the process of transition to alternative benchmark rates?

Users are likely to be interested in disclosures of how the entity is managing the transition process, since this will give information about the extent to which management is prepared for the transition. For example, if fallback provisions differ significantly between the hedged item and the hedging instrument, this might be a relevant aspect of the transition process to explain.

The IASB’s non-mandatory practice statement, ‘Management commentary’, recommends that management’s commentary should be entity-specific, including principal risks and management’s plans for managing those risks. Entities should therefore consider whether further disclosure of the impending replacement of IBOR and associated considerations should also be provided in other parts of the annual report. Entities that have not yet adopted the Phase 2 amendments should consider disclosing the anticipated impacts of those amendments, in particular where there are critical accounting judgements or estimates to comply with paragraph 30 of IAS 8. The Phase 2 amendments, issued in August 2020, require additional IFRS 7 disclosures related to IBOR reform (see para A3.42).
FAQ A3.35.3 – How could IBOR reform impact other disclosures?
Reference to standard: IFRS 7 para 24H Reference to standing text: A3.35
How could IBOR reform impact other disclosures?

In addition to the disclosures specifically required by the Phase 1 amendments, entities should consider the impact of IBOR reform on other required disclosures. For example, accounting policies relating to hedge accounting will need to be updated for the Phase 1 amendments, and disclosures under IFRS 13, might be impacted due to transfers between levels in the fair value hierarchy as markets become more or less liquid.
The Phase 2 amendments, issued in August 2020, require additional IFRS 7 disclosures related to IBOR reform (see para A3.42).
